This study presents a theory regarding the validity of synthetic controls and outlines methods for assessing the reliability of their causal inferences. We propose a framework to evaluate the causal validity of synthetic control constructions by addressing two critical questions: (1) How precisely must the synthetic control represent the pre-treatment data to ensure that synthetic control differences accurately reflect treatment effects? and (2) How can we quantify the certainty that a specific synthetic control will yield a valid inference? To address the first question, we derive a functional theory of validity, which incorporates the functional forms of both treatment effects and pre-treatment distributions. According to this theory, causal validity hinges on the level of detail within the synthetic control's pre-treatment distribution, determined by the number of actual units incorporated into its construction. Regarding the second question, we develop a recognition framework based on kernel approximation theory, which quantifies the capability of synthetic controls to capture the unit-specific pre-treatment distributions required for valid treatment effect inference. Furthermore, we introduce a statistical test to empirically verify whether a particular synthetic control structure sufficiently recognizes the unit's pre-treatment distribution. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of this framework through an application to a previous causal inference involving the impact of the 1965 Elementary and Secondary Education Act on US states' K-12 education systems. The results indicate that the impact of the Act on a state's education system can only be reliably inferred if the state is paired with at least four neighboring states in the synthetic control formulation. Additionally, simulations reveal that the recognition framework is adaptable to various synthetic control settings, offering a general approach for evaluating the certainty of causal inferences. Our findings suggest that the recognition framework offers a practical tool for causal analysts to select the appropriate number of control units to ensure a reliable synthetic control. Ultimately, the recognition framework represents a significant advancement in synthetic control methodology, fostering a more rigorous and scientific approach to causal inference. By enabling analysts to assess the certainty of treatment effect inferences, the framework facilitates the development of a more robust theory of synthetic control validity. This leads to a more nuanced understanding of the synthetic control method, thereby enhancing its application across diverse research and practical contexts. This study investigates a decentralized approach for estimating the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) divergence between two metric measure spaces that lack direct access to one another's data. Decentralization is realized through a localized algorithm wherein each agent exchanges information only with its neighbors. The primary algorithmic challenge stems from the fact that, in a distributed setting, agents cannot directly estimate the target GW divergence; instead, they must reach a consensus on the divergence based on restricted observations. To address this, the proposed solution integrates the distributed averaging algorithm with a regularized GW divergence and carefully designed initialization strategies. These strategies leverage the topological structure of the metric spaces, specifically assuming that agents possess knowledge of their local metric structure relative to the global space. We demonstrate that these initializations steer the distributed algorithm toward an equilibrium state that approximates the true GW divergence. Furthermore, under a connected communication graph assumption, we prove that agents achieve consensus on this equilibrium. We also establish an error bound quantifying the discrepancy between the agent-based estimate and the true GW divergence, which depends on the condition number of a Laplacian matrix, the regularization hyperparameter, and the error in graph approximations. Finally, we validate the distributed algorithm through numerical experiments, showing promising convergence to the true GW divergence and robustness against communication noise. These results suggest that the proposed method is well-suited for decentralized estimation, rendering it valuable for applications where multiple entities must collaboratively learn the divergence between unknown metric spaces without direct access to one another's data. This contrasts with existing centralized methods, which are impractical in real-world decentralized environments due to data privacy and security concerns. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: (i) a distributed algorithm for estimating the GW divergence between metric measure spaces, applicable to both discrete and continuous domains; (ii) distributed initializations that utilize local metric information to ensure agents converge to the true GW divergence; and (iii) an analysis of security and robustness, specifically addressing communication noise and local data breaches. In this work, we model data breaches using a detection mechanism that allows agents to identify and exclude compromised data from processing. This approach significantly enhances security, providing a more robust estimation of GW divergence. Additionally, we propose a security analysis for GW divergence, a topic that has not been explored in prior literature. Our numerical results demonstrate that these contributions are effective, as evidenced by experiments on synthetic data, real-world images, and social network data. We propose utilizing a polarization-modulated laser to drive an electron injector into a contact liner, with the modulation frequency aligning with the incoherent jitter of the liner. This synchronization allows for the averaging of jerks acting on the injector in one polarization direction, thereby minimizing current profile distortion. The input liner velocity is subsequently amplified through a shock driver, which is powered by the steepening front of the laser. This power is directed into an accelerator that employs transverse field boosting via a bubble with a flattened profile. The resulting electron beams are optimized for applications including hard X-ray and gamma-ray generation, as well as particle therapy. This approach eliminates the need for complex multi-stage designs, expensive magnetic components, and extensive precompression of the liner. The proposed laser scheme is straightforward and can be implemented on existing platforms. We outline the necessary research and provide a roadmap to achieve this single-stage concept. Additionally, we present a detailed discussion of the physical principles and their interplay. Finally, we provide a proof-of-principle simulation of the complete system, including a specific example of gamma-ray production. The entire process takes approximately 100 femtoseconds. We demonstrate that the proposed system can deliver a hard X-ray flux of $10^{14}$ photons per shot at 10 keV with a spectrum extending up to 100 keV, and a flux of $10^{12}$ photons per shot at 1 MeV with a spectrum reaching 10 MeV. These results are comparable to those obtained via the more conventional two-stage method. Furthermore, we show that particle jams with energy spectra extending to 2.5 GeV can be achieved. To reach these energies, the laser must deliver a flux of $10^{19}$ photons per second at 1000 $\mu$m, with a spectrum extending to 1 $\mu$m. This laser power is approximately 1 TW, a level accessible with current technology. Our proposed system can also generate particle jams with average bunch charges of $10^{10}$ electrons, exhibiting energy spread fluctuations of $\sigma/E \leq 1\%$. These characteristics make the system suitable for use as a free electron laser. We demonstrate that a jam with an average energy of 250 MeV and a spectrum extending to 300 MeV can be produced. This requires a laser with a flux of $1 \times 10^{19}$ photons per second at 800 nm.

The superheavy island of stability, potentially located in the Z=76-84 range, has attracted significant interest for applications in nuclear medicine, catalysis, energy generation, and energy storage. Within this region, certain nuclei are hypothesized to exhibit kinetic (zero-point) stability, which could fundamentally alter current nuclear physics principles. This study investigates two scenarios: one involving a new dark matter-triggered reaction in Pt isotopes, and another revising the achievable double beta decay boundaries for various nuclei. Both scenarios offer unique opportunities to enhance existing knowledge of the region. We present experimental data on the dark matter-induced reaction $^{194}$Pt($\phi$, $\gamma$) and conduct a comparative analysis of double beta decay pathways in Pt and neighboring nuclei. These investigations aim to deepen our understanding of the island of stability and its broader implications. Additionally, we explore the potential for utilizing nuclei in this region for quantum computing. This research was conducted under the framework of the Russian Quantum Center. The renormalization group behavior of the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge under the dimension regularization scheme is derived from the renormalization of composite operators using a momentum-subtraction renormalization scheme. Furthermore, the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge and its anomaly mass-term coefficient scheme-conversion factors, shifting from momentum-subtraction to the widely used modified minimal subtraction scheme, are calculated through four-loop order in quantum chromodynamics. These results facilitate the proper handling of the renormalization group evolution and scheme conversions for the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge, addressing a long-standing issue in high-precision QCD evolution applicable to various physical contexts, including Tevatron and LHC data analyses. Additionally, the results provide a direct means to compare the mass-dependent evolution of the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge across different renormalization schemes at any order. Finally, the computed results have been incorporated into the recently released REvolver package for use in further analyses. Specifically, utilizing this package, we have calculated the mass-independent evolution of the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge from four-loop order in the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme and demonstrated its potential impact on the determination of the mass ratio $m_u/m_d$ between up and down quark masses. This demonstration is based on a global QCD analysis of experimental data and theoretical constraints, which is also conducted using the REvolver package. The analysis yields a value for $m_u/m_d$ of $0.4810(11)$, representing a significant improvement over the previous next-to-next-to-leading order result of $0.495(35)$. The updated value is also substantially more precise than the leading-order estimate of $0.50(10)$. This represents the first time that the up quark's contribution to the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge has been calculated to the next-to-next-to-leading order level, significantly enhancing the precision of the result. Consequently, the up quark is confirmed to contribute approximately half as much as the down quark to the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge. This outcome is consistent with the QCD sum rule analysis of the pion electromagnetic form factor, which has also demonstrated a significant contribution from the up quark. Our findings also align with the recent analysis of the pion electromagnetic form factor conducted by the BABAR collaboration. While deep colorization models excel at generating realistic pixel-level results, they frequently fail to produce visually convincing color imagery because they rely exclusively on grayscale images, which omit depth and motion data. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel cross-camera deep colorization framework that performs on-movie deep colorization using only grayscale films as input. Specifically, our approach leverages on-movie camera tracking and 3D depth models to address failures caused by depth and motion limitations, while employing a two-stage model design to boost performance on films characterized by diverse color palettes. We successfully applied our method to deeply colorize out-of-copyright feature films, achieving state-of-the-art results in tests against deep colorizers on a grayscale-film-based challenge. Additionally, we demonstrate that our solution can be readily adapted to generate colors for live video feeds by utilizing a single camera. To our knowledge, this represents the first effort to apply deep colorization to films, marking a significant step toward realizing color enhancement for black and white films. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/1000000000000000000/cross-camera-deep-colorization. The accompanying video demonstrates the application of our method to live video feeds. Furthermore, we introduce a new challenge based on grayscale films, featuring three tracks with progressively harder tasks: Track 1 focuses on local pixel coloring, Track 2 adds global coloring consistency, and Track 3 requires a deep colorization model that generalizes across multiple grayscale films. The Ermakov system represents a well-established two-dimensional nonlinear framework that is closely linked to linear harmonic motion. In recent years, numerous generalizations of this system have been proposed, often motivated by the exploration of additional symmetries and their associated conservation laws. This paper examines symmetric structures within $n$-dimensional generalized Ermakov frameworks, extending prior findings by incorporating an arbitrary number of extra symmetric generators. We then derive the corresponding conservation laws linked to these symmetries. Furthermore, we present an explicit solution for the Lagrangian associated with the multi-dimensional generalized Ermakov system, building upon previously published results. Finally, we apply these findings to specific examples, highlighting their relevance to non-relativistic quantum mechanics. As an illustration, the generalization of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator is analyzed. This example demonstrates that the generalized structure yields both first- and second-order conservation laws, alongside fractional-order laws derived from conserved quantities linked to multi-symmetric properties. Additionally, the number of such conserved quantities varies depending on the dimension. We also explore the relationship between these conservation laws and the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equation, showing that dimensionality reduction of certain solutions to the EPD equation generates symmetric structures for specific classes of $n$-dimensional generalized Ermakov systems. Consequently, this reveals an intrinsic connection between the EPD equation and the symmetries of generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov systems. Finally, the EPD equation is further explored, particularly regarding its multi-symmetric characteristics, with examples provided to substantiate this analysis. Overall, the EPD equation exhibits rich symmetry and conservation law properties, and this study demonstrates how to leverage these features to derive the general solution of the $n$-dimensional inhomogeneous Laplace equation. These findings may have significant applications in physics, including the resolution of the $n$-dimensional Schrödinger equation. The full manuscript is accessible via the following link: https://doi.org/10.3390/math9010089. Brazil's available and unavailable public transport systems are designed to be complementary, collectively covering all mobility needs. However, when only an unavailable system's data is accessible, satisfying travel demand becomes impossible without data from the available system. This paper demonstrates how neural networks can be utilized to render unavailable public transport services operational by repurposing their route planning algorithms. We focus on a routing problem within an available network that must satisfy a given travel demand. By analyzing the sequential and repetitive nature of dynamic programming used in Dijkstra's algorithm and the greedy approach, we show that an available network's neural planner can effectively function as an unavailable one. Specifically, we propose using an available neural planner to solve the routing task by feeding it outputs from a previous pass as initial conditions for the next. This approach allows the model to adapt its decisions based on prior results. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function for training neural planners that accounts for both available and unavailable demand, thereby improving results in data-sparse scenarios. Extensive numerical experiments on real-world travel demand in São Paulo, utilizing the available metro network, validate our approach. Compared to the standard training method, our proposed technique reduces average weighted delay by 10% and increases route coverage by 2.5%. Furthermore, results demonstrate consistent performance gains even when the training demand is reduced to 10% of its original size. Finally, we explore the application of transfer learning with multipliers in this context. These findings offer a pathway to more robust neural transport planners and enhanced resilience for cities facing data scarcity in specific regions. Finally, we detail the available network's plotters to support this claim. Available at: https://github.com/fernandocosta22/AvailableNetworkPlotters. Although class-level prototypes have demonstrated efficacy in few-shot classification, determining an optimal prototype structure remains a significant challenge. This study addresses that challenge by introducing a class-level prototype pool, which offers a more refined representation compared to existing methods. For each label, the pool incorporates multiple prototypes derived from data distributions across various dimensions, such as spatial, spectral, and frequency domains for image levels, or textual, acoustic, and graph embedding domains for different modalities. The optimal set of prototypes is selected via a gating mechanism. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed A-CPP model outperforms current state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods across multiple datasets and modalities. Additionally, our analysis reveals that diverse prototype distributions within the pool enhance classification accuracy by providing complementary information. The code and models are available at: https://github.com/zhenghao1992/ACPP.

In systems featuring an infinite volume limit, a first-order phase transition characterized by a non-reversible continuous symmetry occurs if and only if the associated charge fails to commute with the generator of the equilibrium state within the weak operator topology. This state corresponds to the product of local states derived from taking the thermodynamic limit for + boundary conditions on the half-line and - boundary conditions on the other half. We demonstrate this goldstone theorem for a broad category of non-reversible continuous symmetries. The method involves analyzing the current operator linked to the symmetry transformation and the charge, demonstrating that their expectation values diverge. We further illustrate this methodology with an explicit example: a non-reversible continuous symmetry in the 2D Ising model perturbed by longitudinal magnetic fields. In this instance, we prove that both the current operator, derived from energy momentum in the thermodynamic limit, and the magnetization exhibit expectation values that diverge. The demonstration of diverging expectation values for both operators relies on properties of boundary states at the interface between + and - phases. Specifically, we show that the current operator exhibits divergent expectation values between vacua, while the charge operator yields divergent expectation values when acting on the vacuum. To achieve this, we employ a generalized version of the transfer matrix, known as the transfer-matrix-matrix. Furthermore, we provide an alternative derivation for the case of non-reversible continuous symmetries in 1D quantum models, such as the transverse field Ising model, by mapping them to non-reversible Markov processes and applying recent findings by Uchiyama. This approach confirms that the charge operator possesses divergent expectation values between ground states, thereby inducing a divergence in the expectation values of the momentum operator between the vacua. This outcome aligns with the expectation that the expectation value of the momentum operator diverges at the phase transition. Additionally, this method offers an alternative proof for boundary transfer-matrix eigenvalue asymptotics, which are instrumental in deriving boundary vacua within the conformal field theory framework. Finally, we extend these findings to the more general scenario of perturbed 1D quantum models featuring both anisotropic and non-reversible magnetic field terms. Unlike perturbed 1D quantum models with only a non-reversible magnetic field term, this specific case does not possess a corresponding classical model, rendering the second proof inapplicable. Consequently, we depend on an alternative method to show that the magnetization operator yields divergent expectation values between the ground states. A graph $G=(V,E)$ is defined as semi-transitive if, for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, either all neighbors of $u$ are also neighbors of $v$ ($N(u) \subseteq N(v)$), or $u$ and $v$ share at least one common neighbor. It is established that semi-transitive graphs can be recognized in linear time. Building upon this result, we demonstrate that for any semi-transitive split graph, a maximum clique can be identified in $O(V + E)$ time. Furthermore, for such graphs, finding a minimum vertex cover, maximum independent set, maximum independent set of size $k$, and a minimum clique cover can all be accomplished in $O(V + E)$ time. We also extend the concept of semi-transitivity to split graphs and provide an efficient recognition algorithm. Additionally, we prove that a semi-transitive split graph $G$ possesses a maximum clique of size $k$ within $O(V + E)$ time, whereas determining whether $G$ contains a clique of size $k$ requires $2^{\Omega(k)}$ time. Finally, we examine the relationship between transitivity and the existence of large induced subgraphs. Specifically, we show that in a semi-transitive graph $G$, the presence of a clique of size $k$ or an independent set of size $k$ implies the existence of a induced cycle of size 5 or a tournament of size 7, respectively. Consequently, the chromatic number of a semi-transitive split graph is bounded by a polynomial in $k$. We also demonstrate that for a split graph $G$, identifying $k$-colorability can be achieved in $O(V + E)$ time. Our findings indicate that a maximum independent set of a semi-transitive split graph of treewidth $k$ can be found in $O(V + E)$ time, whereas independent sets of size $k$ require $2^{k \log k}$ time to determine. Finally, we establish that a maximum clique of a semi-transitive split graph of treewidth $k$ can be identified in $O(V + E)$ time, while cliques of size $k$ can be found in $2^{k}$ time. The identification of tau leptons that have decayed into hadrons is crucial for many physics analyses at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This study demonstrates that a deep neural network, utilizing an analysis framework comparable to those employed in recent literature, can achieve significant enhancements in both identification efficiency and subsequent physics measurement precision. We evaluate this method for tau reconstruction within simulated data corresponding to $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, derived from proton-proton collisions at the LHC. The results are assessed using the Higgs boson $\tau\tau$ decay channel and the search for supersymmetric $\tilde{q} \to q \tilde{\chi}^0_1 \to q \tilde{\chi}^0_\mathrm{LSP}$ decays. Furthermore, we note that the neural network approach utilized here is highly adaptable to various physics objectives. The findings presented here were reported at the 18th International Workshop on Tau Lepton Physics (TAUP 2017) in Hamburg. Additionally, this work represents an expansion of our prior publication (TAUP 2016-014). The analysis code is publicly accessible via GitHub. This paper is designated as TAUP 2017-014. The abundance of public data from the Virtual Observatory's vast archives presents a significant challenge for data categorization tasks. This difficulty is exacerbated by the "curse of dimensionality," where high-dimensional data lacks sufficient samples, and by the scarcity of theoretical knowledge regarding the underlying data-generating processes. To address these issues, we propose a solution based on Bayesian Neural Networks, which serve as universal function approximators, combined with Transfer Learning strategies. This approach aims to overcome the challenges of sample scarcity and limited theoretical understanding in the context of data categorization tasks within the vast data era. The effectiveness of our method is validated through the application to the Pan-STARRS3 survey. Specifically, we demonstrate that Bayesian Neural Networks, when trained on a related dataset, can successfully perform tasks such as distinguishing between stars and galaxies. We present a theoretical framework to forecast intermodal forward Brillouin scattering between the fundamental and higher-order modes in a photonic crystal thread. This model accounts for the spatial and spectral broadening of this nonlinearity, which stems from variations in mode overlap and propagation constant as the pitch gradually expands. Additionally, we outline a method to generate a narrow-band higher-order mode that leverages the fundamental mode's large cross-sectional area and in-air propagation characteristics. This approach offers a pathway to utilize the intermodal Brillouin effect for sensing and filtering applications, while also supporting future research into dissipationless, chip-based photonic crystal fiber devices for quantum and nonlinear optics. By demonstrating that this phenomenon is an intrinsic property of any waveguide with a variable core size, we establish a broad framework for studying intermodal Brillouin interactions in photonic crystal threads and related structures. Specifically, we illustrate how this mechanism can be harnessed to achieve intermodal filtering and highlight its potential for sensing, including the detection of internal pressure within the thread. Finally, we address the interaction between intermodal and intramodal Brillouin effects, showing how they can be independently controlled to meet specific demands in sensing and signal processing. Overall, these findings provide a robust foundation for the practical application of photonic crystal threads in various areas of photonics. Furthermore, they underscore the significance of intermodality in photonic crystal threads, even though it are often viewed as a drawback during device design. This insight could lead to novel strategies for managing crosstalk and designing efficient couplers based on photonic crystal threads. Finally, we emphasize the relationship between intermodality and exceptional points, a concept that has been previously explored in photonic crystal threads. We also examine how intermodality influences interference, a factor that must be accounted for when developing sensors with ultra-high sensitivity. In this context, we show that photonic crystal threads can outperform other microstructured fibers in achieving large sensing figures. Notably, we predict the existence of a photonic crystal thread exhibiting unidirectional light propagation, a feature that could have significant implications for fundamental research and the development of new devices. These predictions open up new avenues for the study and application of photonic crystal threads. Additionally, we demonstrate that these threads can serve as an effective platform for studying nonlinear phenomena, such as solitary waves and intermodal solitons, thereby advancing fundamental physics research. We present an explicit construction of a spanning tree within the Cayley graph of a B-type Coxeter group, defined by specific generators. Building on this, we establish that a graph homomorphism from this spanning tree to the Cayley graph—mapping the generators to specific generators alongside the identity—functions as an isomorphism when the domain is restricted to a spanning cycle graph. This cycle is generated by a particular set of generators that includes a foundational spanning path as a subgraph. Furthermore, we demonstrate an elegant characterization of this span cycle by linking it to star polygons. These findings collectively confirm the generalization of the foundation theorem proposed by R. Bhat and S. Nair. Additionally, we explore applications related to star polygons derived from regular polygons. Finally, we extend our primary result to the B*-type Coxeter groups, which are dual to the B-type. As a consequence, we derive an explicit formula for the number of spanning trees in the Cayley graph of the B-type Coxeter groups. Last, we examine applications concerning spanning trees of the Cayley graph for the B*-type Coxeter group, dual to the B-type, and present an application detailing the number of spanning trees for this dual group. This work serves as a follow-up to the authors' previous paper, which established analogous results for A-type Coxeter groups. Keywords: Coxeter groups, spanning trees, Cayley graphs, star polygons. This study investigates two multi-objective optimization problems: the Set-Union Rucksack Issue and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Challenge. Both scenarios involve selecting a subset of items with associated costs to maximize the coverage of elements within a defined budget. Items are characterized by multiple attributes, and the objective is to simultaneously optimize total cost and the count of uniquely covered elements. As these problems are proven to be NP-hard, we focus on developing robust and efficient local search strategies. We introduce three novel approaches: the Descent Search (DS), Incremental Descent Search (IDS), and Randomized Incremental Descent Search (IDS-RD). Additionally, we implement a memetic algorithm to further refine the algorithms' performance. Extensive numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate and compare these methods. Comprehensive empirical analysis demonstrates that our proposed algorithms outperform existing state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis is conducted to identify optimal parameter configurations, with findings indicating that the algorithms remain stable across various parameter settings. Finally, the superiority of our algorithms is validated through multiple performance metrics. Notably, for both problems, our approach achieves superior results in significantly shorter execution times. Specifically, IDS and IDS-RD outperform a standard genetic algorithm, while RD (a refined version of IDS-RD) surpasses both a hybrid algorithm and a local search variant of that hybrid. Overall, IDS-RD emerges as the most effective algorithm across all instances, achieving high-quality results in minimal time. A key advantage of IDS-RD is its independence from problem-specific parameters, as it relies solely on randomization. The complete source code is accessible at https://github.com/fernandogarcia2000/SRI-BC. Finally, the authors have established a new state-of-the-art repository for the Set-Union Rucksack Issue, available at https://github.com/fernandogarcia2000/SRI. This repository includes a comprehensive collection of algorithms and a vast set of instances, serving as a valuable resource for the research community. It features performance results on a diverse set of instances, covering both numeric and categorical data, alongside various multi-objective algorithms. Additionally, the repository provides access to all the algorithms employed in this work. Predicting player retention is a core challenge for companies in the online gaming sector. While off-line statistical techniques for customer churn have been widely studied and developed, their direct application to internet-specific contexts remains uncertain. This paper addresses two key issues: first, it evaluates the suitability of standard off-line methods for gaming attrition prediction; second, it identifies drawbacks in current approaches and introduces a novel attrition forecasting framework. Our method leverages game logs to construct a state space that encodes time-dependent features, utilizing Hidden Markov Models to state transition probabilities. This framework offers two main benefits: first, time-dependent states can be learned automatically from raw data without manual feature engineering; second, the model's hidden states naturally generate fine-grained forecasts. We validated our approach across two games from a leading European publisher. The method is accessible at https://github.com/sergioborini/gameloghmm. Results demonstrate that our approach achieves higher accuracy than existing methods, achieving Q-weighted gains of 1.5% and 2.0% for the two tested games, respectively. Additionally, the model can produce granular forecasts across various temporal resolutions. Furthermore, the method is computationally efficient, utilizing less than 100MB of RAM and processing data at approximately 100,000 events per second. Both the model implementation and a demo notebook are included in the repository. The analysis in this study was conducted in collaboration with the publisher. We elucidate how gluon transverse momentum dependent (TMD) parton distributions within an unpolarized nucleon can be derived from "transverse momentum only" (TMD) effective actions in effective field theory (EFT) that incorporate nonperturbative nucleon states. These derivations rely on specific functional structures involving nonperturbative vacuum condensates and correlation functions of transverse-boosted gluon field strengths. Utilizing TMD nucleon states within the effective theory enables the systematic elimination of perturbative contributions arising from initial-state and final-state gluon emissions, thereby yielding the leading-order (LTPD) distribution. Furthermore, this framework allows for the calculation of the first-order perturbative correction to the LTPD. Finally, we demonstrate how the TMD nucleon states of the effective theory can be connected to the conventional TMD framework utilized in phenomenological analyses. This connection enables the prediction of TMD nucleon states in the effective theory, which subsequently generates testable predictions for the TMD of the proton and other hadrons. These predictions include the proton's LTPD, the correction from initial-state radiation (ISRC), and final-state radiation (FSR) corrections, all of which are accessible at the LHC. Additionally, we present predictions for the polarized gluon helicity PDF, which are accessible at the future ILC and can be applied in proton-proton collision experiments, such as those conducted at RHIC. Our predictions for the polarized gluon PDF are consistent with existing proton-proton data and are also applicable to proton-nucleus collisions. We further explore predictions for FSRC corrections to the polarized gluon PDF, which are accessible at the EIC. Our findings suggest a significant enhancement in precision for LTPD and polarized PDFs, including proton and nuclear distributions. Specifically, we predict a 10% improvement for the proton PDF and a 20% improvement for nucleons. These results are expected to substantially advance the precision of global fits for TMDs and PDFs. Beyond the proton, we also examine predictions for the gluon TMD of the pion and eta mesons, which are accessible at the EIC. Our findings indicate a significant enhancement in the precision of the pion TMD, with an expected improvement of approximately 10%. Regarding the eta meson, we predict an improvement of about 20%. Utilizing the Monte Carlo event generator LHC-UCIN, we investigate the potential for electromagnetic interactions between lead nuclei at the CERN Lead-Lead Ultra-Compressed Ion Experiment (AAUCHE) within ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. We demonstrate that electron and positron transverse momenta can be suppressed below 1 GeV/c, indicating the presence of low transverse momentum electrons and positrons. These particles emerge from photon-photon interactions involving both the electron and nuclear sources. Furthermore, we quantify the enhancement factor of low transverse momentum electrons and positrons relative to those from proton-proton collisions, as well as in single-electron and single-posatron sources, which reaches several thousands at a transverse momentum of 1 GeV/c. We also examine the feasibility of a radiative signature involving both nuclei and propose that the photon-photon fusion process can be studied in this ultra-peripheral collision environment. Additionally, we address the advantages of this radiative signature for polarisation studies. Finally, we discuss the feasibility of measuring the polarization of these particles and their application in photon flux calibration. Our findings suggest that this signature could serve as a valuable tool for calibrating low transverse momentum electron and positron detectors in the near future. Additionally, we propose a new method for calibrating the energy of low transverse momentum electrons and positrons. This work is of significant interest to the AAUCHE and ALICE Collaboration. Cyclists face significant injury potential due to their visibility, making the reduction of road collisions a critical priority for authorities. Although risk identification is a key component of risk management, existing solutions fail to fully address collision hazards because they rely on static data and ignore the dynamic nature of the cycling environment. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces the development of the Video-driven Intelligent Risk Identifier for Cyclists (VIDIC). VIDIC integrates dynamic cyclic cues to detect potential collisions and operates within a cycling context to mitigate environmental risks. The system utilizes video streams from cyclists' devices, applying deep learning to identify dangerous objects and situations. Dynamic cyclic cues are extracted using deep neural networks, which are then combined with context cues to identify collisions and alert cyclists to potential hazards. The VIDIC system demonstrates promising performance in both laboratory and real-world settings. These findings offer valuable insights for implementing intelligent risk identification, potentially enabling the mass deployment of smart cycling infrastructure. Furthermore, the VIDIC framework supports intelligent intermodal connections, advancing the development of smart multimodal networks. This approach contributes to sustainable urban mobility by promoting greener travel options and enhancing the quality of life for city residents. Additionally, the VIDIC framework is designed for interoperability, ensuring seamless integration with other intelligent cycling solutions. The VIDIC code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1989/VIDIC. The integration of robotics and cybersecurity is essential for the successful integration of robotic systems into society. This paper introduces a motion planning framework for dynamic robots that ensures security and resilience against both real-time signal processing delays and off-line model perturbations within communication networks. The primary goal is to generate motion plans capable of completing specific tasks while simultaneously avoiding both static and moving obstacles, including cyber cyber-attacks. To achieve this security objective, we employ control barrier functions (CBF) to model the robot as a Control Linear Quadratic Regulator (CLQR), utilizing model predictive control (MPC) to solve a constrained optimization problem. The resulting CLQR-CBF-MPC motion planning algorithm is free parameter, meaning it does not require prior knowledge of potential attack scenarios. We provide a theoretical analysis of the motion plans produced by this algorithm, demonstrating that the robot can reach its target, adapt to communication delays, and prevent penetration into forbidden regions defined by dynamic or static obstacles and cyber attacks. Furthermore, the proposed approach is computationally efficient, making it suitable for robots with complex dynamics. Our numerical simulations on a second-order CLQR system illustrate the method's ability to resolve conflicts between multiple CBFs in real time, effectively balancing performance and security in motion planning. Finally, the results are validated through a case study involving a mobile robot equipped with a manipulator. The paper concludes by outlining several avenues for future research. In summary, the CLQR-CBF-MPC algorithm is a powerful tool for planning secure motion in dynamic environments, making it highly relevant for applications in autonomous driving, robotic surgery, and security-sensitive industrial settings. Additionally, the framework is versatile and can be extended to address other security concerns in motion planning, such as privacy leakage and trustworthiness. Finally, the proposed solution is versatile and applicable to a wide range of robotic platforms, including spacecraft, aircraft, and unmanned aerial vehicles. For each natural number $n$, we define the $n$-encompassing number $e_n(R)$ of a ring $R$ as the greatest possible length of a sequence of $n$ distinct ideals that are not multiplicative, yet their union is a multiplicative ideal. We establish that $e_n(R)$ exists and equals $n$ for both commutative rings and associative rings with identity; in these cases, such a sequence of length $n$ can indeed be constructed. Furthermore, we determine the value of $e_n(R)$ in specific scenarios where the ideals involved lack an associated prime. Our findings indicate that, contrary to the commutative case, the existence of such a length-$n$ sequence in an arbitrary ring does not guarantee that $e_n(R)$ is defined. Additionally, we pose several questions and offer insights regarding these encompassing numbers, demonstrating that various invariants of Boolean rings and rings of continuous functions are bounded by them. Finally, we note that encompassing numbers do not generally apply to nonassociative rings.

This study investigates the interaction between model training and data within deep learning contexts. Specifically, it explores how models trained on adversarial data can be utilized for beneficial purposes. The authors demonstrate that models trained on adversarial examples develop an unusual form of semantic richness, characterized by a significant number of new, valid concept associations that differ from those found in clean training data. Building on this finding, the paper proposes an in-principle framework for the organic deployment of deep learning models. In this approach, model behavior is assessed by comparing its predictions on new data against a distribution of acceptable concept associations, referred to as "memes." Consequently, the model's deployment in a specific context is determined by whether its interactions with that context's instances fall within the range of its acceptable memes. To illustrate the utility of organic deployment, the work presents a use case involving the automated customization of educational materials for students. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research in this area. </s> Finally, this paper examines semantic interactions between models and data to demonstrate how model training using adversarial examples can enhance efficiency. Furthermore, educational and automated customization are explored as effective contexts for deploying such models. The study validates that adversarial training not only improves adversarial robustness but also fosters semantic resilience, thereby increasing the number of valid concept associations in the model. Building on this finding, an educational use case is presented to illustrate an in-principle approach to model behavior analysis. This analysis compares adversarial models against both clean and clean-updated models, revealing that incorporating adversarial examples significantly shifts the model's acceptable concept associations. Specifically, while adversarial training does not increase the total number of acceptable associations, it substantially expands the range of valid concepts for the application, thus enhancing the model's deployability. Based on these findings, an approach to determining the acceptability of model usage is developed. This involves comparing the model's interactions with new instances to the range of its acceptable concepts and utilizing this comparison to inform deployment decisions. To validate this, the paper explores how educational material can be customized for a student based on the student's acceptable concepts, utilizing automated customization as a use case for model resilience. The congestion differential inclusion developed by subagregation teams at the Paris congestion hub is widely recognized for its zero singularity property. This includes formulations by Leland and Barthelemy [J. Phys. A 42 (2009) 334002], subagregation groups at the Paris congestion hub [Phys. Rev. E 89 (2014) 022702], and the work of Liang and Liang [Phys. Rev. E 100 (2019) 052317]. These models are typically analyzed using measure-valued solutions. In contrast, we demonstrate that the model with the highest aggregation level admits a unique continuous solution. We establish that analyzing the singular limit of this congestion differential inclusion within the space of continuous functions results in zero agglomeration. Furthermore, we prove that the inclusion exhibits monotonicity and global Lipschitz continuity. Finally, we examine the well-posedness of a nonlocal congestion partial differential equation featuring general functions. We confirm that entropy solutions exist and are unique, showing that the inclusion derived from the characteristic method is included within this solution and converges to it. Entropy solutions provide a more precise description of the model's behavior near the boundary. Additionally, we demonstrate the stability of this solution and discuss its connection to minimizing a specific cost functional. Notably, we find that entropy solutions do not experience agglomeration. Our findings indicate that stochastic modeling of the congestion hub is viable when agent numbers are not excessively large. Finally, we note that convexity is not required to ensure the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the congestion differential inclusion. This paper extends and enhances the research of Liang and Liang [Phys. Rev. E 100 (2019) 052317]. Key topics include congestion, differential inclusions, singularity, agglomeration, nonlocality, uniqueness, Lipschitz continuity, monotonicity, partial differential equations, boundary layers, entropy solutions, stability, and convexity.

We present a topological generalization of the affine properties seen in closed hyperbolic surfaces, termed "Morse-Smale dilation surfaces." These structures arise by gluing together horizontal strips using complex conjugates under dilations; they feature a horizontal flat metric with singularities and possess a holonomy group limited to $\pm 1$. The mapping class group actions on their horizontal and vertical homology are characterized by specific dynamical behaviors within $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, the mapping classes represented by Dehn twists along horizontal and vertical cylinders correspond precisely to these dynamical traits. The mapping class groups of horizon saddle links exemplify Morse-Smale dilation surfaces, exhibiting identical homological mapping class groups, spectral properties, and realization via mapping cylinders. Finally, we introduce the "dilation spectrum" of a mapping class $\varphi$ as a novel invariant that simultaneously encapsulates several existing invariants for mapping classes and surfaces, demonstrating its efficacy on mapping classes derived from horizon saddle links, once-punctured tori, and once-punctured genus-2 surfaces. Additionally, we define a mapping class invariant based on the joint spectral radius of its associated horizon dilation group, which remains constant across all such groups generated by horizon saddle links, and explore its relationship with the mapping class's dilation spectrum. The proof of our primary theorem serves as a source of new mapping class invariants. Specifically, both the horizon dilation groups and their associated mapping classes constitute a source of novel invariants for closed geodesics on surfaces. The investigation of these horizon dilation groups yields novel findings regarding hyperbolic surfaces containing short closed geodesics. Moreover, our work establishes a new invariant for mapping classes through the "dilation spectrum," which offers a framework for analyzing mapping classes via complex geometry. Notably, the dilation spectrum for a horizon Dehn twist is $\{1\}$, while the horizon braid's mapping class spectrum is $\{\phi, \phi^{-1}\}$, where $\phi$ denotes the golden ratio. Our findings provide a comprehensive framework for studying mapping classes supported by horizon saddle links, including their mapping class groups, braid groups, and invariants. Specifically, we demonstrate that the mapping class groups of horizon saddle links and braids of horizon braids are identical. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research concerning this class of Morse-Smale surfaces. Notably, we extend the concept of the "dilation spectrum" to a broader category of Morse-Smale surfaces by dilating horizontal bands

This study introduces a simplified framework for analyzing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. We treat functional connectivity as defining a directed graph where nodes represent brain regions and edges represent the conditional probability distributions between them. The proposed method constructs this graph using a fully connected structure, calculating each edge from the empirical conditional probability distribution. Our approach demonstrates that these distributions can be accurately modeled using neural variational free energy, yielding a computationally efficient algorithm for analyzing fMRI scans. We validate the method by comparing its functional connectivity profiles against those of an established fMRI analysis tool. Furthermore, we apply the framework to fMRI data collected from 20 subjects engaged in a cognitive task involving color discrimination, with results indicating that the generated functional connectivity graphs successfully capture task-related brain activity. Additionally, we discuss the method's applicability to resting-state fMRI analysis. Given that the computational complexity scales linearly with the number of subjects, the framework is also well-suited for meta-analysis. Finally, the functional connectivity graphs are shown to be effective for brain region classification. The high degree of interpretability of the analysis tool facilitates the design of cognitive experiments and aids in formulating hypotheses regarding brain function. We present an explicit unitary transformation linked to the Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transformation and prove its correspondence to the extended affine Weyl operator. Both the primary transformation and the Weyl operator extend naturally from the real to the Clifford algebra setting. The proof of this isomorphism relies on the explicit formula for the Clifford algebra-valued Segel-Bargmann transformation. Additionally, we derive explicit formulas for the inverse transformation. The development of these results is grounded in explicit calculations. Furthermore, we explore applications within quantum mechanics and quantum field theory. We also examine a transformation analogous to the Segal-Bargmann transformation that involves a rotation in the complex plane. Using explicit formulas, we demonstrate that it corresponds to a shifted Weyl operator. The significance of this paper lies in its explicit approach, which facilitates applications through computational means. All conclusions are supported by direct verification. The paper is structured into four sections. In the first section, we review the quantum Hilbert space, which is a tensor product of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and a Clifford algebra, and provide a brief overview of the Segal-Bargmann transformation. We also review a specific unitary transformation that maps the quantum Hilbert space to a complex Hilbert space of "Clifford analytic functions," serving as an extension of the Segal-Bargmann transformation to a complex vector space. In the second section, we define an operator formulation for rotations of the complex plane and prove that this operator maps constant functions to constants and function derivatives to derivative operators with shifted arguments. In the third section, we prove that a rotation of the Segal-Bargmann transformation corresponds to a shifted Weyl operator by verifying the operator form and utilizing explicit formulas. In the fourth section, we investigate applications in quantum mechanics and quantum field theory, demonstrating that analyzing operator formulations is more efficient regarding both time and space. We illustrate this by examining time evolutions for functions of space and analyzing the quantum field for a scalar field. The significance of this work stems from the explicit verification of operator forms using computational methods. We emphasize that the quantum field theory developed here is fundamentally classical field theory expressed through operator formalism. In conclusion, we show that operator formulations can serve as classical field theories, providing a new perspective on quantum mechanics. The quantum field theory arises when analyzing operator formulations across both real and complex domains. The section begins with a review of time evolution functions of space, followed by an analysis of the quantum field.

This work introduces a pathwise conditional measure designed to regularize Gaussian processes according to the trajectory of a function $y: [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$. Given samples $((x_i, y_i))_{i=1}^n$ generated from a Gaussian process and a target function $u$, the study constructs a conditional measure that approximates the Gaussian process conditioned on the event $\{g \text{ is close to } u\}$. To address challenges arising from the condition's infinite dimensionality and complexity, the authors develop innovative kernel techniques, including random feature kernels and distance kernel functions, alongside regression algorithms to construct data-driven approximations of $u$. These approximations serve as pathwise conditioning functions, yielding consistent estimates of the conditional expectation and covariance of the Gaussian process along with related quantities. The proposed methods are validated through simulations and applications within geometric deep learning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianRiedel13/pathwise-gp. This paper introduces a ground-based sensor network augmented with a second layer of wireless sensors positioned in the atmosphere. The study presents a formula calculating the coverage probability for a ground sensor line, accounting for atmospheric turbulence-induced scattering and blocking effects on both the signals received by the ground layer and by the atmospheric layer. Numerical results are provided, comparing the impact of acoustic and optical turbulence, and an analysis is conducted regarding coverage probability as a function of the height above the ground.

Over the past few decades, particle physics has witnessed a series of groundbreaking discoveries in its fundamental parameters, including the top quark mass, the neutrino mixing angle $\theta_{13}$, the super-Kamiokande neutrino oscillation discovery, the Higgs boson, the T2K and NOvA experiments, and the 7 TeV. Among these, the neutrino oscillation discovery stands out as the most remarkable, prompting the initiation of the extensive Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) at Fermilab. DUNE aims to conduct high-precision measurements on neutrino oscillation parameters, CP violation, and the neutrino mass hierarchy. This document outlines the DUNE design and its future scientific potential. Implemented in multiple stages, the initial DUNE-IA phase will deliver world-class results regarding $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay, supernova neutrino detection, georeactor studies, and long-baseline neutrino oscillation phenomena. Subsequent upgrades, referred to as DUNE-ABCD, will significantly enhance the sensitivity of these core missions while introducing new capabilities to address dark matter and dark energy. Furthermore, the massive data volume generated by DUNE-IA will facilitate discoveries in nuclear physics. Consequently, DUNE represents a comprehensive new endeavor that uniquely integrates fundamental particle physics with astrophysics, cosmology, and nuclear physics. Ultimately, DUNE holds the promise of uncovering new physics beyond the Standard Model. Shapley values originate from cooperative game theory and have recently been suggested as an alternative to current interpretability techniques for machine learning models. This study investigates the potential utility of Shapley values within the context of modern particle physics. The primary objective is to enhance top-taggers employed in jet-to-top quark discrimination tasks. As a starting point, we construct a top-tagger utilizing fully differentiable convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) applied to sub-jet information, achieving an efficiency comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Leveraging our DCNN model, we introduce an enhanced local top-tagger that surpasses existing approaches by approximately 5% in discriminative power, as quantified by the ROC-AUC metric. Furthermore, utilizing Shapley values, we develop a global sub-partition-sensitive top-tagger by integrating multiple sub-taggers with varying weight distributions across jet sub-partitions. This innovative method surpasses all current top-taggers in discriminative capability, representing the first step toward sub-tagger collaboration techniques that offer more comprehensive interpretability insights. Our results demonstrate that DCNN-based tagger optimization can yield significant improvements in classification performance. Additionally, the use of Shapley values establishes a framework for analyzing tagger performance and may facilitate the discovery of previously unexplored optimization strategies for various physics challenges. Our analysis also uncovers the internal working mechanisms of taggers, offering valuable information regarding their performance. The complete code for all taggers and analysis procedures is publicly accessible. \newline

This work aims to further enhance policy performance by applying the VDL principle to the selection of training data. Since variations across different tasks necessitate diverse strategies, this task-independent approach prioritizes training samples that significantly contribute to the task, utilizing two variance-reduced datasets prepared for each episode. To evaluate the method's effectiveness, it was tested across various tasks within the Roboschool Gym environment. The results demonstrate that two distinct variance-reduced policies yield superior performance compared to a single policy. Furthermore, when integrated with established reinforcement learning algorithms, the proposed two variance-reduced versions outperform their traditional counterparts. Spatiotemporal learning is essential for numerous real-world applications, including traffic forecasting, weather prediction, and forecasting. However, these fields often suffer from significant data scarcity and the complex nature of spatiotemporal data. This study investigates the impact of anomalous data on forecasting accuracy and explores utilizing the correlation between anomalies and temporal features to enhance performance. To achieve this, we introduce two methods that leverage motion insights from anomalous data for training. First, the Motion-Distortion Residual Learning (MoDeRNN) technique refines training datasets by applying motion distortion to normal data, ensuring it mirrors the distribution of anomalous data. Second, the Adversarial Motion-Distortion Residual Learning (AMoDeRNN) method incorporates adversarial training to simultaneously capture motion insights and minimize prediction errors. Experimental results demonstrate that both proposed methods significantly outperform existing approaches on traffic prediction tasks. Furthermore, case studies reveal that the impact of anomalous data is more pronounced during peak hours and at longer prediction intervals. Finally, extensive experiments confirm that adversarial training effectively improves the robustness of predictive models. Although Rust is widely recognized for enabling safe and efficient concurrency by precisely managing low-level hardware resources, it is often perceived as unsuitable for high-level domains like web development due to its strict and verbose memory safety guarantees. This paper introduces Josephine, a hybrid programming model that securely integrates Rust and JavaScript by leveraging JavaScript to manage the lifetimes of Rust resources. To achieve this, Josephine extends JavaScript with optional safety contracts and employs a safety checker to enforce them at runtime. Our contributions include: (1) the Josephine programming model, (2) the Josephine language, (3) safety contracts within that language, (4) formal semantics incorporating both JavaScript semantics and optional safety contracts, (5) proofs demonstrating that our proposed weak-safety contracts imply core Rust safety properties, (6) manual verification of Josephine-to-Rust correctness for selected examples, (7) Rust2Josephine translation rules, (8) an Josephine language implementation featuring an optional runtime safety checker, and (9) a demonstration utilizing the Rust WebAssembly ecosystem. We anticipate that Josephine will serve as a foundation for future research and practical applications aimed at securely integrating Rust and JavaScript. The full version of this paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03305. Our Josephine language implementation can be accessed at https://josephine.github.io, where you can also try the runtime safety checker online. The paper itself was typeset using Rust, highlighting both the challenges and opportunities inherent in our research direction. Specifically, we utilized Rust 1.46, which contained 11,000 lines of code when we began work, a figure that has since nearly doubled. To facilitate expressing our language and proofs in Rust, we developed an internal library named `josephine_internal`, which we hope will inspire similar initiatives in the Rust community. Ultimately, we believe that exploring the intersection between Rust and JavaScript represents a promising avenue for future research. We investigate neutrinoless double-beta decay occurring both at nuclei and within colliders. Inspired by recent proposals from the CERN FCC and ILC [A. Pilaftsis and C. Wagner, Phys. Dark Universe 30, 100704 (2020); D. Veltman, Acta Phys. Pol. B 51, 1551 (2020)], we assume a heavy neutral $Z'$ state coexists with the Standard Model Higgs. This framework necessitates the presence of additional neutral neutral leptons. Assuming lepton number is violated exclusively through neutrinoless double-beta decay, we derive a lower bound on the mass spectrum. We demonstrate that multiple neutral neutral lepton states can interfere destructively, thereby significantly suppressing the decay. We explicitly calculate this suppression for a scenario featuring two additional heavy neutral leptons with masses substantially different from the Standard Model Higgs. We estimate the required parameter space to achieve decay rates detectable at colliders and provide an outline of the experimental procedures required to observe such decays within the proposed $Z'$ framework. Additionally, we address a potential conflict between nuclear and collider searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay. We show that this conflict can be resolved if additional neutral states possess mixing angles that are highly suppressed compared to the dominant channel. We conclude by discussing how these suppressed states could be detected at colliders. Finally, we outline a broader strategy for conducting neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments using collider data as a complementary approach. Specifically, we suggest that even a light $Z'$ mass inaccessible to current experiments can be constrained by analyzing the kinematics of $e^- e^- + Z'$ production at colliders. We also examine the sensitivity of this method and the necessary improvements to achieve competitive limits. Finally, we emphasize that this approach offers a unique opportunity to directly probe lepton number violation, a feature otherwise difficult to detect in neutrino physics. This capability is particularly valuable for interpreting the negative or inconclusive results from neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments. We demonstrate that a combined analysis of nuclear and collider data can substantially enhance the sensitivity of neutrinoless double-beta decay searches. Furthermore, we argue that neutrinoless double-beta decay remains the most sensitive probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model, with the potential to uncover phenomena such as extra heavy neutral leptons that may have been missed at colliders. We also highlight that this framework can address discrepancies in octet leptons that have been observed in various experiments

This study addresses the challenge of designing efficient and robust list-decoding algorithms for polar codes under belief propagation (BP) decoding conditions. We introduce a novel list-decoding framework that leverages the advantages of polar subcodes. Specifically, we develop a new polar subcode identification strategy that goes beyond the traditional method of selecting subcodes based on known or estimated channel reliability. Our proposed approach enables the construction of a list-decoding algorithm that maintains strong error-correction performance despite decoding errors in the polar code's tail channel. This method significantly lowers the computational complexity compared to existing polar code list decoders. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can achieve the polar code capacity with a computational complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n^{1.25})$. Simulation results confirm that this algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, we validate the scheme's effectiveness in downlink communication scenarios where certain tail channels are prone to decoding errors. In these scenarios, our approach achieves better tradeoffs regarding error-rate performance, spectral efficiency, and computational complexity. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of polar subcodes in a list decoding context. Finally, we show that the proposed algorithm is highly adaptable to various polar code constructions, such as sparse polar codes and group polar codes, which further enhances its robustness. Extensive simulations across multiple communication scenarios underscore these benefits. In summary, our findings indicate that polar subcodes hold significant potential for future list decoding architectures. By capitalizing on the ability to eliminate unreliable tail channels, polar subcodes can substantially improve the reliability of polar code list decoding. This work opens a promising avenue for future research into polar subcode exploitation within list decoding systems. **Index Terms:** Polar codes, polar subcodes, belief propagation decoding, list decoding, computational complexity. When two images are combined, their point spread functions (PSFs) must be matched. The standard approach involves blurring one image to mimic the pixel response function (PRF) of the other. However, this method is often inefficient and fails to produce the theoretically correct solution. A faster alternative is to blur the images based on their full PSFs. In most cases, the PRF is an adequate representation of the PSF, as it captures the primary characteristic of interest: the total flux. Nevertheless, when PSF shape is critical, such as in photometry, the PSF is defined as the PRF normalized to unity and scaled accordingly.

A common misconception exists regarding the PRF of a stack of images, specifically in weighted average and median combiners. It is widely believed that the PSF is simply a weighted average of the individual PSFs, a notion that is incorrect. This paper demonstrates that such a definition is flawed and that the correct PSF for a stack is, again, the PRF normalized to unity. While an exact calculation is computationally prohibitive, an approximation that is both highly accurate and efficient can be derived. Numerical examples illustrate this methodology. Furthermore, while media combiners are theoretically incorrect for this purpose, they are occasionally used for visualization and can be adapted to accurately reflect the PRF.

Determined from experimental data within the soft-potential model framework, the tensile fracture strength for crystals exhibiting face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC) crystalline structures is calculated. This is achieved by determining the critical strain at which the amorphous-to-amorphous shear transformation, characteristic of soft-potential materials, transitions into a fracture event. The findings align with experimental measurements for real crystalline materials, accounting for an approximate 80% increase in fracture strength observed in metals compared to non-metals. Additionally, the methodology is applied to the quasicrystal-Al$_{65}$Ni$_{25}$Fe$_{10}$, which is composed of decagonal icosahedral (DI) and pentagonal icosahedral (PI) local environments. The resulting fracture strength for this quasicrystal matches experimental results to within 10%. Finally, the computed fracture strengths for nonmetallic FCC and BCC crystals are compared, yielding a ratio of 2. That this ratio exceeds the typical difference between the tensile fracture strengths of nonmetallic and metallic crystals underscores the role of crystalline structure in fracture behavior. Finally, the results are reconciled with the well-documented experimental observation that fracture strength increases as the material approaches absolute zero. This is attributed to the disappearance of dislocations in the lattice and the emergence of a finite energy barrier separating the ground state from the fractured state at temperatures near absolute zero. The latter effect is noted as the reason for the finite fracture strength even at zero temperature. The current study is restricted to the tensile fracture of materials. This work investigates random surfaces generated by multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs) and the random Gaussian free field (GFF). Building upon the framework established in arXiv:1905.03332, our approach models these random surfaces using random log-gases. Consequently, the random surfaces are defined by the trajectories of interacting charged particles. On one hand, we demonstrate that a specific choice of these charged particles yields a random GFF; however, this requires the particles to interact via a modified kernel that accounts for conformal changes. We establish the Markov property of the resulting random surface and identify this family of random GFFs as a Markov chain. On the other hand, we show that these random GFFs possess a remarkable property: they can be realized as boundary values of a holomorphic function within a simply connected domain. Furthermore, we elucidate the relationship between these GFFs and the classical free fermion model previously analyzed in arXiv:1905.03332. Finally, our methodology offers a fresh perspective on the connection between the free fermion model and the free boson model. Specifically, we demonstrate that the free boson model comprises a family of coherent states parameterized by charged particles, where the fermion and coherent state evolve concurrently. This insight may prove valuable for advancing our understanding of the fermion-boson duality. Additionally, we explore the relationship between our findings and the conformal bootstrap program initiated in arXiv:1905.07693. This program examines the partition function of a free boson on a two-dimensional surface, revealing a remarkable structure within its Fourier expansion. By analyzing the coefficients, we observe a clear pattern: some align with the conformal weights of the free boson model, while others correspond to the partition functions of coherent states on a two-dimensional surface. This structure appears consistent with the concept that a coherent state represents an excited free boson. Overall, this paper presents a unique viewpoint on the relationship between the free fermion model, the free boson model, and the conformal bootstrap program. Through the random GFF derived from multiple SLEs, we illustrate the relationship between charged particles, coherent states, and the concept of "towers." This framework may offer a new perspective on the relationship between the Virasoro module and the conformal bootstrap program. Generative modeling for the purpose of generative design is an established technique in engineering, yet it is novel and promising within biophysics. This study introduces a framework for generating the shapes of biological cells, such as red blood cells and neutrophils. By utilizing the advantages of recent deep learning advancements, we develop and assess the practical utility of systems capable of producing complex biological cell shapes. Our approach is grounded in the concept of implicit representations, which represent implicit functions via neural networks; these functions define the boundaries of shapes in 2D and 3D space. By training these networks on real biological data, we can produce new shapes that adhere to specific criteria. This work holds significant value for biophysics, as it facilitates the creation of realistic data for modeling data-driven problems in biological cell mechanics. Additionally, our findings are expected to be highly relevant to computer vision tasks focused on detecting and segmenting biological cells in images. The proposed method is robust, and the resulting shapes are realistic, consistent with established statistical characteristics derived from real data. To demonstrate this, we present and analyze statistical metrics—including histograms, Fourier descriptors, and geodesic distances—computed from both synthetic and real shapes across various cell types. The source code for this project is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ehsan-rahimian/implicit-cell-shapes. Document accessibility ensures that individuals with challenges in reading, hearing, or vision can access information. Access to these documents is typically granted through two main approaches: providing alternative media such as audio, video, or text, or converting documents into accessible formats. Accessibility requirements are inherently diverse and depend on specific user constraints, making their identification and implementation a complex task. This paper introduces a heuristic algorithm designed to suggest the optimal conversion method and alternative type for a given document and user profile. We integrated this algorithm into a web-based tool and conducted an evaluation to demonstrate its effectiveness. The transformation strategies generated by our method align with current practices and user feedback found in related research, indicating that the proposed approach is effective and suitable for real-world deployment. We introduce a straightforward, universal algorithm designed to serve as a universal representation within the autoregressive family for linguistic comprehension tasks. This approach utilizes an autoregressive family of distributions capable of performing sequential prediction in various orders, such as predicting based on positions prior to or following a masked token. We synthesize these representations into a unified, versatile model capable of prediction through positional masking. Our findings demonstrate that this pretraining strategy achieves state-of-the-art results on RoBERTa-baseline benchmarks for linguistic comprehension. Additionally, we extend the method to XLNet-LN by integrating a normalized layer in the encoder block, thereby matching the performance of the state-of-the-art UAN model. On the CoNLL 2003 named entity recognition benchmark, XLNet-surpr and XLNet-LN-surpr achieve F1 scores of 90.2 and 90.3, respectively, surpassing BERT and XLNet by 1.1 and 0.2 points. Similarly, on the BioNLP shared task for named entity recognition in biomedical literature, XLNet-surpr and XLNet-LN-surpr reach F1 scores of 85.0 and 85.1, improving upon BERT and XLNet by 1.4 and 0.9 points, respectively. Finally, XLNet-LN-Lite, a streamlined variant of XLNet-LN featuring a two-layer transformer, matches the performance of XLNet-LN while reducing both FLOPs and parameters by 90%. This work underscores the potential of autoregressive pretraining for linguistic comprehension. The code and models are accessible at github.com/AlibabaResearch/Model Zoo/XLNet.
