Although social networking platforms have become integral to daily life, barriers remain for many Deaf, Hard-of-Hearing, and hearing-impaired individuals (DoH) regarding the creation, rather than just consumption, of social media. This study qualitatively examines the specific challenges and opportunities DoH users face when producing content on these platforms. Through a mixed-methods approach, we conducted an accessibility audit of Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube, followed by interviews with 15 DoH participants. The findings highlight key obstacles such as unfamiliarity, difficulty, and inconsistency, while also uncovering enabling factors like familiarity, ease of use, and personalization. These insights offer a comprehensive framework for designing more accessible social media environments. Additionally, we present a taxonomy of design practices used by DoH users, which reveals how they adapt platforms to meet their unique communication and content creation needs. This research addresses the identified gaps and establishes a foundation for future work. Specifically, it enables the quantification of the accessibility gap between hearing able-bodied individuals and DoH users, and it sets a trajectory for developing assistive technologies that draw inspiration from the practices of their intended users. Consequently, this study advances the goal of democratizing social media. Finally, we outline actionable recommendations for both the social media industry and researchers to ensure no one is left behind. Ultimately, this work seeks to foster a more diverse and inclusive digital society. This paper is grounded in the outcomes of the 1st Edition of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). This paper introduces a geometric non-commutative geometric approach to the tensor union of hypergraphs, which unifies the tensor product and disjoint union of matrices. We demonstrate that the spectral properties of a hypergraph's tensor union are directly derived from the spectra of its projection classes. Furthermore, we establish that the tensor union of highly transitive hypergraphs (which are not necessarily regular) is itself highly transitive. The paper concludes with examples and applications of this construction. This geometric method leverages the algebra of hypergraph functions, which is isomorphic to the tensor product of hypergraph algebras. Additionally, we explore the unitization of this function class by connecting it to local hypergraph projection classes, which are isomorphic to the tensor product of a hypergraph function class and the algebra of scalars. The construction of hypergraph projection classes arises from the tensor product of matrix algebras. We derive the tensor union of hypergraphs and develop its matrix representation, which is based on the tensor product of matrix representations. We verify that the spectrum of a hypergraph's tensor union is determined by the spectra of its projection classes. Our findings enable the development of new methods for analyzing hypergraphs using algebraic and geometric techniques.

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is currently evaluating a mid-term space telescope mission, for which we have submitted a proposal outlining a novel space telescope designed for both spectroscopic and imaging applications. This instrument, named the Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST), is engineered to deliver high-resolution spectra ($R$=10,000) of both point sources and extended objects across the 0.4 to 2.5 $\mu$m wavelength range. The primary scientific objectives of INSIST include determining the ages and metallicities of stellar populations in nearby galaxies, characterizing the chemical abundances of stars and their surrounding environments, and conducting a comprehensive survey of the high-mass stellar population in the Galactic Center. By utilizing a 1.2-meter aperture and a 0.2-second integration time, the mission is projected to achieve a factor of 10 improvement in statistical precision for $[Fe/H]$ measurements compared to existing high-resolution spectrographs on the Hubble Space Telescope, while also offering extended wavelength coverage. Furthermore, the multi-mode imaging capability is expected to generate 10 times more data than comparable high-resolution imaging surveys. This document serves to outline the anticipated scientific outcomes of INSIST and to inspire the future scientific community to engage with this promising mission concept. We anticipate that the Indian astronomical community will soon begin formulating scientific proposals to support this endeavor. The remaining challenge is to initiate the process of selecting the team that will bring this proposal to fruition. We hope that the scientific community will now work to realize the INSIST mission. This study investigates the use of natural cubic splines for modeling longitudinal data in Alzheimer's research. As a nonparametric approach, this method is particularly valuable for analyzing studies where treatment effects remain uncertain. We propose employing the integral of a function as the parameter of interest, utilizing the Bayesian framework to address challenges associated with natural cubic splines. The algorithm's reliability is validated through various numerical examples, including one specifically tailored to Alzheimer's data, with further discussions on its application to Alzheimer's clinical studies. This methodology is implemented via the 'NCSmod' package, available on Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) at: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/NCSmod/index.html. A R package featuring numerical examples can be accessed at: https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/NCSmod. Additionally, the Alzheimer's dataset utilized in this work is available at: https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/NCSmod-Alzheimer's. The findings are detailed in the paper accessible at: https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/NCSmod-Paper. R scripts can also be found at: https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/NCSmod-Paper-Scripts. The analysis was conducted using the NCSmod package, which is accessible at: https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/NCSmod-Package. Finally, the Alzheimer's dataset can be downloaded from: https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/NCSmod-Alzheimer's-Dataset. We conclude that the proposed Bayesian method for natural cubic splines is a viable tool for numerical applications. Its nonparametric nature allows for the detection of nonlinear effects, making it an excellent choice for clinical studies where determining treatment effects is of primary interest. The NCSmod package offers a user-friendly interface that simplifies model specification and provides comprehensive output for assessing treatment impacts. We show that the optimization of decision variables, derived by globally enhancing the contribution of action in trajectory optimization frameworks, can identify multiple Transition Paths (TPs) governing the interconversion of biomolecules. The nature of the decision variables depends on the chosen framework: while Transition Path Sampling (TPS) optimizes entire trajectories, the Enhanced Sampling (ES) method optimizes individual paths anchored to specific sampling points. By applying this approach to both methods for a biomolecular switching process, we identified multiple TPs with distinct characteristics, including those representing the prevailing transition routes. These TPs exhibit unique features, such as the relative importance of the molecular parts involved in the transition, and are consistent with domain knowledge regarding the switching mechanism. Furthermore, the time series generated from these TPs show distinct deviations from the wild-type, providing a basis for comparing the switching processes of the wild-type and a mutant. Finally, we propose that these TPs, representing prevailing transition routes, can be incorporated into simulations using the Adaptive Biasing Potential (ABP) method to generate unbiased equilibrium distributions. This enables the direct verification of enhanced sampling results against equilibrium distributions, thereby facilitating the systematic identification of the most reliable TPs. To achieve this, we propose regular lambda calculi, extensional type calculi, and spectrum classes derived from lambda calculi, monad, and order categories. Additionally, we demonstrate that the functions generated by these formalisms constitute (multi-dimensional) Walsh systems, which serve as the regular function equivalent of piecewise linear functions. This finding represents the primary contribution of the study. As practical applications, we detail regular lambda calculi and (multi-dimensional) Walsh systems constructed from carefully selected function spectra. These constructions include lambda calculi capable of generating absolute value, maximum, minimum, sum-of-magnitude, and Chebyshev distance functions, alongside regular function equivalents for fundamental mathematical operations involving integers and rationals. This latter aspect specifically addresses their utility in computer vision and image processing. Finally, we examine existing (lambda) calculi that are functionally equivalent to the regular lambda calculi developed in this paper. This equivalence arises because total functions in (lambda) calculi can be viewed as discrete extensions of regular functions, and by applying "relaxation," they can be approximated by regular functions. Consequently, functions from (lambda) calculi that are equivalent to regular functions can be utilized in computer vision and image processing as regular, "well-behaved," non-smooth kernels and kernels modified with Gaussian smoothing. The relevance of this equivalence is underscored by the emergence of the "Soft Kernel Method" as a distinct approach to computer vision and image processing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the functions associated with the Soft Kernel Method correspond to regular functions generated by the lambda calculus $\lambda_{WL}$. This observation is significant because it establishes that $\lambda_{WL}$ is, alongside $\lambda_{GL}$ and $\lambda_{BL}$, the first regular lambda calculus developed within the context of computer vision and image processing. The paper concludes by outlining open problems and potential future research directions. Overall, the findings presented herein may inspire the creation of new formalisms for reasoning about and implementing regular functions, as well as their application in the field of computer vision and image processing. Conditioned dynamic systems represent a dynamic version of conditional models, which represent an conditionally invariant model as the product of the unconditioned model and a conditioning function. This function, known as the model's conditionally invariant manifold, is derived from the conditional distributions of the conditioned state variables within a conditioning variable system. The dynamics of these conditional distributions are governed by the conditionally Fokker-Planck-Petrovskii (CFPP) and conditionally Kolmogorov forward (CFK) equations, while conditionally Fokker-Planck-Petrovskii (CFP) matrices are defined by the conditions under which a stochastic dynamic system is conditioned. The motion of a conditional model constitutes a conditionally model flow, a concept that has been utilized in various applications, such as estimating the state of a dynamic system via the conditional mean and determining the state of one system using the state of another. This flow is referred to as a conditional model flow, representing a conditionally invariant model with standard Itô noise. However, when the model conditionally invariant manifold is determined by the state joint probability density function (PDF) of a dynamic system, the conditionally model flow is instead termed a conditional distribution flow. This article demonstrates that the transition from an Itô to a Stratonovich integral in a conditionally model flow can be achieved by modifying the conditional Kolmogorov forward (CMF) and conditionally Fokker-Planck-Petrovskii (CFP) matrices, as well as the conditionally Fokker-Planck-Petrovskii (CFP) matrices, which are components of the conditionally model flow. Furthermore, it is shown that applying the conditionally Fokker-Planck-Petrovskii (CFP) matrix to the conditional distribution flow results in a conditionally Stratonovich model flow. Finally, the paper illustrates several examples of conditionally model flows, demonstrating the impact of changing from an Itô to a Stratonovich integral. Additionally, an application of a conditionally Stratonovich model flow is presented, which is a conditionally parameterized model flow. Parameterization of a conditionally parameterized model flow is achieved through the application of conditionally parameterization operators, which are composed of the conditions under which the conditionally parameterization operator is applied. Consequently, the conditionally parameterization operator is applied to the conditional distribution flow. We introduce a novel spectrum grounded in ideals, showcasing its relationship with other analogous spectra and highlighting its potential utility in group theory. This discussion is primarily motivated by applications in noncommutative algebraic geometry. Specifically, we investigate structure spaces associated with ideals within group rings, demonstrating how these can serve as a tool for investigating various group-theoretic properties. Furthermore, by applying Shirokov's technique, we render the problem of distinguishing simple groups via structure space technology, thereby proving that this method can successfully differentiate simple groups. Additionally, we address torsion and simplicity through spectral means, utilizing torsion-free ideals to define specific classes of groups and proving that the structure space captures information regarding group simplicity. Finally, we employ this new spectrum to provide a positive solution to a question posed by Jategaonkar and Zaraliadis concerning finitely generated ideals in noncommutative polynomial rings. Notably, we identify a particular class of rings where all ideals satisfy the Shapira condition, and we propose an open problem regarding the possibility of distinguishing between two specific groups using structure spaces. For readers interested in the connection between groups and rings, we provide a comprehensive table of concepts in group rings with established counterparts in ring theory. Ultimately, we view the standard structure space as a valuable instrument that bridges group theory and noncommutative algebraic geometry. To facilitate this, we also incorporate a chapter on the fundamentals of algebraic geometry and include an extensive bibliography on the topic. Overall, this work represents a significant endeavor to extend the concept of standard structure spaces from rings to groups, and it serves as a foundation for future research in this direction. Additionally, the book features exercises alongside remarks and comments. Given the length of the project, we have segmented the content into multiple monographs, with this volume focusing exclusively on groups and their rings. In subsequent works, we intend to explore other groups by employing suitable functors to translate them into rings, subsequently analyzing their structure spaces, topology, and geometric properties. Furthermore, we aim to extend these structure spaces to broader categories of groups and rings. For readers seeking to delve deeper into structure spaces, we have compiled a bibliography on the subject. Interested parties are also directed to the bibliography on polynomial growth within groups and on polynomial rings over groups. Cross-domain Text-to-SQL generation presents a complex challenge due to the scarcity of annotated data and the difficulty in encoding both semantic and syntactic structures. To address this, we introduce an end-to-end cross-domain model that employs a meaningful parser, utilizing a supportive task to jointly encode these crucial elements. Additionally, we develop and release a new dataset, CodeSQL, which includes rich semantic and syntactic annotations. CodeSQL comprises 2,000 manual annotations, each featuring multiple sentences with varying degrees of semantic equivalence relative to their SQL labels, alongside 2,000 automatically annotated examples. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses baseline approaches. Furthermore, CodeSQL will be made publicly available to facilitate enhanced research in this domain. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang/MeaningParser. This work was presented at the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

This study addresses the navigation of a multi-robot system within a congested multi-port corridor, utilizing data inference to estimate traffic flow and model predictive optimization (MPO) to generate secure navigation trajectories for all robots. The research focuses on enhancing safety by incorporating both individual robot risk aversion—specifically collision avoidance—and collective risk aversion, which aims to prevent traffic jams. Furthermore, model uncertainty is integrated into the MPO framework, with its impact on the overall navigation performance, safety, and robustness thoroughly examined. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed risk-averse MPO approach outperforms both the traditional receding horizon control method and a naive risk-aversion-based model predictive control scheme across various scenarios. Additionally, the proposed method is noted for its model simplicity and computational efficiency. Finally, the efficacy of this risk-aversion-based MPO approach is validated through a multi-robot navigation case study conducted at a real-world airport in South Korea.

We introduce Andromeda XXV, a dwarf galaxy characterized by a low mass of dark matter at its center. Its physical properties were determined through photometric and spectroscopic data gathered by the Andromeda Dwarf Survey. The galaxy's total stellar mass is estimated at approximately $1.5 \times 10^6 M_{\odot}$, with a stellar mass within the half-light radius of roughly $1.0 \times 10^5 M_{\odot}$. Stellar velocities relative to the Andromeda Galaxy suggest a distance of 770 kpc, accompanied by a stellar mass velocity dispersion of 10 km/s. Stellar kinematics indicate that Andromeda XXV is in virial equilibrium, with the dispersion in line-of-sight velocities averaging 8 km/s. Stellar kinematic ages range from 1.5 to 10 Gyr, peaking at 1.5–8 Gyr, implying that the majority of its stars formed during the Andromeda Group's initial assembly. The dark matter density within the half-light radius is estimated to be no more than $1.5 \times 10^8 M_{\odot} kpc^{-2}$, which is approximately 10 times lower than that of other dwarf galaxies. Stellar abundances are metal-poor, with a metallicity of $-1.5 \pm 0.2$ dex. We propose that Andromeda XXV is a genuine member of the Andromeda Group, likely a stellar remnant from the initial collapse of the Andromeda halo. Its high stellar density and low central dark matter density make it an ideal candidate for studying the stellar core dynamics of dwarf galaxies. Additionally, Andromeda XXV is a prime target for investigating the dark matter density in the inner regions of the Andromeda Group. The Andromeda Group is considered a relic of the early Universe, offering a unique opportunity to study the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies. This research examines various modeling approximations for simulating the thermodynamic interactions between water and vapor within humid air. The study analyzes the thermodynamic coherence of these models and evaluates their respective errors. Initially, several fundamental properties of thermodynamic potentials, including convexity and adiabatic entropy invariance under adiabatic processes, are established and utilized to assess a simulation's thermodynamic coherence. This assessment involves comparing numerical solutions against analytic solutions representing an isolated system over extended time periods. Following the analysis of basic model approximations, the analysis is extended to the Pierce model, a widely utilized simulation framework for humid air. Our findings indicate that the practical model currently employed in simulations can be enhanced to ensure strict thermodynamic coherence with minimal impact on computational performance. These results provide a solid basis for selecting model approximations when developing simulation systems for humid air. Furthermore, several interesting numerical phenomena are observed and discussed. Finally, the code utilized in this study is released under an open-source license. Open access to simulations of humid air thermodynamics is crucial for advancing our understanding of the field. This work establishes a foundation for reproducibility and a baseline for ensuring thermodynamic coherence in such simulations. Additionally, the established methodology can be extended to address other widely used models for humid air simulation. This understanding of model approximations in humid air simulation is a significant contribution to the field of virtual reality. Specifically, our work addresses a problem within head-mounted display simulation, a critical component for VR. By utilizing our approach, the thermodynamic behavior of these systems can be understood with greater precision, leading to more realistic and convincing virtual experiences. This, in turn, may result in reduced simulation times and lower power consumption for VR headsets. Ultimately, VR developers can make more informed decisions regarding the selection of appropriate model approximations. To support this, we have made all simulation codes and results available for reproducibility. Additionally, we have provided access to all intermediate results required for verification and have detailed the procedures for ensuring thermodynamic coherence. This transparency enables other researchers to replicate our findings and further the understanding of model approximations in humid air simulation. The concept of "subalgebras" within matroid lattices was introduced by H. Nakamura. This paper extends Nakamura's study by defining and investigating the complementary notion of "quotialattices" or "outer subalgebras." We present several examples and establish a series of open problems. Furthermore, we establish a general method for constructing outer subalgebras from arbitrary lattices sub lattices related to matroids. In a specific instance of this procedure, the outer sublattices constructed correspond to matroid "grothendieks." Additionally, we demonstrate that this outer subalgebra serves as a significant invariant for matroids. Specifically, we show that two matroids possessing isomorphic outer subalgebras of the lattice of flats may still be non-isomorphic. The paper concludes with a series of problems arising from this approach.

Although Dialogue State Monitoring (DSM) systems have demonstrated efficacy in conversational virtual assistants, they rely on the assumption that prior Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) transcriptions are accurate. However, this reliance overlooks errors inherent in both human and computer-based ASR systems. To address this, we propose a DSM framework that incorporates uncertainty-aware robustly modeled ASR transcriptions, generated from Word Confusion Networks (WCNs). Experimental results indicate that WCN-based modeling enhances performance on both automatically and manually labeled datasets. Furthermore, our analysis of the impact of ASR uncertainty on DSM reveals that the model benefits more significantly from uncertainty-aware processing when using automatically labeled datasets rather than manually curated ones. Finally, we examine the specific limitations and future research directions regarding the integration of uncertainty-aware ASR with DSM systems. Given that this work represents one of the first attempts to model uncertainty within DSM, it opens several avenues for future inquiry, such as developing generalized methods for creating uncertainty-aware transcriptions and conducting extensive human-in-the-loop studies to evaluate the practical applicability of these models in real-world conversational systems. Overall, we aim to foster research that fosters greater collaboration between researchers specializing in dialogue systems and those focused on natural language understanding. By promoting greater interdisciplinarity, the field can achieve more significant progress in dialogue state monitoring. Our work demonstrates that by acknowledging uncertainty in ASR transcriptions, DSM systems can be improved, a principle that is particularly relevant for virtual assistants handling the full spectrum of user inputs, from clearly articulated speech to highly uncertain utterances. Acknowledging and addressing this uncertainty is essential for building virtual assistants that are not only accurate but also robust in diverse real-world interactions. Our findings provide a foundation for future research dedicated to enhancing the reliability and adaptability of conversational virtual assistants. Our analysis underscores the need for greater interdisciplinarity in the field, fostering collaboration between dialogue system researchers and natural language researchers to drive further advancements in dialogue state monitoring. Recognizing and mitigating the uncertainty inherent in user speech is crucial for virtual assistants to deliver accurate and reliable responses across a wide range of interactions. By addressing these uncertainties, virtual assistants can achieve a new level of reliability and user satisfaction, ultimately setting a new standard for conversational AI systems. Our findings highlight the critical role of interdisciplinarity in advancing the field, as the convergence of dialogue system expertise and natural language understanding research holds the key to unlocking the next generation of robust virtual assistants. We examine the properties of universal machine learning models, such as deep neural networks and polynomial neural networks, necessary for approximating any function within a specific domain. Intricacy measures are derived from the minimal resource counts required to represent target functions using these frameworks, accounting for parameters, input depth, and additional resources influencing learning capabilities. By establishing bounds on these measures across various domains, we demonstrate that universal models can exhibit substantial differences in resource efficiency when representing functions in specific regions. Leveraging these findings, we highlight the role of over-parameterization in the efficacy of universal learning frameworks and elucidate the intricate relationship between parameter count, model capacity, and learning ability. Furthermore, we establish that certain functions can be represented by universal frameworks with a number of parameters scaling linearly with the domain size, yet require exponential resources to learn from data within that domain. These results offer valuable insights for selecting optimal learning frameworks for domain-specific tasks, an issue frequently debated in recent literature. Finally, our methodology for constructing universal learning frameworks relies on a systematic approach, facilitating the generation of analogous or complementary constructions, including universal entry frameworks based on ReLU gates, polynomial neurons, and Gaussian neurons. We derive general formulas for the fidelity required to confirm entanglement between two qubits using optimal measurements. For qudit systems, we demonstrate that the Furer state is always optimal under the condition that its reduced density matrices share identical purities. Furthermore, we establish that any entangled state can be approximated to arbitrary precision by qudit systems that possess equivalent reduced purity, thereby extending this finding to systems with a general number of particles. We subsequently apply these results to experimentally accessible schemes for verifying entanglement in photonic qubits. We formulate optimal measurements based on the system's characteristic functions, calculated from experimental data obtained through homodyne detection. Our results indicate that the optimal fidelity needed to prove entanglement varies depending on the specific measurement protocol employed. Finally, we show that the optimal fidelity corresponds to the minimum eigenvalue of the reduced density matrix, a quantity readily accessible in experiments. These findings hold significant implications for the practical verification of entanglement in real-world optical quantum systems. For instance, they provide a framework for designing new experiments capable of verifying entanglement in photonic quantum channels. Specifically, we demonstrate that the entanglement of this channel can be unambiguously confirmed using measurements that deviate minimally from the optimal Gaussian state, a fact established as the first time. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on the measurement precision required to detect entanglement in an optical quantum system, thereby offering a basis for the robustness analysis of future experimental designs. In conclusion, this work offers a valuable reference for the optimal assessment of entanglement in optical quantum systems. It facilitates the advancement of new proposals for generating and applying entangled states, ultimately driving the exponential growth of quantum information technology. Furthermore, this research may inspire approaches to optimizing the measurement of other quantum resources, such as quantum coherence and quantum steering. Finally, the methodologies developed in this study may prove useful for the optimal certification of other target resources in quantum technologies. The JET tokamak exhibits persistent, robust, and regular 1.5 Hz rotation in its plasma rotation spectrum, a phenomenon known as the Palm Tree Mode (PTM). This mode is named for its spectral appearance, which closely resembles the fronds of a palm tree. We contend that the PTM is not an intrinsic property of the system, but rather a byproduct of the limited number of toroidal modes available for measurement. Specifically, when a non-axisymmetric mode is well-resolved by the diagnostics, it generates a strong peak. When this mode rotates at the frequency of the poloidal field harmonic, it produces a peak located on the first branch of the Palm Tree. Conversely, if the mode is poorly resolved, it leaves two small, distinct peaks instead of a single prominent one. We demonstrate this mechanism using both theoretical analysis and the GATO diagnostic code. This insight is crucial for interpreting PTM data, as it prevents the attribution of the mode's origin to the diagnostic setup rather than the tokamak itself. Additionally, we note that the PTM is likely composed of multiple toroidal modes, as it is more accurately described as a Fan mode due to its spectral resemblance to a palm tree fan. Finally, we discuss the limitations of this explanation in light of recent findings that have challenged its validity. Ultimately, we conclude that while a comprehensive explanation for all PTM features remains elusive, this understanding covers the majority of the observed characteristics. Furthermore, we highlight that this mechanism offers a valuable tool for interpreting the regular toroidal rotation peaks in JET data. A potential candidate for the origin of PTM is the Neoclassical Toroidal Alfvén Eigenmode (NTAE), which is regular, non-axisymmetric, and has been detected in JET. The NTAE is driven by energetic neutrons from D-D fusion reactions, which align with the observed frequency of 1.5 Hz. The NTAE is expected to rotate at the poloidal frequency, consistent with the position of the PTM peak. We also address the origin of PTM peaks on the second branch, which the current explanation does not fully account for. We propose that these peaks arise from the toroidal mode with the highest mode number, which is well-resolved by the diagnostics. This mode is expected to rotate in the opposite direction of other PTM peaks, consistent with the location of the second-branch peaks. The recent surge in interest surrounding large pretrained models has spurred significant advancements in natural language processing. However, most evaluation metrics fail to adequately assess a model's limitations, often leading to the misleading impression that performance is merely a matter of fine-tuning. This paper identifies two primary challenges: (1) catastrophic forgetting and (2) bias towards training data, which are inherent to the self-supervised learning techniques used in model pretraining. Consequently, we introduce the Ongoing Learning Basic Benchmark for Question Answering to test whether pretrained models truly possess application-ready capabilities or if their integration into ongoing learning requires further investigation. Furthermore, we propose several practical strategies for reusing knowledge from large pretrained models, which effectively mitigate both catastrophic forgetting and data bias while enhancing performance. Our experiments and insights aim to foster more robust and transparent research practices within the natural language processing community. Additionally, our repository offers a user-friendly interface for easily implementing the proposed knowledge reuse methods. We provide pre-trained BERT-based classifiers for tasks A, B, and C, along with the necessary configurations to replicate our findings. Identifying hate speech has garnered significant attention recently. While prior research has utilized single-modal approaches based on text alone or using images and text separately, this study introduces the task of identifying hate within multi-modal inputs. Specifically, we present the Understandable Multi-Modal Hate (UMMH) dataset, which comprises 1,000 Instagram posts featuring co-aligned images and text, annotated by human judges to identify offensive content. We offer a comprehensive analysis of this dataset and introduce UMMH-Label, a human-understandable multi-modal method that integrates multi-head attention mechanisms with a multi-modal fusion layer. On the state-of-the-art benchmark IMMHO, our model surpasses all existing models by achieving a 11.1% improvement in accuracy, reaching 91.0%. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of model performance and human evaluation confirms that our model effectively leverages the multi-modal data. Finally, we examine human judgments to enhance the robustness of multi-modal models, with results demonstrating that human evaluations align closely with our model's performance. Program repair systems generate numerous false positives by suggesting repairs that are either incorrect or insufficiently precise. An effective system must eliminate these spurious repairs. We posit that spurious repairs arise because a repair candidate is classified as valid at the program level despite being invalid in context; this occurs because the set of antagonistic context features that should invalidate it has not yet been discovered. We introduce Antagonistic Patch Creation (APC), a technique for generating context features. APC employs a rule-based strategy to synthesize context features capable of refuting spurious repairs. Evaluated on the Defects4J dataset, our approach surpasses the existing state-of-the-art program fixer, showing that the produced features can resolve up to 10 previously unresolved bugs. Additionally, we provide practical guidelines for integrating feature synthesis into the repair process and discuss how APC can enhance other software engineering tasks involving the generation and rejection of patch candidates, such as conformance testing. Our Python implementation of APC is available as open-source software. Our findings demonstrate that APC holds promise for enhancing program repair systems. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of program synthesis techniques to the field of automated program repair. Our work offers a novel method for creating context features, a tool for spurious repair refutation, and a framework for advancing the field of automated program repair. The capability region (CR) defines all potential outcomes achievable through various protocols within a given physical theory. This study introduces a data spectrum approach to constructing the CR in probabilistic quantum theories, which extend quantum mechanics and are applicable to physical scenarios involving signaling. We demonstrate that the theory's basic building blocks serve as an effective basis for describing the CR, facilitating its geometric and resource-theoretic investigation. This study proposes privacy-preserving early warning training using adversarial training to facilitate the early detection of COVID-19 from clinical data. We applied this method to create an early warning system for COVID-19. Training was conducted using an imbalanced dataset of 1,078 patients from the MIMIC-III database, which included 92 non-COVID cases and 1,006 COVID-19 cases. The model integrates 18 clinical features representing vital signs, laboratory results, and medication history. Adversarial training employs Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to enhance training data by generating new samples of features from non-cases to create augmented training sets. Results indicate that the system achieves 99.6% accuracy, 99.1% precision, and 99.6% recall in early identification. Additionally, a data ablation study demonstrates that the system remains robust even when trained on a significantly reduced number of cases. Furthermore, Adversarial GAN training outperforms other methods for data augmentation. These findings suggest that GAN-based augmentation improves model training, enabling reliable early warning system performance even with a highly imbalanced dataset containing a limited volume of positive cases. This research establishes a foundation for developing an early warning system for COVID-19 and other diseases, with potential for integration into hospital information systems for data analysis and decision-making. By enabling rapid identification of cases, this system can assist in the early detection of various diseases, thereby enhancing the efficiency of healthcare systems. Additionally, the application of adversarial training offers a new direction for future research in medical decision-making. Although clinical data is typically considered private, we demonstrate that generating training data from existing samples can be treated as a public task. This insight advances the field of medical decision-making by offering a new perspective for data augmentation and enhancing the robustness of decision-making processes. Consequently, this work expands the scope of medical decision-making research. Finally, the developed system holds potential for application in diverse healthcare settings, including hospitals, clinics, and other medical facilities. Over recent years, decentralized control has gained significant traction, with wireless transmission systems serving as a primary example through distributed antenna or distributed beamforming setups. A key challenge in these environments is achieving high-performance decentralized optimization without incurring excessive communication costs. A critical insight is that optimizing decentralized graph neural networks (GNNs) for wireless transmission can enhance performance while maintaining low communication overhead. To address this, the present study proposes two GNN variants: one leveraging the channel matrix and the other utilizing covariance matrices as input. Experimental results demonstrate that both architectures outperform all existing benchmark methods and establish these approaches as new baselines for future investigation. Additionally, it is observed that covariance matrix-based GNNs exhibit greater robustness compared to those designed for channel matrix inputs. The efficacy of these proposed solutions is validated using two representative examples of wireless transmission systems. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ehsan-rahimzadeh/Centralized-And-Decentralized-Beamforming. Furthermore, while this work primarily targets antenna and beamforming problems, the developed GNN models are also applicable to other decentralized control systems, such as distributed consensus and multi-agent tracking. The paper concludes by discussing potential future research directions and open problems. Notably, the authors aim to explore the use of model-based learning methods, including domain randomization, transfer learning, and meta-learning, to further improve the efficacy of these graph neural networks. Additionally, extending the framework to other input types, like decentralized model-predictive control, constitutes another potential avenue for future inquiry. Finally, evaluating the efficacy of these GNNs across diverse scenarios and environments represents another potential line of future research. This research was conducted while the author was affiliated with the Department of Electrical Engineering at the University of Maryland, College Park. The author is currently pursuing a PhD in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Texas at San Antonio. For correspondence, please contact me at Ehsan.Rahimzadeh@my.utsa.edu. Keywords: Wireless Transmission Systems, Decentralized Control, Graph Neural Networks, Convex Optimization, Non-convex Optimization.

The state of Goiás, located in Brazil's Central-West region, exhibits notable spatial heterogeneity in mortality rates caused by murder. This study aims to identify spatial clusters characterized by elevated murder mortality and to analyze the socioeconomic and demographic factors associated with these high-risk areas. Utilizing a georeferenced dataset of 10,580 individuals across 39 municipalities, the research examines murder mortality from 2002 to 2014 through spatially and temporally stratified logistic regression models. These models incorporate high-resolution spatial covariates, including the proportion of each municipality within the Formal Economy, the Informal Economy, and the Low Development zone. The findings indicate that spatially adjusted models yield a higher R² value compared to non-spatially adjusted ones. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that adjusting for the percentage of the population in low development zones and the formal economy significantly reduces the likelihood of murder mortality. Finally, the results confirm a strong association between membership in High Murder Rate Clusters and the Low Development Zone. Consequently, targeted public policies are necessary to address the specific social and economic conditions of these clusters to mitigate murder mortality. This spatially adjusted logistic regression method offers a straightforward approach for analyzing spatially heterogeneous data, such as mortality, that is aggregated by geographic units, like census tracts or municipalities. By utilizing geocoded individual data, the technique achieves high-resolution analysis while maintaining the benefits of individual-level data. Additionally, the method is applicable to other types of covariates, such as air pollution, if available. The methodology has been implemented in the R package `sclustergam` and its associated functions. Finally, the authors propose an alternative approach utilizing Lasso techniques to handle multicollinearity among spatially lagged covariates. This method is detailed in a thesis by the first author, which is accessible at the following link: https://repositorio.ufu.br/bitstream/ufu/19965/1/Dissertacao_Jorge_Ferreira_Silva.pdf. The associated R code can be found here: https://github.com/jfbsilva/SpatialLasso. The dataset used in this study is available at: https://github.com/jfbsilva/SpatialLasso_Dataset. This work addresses a long-standing issue in optimization by proposing the development of a method capable of adapting to environmental noise. Specifically, in stochastic optimization contexts, a response to algorithmic noise is essential for determining the necessary acceleration level. By applying the biologically derived "caloric attention" hypothesis to the learning process, we achieve a biological neural network capable of adaptive learning acceleration. Achieving a noise-responsive calculation method required two key innovations: first, the application of stochastic resonance to continuous-time gradient ascent, and second, the modeling of a dual system featuring negative feedback to regulate speed. We demonstrate that this dual system functions as a negative feedback loop, enabling adaptive negative feedback control. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for faster, more efficient biological and artificial neural networks. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between this dual-system approach and modern techniques involving challenge adaptation and Curiosity-driven learning. Ultimately, our research offers both a theoretical justification and practical utility for designing learning algorithms that dynamically adjust their speed based on noise and difficulty. The proposed method, referred to as Dual System Local Dynamics (DSDL), is implemented in Python and made available on GitHub. Additionally, we provide open-source code for a model exhibiting curiosity-driven learning within a maze environment, alongside a Python library supporting DSDL. This availability facilitates the rapid, efficient, and noise-responsive calculation of enhanced biological and artificial neural networks. IAXO represents the next generation of solar neutrino detectors, designed to uncover astrophysical phenomena previously inaccessible, particularly the Sun's core. This next era will be defined not only by enhanced precision in measuring known neutrino fluxes but also by groundbreaking discoveries in novel neutrino channels. This study presents a white paper for BabyIAXO, the initial small-scale implementation of the IAXO concept, specifically targeting neutrino observations of the Sun. The analysis examines BabyIAXO's anticipated scientific outcomes, including an order-of-magnitude improvement in solar neutrino data from IAXO's primary sources: hep, he, and hep neutrinos from the pp chain; the CNO cycle's 7Be and 13N neutrinos; hep neutrinos from the CNO chain; and events from 8B neutrinos. The work also explores potential observations of non-Standard Model physics, such as sterile neutrinos and solar axions. Finally, the report addresses the construction timeline and budget requirements, recommending a scientific runtime of approximately 3 years. To fully leverage IAXO's scientific potential, a dedicated agency is deemed necessary to manage the project's ambitions. Such an agency would oversee project management, ensure adequate funding, and foster a diverse, international collaboration. This approach is considered essential for the project's success. Additionally, the paper outlines a roadmap for the upcoming years, including the adoption of a definitive science goal statement, a thorough review of construction plans, and a detailed design study. These steps will serve as a robust foundation for the next phase of IAXO: a medium-scale prototype. Ultimately, this will lead to the realization of a large-scale IAXO detector capable of delivering transformative science. Keywords: neutrinos; Sun; sterile neutrinos; axions; non-Standard Model physics.

This work introduces a new self-exciting and self-exciting dissipative (SESD) system exhibiting complex dynamics, characterized by the lack of continuous symmetry breaking. We demonstrate that the model displays complex behavior driven by negative feedback mechanisms rather than symmetry breaking, featuring rich dynamics including period-doubling cascades, quasiperiodicity, and chaos. Notably, the system undergoes a novel type of crisis, as detailed in Ref. [Physica D 400, 132408 (2019)]. The system's parameters can be interpreted as representing the total population, per capita birth and death rates, and a single control parameter. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the emergence of time crystals and glass-like states from initial conditions, even without explicit coupling to thermal baths. These findings suggest that the proposed model holds significant potential for applications in physics, including the description of population dynamics and the formulation of a thermodynamics for time crystals. Additionally, the model serves as a valuable example for studying complex dynamics and crisis phenomena. Our analysis of the parameter space includes the identification of new regions with complex dynamics and the observation of period-crisis phenomena. We also map out various bifurcations, such as period-doubling, torus-doubling, and period-quadrupling, as well as crises involving the breaking of quasiperiodicity and chaos. Finally, we calculate Lyapunov exponents and utilize them to characterize the system's crisis. Overall, the SESD model represents a new class of dynamical systems, and the comprehensive analysis of its parameter space provides a foundation for future research. Furthermore, the parameter $r$ acts as a control variable, while $a$ and $b$ can represent birth and death rates, respectively, and the total population is denoted by $N$. The model's versatility is also evident in its application to the Lorenz system, where it yields results consistent with those of the original framework. The model's simplicity and the broad scope of the analysis make it an ideal candidate for a wide range of applications. The findings of this work are expected to have a significant impact on the fields of nonlinear dynamics and complex systems. The SESD model is anticipated to serve as a basis for future research into the properties of time crystals and glass-like states. The comprehensive analysis of the parameter space provides a solid foundation for further investigations into the properties of the SESD system. Robotic grasping remains a persistent challenge in robotics due to factors such as diverse object geometries, textures, and the need to avoid collisions. While simulation has become a standard approach for accelerating grasp generation, it frequently suffers from unrealistic environments and the "sim-to-real" gap. To address these issues, we present DexGraspNet, a large-scale synthetic grasp database comprising 1.5 million synthetic grasp labels derived from 420,000 unique objects. Our method employs a two-stage strategy to synthesize dexgrasps, which are then validated against real-world data. In distinct contrast to prior research, our analysis reveals that the distribution of z-rotation values is random and independent of diverse graspable objects, and that a single dexgrasp instance can support multiple valid grasps. These findings are further supported by the observation that robust grasp stability relies on a single point of contact. Leveraging DexGraspNet, we develop GRASPN, a real-time, universal object grasp generator. By integrating DexGraspNet and GRASPN, we pave the way for robust, universal, and fast grasp generation. The DexGraspNet dataset and GRASPN framework are accessible at https://github.com/rogerslab/DexGraspNet. Additionally, our real-world dataset is available at https://github.com/rogerslab/DexGraspNet-Real-Data. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D (where 4D represents 3D spatial resolution plus respiratory phase encoding) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TESE) sequence designed for visualizing the chest and abdomen. The sequence employs variable turbo factor, repetition time, and echo train length adjustments throughout the k-space acquisition. These motion adjustments occur over multiple 4D datasets, each corresponding to a distinct respiratory phase. By acquiring and combining these datasets, the method compensates for free-breathing motion, enabling the generation of high-resolution, isotropic, multi-contrast, and fully sampled images. The free-breathing 4D-T2-TESE sequence was evaluated on a healthy human volunteer using both a 1.5T and a 3.0T clinical MRI system. The resulting images demonstrated high resolution with no visible signs of respiratory or cardiac motion artifacts. Furthermore, the free-breathing 4D-T2-TESE sequence proved to be both feasible and efficient for clinical use. The study concludes that this technique is effective for generating motion-adjusted, free-breathing, 4D isotropic T2-weighted images of the thorax and abdomen. Additionally, it offers flexible trade-offs between scan time and image resolution, making it suitable for a broad spectrum of clinical applications. The potential for expanding this approach to other imaging sequences is also explored. Model compression and acceleration are essential for deploying Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) on resource-constrained mobile and IoT devices. While recent studies have demonstrated that Knowledge Distillation (KD) can significantly enhance inference speed, existing KD frameworks typically ignore the internal data flow of both teacher and student networks. This oversight often leads to substantial reductions in accuracy, particularly in Student-Teacher pairs with heavily skewed architectures. To address this, we introduce **InDistill**, a novel KD approach that maintains the data flow within teacher networks and preserves critical information across diverse layers. InDistill employs a selective distillation strategy that adapts to the data flow of both teacher and student networks, enabling a more robust transfer of vital information from teacher to student to student from teacher. We validated our method across various compression scenarios and applications, including image classification, semantic segmentation, anomaly classification, and object detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that InDistill consistently delivers superior performance compared to state-of-the-art KD techniques. Specifically, it improves accuracy by 1.1% to 16.1% across diverse datasets while maintaining comparable model sizes. The source code is available at: https://github.com/DeepVisionLab/InDistill. We demonstrate that a substantial subset of submersion functions, defined on the affine plane and subdivide it into straight lines, exhibits topological similarity under linear homeomorphisms of the plane. The resulting topologically equivalent functions can differ significantly in their "local" and "global" characteristics, which are formally specified in this article. We explicitly identify conditions for topological equivalence based on local and global properties, considering both cases where lines are parallel at infinity and when they are not. Furthermore, we propose the concept of "pieces" of submersion functions, enabling the construction of explicit pairs of function "pieces" that are topologically equivalent yet lack global line-topological similarity. Consequently, two submersion functions may consist entirely of "equivalent pieces," even though they themselves are not globally topologically equivalent. Additionally, we examine specific classes of submersion functions, including those quadratic in coordinates and specific subsets of cubic functions. For each class, we detail the conditions for line-topological similarity among its members. In the case of quadratic functions, we derive the line-topological invariants and classify all such functions using these invariants. For functions quadratic in coordinates that are rational of degree 2, we determine the line-topological invariants and establish their line-topological classification. Finally, we present explicit line-homeomorphisms between subsets of quadratic and cubic function classes that induce topological equivalences between their associated foliations on the plane. These examples illustrate various types of local and global properties, including simple and non-simple cases regarding the line-topological equivalence of submersion functions. Throughout, the line-topological invariants of submersion functions and the line-homeomorphisms between their level sets are derived from the asymptotic behavior of non-proper functions and the line-homeomorphisms between their level sets at infinity. We argue that a comprehensive classification of submersion functions via line-topological invariants is unlikely, as the invariants for functions quadratic in coordinates appear to mark a significant threshold. Nevertheless, for functions quadratic in coordinates, we identify line-topological invariants derived from local properties, specifically near points at infinity. We also establish the conditions for line-topological equivalence between subsets of these functions. Finally, we outline directions for future research regarding global line-topological equivalence, particularly in scenarios involving multiple non-simply connected regions bounded by level lines. Ecosystem services are compromised when spatial heterogeneity in resource distribution and consumption is ignored. This study assesses the validity of the common "local foraging" hypothesis, which posits that granivorous animals deplete local seed resources, thereby stabilizing plant populations through negative feedback. By employing Fourier analysis, we demonstrate that "non-local foraging" contradicts this hypothesis, as such animals amplify spatially oscillatory patterns in seed density. We show that these dynamics involve traveling waves of seeds and animal populations, which can be characterized by their speed and direction relative to resource production sites. Utilizing mean-field theory, we derive approximate formulas for wave speed as functions of system parameters. Our findings indicate that when system size is insufficient, system boundary effects will inevitably cause local extinctions of either the plant or animal species. This underscores the critical role of spatial heterogeneity in sustaining both plants and animals. Furthermore, our results suggest that animal-induced oscillatory patterns can coexist with traveling waves under conditions of spatially periodic system parameters. These predictions are supported by direct numerical simulations of the full system. Our models provide a framework for understanding how spatially heterogeneous ecosystems are maintained and how spatial heterogeneity influences ecosystem services. CountSketch is a well-established, efficient, and scalable technique designed to identify approximate $k$-sparse vectors within the $\ell_1$ unit ball in high-dimensional spaces. Despite its popularity, theoretical research has largely concentrated on static datasets, whereas practical applications often encounter dynamic and potentially adversarial data. This study investigates the resilience of CountSketch against adaptive data. We demonstrate that a modified version of the technique remains resilient to data adaptivity by incorporating randomized row permutations. Furthermore, we present a lower bound showing that such transformations are essential for maintaining this resilience. Finally, we analyze the sample complexity required for adversarial data and reveal that the count and sign components of CountSketch exhibit different behaviors in this context. Specifically, the sign component necessitates $n = \Omega(k^2 \log k)$ samples to guarantee constant approximation accuracy, which is optimal for this variant of the sparse mean estimation problem. In contrast, the count component can achieve constant approximation accuracy with $n = \Omega(k^3 \log k)$ samples in the adversarial setting, a bound that is sub-optimal. To address this, we propose an enhanced CountSketch variant that achieves the optimal sample complexity of $n = \Omega(k^2 \log k)$ even under adversarial data conditions. Our proofs utilize a combination of convex geometry and game theory, while our lower bound is derived from the graph theory concept of graph separators. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the streaming setting, demonstrating that our optimal sample complexity holds in this scenario as well. Notably, this result is unattainable by any linear algorithm. Our findings are supported by experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of game theory to address the resilience of count-based sketching techniques to adaptive data. Our results offer the first theoretical insights into the robustness of these methods when faced with adversarial data. Furthermore, our work provides the first lower bound regarding the sample complexity of sign estimation for sparse vectors in adversarial environments. This result also establishes the first lower bound for sparse mean estimation in this setting, thereby clarifying the trade-off between sparsity and dimensionality. Our results also shed light on the relationship between sparsity and sparsity-free estimation. Finally, our work offers the first lower bounds for both sign and mean estimation problems, which are derived from the graph separator problem. We introduce ipie, a Python-based Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) framework designed for the versatile and efficient simulation of both bosonic and fermionic quantum many-body systems on CPUs and GPUs. The ipie code is accessible at https://github.com/ihmiao/ipie. Furthermore, we have developed a flexible set of libraries utilizing C++11 that can be integrated into the ipie code, allowing users to extend its functionality with ease. Finally, we showcase recent, state-of-the-art applications of AFQMC implemented with ipie across various recent publications. These cases demonstrate that our method, powered by ipie, can explore the ground states of strongly correlated systems with challenging sign problems, achieving quantum-level scaling with respect to basis size. Additionally, we demonstrate that the ipie algorithm surpasses other Monte Carlo methods in accuracy, offering an effective approach to solve these systems. The combination of versatility, efficiency, and ease of use makes ipie an ideal choice for both bosonic and fermionic AFQMC applications. This is evident from numerous recent publications that have employed ipie to address a wide spectrum of bosonic and fermionic problems, ranging from quantum phase transitions and Fermi liquids to Mott insulators, superconductors, and magnetic phases. The ipie algorithm's versatility is further illustrated by its ability to calculate ground state wave functions, excitation spectra, dynamical correlation functions, and finite-temperature properties. The ipie code's effectiveness is similarly demonstrated by its performance in quantum chemistry calculations, where it has solved electron correlation problems in molecules and materials with large basis sizes and system sizes. The ipie method's scalability is also highlighted by its success in solving electron correlation problems on supercomputers with up to 100,000 cores. The "Prisoner's Dilemma" serves as a foundational model in game theory, designed to illustrate why rational individuals often fail to achieve the optimal collective outcome. This paper adapts that dilemma for use in High-Frequency Trading (HFT) within the financial sector, aiming to demonstrate how quantum strategies can generate superior returns for all market participants involved. "Quantum Elevated Frequency Trading" represents a practical application of "Global Cooperation" within the "Quantum Prisoner's Dilemma," where all traders achieve mutual benefit. To address "Information Asymmetry" common in HFT contexts, the study leverages emerging Quantum Cloud Technologies, which provide superior market data to everyone, thereby enabling wins for all. The paper also highlights the "Bounded Rationality" inherent in HFT and the "Nash Equilibrium," and provides real-world evidence from trading actual shares on the Quantum Cloud to support these claims. Ultimately, this research aims to serve as a catalyst for the development of quantum algorithms and software for financial markets, as well as to promote the adoption of Quantum Cloud Technology for market data provision, ultimately benefiting all human traders, investors, and the financial system. Specifically, the study demonstrates the value of Quantum Cloud Technology in delivering enhanced market data to all users, the necessity of quantum strategies in HFT, and the challenges of global cooperation within the Quantum Prisoner's Dilemma. This research examines the impact of intermediaries on investor income, specifically analyzing how their fee structures influence revenue. Intermediaries influence investors by recommending or discouraging specific trades, the consequences of which are reflected in interbank rates. Using a computational approach, the study employs a Monte Carlo simulation to track multiple traders and interbank rates over time, optimizing income for each agent based on the cost benefits introduced by intermediaries. The findings indicate that agents typically achieve higher incomes when intermediaries adopt pricing strategies that favor long-term trading. Additionally, among short-term traders, those positioned in the middle of the distribution exhibit higher incomes than those at the extremes. The study further reveals that certain agents exhibit behavior consistent with the disposition effect, evidenced by their decision to sell winning trades rather than allowing them to appreciate further. Overall, these results suggest that intermediaries can enhance individual incomes, although this improvement does not necessarily extend to the aggregate system. This conclusion is supported by evidence of the second-order effects of interbank rate changes and a computational analysis of the stock market system's behavior with and without intermediaries. Consequently, this model offers a framework for examining the effects of market changes on the system as a whole. Building on the entity centrality hypothesis, we contend that entities highlighted in the input data hold paramount importance for summarization. Consequently, we aim to generate writing plans by identifying and prioritizing salient entities, subsequently organizing content through these prioritized entities to ensure the output aligns closely with the specific data provided. To achieve this, we introduce Deep Planning with Acquired Entity Prompts (Deep E2sum), a neural sequence-to-tree deep planning framework enhanced by acquired examples. This plannar algorithm integrates both content-based and structure-based steps, utilizing structure-based planning to refine the initial content-based draft. Experimental results on the DUC2002 and CNN/DailyMail datasets demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, a human evaluation by three professional writers confirms that our model produces higher-quality summaries compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. "Vocal entrainment" describes the synchronization of one's speech rate to match a conversation partner during dialogue. Given its established link to dynamic interpersonal behaviors like responsiveness and engagement, this phenomenon holds significant promise as an indicator of dialogue quality. However, the current literature lacks a comprehensive understanding of how such speech rate adaptations evolve within the broader context of interaction dynamics. Consequently, there is an urgent need for objective, automated metrics to quantify entrainment and a nuanced comprehension of its relationship with interaction dynamics. This study introduces a novel metric that evaluates entrainment by examining speech rate similarities across the immediate prior utterances. Using the Dialogue Corpus, the method is validated through an examination of how entrainment evolves within the contextual space of preceding utterances and how it serves as an indicator of specific interaction dynamics. The findings reveal that speech rate adaptations are more predictive of quality assessment than previously thought and demonstrate the existence of distinct entrainment patterns in dialogues rated as high versus low in interaction. Ultimately, this research advances the measurement of entrainment by accounting for contextual sensitivity, while also deepening the understanding of its role in interaction and its relationship with perceived dialogue quality. This paper aims to quantify the spherical symmetry of pure quantum operations. Leveraging recent advancements by the authors and their colleagues, we examine how to parameterize global symmetry within the geometry of the unitary sphere. We demonstrate that the resulting symmetry measures are anchored to specific Fubini-Study geodesics. Offering a fresh perspective on existing spherical symmetry methods, we emphasize that these techniques are adaptable to various contexts, such as assigning origin points to spherical symmetry measure (L-S2) along Fubini-Study geodesics or facilitating category-theoretic generalizations. Employing a categorical approach, we extend the method to any monoidal category enriched with abelian groups. We explore generalizing both spherical symmetry to monoidal categories and the global symmetry quantifiers to any symmetric monoidal category. Furthermore, we generalize the lambda-sphere to any monoidal poset and the sphere-to-sphere map to any functor category. Ultimately, this work provides foundational tools for quantifying symmetries within quantum logic and topological phases of matter. Specifically, we introduce a framework for measuring the symmetry of any categorical construct, encompassing any collection of morphisms, any subcategory, and any monoidal category. Additionally, the method establishes a pathway for developing symmetry measures in any enriched category where the enrichment consists of an abelian group. This approach also addresses the symmetry of any monoidal functor and extends the lambda-sphere concept to the setting of any monoidal poset. Finally, the framework establishes a foundation for developing symmetry measures in any construct where universal properties define symmetry through specific commutative diagrams. Consequently, this research offers a comprehensive foundation for investigating symmetry measures across a broad spectrum of categorical structures. We introduce DUVET (Dual-View Outflow), the first multi-wavelength, spatially resolved survey of a massive, co-spatial outflow in the nearby starburst disk galaxy 3C 295. This survey uniquely combines data from the VLA, ALMA, Spitzer, and HST, all aligned to a common astrometric frame. These observations highlight the critical role of feedback from star formation in driving and sustaining AGN-driven outflows. This study introduces the concept of a Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS), which encompasses multiple robots operating in close proximity to execute tasks that a single unit cannot accomplish alone. Structure formation involves simultaneously optimizing the robots' communication topology, control inputs, and configurations. We address the specific challenge of forming a 2-D polygonal SRS with nonholonomic agents subject to nonholonomic constraints. A model problem is defined, solved, and analyzed, revealing that the solution set is generally non-convex and disconnected. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution space is typically disconnected when the polygon has 5 or more vertices and requires disjoint interior angles of at least $\pi/2$ in the worst-case scenario. Finally, the proposed formation control law is shown to ensure practical stability. Numerical simulations are included to validate the theoretical findings. The main contributions of this work are the definition and initial characterization of 2-D SRS problems, an algorithm for solving the 2-D polygon case, and the subsequent theoretical analysis of the solution space, practical stability, and simulation results. The remaining problem of forming a general 2-D SRS, along with solution characterizations for higher dimensions, will be addressed in future research. The term SRS is selected to emphasize that these structures represent a novel class of systems within multi-robot and multi-agent frameworks. Additionally, the term underscores the simultaneous nature of the optimization, which contrasts with traditional approaches where the topological structure is often designed independently of the configuration. This distinction is significant because, in many classical problems, the resulting structures are typically stars or complete graphs, a limitation we aim to overcome. Topological formation design is also considered a distinct problem. Recent research indicates that pre-training on monocular depth estimation yields superior results compared to both direct training and other self-supervised tasks when performing semantic segmentation. However, the specific advantage that distinguishes depth pre-training from other shallow metric estimation tasks, such as scale estimation, remains unclear. This study investigates the efficacy of depth pre-training in semantic segmentation by benchmarking it against other self-supervised depth and non-depth tasks. We demonstrate that other self-supervised tasks, including classification, can match or exceed the performance of depth estimation in semantic segmentation, thereby validating the hypothesis that depth pre-training does not inherently provide benefits for this task. Additionally, we explore the possibility that it is the transfer of representation rather than the metric that explains the observed gains from depth pre-training, given that other similar tasks do not reproduce these results. Finally, we propose an alternative explanation for why depth pre-training excels in semantic segmentation, emphasizing its role as a representation that encodes scene geometry. Kendall's tau is a robust, parametric-free, and distribution-agnostic metric for assessing a predictor's association with an outcome, yet its computational complexity scales quadratically with sample size, limiting its applicability in large-scale settings. This paper introduces a validated method to reduce computation time by approximately two orders of magnitude by leveraging the effective support of a Markov chain, a concept from sensitivity analysis. Our approach involves calculating the Kendall's tau of the effective support and proving that this value equals the original Kendall's tau for the full chain. We also present a general strategy for constructing the effective support of a Markov chain, which includes two new algorithms for specific cases: a discrete Markov chain with a uniform stationary distribution and a continuous random walk on a regular graph. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of this work through two large-scale examples: a network that tracks daily page views for over 100,000 networks and a continuous-time Markov process modeling the spread of COVID-19 across the United States. These applications highlight the method's potential for use in large-scale network and epidemiological models. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashokkumar2000/EffectiveSupportKS. Furthermore, we have developed a new R package, EffectiveSupportKendallTau, to facilitate the calculation of Kendall's tau for the effective support of the discussed Markov chains. This package is available on CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/package=EffectiveSupportKendallTau. Additionally, the package is being considered for inclusion in the Bioconductor project, which serves the bioinformatics community, at https://www.bioconductor.org/. The rise of Edge Cognition represents a significant paradigm shift for future automotive networks, aiming to lower computational demands on vehicles and enhance overall performance. However, this approach introduces critical challenges regarding data privacy and security, as well as resource constraints in network infrastructure. To address these issues, we propose the Collaborative Structure for Privacy-protecting Edge Cognition (CSP-Ec), designed to intelligently manage tasks and data alongside privacy preservation measures across networks of vehicles and road infrastructure. This framework leverages the parallel computing capabilities of wheels and utilizes homomorphic encryption for encryption and decryption at wheels, road signs, and infrastructure Edge Computing Nodes (ECNs). Consequently, this allows for privacy-preserving computations within the CSP-Ec structure. We evaluate the performance of this structure regarding computational efficiency and data privacy, demonstrating that wheels and infrastructure ECNs can effectively execute private tasks while significantly enhancing computational power and reducing latency. Furthermore, we introduce an optimization strategy based on the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) to optimally assign the most suitable road sensors and ECNs for handling private tasks. Experimental results indicate that the proposed structure can reduce latency by up to 50% and improve computational efficiency by as much as 40%. Additionally, our privacy-preserving Edge Cognition architecture is capable of safeguarding sensitive data during transmission and processing on wheels and ECNs, thereby maintaining data privacy and confidentiality. Overall, this structure offers a promising solution for secure and privacy-preserving Edge Cognition services in future automotive networks. Significance surfaces are created by applying a statistical test to every voxel within a brain image. While these surfaces effectively highlight statistically significant regions, they fail to display the magnitude of the effect at each location. This paper presents a novel surface method that incorporates effect size without relying on statistical thresholds. Specifically, we propose two new surfaces: one utilizes the \emph{Euler characteristic surface} to measure the surface area of spherical contours derived from a one-dimensional nonparametric estimate of the pointwise \emph{Euler effect}, and the other employs a weighted sum of spherical shells based on a unidimensional \emph{Gauss-Jackson effect surface} derived from the Euler characteristic surface. Both surfaces derive their name from the fact that their construction relies on the \emph{Euler-Poincar\'e relation}, a topological formula that connects the counts of vertices, edges, and components in a mesh. The proposed surfaces serve an aesthetic function, enhancing the visualization of the functional data underlying the image, and demonstrate that this functional information can be accurately represented by the mesh's numerical invariants. Numerical simulations and examples applied to real fMRI data confirm that the numerical characteristics of the mesh accurately reflect the properties of the underlying image. Consequently, the numerical content of this mesh can be utilized for the automatic segmentation of the corresponding image. We conclude by addressing several challenges related to the visualization of functional images and suggesting potential future research directions. This work serves as a sequel to \cite{Bergamasco2019}. The numerical methods for the segmentation example are currently under preparation for submission to a future joint paper.
