Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) serves as a widely accepted framework for secure communication, yet it relies on the assumption that an eavesdropper possesses uniform randomness over any system not explicitly defined in the protocol. This assumption is unrealistic, as an adversary can construct non-uniform, private states from publicly accessible resources. This work addresses the issue of bounding key rates under such conditions by integrating a non-uniform private state into the QKD key generation process. Using the quantum information-theoretic framework for one-shot hypothesis testing, we derive a safe bound on the achievable key rate. This bound is derived by analyzing the mutual information between the Eavesdropper's state and the legitimate users' measurement outcomes, integrated with the hypothesis testing limit. We demonstrate the bound through numerical simulations representing a non-uniform depolarizing channel within the BB84 protocol. Furthermore, we compare this approach to standard QKD security analysis; while our method yields a more conservative key rate bound, it remains feasible for practical implementation. Our findings offer a foundational step toward safe bound evaluations in practical QKD systems. Additionally, this theoretical approach can be applied to other quantum technologies that depend on the independence postulate. Ultimately, our results provide a pathway for safely assessing performance metrics in quantum devices utilizing non-uniform random resources for privacy enhancement. These outcomes can aid decision-making regarding the deployment of emerging quantum technologies in real-world settings. Our theoretical findings are supported by supplementary materials available in the online repository. The code used in this work can be accessed at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10400008. Future research will aim to derive tighter bounds, offer recommendations for practical QKD deployment, and extend these theoretical results to broader quantum information processing scenarios. To facilitate this, we have developed a Python package named "QKD-safe-bounds" to implement our theory, which is detailed in Section 5. The package is available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Computing-Group-TU-Darmstadt/QKD-safe-bounds. We believe our approach offers a safe bound calculation for any QKD system, enabling practical performance analysis. Specifically, we have outlined a procedure to derive safe bounds for any QKD protocol by inputting mutual information and error rates from raw key data, as demonstrated in our simulations. This method allows for the evaluation of system performance in practical deployments. The Feller process, or Feller diffusion, represents a diffusion on the non-negative half-line governed by specific generator conditions. This format models the evolution of a quantity subject to stochastic fluctuations that are asymmetric and dependent on its current value. Such processes are widely applicable, including as continuous approximations for branching processes and economic models featuring increasing returns to scale alongside asymmetric individual behaviors. Furthermore, they can be derived from coalescent point processes on the non-negative half-line. This article presents a unified framework for analyzing Feller diffusions by linking them to one-dimensional stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and SDEs on the half-line. It also offers a method for approximating the diffusion using the solutions to a specific type of non-linear integral equation. Additionally, we construct a SDE for the 1/2-contraction coalescent point process based on a half-line kernel and demonstrate that its coalescent measure corresponds to the solution of a non-linear integral equation. We also derive the measure that describes the difference between two points in the process, known as the diffusion-in-diffusion measure. Finally, we establish that the distribution of the diffusion at any time $t$ is a solution to a family of integro-differential equations. This finding enables the sampling of the diffusion from its $t$-distribution by combining the coalescent measure with the diffusion-in-diffusion measure. We provide several examples of Feller diffusions, including those with superlinear growth, power growth, logistic growth, square root growth, and negative growth. For each example, we present the corresponding non-linear integral equation, its solution, and an approximation to the process's distribution. For all cases, we calculate the coalescent measure and the diffusion-in-diffusion measure, illustrating how to sample from their respective distributions. In cases with power, logistic, square root, or negative growth, we observe that the coalescent measure is either a stable law or a stable law shifted to the right. For the superlinear growth case, we identify the process as the solution to an It\^o SDE and provide a derivation of the coalescent measure. Additionally, we include an appendix with a proof of the non-existence of the $L^1$ coalescent measure for the superlinear growth case. These findings were motivated by an economic model of a firm's market share, where growth follows a logistic pattern with a square root component. We illustrate the theory by simulating the process and comparing its distribution at various times

Research indicates that dark matter (DM) diffusion, driven by its spin, can significantly impact direct detection experiments. This concept originated from the work of Gnedin et al. [Phys. Rev. D 98, 023527 (2018)], which demonstrated that thermal neutron flux could reduce DM–nucleus scattering cross sections by up to 10 orders of magnitude. While the original focus was on scalar neutrons, this study investigates a spin-related diffusivity for axial-vector neutrons, comparing the two regimes. We demonstrate that a low thermal neutron flux, increasing with distance from the source, similarly suppresses DM scattering off nuclei through the spin degree of freedom. Notably, this suppression offers a distinct advantage over scalar neutrons: it can be fully recovered by recoiling nuclei upon collision, thereby preserving the potential for direct detection. Furthermore, we calculate the one-order-of-magnitude zone surrounding the Sun where this spin-related diffusion efficacy is maximized. We also examine how this region influences direct detection prospects and explore its broader implications for astrophysical processes involving DM. Finally, we establish that spin-related diffusion does not suppress the overabundance of DM around the Galactic center, a phenomenon known as the cusp-core problem. The findings presented here are expected to advance future direct detection experiments by expanding the parameter space for axial-vector dark matter. Additionally, these results offer new avenues for investigating axial-vector DM interactions with nucleons, the spin-dependent component of the cosmic gamma-ray spectrum, and the effects of DM on the evolution of compact objects. Our work serves as a foundational reference for future studies on axial-vector dark matter. Finally, we provide open-source code to facilitate these efforts. **Keywords:** Dark Matter, Direct Detection, Diffusion, Spin-Dependent Cross Section. **Abbreviations:** DM: Dark Matter; DM-SN: Dark Matter–Standard Neutron; SN: Standard Neutron; SVN: Spin-Dependent Vector Neutron; sDEDSN: Spin-Dependent Effective Diffusion Coefficient of SVN; ADEDSN: Effective Diffusion Coefficient of Axial-Vector Dark Matter–Nucleon Interaction; SDDIC: Spin-Dependent Direct Interaction Cross Section; SDSC: Standard Scattering Cross; ADEDSN: Axial-Vector Dark Matter–Nucleon Standard Scattering Cross; AVEDSI: Axial-Vector Effective Diffusion Coefficient of DM–SN Interaction; AVEDSI: Axial-Vector

While Faulhaber identified the solution set $c_1=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdots$, Euler was intrigued by this property and sought to extend it to $n=2,3,4,\ldots$. This study investigates the delay enhancement of a traditional delay-coherent detector when applied to delay-coherent differential detection. It demonstrates that, unlike delay-coherent detection, differential detection renders the detector linear and time variant. Furthermore, it shows that the traditional detector achieves delay enhancement by exploiting the inherent memory of differential detection and suggests an alternative detector that improves performance over the traditional one. Finally, the study confirms these results through simulations based on representative examples. Notably, the findings indicate that, unlike conventional delay-coherent detection, differential detection enables the input to the delay adder to be real-valued, facilitating a straightforward implementation of delay enhancement. Consequently, this results in both enhanced performance and reduced complexity for the delay adder. Additionally, the proposed alternative detector surpasses the traditional detector, particularly in low signal-to-noise ratio conditions. Overall, the paper demonstrates that, through suitable design, differential detection can achieve delay enhancement more effectively than traditional CPM with non-coherent detection. This capability not only improves performance but also enhances spectral efficiency by allowing for a more compact spectral design. Keywords: Continuous Phase Modulation, Differential Detection, Delay Coherent Detection, Delay Coherence, Delay Coherent Detection.

Reward learning seeks efficient approaches for automatically designing rewards, yet it faces significant hurdles, including high-dimensional policy spaces, suboptimal random rewards, and the difficulty of obtaining sufficient expert data. To address these issues, recent research has shifted toward aggregating partially labeled state-action pairs through ranking. However, existing methods often neglect environmental dynamics, rely on computationally expensive off-policy algorithms, and struggle with data scarcity. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes visually assisted reward learning by introducing VACRE: Visually Assisted Cluster Ranking via Expert comparisons. VACRE first partitions state-action pairs into clusters based on environmental dynamics, then identifies preferred clusters using expert labeling. These comparisons enable the rapid and accurate aggregation of human preferences, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Furthermore, VACRE effectively manages fully or partially observable environments, ensuring stable and robust learning. We evaluated VACRE across various expert data scenarios using a broad suite of benchmark tasks. The results demonstrate that VACRE achieves superior sample efficiency and significant reductions in training time, with an average time savings of 40% on linear-quadratic regulator tasks. Additionally, an ablation study confirms that the visual aggregation component is essential for achieving these advantages. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/kuangyuan/VACRE. By promoting more efficient and accessible reward learning, this work aims to facilitate the broader adoption of reinforcement learning in real-world applications. Our accompanying video offers an in-depth analysis of the proposed methods. Finally, the expert comparison datasets utilized in this work are available at https://github.com/kuangyuan/VACRE_experts. Specifically, the VACRE_Ecpts dataset contains comparisons of state-action pairs across 11 tasks from 11 domains, while VACRE_Openspace provides comparisons for 20 Openspace tasks. Furthermore, VACRE_Openspace offers an option for fully labeled data to support the evaluation of comparison-free methods. We anticipate these datasets will assist researchers in developing effective and efficient reward learning techniques. We also acknowledge the substantial effort required to construct these datasets and encourage interested parties to contact us for access. Finally, our demonstration video offers a more detailed overview of the datasets and evaluation code. We hope these resources will be beneficial to the community. The demonstration can be viewed here: https://youtu.be/4Yq14444444. The datasets are located at: https://github.com/kuangyuan/VACRE_experts. (Version 1.0)

Our findings indicate that these matrix elements remain dependent on the noncommutative parameter even at second order, at least for the quark distribution function. Consequently, this indicates that the symmetry arguments previously used to argue the irrelevance of second-order terms do not hold in our framework. Finally, we present predictions for the quark vector and space-like baryon magnetic form factors, which can be experimentally tested. These results align with the observation that the nucleon's magnetic moment exceeds that of any of its constituent quarks. Furthermore, our computed distribution functions satisfy all relevant experimental constraints, including those derived from the spin-dependent structure function $g_1$. This paper investigates large-scale pre-training for conversational understanding, focusing on the challenges of conversational contexts where utterances possess distinct meanings and rely heavily on prior dialogue history. We observe that standard language models, such as BERT, are ill-suited for these tasks because they are trained on monologic, written text and fail to capture the interactive dynamics inherent in conversations. To address this, we introduce CONVEML, a dataset comprising over 100 million utterances from chat rooms and social media platforms, complete with utterance-level interpretations. This dataset enables the training of CONVEML-EM, a transformer-based model designed for continuous interpretation of utterances within conversational exchanges. We evaluate this approach using two tasks: conversation interpretation and factoid question answering. Our results demonstrate that CONVEML-EM significantly outperforms BERT-based baselines, achieving an accuracy improvement of 11.5% on conversation interpretation and 7.4% on question answering. Although algorithmic interpretability is essential for machine learning (ML) success, there remains no consensus on how to measure it. This paper presents a framework for evaluating algorithmic interpretability based on the core principle of human learning: the cognitive complexity required to understand an ML model's decision-making process. Within this framework, we propose the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS), which quantifies this requirement. The theoretical foundation for CCS draws from the classical concept of state machines and their order, as well as the hypothesis testing framework. To illustrate the framework's utility, we detail two state machine models that correspond to the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) and the Generalized Post Correspondence Problem (GPCP). Furthermore, we introduce the Algorithmic Complexity Score (ACS), another metric for measuring interpretability derived from this same framework. The CCS and ACS serve as practical tools for assessing the interpretability of ML models. By demonstrating how to construct state machines from ML models, we calculate their respective CCS and ACS values, thereby providing a practical method for interpretation. These findings offer actionable tools for interpreting ML models, helping to address the current lack of consensus on how to do so effectively. Unsupervised anomaly detection is unsupervised machine learning designed to identify outliers without prior knowledge. Isolation Forest (iF) is a widely adopted anomaly detection method that excels in large-scale environments by isolating anomalous data points. However, in tiny machine learning (tinyML) contexts where training data is scarce and computational resources are limited, iF often struggles due to the need for extensive feature engineering and the high training costs associated with processing massive datasets. To overcome these challenges, we introduce TiWS-iForest, an optimized anomaly detection algorithm tailored for tinyML scenarios. TiWS-iForest merges the strengths of iF with the parameter-efficient, data-hungry anomaly detection technique TiWS. Its primary objective is to enhance iF's performance by reducing the volume of training and testing features, thereby enabling deployment on small hardware devices. Experimental results using the CIFAR dataset demonstrate that TiWS-iForest reduces computational complexity by 99.9% and memory usage by 99.99% compared to the baseline iF, while maintaining comparable accuracy. Furthermore, TiWS-iForest successfully detects anomalies on CIFAR data with only 10 training images per class, achieving results similar to those obtained with 64 training images per class. This research investigates a specific bi-parameter Poisson process distribution designed to model extreme values. A primary advantage of this distribution is that its cumulative distribution function relies on only two parameters, facilitating straightforward fitting. The study addresses two key areas: first, it establishes sufficient and necessary conditions for validity, ensuring the distribution remains well-defined for all real numbers; second, within a Bayesian context, it develops estimation methods for the unknown parameters, including self-consistent estimators and fully Bayesian confidence intervals. To address potential challenges in estimating the tail index, a reparametrization is introduced that approaches zero rather than positive values. Finally, the paper proposes a new transformation that ensures bounded support, which is particularly effective for data representing physical quantities. Throughout, estimation and inference are applied to both transformed and original scales to derive confidence intervals for the quantile function. The Bayesian estimators are shown to be consistent, and their asymptotic normality is demonstrated. This method is validated as a reliable approach for practical data fitting through a series of real-world case studies. Additionally, a simulation study is conducted to verify the accuracy of the derived confidence intervals. From a theoretical perspective, the fully Bayesian confidence intervals are proven to be asymptotically correct with a non-vacuous convergence rate. Overall, this work demonstrates the versatility and robustness of the bi-parameter Poisson process distribution in modeling extreme phenomena. Notably, the distribution is unimodal, exhibiting a peak at zero and increasing monotonically for positive data. Furthermore, it successfully captures the distinct behaviors characteristic of extreme phenomena within a single distribution. By adopting a non-regular framework, the study avoids the need for separate analysis for bounded and unbounded domains. The paper includes detailed technical proofs for all theoretical assertions. From a practical standpoint, a fully Bayesian approach is advocated for this distribution, with fully Bayesian confidence intervals recommended for practical applications. Moreover, the fully Bayesian approach circumvents difficulties in determining the tail behavior at large $x$. **Context.** Globular clusters (GCs) serve as valuable laboratories for studying low-metallicity stellar populations, with NGC 2808 being a prime example due to its well-defined blue horizontal branch (BHB) and the recent confirmation of dual horizontal branch (B) populations.

**Aims.** This study aims to determine the ages and chemical compositions of NGC 2808's main sub-populations.

**Methods.** We conducted a comprehensive analysis of 100 BHB stars, measuring equivalent widths of 13 spectral lines to derive abundances of Fe, O, Na, Al, and Mg. Additionally, we utilized color-magnitude diagram (CMD) analysis to constrain the abundance of C.

**Results.** Our findings reveal two distinct groups within the BHB:
1. **Blue Group:** Characterized by low metallicity ([Fe/H] = -1.91 ± 0.05), high sodium ([Na/Fe] = 0.40 ± 0.10), and low aluminum ([Al/Fe] = -1.10 ± 0.10).
2. **Red Group:** Marked by higher metallicity ([Fe/H] = -1.55 ± 0.05), lower sodium ([Na//Fe] = -0.20 ± 0.10), and higher aluminum ([Al/Fe] = -0.60 ± 0.10).

**Conclusions.** The differences in chemical abundances between these two groups, alongside the previously established spread in horizontal branch colors, provide strong evidence for multiple populations within the GC. Furthermore, the derived ages of 11.8+1.5-1.1 Gyr and 12.0+1.3-0.7 Gyr for the blue and red groups, respectively, suggest that NGC 2808 formed through a multi-stage process. This is further supported by the detection of a third sub-population in the CMD, which aligns with recent dynamical studies indicating that BHB stars in the blue horizontal branch sequence possess distinct dynamical properties. Finally, we propose that the observed composition spread in NGC 2808 may be a result of mergers between stars of different compositions. The implications of these findings are discussed.

The intensity of intergalactic Lyman-$\alpha$ emission, generated by star-forming galaxies and driven by neutral hydrogen, creates a strong Lyman limit flux discontinuity. This phenomenon causes Earth's atmosphere to become highly opaque to Lyman limit ultraviolet (UV) radiation, necessitating observations from space. However, space telescopes face significant challenges, including high costs, limited availability, and the inability to adapt to changing observing conditions. Consequently, ground-based space-UV observations are restricted to brief windows during astronomical twilight, when residual Lyman-$\alpha$ emission is sufficiently suppressed to facilitate the study of intergalactic medium properties and high-redshift galaxies. This article introduces the design of the Lyman-alpha Screen (LAS) prototype, a device intended to block interstellar Lyman-$\alpha$ emission, thereby enabling ground-based UV astronomy during twilight. The proposed prototype will be deployed at the El Leoncito High-Atmosphere Observatory (OEA-LE) in Argentina's Atacama Desert. We demonstrate that utilizing the LAS prototype at OEA-LE can achieve ground-based UV astronomy during twilight with photometric quality comparable to that of current space-based observatories. Additionally, we examine the advantages of conducting observations from the ground, such as cost-effectiveness and the flexibility to adjust to varying conditions. Finally, we evaluate the optical and atmospheric transmission characteristics of the LAS prototype and the OEA-LE site. Our analysis indicates that the LAS prototype combined with the OEA-LE observatory can achieve space-quality photometry approximately 10 hours daily, roughly 4 months per year, representing a three-fold increase in observing time relative to existing space UV telescopes. We conclude by discussing potential applications of the LAS prototype and the OEA-LE site for high-quality UV astronomy during twilight. The LAS prototype is currently being developed for deployment at OEA-LE. Future research will address optical modeling, systemization, and the construction of UV photometric filters. This study focuses specifically on the optical modeling of the LAS prototype. The results presented here are preliminary; further analysis is required to account for atmospheric transmission and sky background effects. Ultimately, our analysis confirms the viability of achieving space-quality UV astronomy from the ground during twilight, provided the Lyman-$\alpha$ emission screen is successfully implemented. Achieving UV astronomy from the ground during twilight could revolutionize the field, fundamentally altering the approach to UV astronomy and its future trajectory. Such a breakthrough could also influence the development of future UV astronomical facilities, whether space- or ground

This paper investigates the distributed generation of graph symmetric transformations within communication graphs equipped with directed communication links. We assume that each node possesses a directed communication link to its right-hand neighbors and possesses knowledge of the graph's symmetries. The primary objective is for all nodes to converge to a common value through a distributed algorithm. First, we address networks featuring directed rings of neighbors, demonstrating the ideal (exact) achievement of graph symmetry using a node-centric algorithm. Subsequently, we extend these findings to more intricate network topologies. Our approach relies on a novel resource termed "graph devices," which encapsulate the collective information of the network's directed graph symmetries. We prove the existence of these graph devices under specific assumptions about the input network's directed symmetries and design a distributed algorithm to compute them. Finally, we show that all nodes can exactly simulate these graph devices using the proposed node-centric algorithm, thereby precisely achieving the desired goal. Our results hold for both infinite and finite networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate ideal achievement in finite networks by adapting existing synchronous algorithms; specifically, we highlight that our work generalizes the well-known average consensus algorithm for networks with directed connected graphs. For infinite networks, we prove convergence under mild assumptions. In this context, we extend our results beyond average consensus to the broader scenario of distributed distribution, wherein a node distributes its local value to the entire network based on the network's symmetries. This research paves the way for the distributed management of communication networks, a field that has garnered significant interest in recent years.

Image Catalogs are collections of images tagged with metadata. While traditional catalogs rely on static annotations, modern approaches leverage deep learning to enable image tagging as a predictive task. Existing methods typically depend on carefully curated, high-quality annotations to train robust cataloging models, yet obtaining these annotations is often expensive and time-intensive. This paper addresses the image tagging problem within the Quadruped dataset using a dynamic cataloging framework. We demonstrate the application of active learning and transfer learning techniques to dynamically expand the cataloging catalog. Specifically, we employ active learning to selectively sample and annotate a subset of images, utilizing these new annotations to refine the cataloging model. Furthermore, we investigate transfer learning strategies to enhance cataloging performance by adapting pre-trained models across different subsets of the Quadruped dataset. Our results demonstrate that dynamic cataloging effectively improves both the accuracy and efficiency of image tagging. Additionally, we analyze the impact of active learning and transfer learning on cataloging performance across various experimental configurations. Finally, we examine how the initial catalog influences performance and explore potential strategies for initial catalog construction to further optimize cataloging accuracy. The keyless communication framework eliminates the necessity for a shared key between the transmitter and receiver, substituting it with a common noise realization drawn from a established distribution. This structure is notably advantageous for physical layer security (PLS) applications because extracting noise from the channel is inherently more robust than extracting keys from communication channels. Among various schemes, keyless verification stands out as it allows the noise realization to function as a network code, thereby enhancing security for single-antenna systems. This paper investigates the optimal keyless verification strategy within an AWGN channel affected by an active eavesdropper. To address this, we introduce an optimization problem that maximizes the eavesdropper's mutual information. Subsequently, we derive an iterative algorithm capable of solving this problem. Our numerical findings demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms the optimal traditional key-based approach. Additionally, we prove that the developed algorithm converges to a stationary point. Finally, to improve the algorithm's efficiency, we propose two variants, which are evaluated in terms of runtime. Furthermore, our results indicate that these algorithm variants achieve the same stationary point as the original formulation. Ultimately, for both single and multiple antenna configurations, the proposed keyless verification approach yields superior security performance compared to traditional key-based methods. In the single antenna scenario, we observe that with a fixed eavesdropper power, reducing the number of iterations leads to a significant decrease in the eavesdropper's achieved rate. However, in the multiple antenna case, the algorithm requires more iterations to converge, yet it still outperforms traditional key-based techniques. These outcomes highlight the versatility of keyless communication frameworks and their potential to advance communication security. Additionally, we demonstrate the benefits of keyless communication in a wireless-powered network where an active eavesdropper attempts to intercept transmitted messages. For this specific application, traditional key-based communication fails to offer any security advantage. We evaluate the performance of two keyless communication approaches—traditional keyless communication and keyless verification—using a proposed algorithm variant. Our results confirm that the keyless verification approach provides greater security against eavesdropping than the traditional key-based method. Moreover, the proposed keyless verification scheme outperforms traditional keyless communication when the eavesdropper's power is low. Conversely, at higher eavesdropper powers, traditional keyless communication exhibits a slight security advantage. These findings underscore the benefits of keyless communication frameworks in enhancing communication security. Ultimately, the research demonstrates the efficacy of keyless communication in mitigating eavesdropping risks.

The problem of a particle rolling without friction on a dispersion-covered wavy surface, governed by a periodic washboard potential, is formulated as an ordinary differential equation. By applying general theorems and making specific estimates, we analyze the dynamics of rolling and jumping within the system, identifying the two integrals of motion that define particle state spaces. We also present numerical simulations of state trajectories and phase transitions. Given that the differential equation includes a term raised to a fractional power, we first establish mathematical properties of the potential, including its curvature, and discuss the implications of this specific form for particle dynamics on the surface. Additionally, we explore the connection between rolling and sliding surface processes, as well as their link to surface roughness and surface energy. We present a new framework for estimating impulse response functions (IRFs) using local projections, designed to enhance accuracy and minimize the burden of hyperparameter selection. This approach combines multiple impulse estimates into a single response estimate through an optimal linear combination, where weights are selected to simultaneously minimize the estimated multivariate mean squared error (MSE) of the impulse response and its associated forecast error. Unlike previous adaptive methods, our proposed criterion explicitly accounts for the forecast error of multiple variables simultaneously and directly addresses the trade-off between impulse estimate precision and bias. We demonstrate that adaptive estimation yields tighter confidence intervals and superior overall performance compared to naive methods. Furthermore, we introduce a data-driven technique for determining the number of impulse points to aggregate in high-dimensional settings, effectively balancing the benefits of adaptation against the costs of increased variance due to overfitting. Finally, we apply this adaptive IRF estimator to analyze how monetary and fiscal policy shocks influence the US economy during the COVID-19 pandemic. The results indicate that both monetary and fiscal policies have significant effects on the economy, that these effects are relatively stable over time, and that the economy exhibits asymmetry in how it responds to expansionary versus contractionary shocks. These findings align with existing literature regarding monetary policy but present new insights concerning fiscal policy. Additionally, we observe that responses to monetary and fiscal shocks are asymmetric across different types of economic variables. Specifically, we find evidence supporting the existence of a "fiscal dominance" regime, characterized by: (i) fiscal stimulus having a more pronounced impact on output and inflation than monetary stimulus; (ii) asymmetric responses to monetary and fiscal expansion; (iii) reduced inter-variability during expansionary shocks; and (iv) decreased co-movement between output and inflation during expansionary shocks. These results align with theories of zero lower bound (ZLB) and inaction traps. However, these effects are not observed during contractionary shocks, suggesting that the asymmetry in responses is primarily driven by the presence of zero lower bounds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within our framework, all these results can be derived from a single, unified model. Finally, we release an R-package implementing this local projection-based adaptive IRF estimator alongside a demonstration dataset. This dataset allows users to replicate our empirical analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic and explore additional applications of adaptive impulse estimation. Empirical results confirm that our framework delivers performance gains over traditional methods. Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a critical Natural Language Processing task that identifies entities within sentences and determines their types. The combination of text and sentence-level embeddings has proven highly effective for this task. However, text embeddings within hyperbolic space offer a distinct advantage by incorporating distance information, a feature absent in other embedding spaces. This study explores the application of hyperbolic embeddings for NER. To manage the scarcity of labeled data, we employed a self-supervised learning approach utilizing a transformer model trained on both labeled and unlabeled datasets. The resulting model was fine-tuned for detailed NER using specific loss functions designed for hyperbolic spaces. Evaluated on two German sentence-level datasets, our experimental results demonstrate that hyperbolic embeddings significantly enhance NER performance. Furthermore, we utilized visualizations within hyperbolic space to reveal the model's acquisition of entity-related knowledge through self-supervised pre-training. Given that our proposed self-supervised training method is independent of the specific embedding space, it holds potential for future research. Additionally, we have open-sourced our code and models to assist researchers in advancing hyperbolic deep learning research. The widespread adoption of cloud computing has enabled the mass production of results across various scientific and educational fields. Virtual machines, hosted on physically distinct servers within a cloud environment, are typically allocated using specialized tools. However, these tools often fail to account for the computational capabilities of the underlying physical machines, leading to uneven result distribution. To address this, we have developed and evaluated a new load-balancing strategy called Prepartition. We conducted six experiments, comparing Prepartition's result distribution to that of a baseline method. The study involved tasks ranging from small to large datasets, with VMs and physical machines scaled accordingly. We tested two task types: one simple and parallelizable, and another more complex that is not fully parallelizable. The findings demonstrate that Prepartition significantly enhances load balancing, reducing the time required to complete tasks and ensuring that performance is not limited by specific VMs or their host physical machines. Overall, Prepartition outperforms the baseline in both result distribution and completion time. These results indicate that the proposed load-distribution method is highly effective for use in cloud environments. This work was supported by the Russian Science Foundation (Grant 18-11-00001). Our source code can be found at: https://github.com/avd2000/prepartition. Dynamic models are essential for predicting future market outcomes, such as equilibria, in fields ranging from energy to telecommunications. These models typically comprise a system of nonlinear algebraic equations where variables represent future market states and parameters reflect current conditions. However, the high dimensionality of both variables and parameters, combined with the nonlinearity of the equations, makes finding accurate solutions difficult, especially when observation data is scarce. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the Fixed Point Network (FiNet), a type of Residual Solving Network (RSN) designed to learn the solution operator for dynamic model equations. Unlike traditional methods, FiNet simultaneously optimizes the model's parameters, initial guesses, and relaxation parameters alongside the learning of the solution operator. We establish the conditions under which FiNet is well-posed and provide both theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrating its ability to accurately forecast equilibria for the Cournot and Bertrand games. Furthermore, we extend FiNet to enhance robustness against noisy data and FiNet Variational Autoencoders (FiNet VAEs) to improve solution quality when observation data is limited. Experimental results confirm that FiNet and FiNet VAEs achieve accurate forecasts even with noisy data or restricted data, offering a significant advantage over baseline approaches. Additionally, FiNet VAEs offer the novel capability of learning latent nonlinear models even when only linear ones are observable. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/epiclab/epic-dynamics. This work serves as an introduction to our epic-R package, which integrates Model-Based Machine Learning techniques. This paradigm shifts the focus from learning operators from data to learning operators that map from data to models. We demonstrate that FiNet and FiNet VAEs excel at solving and predicting the dynamics of both linear and nonlinear models, even when those models are partially unknown. This represents a significant advancement over conventional machine learning methods that primarily rely on data-driven approaches. Ultimately, this framework enables the integration of rich domain knowledge into machine learning models, thereby enhancing their generalizability and robustness. This introduces a new category of knowledge-driven models grounded in the principles of Model-Based Machine Learning. These fields are explored within our epic-R package, which is the outcome of the epic group's research. The package also demonstrates the high generalizability of our approach, as it has been successfully applied to solve nonlinear inverse problems in energy, telecommunications, and chemical engineering. Furthermore, the package illustrates the effectiveness of model-based machine learning in variational deep learning, a strategy that has yielded substantial benefits for imaging

This study presents observation-based statistical inference techniques for estimating causal impact limits within high-dimensional contexts. The first approach derives bounds on causal attribution across generalized mutual information (GMI) [1], adapting recent information-theoretic limits regarding causal discovery and inference. The second approach employs a Bayesian framework to calculate the probability of causal attribution, extending these bounds into a multi-dimensional framework capable of handling effect sizes in independent, non-identically distributed random variables. We validate the method using synthetic data and demonstrate its application to causal inference challenges in large genomics datasets. Ultimately, this work introduces a multi-dimensional extension to causal attribution bounds that facilitates high-dimensional causal inference through statistically rigorous accuracy estimates. The method is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/alexmccullough/causal_bounds.

This study introduces a method for building an effective predictive surveillance system for linear time-invariant systems subjected to covert attacks. The attack detection framework combines a linear filter with a nonlinear filter. The linear filter functions as a standard predictive surveillance system, whereas the nonlinear filter is designed to detect attacks targeting the system parameterized by the filter's state. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed approach can identify attacks that linear-only systems miss. Additionally, the convergence of the prediction error covariance matrix and the asymptotic behavior of the surveillance system are analyzed. These findings indicate that the proposed systems achieve convergence and maintain a constant, positive definite error covariance matrix. Furthermore, it is shown that the detection performance of both the linear filter and the proposed hybrid method remains robust against model mismatch. Finally, the application of these predictive surveillance systems to detect attacks in a power grid simulation is presented. Power flow equations are solved using the Matpower package, with attack detection evaluated based on the distance between estimated states and the known nominal system. Results confirm that the surveillance systems can detect attacks in the transmission network, including both partial and complete outages of transmission lines. Notably, the linear filter successfully identifies attacks on individual lines, while the nonlinear filter is capable of detecting attacks on multiple lines. Overall, the predictive surveillance systems developed in this work offer the advantage of providing an early warning for attacks, enabling timely responses and mitigating damage. Furthermore, the computational cost of the proposed predictive surveillance approach is relatively low. Specifically, the linear filter requires $O(n^2)$ operations, where $n$ is the state dimension, and the nonlinear filter requires $O(n^3)$ operations. In contrast, standard Kalman filtering-based surveillance systems require $O(n^3)$ operations. Given that the state dimension of the power grid in our simulations is approximately 100, the computational burden of the proposed predictive surveillance system is considered negligible. Finally, the predictive surveillance systems are shown to be robust to noise. However, it is important to note that the predictive surveillance approach is not suitable for detecting attacks on a very large number of lines, as this may lead to a high false alarm rate. Therefore, a decision-making mechanism is required to determine an appropriate threshold for the surveillance system. The predictive surveillance systems developed in this work hold the potential to serve as a foundational component for future research in advanced surveillance and decision-making frameworks. Additionally, the predictive surveillance approach can be extended to nonlinear systems. Document summarization focuses on creating concise abstracts for text collections. While most existing research targets English, there is significant scarcity in developing multilingual summarization systems for Indian languages. This paper introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised model designed for language-specific document summarization across Indian tongues. The system begins by pre-training a graph auto-encoder (GAE) using language-independent document texts to generate latent vectors for language-specific vocabularies. Subsequently, these vectors are fine-tuned to produce language-specific scores for individual words. Summarization is then executed by constructing a word-level graph from these scores and identifying the most representative word communities through community detection algorithms to select the summary words. To ensure the selected words form coherent sentences, we introduce an entropy-based cost function that guides the shuffling of communities into the original sequence. We evaluate the model's efficacy through experiments across six Indian languages, demonstrating its success in summarization. Furthermore, we expand the dataset with additional texts to test robustness. The results confirm that our approach effectively achieves language-specific document summarization for Indian languages, surpassing baseline methods. The code and data associated with this project can be accessed at: https://github.com/Ankit-1234/GAE-ISumm.

This paper introduces the concept of S-rings of Noether type and establishes several characterizations for them. Additionally, we demonstrate a series of fundamental properties of these S-rings, which enable the transformation of certain "wild" covering problems—specifically those involving Galois covering groups of type $A$—into "tame" ones. Furthermore, we derive a generalization of Ito-Schmidt's theorem regarding the transitivity degree of permutation groups and offer a characterization for an S-ring $\mathcal{S}$ within a finite group $G$ where $\mathcal{S}$ constitutes a maximal Noether type S-ring in $G$. The discussion begins with basic definitions and properties of S-rings and covering groups, followed by an exploration of S-ring chains in Galois covering groups of type $A$. The text also examines transitivity degrees in S-rings, maximal S-rins of the Noether type, and Noether-type S-ring chains. The study concludes with an analysis of the relationship between transitivity degrees and S-rings of the Noether type. Ultimately, the paper presents a comprehensive characterization of Galois covering groups of type $A$ utilizing covering groups of type $S_n$, alongside a detailed examination of type $A$ covering groups for specific groups of Lie type. Finally, the authors aim to extend this characterization to general linear groups over finite fields in their subsequent publication. This study investigates hidden companions influencing the motion of five nearby stars with accelerating space-based data from Gaia DR2. By utilizing the parallax-centred mean position of each star, we model their observed motions as a superposition of astrometric wobble, constant velocity, constant acceleration, and a Reimers' perturbation caused by the gravitation of unseen companions. The model yields unique solutions for up to two companions per star, providing estimates for each companion's total mass, orbital distance, and distance relative to the line of sight. Results indicate that four of the five analyzed stars possess unseen companions with combined total masses of 1.02±0.04 and 0.90±0.04 solar masses, distances of 1.70±0.08 and 1.40±0.07 AU, and distances of 0.89±0.04 and 0.77±0.03 AU along the line of sight, respectively. For HD 142904, the model identifies two companions with a combined mass of 1.01±0.04, but the model-fitting process reveals that one companion is likely a spurious solution. The identified companions are predominantly low-mass M dwarfs, and their orbits are generally tight, suggesting they may be brown dwarfs. These findings offer potential explanations for the accelerating motions of the five target stars. Additionally, we introduce a Python package named `compfit`, which implements the presented model and automatically calculates the model-to-data fit quality. This tool is applicable to any dataset exhibiting accelerating motion. Finally, we demonstrate that the model can be extended to incorporate light pollution from a luminous unseen companion, allowing for the estimation of its absolute distance within the plane of the sky. This extension is particularly relevant for stars showing apsidelution, which may indicate the presence of a single, massive unseen companion. These results highlight the utility of accelerating datasets for detecting very low-mass companions with orbital periods under 100 years. The presented model offers a promising alternative to astrometric binary solutions for a subset of sources displaying strongly non-symmetric wobbles. Furthermore, it can be adapted to account for other non-linear motions, such as those resulting from tides, mass loss, or radiation pressure. A detailed examination of these effects will be the focus of future research. The five target stars are HD 142904, HD 1698

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are extensively utilized for dimensionality reduction and feature extraction. To further refine the learned features, we introduce a constrained VAE with minimum square (CVAE) that incorporates a prior on feature dimensions. Specifically, the proposed method employs an asymmetric Laplacian prior to enforce dimensionality reduction, resulting in more effective features. Convergence tests and statistical comparisons (involving t-tests and F-tests) on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that CVAE outperforms standard VAE and PCA in terms of reconstruction quality and feature significance. Furthermore, CVAE achieves superior results compared to PCA and limited PCA (l-PCA) when evaluated under cross-validation across various classification algorithms. Finally, the method's effectiveness is illustrated through its application in reconstructing and extracting features from high-dimensional single-cell RNA sequencing data for cancer classification. The associated Python code can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmedfalahi/CVAE.

This paper explores private Blockchain technology for home appliance monitoring, targeting security-conscious users who prefer not to have their data stored on public networks. We outline the system architecture and demonstrate that, given current hardware capabilities, the network can support up to 175,000 home appliances. Furthermore, we detail an Intelligent Appliances Tracker (IAT) system that leverages Blockchain to create a secure framework for home appliance tracking, utilizing a Ray Tracing (RT) simulation to model 5G network performance. This RT simulation effectively serves as a positioning system, providing precise location data for each appliance within the home. The paper also examines security and privacy challenges associated with private Blockchain, proposing countermeasures to mitigate threats such as DDoS attacks. Ultimately, the study argues that private Blockchain offers a viable solution for secure home appliance tracking, with the RT simulation showing high potential for accurate localization in this context. Additionally, the RT simulation can be executed on both smart home devices and home appliances, further enhancing the reliability of the appliance tracker. The paper concludes with an analysis of the proposed system's security and privacy mechanisms. Specifically, the RT simulation achieves an 80% localization error rate, while the IAT employs SHA256 hashing for data integrity, Ring Signatures for privacy, and Naive Bayes classification to detect malicious nodes. Additionally, to address double-spending issues, the system proposes a new consensus mechanism called the Naive Bayes Voting (NAV) algorithm. Finally, the study identifies potential future research directions, including the application of RT simulations in both indoor and outdoor environments. Overall, this work highlights the promise of private Blockchain in home appliance tracking and successfully validates the feasibility of the RT simulation approach for localization within this framework. The proposed IAT system represents a significant advancement in home appliance tracking technology. Additionally, to address privacy concerns, the paper introduces a new algorithm named the Smart Home Distributed Algorithm (SHDA), which functions as a privacy-preserving method to detect malicious nodes in a distributed environment. This algorithm employs smart home devices as sensors to gather information about malicious nodes. Simulation results indicate that the proposed algorithm achieves a 90% detection rate for malicious nodes. ShDA operates with low computational complexity, making it highly efficient for home appliance tracking. Ultimately, the proposed IAT system holds great potential to revolutionize the field of home appliance tracking technology. The algorithm's ability to detect 90% of malicious nodes ensures a secure environment for users, while its low complexity ensures efficient and reliable data management within the system.

The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm is a fundamental instrument in modern error correction, widely utilized in contemporary communication systems. However, its computational demands are high, making it impractical for deployment on energy-constrained devices. A viable solution involves substituting it with a lighter alternative, such as the L-value algorithm, which serves as a soft decision decoder for CRC-based error correction when paired with a syndrome-based erasure strategy. This paper introduces a novel method to enhance the efficiency of the L-value algorithm by employing deep learning to dynamically adjust its complexity. Our results indicate that this adaptive approach can reduce power consumption by up to 40% while maintaining equivalent or superior decoding performance compared to the traditional L-value algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this deep learning-driven quantization method can be implemented in hardware with minimal learning overhead. These findings confirm the practical application of our method, which is particularly beneficial for resource-limited systems, including those utilizing software-defined radio. The corresponding code and hardware models are available at \url{https://github.com/DeepSenseLab/DeepSense_Lvalue}. Notably, this work was partially presented at the Design Automation Conference 2022. Our contributions are part of the first open-source repository dedicated to DeepSense algorithms, which are energy-efficient deep learning techniques specifically designed for edge-of-network applications. This repository, which includes comprehensive hardware models for FPGA and ASIC synthesis, is the foundational element of the DeepSense project, an Aalto University research initiative funded by the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program (Grant Agreement No. 871425). The project's outcomes are detailed in the recently published book, *DeepSense: Energy-Efficient Deep Learning for the Edge-of-the-Network*, released by Springer. This study examines the problem of Uppward Planarity Deletion, which involves identifying a deletion set for an undirected acyclic graph with designated source and sink vertices to ensure the remaining subgraph admits an upward planar drawing. While parameterized complexity has been explored for various graph problems, the question of whether this approach applies to upward planarity deletion remains unresolved. We address this by presenting a parameterized algorithm with runtime $O((3.828)^k \cdot n)$, where $k$ represents the deletion set size. Our method relies on a dynamic programming algorithm that achieves exponential-time performance on graphs with bounded treewidth and is supplemented by an embedding lemma. These findings are derived from an algorithmic extension of a graph modification problem, which interests us independently. The research is supported by the first author's grant from the Czech Science Foundation (19-02931S). Furthermore, we establish bounds on the upward planarity of digraphs based on their number of sources, sinks, and vertices, demonstrating that the upward planarity deletion problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the difference between this count and five. The outcome is $O(4^k \cdot n^2)$. The study concludes with several complexity results, including fixed-parameter intractability for specific deletion set parameters and fixed-parameter cruder algorithms for parameterizations by number of edges, sources, sinks, and nodes. Finally, the paper ends with a fixed-parameter algorithm for identifying irreducible digraphs, a class characterized by the property that all acyclic superdigraphs are upward planar. This is achieved via a dynamic programming algorithm that determines upward planarity in $O(2^k \cdot n)$ time. Our findings expand the set of known irreducible digraphs and provide an efficient fixed-parameter algorithm for verifying if a digraph belongs to this class. Strategies designed to mitigate noisy, crowdsourced data remain scarce within algorithmic trading, despite the significant financial losses caused by such errors. This paper introduces a method that leverages the uncertainty metrics inherent in ensemble models, including maximum entropy and minimum $\lambda$-divergence, to address noise in crowdsourced information flows. These metrics are integrated into an algorithm called the Uncertainty-Adjusted Consensus Tracker (UACT), which utilizes decision thresholds to filter out noisy data points. By employing an entropy-based significance test, the study assesses whether a signal is significant enough to generate trading opportunities. The research demonstrates that UACT outperforms both the standard Consensus Tracker and traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) in classification accuracy. Furthermore, in an algorithmic trading context, UACT achieves superior risk-adjusted returns compared to the standard Consensus Tracker while simultaneously reducing transaction costs. These outcomes stem from the narrower trading bands produced by UACT, which result from more precise probability estimates and lead to fewer, yet higher-quality, trades. Ultimately, the study finds that the proposed method is effective for crowdsourced data and offers a promising avenue for noisy data compression, thereby enhancing the reliability of algorithmic trading signals. Finally, future research will explore the application of these uncertainty metrics to other domains, such as image recognition and natural language processing. This research investigates semigroups derived from transfer operators linked to semiflows on compact manifolds. Our primary focus is on estimating the norm of these operators. We demonstrate that the norm decreases at an exponential rate within local charts of the manifold, adhering to a Lipschitz condition, and polynomially from within the manifold. Additionally, we establish a upper bound for the Hausdorff dimension of the fixed point sets of these semigroups. As a consequence, we deduce that the spectrum of the transfer operator semigroup is compact and derive a bound for the growth of its trace. Finally, we explore applications of semigroups formed by transfer operators for semiflows exhibiting hyperbolic recurrence on the manifold. Notably, we derive an upper bound for the Bowen-Lin spectrum and prove the existence of a Markov partition and a countable Markov spectrum for semiflows that possess a dense set of periodic points. Furthermore, the methods employed in this study enable the derivation of an upper bound for the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius spectrum of semiflows on the sphere that admit a transitive periodic orbit. In this work, we examine the transfer operator for the geodesic flow on a compact hyperbolic surface, as well as for semiflows on the sphere that include real quadratic vector fields, the Hamiltonian vector field associated with the z-component of angular momentum, and the gradient flow of the z-component of angular momentum. The methodologies utilized can also be applied to analyze the transfer operator for the geodesic flow on a compact locally symmetric space of rank at least 2, a system previously addressed by S. Klimek and A. Ziemian. Their approach yields an upper bound for the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius spectrum of this geodesic flow, a result that also holds for the semiflows discussed in this paper. Our findings regarding the norm of the transfer operator and the dimension of its fixed point sets are applicable to the transfer operator defined in their work. Additionally, we offer a distinct derivation of the upper bound for the Hausdorff dimension of the closure of periodic orbits for hyperbolic semiflows on the sphere, an result established by J. L. Rodriguez and A. Ziemian.

Strength-$2$ covering arrays are designed to ensure that every possible pair of symbols appears a minimum number of times across all combination tests, thereby optimizing resource usage in tasks like software parameter testing. However, as the array dimensions expand, constructing these arrays becomes increasingly difficult. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new class of covering arrays termed "tiny strength-$2$ covering arrays" (tsCCAs), which are non-square arrays square-bracketed at specific sizes. By developing a construction method based on orthogonal arrays and employing an inflation technique, we successfully generated tsCCAs ranging from 3 to 7 rows. Additionally, we revised the definitions of certain parameters, leading to the discovery of 12 new tsCCAs with bracketed sizes of 8 or 9. Furthermore, recursive constructions were employed to create 15 new tsCCAs with bracketed sizes of 10, 11, or 12. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive framework for tsCCA constructions that fills 27 of the 36 remaining gaps in the open problems table for these sizes. Notably, the largest tsCCA identified in this study has sizes of 7 rows and 13 columns, demonstrating that tsCCAs can achieve high column sizes relative to their small row counts. To the best of our knowledge, this research represents the first exploration of tsCCAs. Our results are available at http://la.utexas.edu/users/fhwa/CCAs/tsCCA.html. Finally, the accompanying code is released under the MIT license. Keywords: Covering arrays, Software parameter testing, Orthogonal arrays, Defining levels.

We demonstrate that the well-established instability of local contests remains valid even when participants possess nonlocal strategies derived from maximally correlated states with noise. Specifically, in the standard public goods game context, noise is sufficient to render all nonlocal strategies incoherent. Consequently, the dynamics of resolvable contests, as previously shown, apply to all noisy implementations of maximally correlated states, implying that all such games are locally equivalent. This conclusion stands in direct contrast to the striking finding by Yu et al. that certain implementations of the GHZ game are nonresolvable. We clarify the origin of this surprising result by highlighting its deep connection to nonlocality as measured by PR-box correlations. Furthermore, we introduce a specific modification to the GHZ game that eliminates this nonlocal component, thereby proving its resolvability. Finally, we examine the application of these results to a simplified model of evolutionary biology. In this model, a population consisting of individuals capable of both local and nonlocal strategies evolves toward a state where only nonlocal strategies survive, resulting in a final population exhibiting nonlocal correlations. This outcome sharply contradicts established expectations, where noise typically diminishes or eliminates nonlocality. Our findings offer significant insights for both game theory and biology, suggesting that the emergence of nonlocality may be more probable than previously believed. Supporting this view, recent experimental data from a local game indicate a surprising prevalence of nonlocal strategies, while our own results from a simplified biological model suggest that nonlocal strategies can be advantageous. These insights may pave the way for new avenues of research in both fields. To facilitate this, we have made our code available online. Automated failure replication serves as a valuable technique for establishing ground truth in hardware testing. The research behind the original paper, titled "Genetic Algorithm Based Automatic Failure Injection and Fault Localization for Black Box Hardware Hardware Test," aimed to develop, assess, and assess a directed automatic failure replication method. This process involves creating a test failure scenario, submitting it to hardware, and attempting to reproduce it. The goal was to minimize operator involvement, specifically reducing the time and effort required to analyze failures. The study examined three primary strategies for this method: state-based, test-based, and coverage-guided testing. To address this, the authors implemented and partially replicate a directed genetic algorithm, having already published their findings under the title "A New Approach to Automatic Failure Injection and Fault Localization Using Directed Genetic Algorithm." This automatic failure replication through directed testing seeks to determine if specific test failures can be consistently reproduced on various devices. By employing directed testing, failure patterns can be more reliably induced, potentially reducing the time and effort needed to capture hardware failures. Furthermore, local search and fault localization techniques are utilized to achieve failure reproduction with fewer test vectors. The authors have also released source code for their work, titled "GDGTFL," which includes a fault model, directed testing, local search, and fault localization capabilities. The following sections detail the research questions, methodology, outcomes, and conclusions of this partial replication. The vortex lattice represents a fundamental characteristic of type-II superconductors, yet its microscopic structure remains unclear due to conflicting experimental findings. This study presents neutron scattering data from a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate that clearly indicates a square-square transition in the vortex grid. This observation resolves previous controversies and demonstrates that vortex-vortex interactions can shift from repulsive to attractive, a phenomenon previously observed in underdoped YBCO vortex lines. These results imply that vortex-vortex interactions in cuprates are mediated by an anisotropic electromagnetic field. Furthermore, these interactions are governed by the pairing gap anisotropy and the electromagnetic field generated by circulating supercurrents, offering compelling evidence regarding the nature of pairing in these materials. Finally, our findings regarding vortex line rigidity align with theoretical predictions for a $d$-wave pairing symmetry. In a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate, the transition between vortex vortex rings is driven by anisotropic electromagnetic forces, confirming the existence of vortex grid transitions in these materials. Directional flow in nuclear collisions at various centralities offers a method to investigate the physical characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). While hadronic viscous pressure contributes to this flow, its impact on anisotropic flow observables is minimal. Conversely, thermal photons, which originate mainly from the QGP, exhibit corrections due to shear viscosity that alter their transverse momentum distribution and directional flow. By analyzing the directional flow of thermal photons across different centralities, researchers can determine plasma parameters, including shear viscosity, through a comparison with Monte-Carlo-Event-Generator-LEB-Plasma (MEG-LEP) simulation results. This approach highlights the potential of thermal photon data as a tool for measuring QGP properties, particularly shear viscosity. Furthermore, incorporating thermal photon signatures from both viscous and inviscid simulations into the publicly available THERMINAR framework could facilitate a more direct extraction of plasma properties from experimental data. A public dataset is available at \url{https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/11421244122222222222222222222222}. We present an analytical framework for investigating magnetic configurations in triangular and kagome lattices featuring short-range isotropic interactions and single-ion anisotropies. This method utilizes a mapping to a lattice spin model to determine the most probable magnetic structures. Our findings reveal various characteristic arrangements, predominantly of type-A and type-C. Notably, we observe multiple first-order transitions between these structures and points where first and second-order transitions coincide. Furthermore, we map the transition landscape between the highest entropy magnetic configurations on kagome lattices, tracing paths through diverse phases and identifying points of order discontinuity on phase boundaries. This research offers analytical and semi-analytical continuations to recent numerical studies on this topic [Phys. Rev. B 104, 094417 (2021)]. We anticipate that the developed approach will prove beneficial for investigating other frustrated systems. Finally, we propose that the method's utility can be expanded to include long-range interactions and interactions with conduction electrons. This capability is particularly relevant for analyzing materials with partially filled bands, where electron-electron interactions and spin fluctuations significantly influence the ground state. Specifically, this would enable the investigation into the stability of electron-spin density waves and magnetic structures with non-zero electron spin moments. This capability is especially pertinent to kagome metals, where such phenomena are currently under active study. This work serves as a foundation for future investigations into this critical issue. To facilitate such studies, we have provided a Python script implementing the mapping and solution procedures, which is available at \url{https://github.com/romanov-alexey/Magnetic-structures-on-kagome-lattices}. Additionally, we plan to extend the approach by incorporating quantum effects and applying it to the type-C state, which remains unexplored. This extension will be addressed in a follow-up paper. The source code for these extensions is also included in the repository at \url{https://github.com/romanov-alexey/Magnetic-structures-on-kagome-lattices}. We conclude that the current code, despite its limitations, is sufficient to explore the entropy landscape on kagome lattices, as demonstrated in the referenced study. This enables the identification of promising candidates for magnetic structures with non-zero electron spins and the investigation into the stability of magnetic structures with type-I and type-II symmetries. New drugs and materials are frequently evaluated through extensive experimental campaigns involving hundreds of related samples, such as those arising in combined toxicological and environmental stressor studies. Traditional statistical approaches, which rely on univariate or bivariate techniques, often lack the sensitivity required to detect subtle effects within these complex settings. Although some research has addressed this by constructing joint confidence regions, they typically assume sample independence. This study introduces an algorithm designed to identify dependent samples exhibiting similar intervention impacts while controlling the false discovery rate at a predefined level. Through rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive numerical experiments, we demonstrate the method's effectiveness and practical utility. Furthermore, the approach is applied to dependent drug-induced liver toxicity (DILT) data, successfully uncovering previously unidentified mechanistic similarities. The method is implemented in an open-source R package, DRiDLE, which is available at \url{https://github.com/Chenchen-chen/DRiDLE}. Additionally, all data and analysis scripts are publicly accessible via GitHub at \url{https://github.com/Chenchen-chen/DRiDLE}. The underlying code was developed during the author's PhD research at Carnegie Mellon University. The supervisor for this work, Dr. Chenyang Liu, holds a position at Carnegie Mellon University; his contributions are detailed in the reference: Chenyang Liu, \textit{Statistical inference for high-dimensional data with applications to drug toxicity data}, PhD thesis, 2020. Although he was no longer affiliated with the university at the time of software release, his contributions remain relevant. His contact information is \textit{chenyangl@andrew.cmu.edu}. The current software version has not been jointly reviewed or released with his, which is available at \url{https://github.com/Liu-Chenyang/DRiDLE}. The fundamental issue in the study of inflation remains the mechanism driving its occurrence. This paper examines whether a simple inwards expansion of a sphere can account for the cosmic expansion of space, specifically addressing whether cosmic inflation can be simulated through external inflation models driven by gravity and momentum. The research concludes that inflation models based on gravity and momentum are not required to explain the universe's expansion, as their essential characteristics—such as the singularity problem, the horizon problem, the flatness problem, and the illusion of randomness—all stem from the external inflation model. Additionally, Section 2 provides a brief explanation of the first law of thermodynamics by analyzing the inwards expansion of a spring, which serves as the foundation for the logic presented in this paper. In the future, I intend to develop a more comprehensive explanation of inflation using a step-by-step approach, as this current presentation is limited to a basic overview. This study examines the type-X two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) as a mechanism for addressing the muon $(g-2)_\mu$ and $W$ mass anomalies. By performing a detailed analysis of 2HDM parameter space, we identify regions where both experimental puzzles can be simultaneously resolved. Furthermore, we assess the model's predictions regarding the 2-loop contributions to the muon anomalous magnetic moment, future precision measurements of the $W$ boson mass, and the Higgs mass. Our findings indicate that the type-X 2HDM offers a viable explanation for the $(2\sigma)$ muon $(g-2)$ result, while also making testable predictions at future colliders. Specifically, we demonstrate that the LHC can exclude certain parts of the parameter space responsible for solving the $(g-2)_\mu$ riddle, whereas the ILC and FCC-ee have the potential to probe the regions that could also address the $W$ mass discrepancy. Finally, we note that within these parameter regions, Higgs boson measurements at the LHC and FCC-ee may reveal significant new physics effects. This would manifest as deviations from the Standard Model in $hZZ$ and $h\gamma\gamma$ couplings, specifically a factor of approximately 2.5 for $h\gamma\gamma$, which would consequently impact future searches for CP violation. Additionally, we have included a list of relevant references and cited papers. Our results suggest that upcoming experiments will be able to test the type-X 2HDM solution to the $(g-2)_\mu$ problem and will also evaluate the possibility of solving the $W$ mass problem within the same framework. We have also considered the effects of a future more precise measurement of $h\gamma\gamma$ by the HL-LHC. Finally, we have included some relevant plots illustrating the effects of additional new physics contributions in the type-X 2HDM. These findings may assist future searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model. In conclusion, our results may help explain the $(g-2)_\mu$ and $W$ mass problems within the type-X 2HDM framework and provide a new perspective for investigating the Higgs boson. We have also presented some relevant plots to explore the parameter space that could solve both of these problems. In recent years, there has been a growing trend of positioning products through online community platforms. This study investigates methods for automatically reformulating product positioner inquiries to enhance matching precision. Our approach leverages crowdsourced data, including product details and reviews, to generate semantically equivalent queries that preserve the original meaning. Our method relies on an automatic process and avoids human intervention. We developed QUICKAR, a system that automatically bridges query and product term gaps using domain-specific knowledge extracted from crowdsourced information. Evaluation on the GITE product positioner dataset, which spans multiple product categories, demonstrates that our method outperforms the baseline in both precision and recall. The source code for QUICKAR will be made available on GitHub. This system is intended for research and educational purposes. Given that product positioners are not search engines, the QUICKAR system is not available to the public. This paper investigates strategies for enhancing the Deep Entrainment Network (DEN), a neural architecture designed to forecast the distance between two consecutive mention of a discourse connective. While DEN demonstrates promising initial results, its authors acknowledge several model limitations that hinder performance. This study examines multiple techniques to mitigate these issues, with a specific focus on increasing the diversity of training data. By leveraging large-scale social media datasets, we trained a network that learns entrainment distance in an unmonitored context and achieves a significant performance gain. Additionally, we evaluate several alternative models and data preprocessing methods, providing a clear assessment of their impact on entrainment distance prediction. Our findings indicate that expanding the vocabulary used to describe entrainment distance yields a more than 10% improvement in F-measure across all connectives. Furthermore, we propose a new classification approach for predicting entrainment distance based on the relationship between the current utterance and its surrounding context. This method utilizes the representation of the immediate preceding utterance and delivers results comparable to those of DEN. Overall, these results provide valuable insights for future research in the field.

Temporal action division for action recognition has recently become a focal point of research. While many approaches rely on action dictionaries learned from annotated data, we introduce an alternative method that divides videos into action units without requiring such labels. Our strategy involves: 1) coarsely segmenting videos into self-supervised co-occurring activity (SSCA) clips based on semantic boundaries, and 2) within each SSCCA clip, unsupervisedly parsing temporal action segments using internal correlation features. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of both mean average precision (MAP) and clustering performance, particularly on challenging datasets. Furthermore, our division results are more interpretable to humans, and our model is the first to separate within-clip actions while maintaining clustering accuracy on external validation datasets. Finally, we propose a temporal action recognition model without pre-training that outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is available at https://github.com/Chongchou/SSCAP. Source code and methods are invited to TACL. Please contact us at ccwu@cs.ubc.ca. The paper is also available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01000.
