This study examines the concealed-charm pentaquark states $Z_c^-(3900)$ and $Z_{c s}^-(4600)$ recently identified by LHCb, analyzing both their formation and breakdown using the present algebra. To represent the pentaquark content of $Z_c^-$, the configuration $[p \otimes [n \otimes (\chi_s \otimes \chi_l)]]$ is proposed, whereas the $Z_{c s}^-$ state, which includes strange quarks, is described by the configuration $[p \otimes [n \otimes (\chi_s \otimes \chi_l)]]$. Both configurations feature a charmed-$\chi_s$ quark paired with a charmed-$\chi_l$ quark. The $Z_c^-$ state is predicted to exist within the isospin $I=0$ multiplet at $1^-$, while the $Z_{c s}^-$ state is anticipated in the spin $s=1/2$ doublet at $1^-$, corresponding to isospin $I=0$ and strange quantum number $S=-1$. Furthermore, the study investigates a possible link between these states and the decay process $J/\psi p$, which is also analyzed using the present algebra. The results indicate that the $Z_c^-$ state arises from this decay, whereas the $Z_{c s}^-$ state does not. This finding aligns with experimental observations, confirming that the $Z_{c s}^-$ state is absent in the $J/\psi \Lambda$ decay channel. Additionally, the $Z_{c s}^-$ state is predicted to exist within the $s-d$ hyperon doublet, a region previously unexplored in theoretical investigations of conscious-charm pentaquark states. Finally, the $Z_{c s}^-$ state is expected to appear in the $J/\psi \Lambda$ decay channel, a prediction awaiting experimental verification. Overall, the present algebra proves to be an effective tool for the theoretical analysis of pentaquark states. This approach offers a promising framework for uncovering new pentaquark states and clarifying the structural properties of those already discovered. The findings of this work are expected to be of significant interest to experimental physicists. Software testing education remains a critical component within computer science curricula. This testing training typically occurs within programming education and project-based learning environments, where students acquire testing knowledge through problem-solving. However, as software engineering is a highly technical discipline, students often struggle to grasp complex theoretical concepts, particularly regarding testing techniques. Consequently, the effectiveness of traditional detailed feedback systems, which are labor-intensive and time-consuming for educators, becomes a bottleneck. This paper introduces the Inquiry-Based Conceptual Feedback (IBCB) system, which allows students to request corrections for their answers by prompting them with specific testing concepts. Through an experiment comparing the BCB system against the traditional approach, we evaluated student engagement, performance, and satisfaction. The findings indicate that the BCB system significantly enhances software testing education effectiveness. The study also offers conceptual insights into the BCB system's effectiveness, which may assist researchers in designing more effective software testing education programs. Finally, the paper presents lessons learned from this empirical research. The completed study is available at: http://www.ibcb.system/ (accessed 10/10/2021). Keywords: Software Testing Education, Feedback Systems, Conceptual Feedback, Programming Education, Project-Based Education.

To mitigate performance loss caused by domain shift, many adjustment techniques rely on a substantial dataset of samples labeled with historical performance, a requirement that limits their applicability. This study introduces an approach to adapt these methods for a source-free, semi-supervised setting that requires no such historical data. The proposed solution, called $\delta$-Transformation, is a theory-based framework that abstracts and integrates existing techniques through a generalized $\delta$-transformation of input data. This input transformation is designed to minimize theory-based input features, which the authors define as data aspects essential for model performance. The work begins by categorizing current techniques into four types based on their underlying theories, then offers a theory-driven classification of inputs into four corresponding categories. Through a rigorous examination of various techniques and input types, the paper establishes guidelines for selecting theories to adjust for domain shift. Furthermore, it provides an a priori method for identifying whether a theory can help or harm performance in a given setting. Finally, input features are analyzed using an information-theoretic perspective, with distributions compared via divergence metrics. Ultimately, $\delta$-Transformation offers a source-free, theory-based framework for domain adjustment that is independent of training data. Empirical evaluations on three benchmarks, including ImageNet, demonstrate that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average gain of 1.6% across 27 experiments. Additionally, an ablation study on 14 experiments reveals that all individual theories contribute a priori to performance improvement, with an average gain of 1.1% across 12 experiments. Finally, a case study on object recognition explores how $\delta$-Transformation identifies theories and their effects, while also highlighting the challenges of theory-based domain adjustment. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffler1992/semi-supervised-theory-transfer. The bibliography can be found at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/341911012_Semi-Supervised_Theory_Transfer_for_Source-Free_Domain_Adjustment. This paper provides a concise overview of utilizing gas-core nuclear reactors for deep space propulsion, primarily targeting an audience with a scientific background but limited exposure to nuclear engineering. The discussion begins by defining the fundamental principles of gas-core reactors, followed by an analysis of their application as a fission rocket propulsion system. Key parameters are examined, with a specific focus on the material properties of the liquid fuel. The study further introduces the nuclear engineering concepts necessary to establish design criteria for these systems. Finally, the potential benefits of gas-core nuclear reactors as a propulsion method are highlighted. While this paper does not aim to provide exhaustive mathematical derivations, it does offer references for readers seeking further detail. Instead, the primary objective is to outline the essential nuclear engineering concepts that must be mastered to develop such systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of relevant research opportunities. Although written primarily in English, the author acknowledges their native language is German and has made efforts to ensure the text remains accessible. Any remaining errors are the sole responsibility of the author. All corresponding source code is available at: https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder1992/gas-core-reactors. Translations of this work into German can be found at: https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder1992/gas-core-reactors/tree/master/German. The manuscript was prepared using LaTeX, and the numerical examples were computed with Python. The author's native language is German, and any remaining errors are their own responsibility. This study evaluates domain-informed neural architectures, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Tabular Sequential Neural Networks (TSNNs), against standard Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) for the task of interaction localization in astroparticle experiments. Data consisting of signals from digital particle detectors following neutrino-nucleus interactions were synthesized, with network performance assessed using aggregated spatial RMSE metrics derived from validation set predictions. Under realistic conditions, the use of spatial label information in TSNNs enhanced localization accuracy by up to 10% compared to TSNN configurations lacking this capability, while demonstrating superior scalability to larger datasets and reduced computational costs compared to TSNNs and MLPs. Furthermore, TSNN architectures exhibited greater robustness to variations in detector geometry and topology, maintaining or improving localization accuracy across all tested configurations. Consequently, TSNNs emerge as the most effective and efficient tool for particle interaction localization. These findings have significant implications for the design of future digital particle detectors in digital particle physics. Specifically, the enhanced generalization capabilities of TSNNs regarding detector geometry and topology suggest that the optimal strategy for maximizing sensitivity in digital particle detectors is to employ a large number of detectors with a compact spatial arrangement. This approach is particularly relevant for digital particle detectors designed to observe rare events, such as those targeting neutrinoless double beta decay. We also provide open-source code for synthesizing interaction data and localizing particles using MLP, CNN, and TSNN methods. Finally, detailed numerical results regarding the sensitivity of digital particle detectors for neutrinoless double beta decay are presented in a companion paper. (arXiv:2209.01065v2 [astro-ph.HE]) Keywords: Digital particle detectors; particle localization; digital particle physics; machine learning.

Atmospheric spectra serve as critical tools for analyzing exoplanet and brown dwarf environments, yet the data reduction process is often hindered by the absence of accurate molecular absorption cross-sections at the extreme temperatures and pressures found in these systems. To address this, we present EXOPLINES, a comprehensive repository of molecular absorption cross-sections designed specifically for the conditions of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets. This database includes over 1,000 molecules, covering species vital for exoplanet characterization, including common constituents like H$_2$, H$_2$O, CH$_4$, and CO, as well as trace gases such as HCN, CS, and TiO. These cross-sections are derived from multiple sources, including laboratory experiments, the HITRAN database, and theoretical calculations. Access to EXOPLINES is available through the Exoplanets package at https://github.com/brunodelim/vlines. We anticipate that these molecular absorption cross-sections will facilitate the identification of new molecular species in exoplanet atmospheres and aid in constraining the internal structures of brown dwarfs and giant planets. The repository will be updated regularly with fresh contributions. The current collection comprises 1,100 molecules and their associated cross-sections, with this number expected to grow continuously. The package is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0. Users are encouraged to cite our work when utilizing EXOPLINES. Furthermore, the team welcomes contributions of theoretical or experimental cross-sections; please contact the authors at bruno.delim@unige.ch or alexandre.murphy@unige.ch. This paper presents a metatheoretical analysis of grounding, defining it as the process of determining which formulas are meaningful within a specific language. We examine grounding from multiple perspectives, including computational, semantic, and relative to various inference rules. Subsequently, we establish a formal model for this phenomenon and develop a algorithm to implement it, with both the model and algorithm validated through proofs. Additionally, a computational report is provided, detailing experiments conducted on answer set programs across four dimensions: semantics, grounding methods, computers, and inference rules. These experiments aim to answer a specific quantitative question regarding the computational complexity of grounding under different inference rules when using multiple ASP solvers. The study concludes with a discussion on possible future directions. The relative computations of grounding presented in this paper can be found at: https://github.com/ashir2000/ASP-Computational-Complexity-of-Grounding. Furthermore, the source code for the ASP program used is available at: https://github.com/ashir2000/ASP-Computational-Complexity-of-Grounding/tree/master/ASP-Computational-Complexity-of-Grounding. Resource theories provide a framework for analyzing physical systems by quantifying the value and functionality of physical quantities like randomness, asymmetry, and entanglement. While previous research has predominantly concentrated on global quantum resources, establishing principled frameworks for initial principles regarding local and bipartite quantum resources remains a significant challenge. This study addresses that gap by developing such frameworks based on the complete set of Local Operations and Entanglement Assistance (LOEA). Specifically, we derive the monotones for both local quantum discord and correlation from the respective $l$-LOA (l-local operations and alignment) sets. Furthermore, we establish the monotonicity of local quantum discord under local operations, confirming its classification as a genuine quantum correlation. These findings are demonstrated through the analysis of isotropic states and Werner states. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the efficacy and power of the proposed framework. Additionally, the initial principles regarding high-order quantum resources constitute an important direction for future research. Finally, the optimal conversion rates between quantum resources remain a significant issue for the quantum information community. By utilizing the proposed framework, the initial principles governing these conversion rates can be determined. This approach enables the calculation of rates for arbitrary quantum states, thereby generalizing the understanding of initial principles for local quantum resources. We introduce two techniques for directly evaluating data from moments, enabling the analysis of moments with varying orders without retraining, rather than fitting the underlying density. The first approach involves training a neural network to evaluate the product of two moments, while the second trains a separate neural network for each combination of two moments. These methods are instrumental in determining the relative importance of different moments for moment matching. Our approaches are straightforward to implement and can be utilized within any density framework that includes a step matching the 1-dimensional marginal of the target density to training data. We demonstrate that these techniques yield promising qualitative and quantitative results in various density estimation tasks, including matching moments to a training distribution, conditional density estimation, and stochastic factor models. Our code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/taehyung-lee/assessing-data-from-moments}. The accompanying paper is available at arXiv:2101.01003. Additional code and papers related to matching moments are also hosted on \url{https://github.com/taehyung-lee/matching-moments}. Furthermore, details on the methods used to generate data for density estimation can be found in our repository at \url{https://github.com/taehyung-lee/matching-moments/data-generation}. Taehyung Lee's website is located at \url{https://taehyung-lee.github.io/}. Any inquiries should be directed to leetahyung@berkeley.edu.

This study examines inference for non-stationary multidimensional time series within the robust-tailed framework. The model integrates a time-varying location time-series regression model with a time-varying multivariate $t$-distribution. We establish the asymptotic properties of the least squares estimator and the associated estimator for the time-varying $t$-distribution's degrees of freedom. The analysis reveals that the former converges at a rate of $o_p(n^{-1/2})$, while the latter is consistent. Additionally, we demonstrate the asymptotic normality of the estimator for the degrees of freedom and develop an estimator for the asymptotic variance of the regression. These contributions enable the construction of an asymptotic $1-\alpha$ confidence interval, thereby facilitating inference. Simulation results indicate that our approach outperforms existing methods. We apply this methodology to a quarterly US dataset covering the period from 1947 Q1 to 2011 Q4, analyzing two separate cases: an 8-dimensional model and an 80-dimensional model. Furthermore, we introduce a new package designed to estimate this class of time series regression models. The R code required to replicate our simulation results and the empirical application is available on GitHub. This work extends our previous research (Choi et al., 2017), which focused exclusively on static models. Our primary contributions are the extension of robust-tailed time series regression models to time-varying nonlinear frameworks and the provision of rigorous inference tools for these models. The empirical results confirm the efficacy of our proposed framework. We have released the estimation code as the R package \texttt{rtst}, which can be accessed at \url{https://cran.r-project.org/package=rtst}. Post-Landau free quantum error-correcting codes (qECCs) featuring efficient decoders operate by mapping the stabilizer group of a system with n physical qubits onto a combinatorial graph, where decoding corresponds to finding a matching. Recently, 2D planar graphs have been demonstrated to support a family of such codes with linear-time decoders; however, these codes lack effective physical distances. This study expands the analysis to include various 2D codes on other topologies, as well as 3D codes defined on 3D graphs. We establish sufficient conditions for both the code and graph structures required to guarantee an efficient decoder with linear complexity. Specifically, we prove that any 2D code defined on a triangulation graph is effective, provided it meets local geometric constraints, while also addressing several open problems. Furthermore, we develop effective families of 3D post-Landau codes, detailing specific constructions with linear-time decoders and their minimum distances. Additionally, we introduce a method to define effective post-Landau codes using 2D graphs, achieving constant decoding times. Ultimately, these findings facilitate the construction of post-Landau qECCs that combine effective distances with linear-time decoding complexity. Notably, one such code achieves effective distances of 10, 11, and 12, respectively, for the 2D, 2D, and 3D instances analyzed. In 2018, Byers, Gavoille, and Kuhn demonstrated that finding a distance-$r$ dominating set is feasible through a randomized algorithm with high probability on extremely dense graphs, provided $r$ is small relative to the dimension of the Dyer-Frieze-Ganapathy selector subspaces. Subsequently, Ghaffari, Ghodsi, and Kuhn established that this approach fails for graphs with girth 4 when $r=1$. This paper extends those findings by proving that distributed distance-$r$ dominating sets cannot be identified in high-girth graphs if the graphs are sufficiently sparse. Consequently, this result indicates that the framework by Byers, Gavoille, and Kuhn reaches its limits in this context. Additionally, assuming the validity of a specific conjecture, we demonstrate that the lower bound is optimal. Networked systems frequently exhibit high graph sparsity and high girth, a phenomenon that can be linked to Benford's law. This connection underscores the necessity of developing alternative methods to construct distance-$r$ dominating sets for such applications. To address this, we propose a novel construction of these sets that surpasses the lower bounds imposed by Benford's law. Furthermore, utilizing this construction, we derive an explicit bound on the graph density that guarantees the success of the randomized approach by Byers, Gavoille, and Kuhn. Finally, we illustrate the tightness of these bounds through the example of random graphs. Notably, our findings regarding distance-1 dominating sets (independent sets) align with recent research by Ghaffari, Ghodsi, and Kuhn. Our work also introduces a new lower bound on the independence number, which surpasses existing bounds in the context of sparse high-girth graphs. Additionally, we present an explicit construction that validates this lower bound under a single conjecture. This specific conjecture is closely tied to the recent conjecture by Khot, Saket, and Shinnar concerning the independence ratio of high-dimensional expanders. In the broader context of distance-$r$ dominating sets, we refer to them as virtual independent sets. Our results offer a partial answer to a question posed by Ghaffari, Ghodsi, and Kuhn, demonstrating that the relationship between graph density and high girth observed in virtual independent sets also applies to distance-$r$ dominating sets. Specifically, we establish that high girth in distance-$r$ dominating sets necessitates a minimum density. This finding is consistent with the recent observation by Byers

Recent research has established connections between bulk, mass, and boundary parameters that dictate the emergence of boundary states within topological insulators. While the significance of the mass-parameter relationship has been well-documented across various $D$-dimensional topological insulators (where $D$ exceeds 1), the mass-boundary correspondence has received less attention. This study investigates disordered 2D and 1D elevated-order topological insators to explore the mass-boundary correspondence. Through numerical simulations, we observe that the time-reversal invariant elevated-order topological insulator exhibits a degenerate zero-energy localized state at one of its corners, which can be precisely predicted by the mass-parameter's sign. Furthermore, we reveal that the mass-boundary correspondence extends to the disordered variant of this system, demonstrating that the mass-parameter dictates the topological nature of the boundary state. These findings offer a promising avenue for achieving predictable corner-localized states with controllable topological characteristics in actual physical systems. Additionally, our results offer valuable insights for the theoretical study of other physical systems exhibiting elevated-order topological phenomena. Finally, we outline several potential experimental applications of our findings. Notably, the $p$-wave topological superconductor and the Haldane chain—both exemplars of elevated-order topological insulators—can be realized using photonic and cold-atom platforms, respectively. By applying our findings to these systems, we can achieve predictable localized zero-energy modes and tunable topological features, thereby advancing our understanding of the physics underlying these materials. Furthermore, our work paves the way for exploring the mass-boundary correspondence in other experimentally accessible systems, such as $p$-wave topological superconductors and Haldane chains. This could lead to the development of new devices capable of exhibiting elevated-order topological phenomena, thereby deepening our comprehension of the underlying physical mechanisms. Finally, the implications of our findings extend beyond fundamental research, with the potential to enable the creation of next-generation quantum computing devices and other practical applications that rely on the reliable manipulation of boundary states in elevated-order topological insulators. The successful realization of the mass-boundary correspondence in these systems would pave the way for significant technological advancements in the field of topological matter. The significance of our findings lies in their ability to bridge the gap between theoretical and experimental realizations of elevated-order topological insulators, thereby advancing our understanding of the fundamental principles governing these systems and enabling the realization of a wide range of practical applications. This document serves as an experimental review focusing on supersymmetry (SUSY) within the context of the CMS experiment during Run 1 (2010–2012) and the initial LHC Run 2 (2015–2018) searches. It highlights several prominent SUSY models, such as the R-parity conserving Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), RPCT, and R-parity violating (R-parity violating) CMSSM scenarios. The review covers a broad spectrum of final states, including multilepton, multijet, and missing energy signatures. Furthermore, it examines the utilization of advanced CMS detector capabilities, including muon spectrums, trigger systems, tracking, and calorimetry, alongside various analytical techniques like multivariate analysis and machine learning. Finally, the text discusses the current experimental status of these SUSY models and outlines prospects for the CMS experiment's future searches. Keywords: Experimental particle physics, Large Hadron Collider, Supersymmetry. 2015. ACM. 15 pages. 10 figures. 1 table. arXiv:1903.07304 [hep-ex] (2019). DOI 10.1145/3290053.3290054.

We introduce a new neural rendering approach designed for dynamic scenes, specifically focusing on characters animated via neural fields. Unlike conventional neural radiance fields (NeRF) that reconstruct scene geometry from camera views, our method prioritizes character geometry relative to their local coordinate system. To address this, we propose a brightness-based factorization, which separates the character's geometry from its appearance, mapping the former to a brightness field and the latter to reflectance. This decomposition is learned through a view-based training process that combines the brightness field with an appearance map to generate novel views. We demonstrate that integrating the brightness field with neural skeleton-based rendering (nSB) results in superior rendering quality and faster convergence. Furthermore, we show how to factor out motion to generate virtual views of characters, a capability with broad applications. Experimental results indicate that character brightness field neural rendering (cbNeRF) produces high-fidelity renders of characters in various poses, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods. This study presents speckle interferometric data for 100 stars, ranging from magnitude 6.5 to 13.5, observed with the Advanced Optical Telescope's speckle interferometry mode during 2020. The observations were conducted under a new data reduction pipeline, featuring an upgraded camera with an enhanced lens. We report 28 new high-resolution images, 111 new angular separations, 11 new relative positions, 147 new full widths at half maximum (FWHM) measurements, and 1,052 FWHM values previously published in other studies. Notable findings include a binary system with a 0.24" separation for HD 133703, a 0.10" separation for HD 168262, and the first resolved high-order eclipse for HD 188007, detected at 0.02". Additionally, we identified a 0.22" separation in HD 189733 and a 0.15" separation in HD 204932. The 2020 observations also confirmed a 0.12" separation for HD 131596 B, a previously detected binary component, and provided the first resolved image for HD 131596 Bc, with a separation of 0.03". The paper concludes with a discussion of these significant results. The data and findings are accessible at https://www.lpl.utoronto.ca/speckle/. The full collection of 2020 observations will be released in 2021. We build and analyze a family of (holomorphic, two-dimensional, stringy) conformal field theories (CFTs) derived from the compactification of 11D and 2D supergravity. By building on recent findings, we identify their central charges, demonstrating that non-zero values arise from the cosmic Jacobian kinematics and magnetic monopole solutions of supergravity. These "cosmic CFTs" exhibit infinite $SU(2)$ current algebras and their level-1 cousins (current, $N=2$ extended supersymmetric) as sub-theories. Their "stringy" nature is highlighted by their large (and unbounded) coupling constants, a feature linked to the cosmic hue-kinematics duality with kinematic and monopole physics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that cosmic CFTs possess integrability. Their holonomy and magnetic properties mirror those of the 11D superparticle projected onto super-isospin. Consequently, our analysis of cosmic CFTs offers fresh perspectives on the interconnections between information, gravity, and non-trivial CFTs. Specifically, our results suggest that (local) information in 2D CFTs may be encoded in (non-local) gravitational theories. This could shed light on the nature of gravity, as cosmic CFTs are closely tied to a novel momentum-space (kinematic) representation of (linearized) (M- and little) supergravity. In this framework, the integrability of cosmic CFTs corresponds to the integrability of magnetic monopole (and, more broadly, nonlinear) solutions in (linearized) (M- and little) supergravity. Finally, we show that cosmic CFTs provide a concrete example of a holographic duality between (two-dimensional) CFTs and (zero-dimensional) matrix models (which are also quantum mechanical). This duality relates to recent (little) supergravity findings, where field equations can be reformulated as quantum mechanical matrix models. Our results may offer valuable insights into (local) information within both CFTs and matrix models, as well as the relationships between them. (Our findings may also help address the black hole information paradox.) (Our work may also contribute to the ongoing (little) superspace, spinor helicity, and integrability programs.) Solar jets are frequently observed across various wavelengths, though their origins remain debated. This study presents LOFAR observations of a solar jet occurring above a delta sunspot pair (DN12), demonstrating that these structures can be detected in the low corona. The image reveals a well-defined, bright loop originating from the sunspot pair, which emits a collimated, high-speed stream of plasma. The jet's morphology indicates a rapid initial expansion followed by the propagation of a shock wave along the corona. This dynamic behavior is characteristic of jets driven by reconnection at a current sheet, a mechanism that also explains their brief duration and small spatial scale. The initial expansion velocity reaches approximately 300 km s$^{-1}$, while the surge and shock wave travel at roughly 500 km s$^{-1}$. Additionally, the surge is accompanied by a burst of hard X-rays and a flare of M1.5 class. The loop's properties align with standard models of jets driven by reconnection at a current sheet. These findings support the conclusion that LOFAR is capable of detecting jets in the low corona. Furthermore, the ability to observe jet dynamics in this region may enhance our understanding of their nature and provide a new tool for studying the coupling between jets and flares. Finally, the loop's stability suggests that LOFAR can be utilized to study the coronal heating problem. We investigate the general two Higgs doublet model, focusing on the contributions of a light charged Higgs boson to various charged current processes at tree level. By employing a "beyond standard model probability density" approach, we analyze their anomalies. Our study examines the implications for the $g-2$ of muon and electron, $B \to X_s \mu^+\mu^-$, $B \to \pi \nu\bar{\nu}$, $B_c^+ \to J/\psi\, \eta(\eta')$, $B_s^0 \to \gamma e^+ e^-$, $B \to (P') K$, and $R(D^{(\ast)})$. We present exclusion contours in the mass-Yukawa parameter space, demonstrating that the observed deviations cannot be accommodated by the model. Consequently, we establish new lower bounds on the mass of the charged Higgs boson. In our analysis, we treated the datasets as independent and did not incorporate experimental theoretical uncertainties. Furthermore, we did not consider the effects of heavier Higgs bosons ($H^{\pm}, A^0, H^0$), as their contributions are suppressed by powers of $m_W^2/m_{H^{\pm,0}}^2$ relative to the light charged Higgs boson. Our findings indicate that the light charged Higgs boson scenario is disfavored by the data. We also examined the neutral Higgs boson contributions to the electron and muon $g-2$ anomalies. Using data from Belle II, LHCb, and LHC, we derived lower mass bounds for the $H^0$ and $A^0$ bosons, finding that the neutral Higgs contributions do not resolve the $R(D^{(\ast)})$ puzzle. Finally, we conducted a scan over the parameter space to determine if the neutral Higgs contributions can account for the muon $g-2$ anomaly. Based on current data, we determined that neutral Higgs contributions are also disfavored. Our study demonstrates that conducting statistical hypothesis tests on the beyond standard model data is highly effective for probing new physics. We also note that the exclusion contours in the parameter space are sensitive to the chosen data set. This work aims to encourage further studies of these hypotheses in the context of possible new physics. Boson sampling is recognized as the inaugural all-optical model for quantum computation that is resistant to classical simulation. While the sampling distribution adheres to a Gaussian distribution and the eigenvalue distribution of the covariance matrix follows a Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE), the model's internal structure remains incompletely characterized. This study investigates the entanglement structure within the "boson sampling space" by examining von Neumann entropy and negativity as metrics for entanglement. The von Neumann entropy of mode $i$ is calculated using the reduced density matrix of that mode, derived from the density matrix of all modes excluding $i$. To quantify two-mode entanglement, negativity is employed as the specific metric. We demonstrate that the sampling probability $P$ is directly proportional to the product of the von Neumann entropy $S_i$ and the negativity $E_{i,j}$ across every mode pair $(i, j)$. This relationship is expressed as $P \propto \prod_{i=1}^{m} S_i \times \prod_{i=1}^{m}\prod_{j=1}^{m} E_{i, j}$, where $m$ represents the total number of modes. These findings offer a novel perspective on the entanglement structure of boson sampling, underscoring the significance of von Neumann entropy and negativity in both quantum information theory and quantum physics. The code utilized in this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongqiangyuan/Entanglement-in-Boson-Sampling. Additionally, the arXiv version of this paper is expected to include supplementary materials, such as extended data and detailed calculations, alongside the published version. Temporal series data from observational studies in life sciences often exhibit complex patterns that challenge conventional analysis and interpretation. We introduce an operator that decomposes these series into a mixture of interpretable components, each characterized by a brief, high-dimensional pattern alongside an unknown modulation function. Through a monitoring mechanism, we automatically detect the presence of these pattern components within the series. By integrating operator theory with operator learning, we develop ConMO (Conditioned Mixed Operator), a model designed to modulate these brief patterns. This framework enables component-wise series decomposition, facilitating pattern discovery and offering a flexible approach for generating synthetic temporal series. Within a controlled biological system, we apply CONMO to identify previously unknown biological patterns and successfully re-discover pre-specified ones. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these brief patterns can be combined to reconstruct the original series and propose a method for generating synthetic temporal series. Ultimately, this work provides a new framework for analyzing temporal series and deepens our comprehension of the processes driving their evolution. For instance, in a yeast growth study, we identified distinct modulation functions governing cell cycle phases and discovered that certain proteins exhibit activity only during specific phases. Additionally, the method allows for the direct construction of synthetic data, which is particularly valuable for addressing challenges in data scarcity and privacy. To support these capabilities, we have created a synthetic data generator. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/DeepMind/life_sciences_temporal_series. Enhancements to the code regarding the temporal series dataset will be published in an upcoming update. This work presents the findings from the 4th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICML 2016) Workshop: Machine Learning for Embodied AI. The paper addresses a reinforcement learning challenge where an agent, similar to a robot operating in a dark room with minimal sensory input, must rely on a model of the environment's dynamics to forecast future observations. We demonstrate that a recurrent, convolutional agent can effectively learn this dynamics model. The term "concealed," which appears in both the title and abstract, refers to state variables that are invisible to the agent but influence the dynamics; we show that these variables remain hidden until their effects become visible in future observations. Furthermore, we examine how this knowledge can be utilized to enhance learning within the primary task. The final section of the paper addresses "convictions," a concept we propose to describe the agent's confidence in its predictions regarding future observations, derived from an EM algorithm. These convictions prove valuable for training recurrent neural networks on this class of problems. The experimental section reports on an application of our method to a mobile robot tasked with navigating a dark room. Overall, this research demonstrates that recurrent architectures are effective for modeling dynamics in environments with limited perception. Additionally, we show that recurrent models act as a bridge between the dynamics model and the primary task, enabling improvements in performance and exploration. This insight is achieved through an EM algorithm that alternates between training the recurrent network and solving the reinforcement learning problem using the dynamics model. We provide empirical evidence supporting the necessity and utility of the recurrent model as an intermediary between the dynamics model and the primary task. Finally, we illustrate how convictions within the dynamics model can serve as a basis for creating useful features for the reinforcement learning algorithm, thereby improving performance. The dynamic nature of this problem presents significant challenges, as the agent must learn to predict future observations despite the hidden nature of the variables governing those observations. This conveys a sense of "conviction" regarding the agent's beliefs about its future observations. In summary, this paper shows that recurrent architectures are well-suited for learning dynamics models from partial perception, that these architectures serve as a bridge between the dynamics model and the primary task, and that convictions regarding future observations can yield useful features for the reinforcement learning process. The primary objective of human action recognition in videos is to identify and detect actions. While deep learning-based methods, particularly those utilizing region proposals, have achieved state-of-the-art results, they remain dependent on region proposals and struggle to capture contextual information effectively. This paper introduces GCN-SAD, a novel deep learning-based weakly-guided action detection framework that integrates context-aware graph convolutional networks. Specifically, we develop a new action detection algorithm that merges deep learning with weakly-guided context awareness. This approach leverages semantic context derived from high-level semantic segmentation or object detection, eliminating the need for time-consuming action recognition and detection during context extraction. Furthermore, our designed graph convolutional networks facilitate efficient feature aggregation and weakly-guided action detection. Extensive experiments on two video action datasets, MSRCV1.5 and MSRCV1.6, demonstrate that GCN-SAD significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. This paper details the methods, results, and new findings from the 2021 Image Resemblance Challenge. The task involved identifying the two most similar images from each of 2,000 randomly generated sets of three. The competition was won by the deep learning-based method developed by Stanford University, followed by the algorithm created by the University of Oxford, which secured second place. Notably, the University of Oxford's approach is fully rule-based and does not depend on image features. Overall, participants achieved a 60.2% success rate. A subsequent analysis using the feature extractors optimized during the competition revealed that 76.4% of all image pairs in the dataset are correctly classified by at least one participant system. The study also identified the three most similar image categories: food, landscapes, and beaches. Finally, a random sampling of 200 pairs from each category allowed for an examination of how participants utilized semantic information from images to determine similarity. Finally, 10 new image datasets were introduced to explore the extent to which features extracted by participants generalize to unseen data. These datasets are categorized into semantic, structural, and semantic+structural similarity groups. The newly released datasets are available at: https://github.com/DeepLearningAtAtwood/IRC2021-Challenge. At the time of release, the code and extracted features were not optimized for these specific datasets. The findings suggest that participants primarily relied on semantic information, with structural details playing a secondary role. Specifically, structural-based methods performed well on structural similarity datasets but poorly on semantic ones, whereas the reverse was true for semantic methods. Furthermore, deep learning-based methods demonstrated the strongest generalization capabilities. Overall, the results indicate that while the Challenge revealed the methods used by participants to extract features from images, it also exposed the limitations of those methods.

Keywords: image similarity, image features, image representation, rule-based, deep learning.

This chapter examines diffusion processes and semigroups that exhibit non-smooth behavior, metastable dynamics, or microstructured characteristics, focusing on how perturbations influence them. The analysis is confined to a finite time interval, addressing boundary value problems within general domains and the associated evolution equations. The theoretical framework relies on weak solutions, metastable sets, and the convergence of semigroups in the strong operator topology. The chapter begins by establishing a general comparison principle within ordered Banach spaces. It subsequently investigates nonhomogeneous elliptic boundary value problems within Lipschitz domains, demonstrating that specific boundary conditions yield well-posed problems even when principal coefficients vanish within the domain. Following this, the relationship between these boundary-value problems and evolution equations is established, leading to the derivation of strong operator convergence in compact time intervals. The discussion then shifts to locally homogeneous problems where stationary solutions represent narrow bands within metastable sets. This line of inquiry reveals that the long-term asymptotic behavior of perturbed solutions can be represented by the convolution of a kernel with finite support and an invariant measure characteristic of the unperturbed problem. Finally, the analysis turns to problems defined on fractals, where the limit problem is characterized by fractional diffusion. This segment presents findings on the local-in-time behavior of solutions to such problems, specifically regarding the convergence of evolution operators to those of the limit problem. The chapter concludes by reviewing recent advancements concerning the convergence of solutions to a large class of related problems toward those of a simplified problem, a convergence driven by the weak operator topology and fractal dimension. These results are supported by numerical simulations and established within the context of periodic coefficients, finite domains, and nonnegative principal coefficients. Notably, the core results extend to broader settings, encompassing nonperiodic coefficients, negative principal coefficients, and problems with measure data. Furthermore, the methodology remains applicable to a wider class of problems, including those involving singular coefficients. However, extending these findings to problems in unbounded domains would require additional assumptions regarding the asymptotic behavior of solutions. This chapter omits the analysis of such asymptotic properties, as this topic has been thoroughly explored in recent literature, including works by the authors. The final section presents an overview of these findings and their applications. This overview begins by establishing the well-posedness of parabolic problems within ordered Banach spaces and introduces an abstract representation of the associated semigroup. It then demonstrates that the principal coefficients need not be nonnegative and that the diffusion mechanism may operate within the domain's boundary. This study investigates the properties of symmetric nuclear matter under intense magnetic fields using the second-order charge-constrained variational theory combined with the constrained variational theory, referred to as the LOCV approach. Findings indicate that both the magnetic field and the constraint parameter significantly influence nuclear substance characteristics. At low densities, the symmetry energy is minimized when the constraint parameter $c$ is approximately 0.25, and the symmetry energy slope $k_{sym}$ is nearly unaffected by the magnetic field in this regime. However, at high densities, nuclear matter transitions to a polarized state, where $k_{sym}$ becomes sensitive to variations in the magnetic field and the constraint parameter. Furthermore, the magnetic field's influence on the magnetic field energy (MFE) is notably more pronounced than on the Coulomb energy (CE). These results suggest that the magnetic field's effect on nuclear matter features is substantially greater than that of the Coulomb interaction. Additionally, we observed that the magnetic field induces a phase transition, leading to an asymmetric configuration where protons align with the field and neutrons oppose it. Finally, our calculated constraints on the magnetic field's impact on nuclear matter properties align with existing literature findings. Specifically, the magnetic field enhances neutron capture cross-sections, potentially facilitating the creation of r-process elements. Ultimately, this research deepens the understanding of how intense magnetic fields affect nuclear matter properties. To achieve this, we computed the energy, number density, and kinetic energy of symmetric nuclear matter, as well as the magnetic moment, within these extreme conditions. Furthermore, to validate the efficacy of the LOCV approach, we compared magnetic moment calculations with those from the constraint variary theory (CVT) and the constrained variational theory (CFT), which yielded consistent results. This confirms that the LOCV method is a reliable tool for calculating nuclear substance properties at finite densities. Ultimately, the influence of magnetic fields on nuclear matter features is expected to be significant, particularly in high-density environments such as magnetars. Consequently, this work aims to provide insights into the behavior of nuclear matter under such extreme conditions. To achieve this, we calculated the symmetrical nuclear matter energy, symmetrical number density, and magnetic moment using the magnetic field energy, demonstrating that the magnetic field's effect on nuclear matter is greater than that of the Coulomb interaction. These calculations provide valuable insights into nuclear matter properties under extreme conditions, thereby advancing our understanding of the structure and evolution of neutron stars. Federated Learning (FL) has become a widely adopted machine learning paradigm, enabling the training of models across multiple institutions by utilizing their local data. Recent advancements have introduced differential privacy (DP) into FL to safeguard institutional data. However, existing DP-FL methods often demand more communication bandwidth than traditional FL due to the need of multiple communication rounds for guaranteeing privacy assurances. To address this trade-off between communication efficiency and privacy, we propose a principled approach called Confidential & Communication-Efficient Training (DP-REC) tailored for federated education. Our core strategy involves employing a communication-efficient stochastic gradient descent (CGD) algorithm within the FL framework, where models are trained to recognize institutional knowledge and skills. Subsequently, we integrate the confidant mechanism into the FL update process to ensure privacy guarantees while maintaining communication efficiency. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence, utility, and privacy properties of DP-REC, demonstrating that DP-REC can achieve the optimal trade-off between communication efficiency and privacy in federated education. Extensive experiments on real-world educational datasets confirm the effectiveness of DP-REC, showing it surpasses conventional FL methods in terms of both privacy and communication efficiency within a practical setting. Furthermore, DP-REC outperforms state-of-the-art privacy-preserving techniques for FL. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) imaging observations of the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga molecular clouds using the {\it Galaxy Evolution Explorer} (GX-UVW1 and GX-UVW2 filters) to investigate the conditions of young stellar objects (YSOs) in these regions. Our analysis successfully identified 1,001 YSOs in Taurus, 1,100 in Perseus, and 1,000 in Auriga. By examining the color-color diagrams, we observed that Taurus YSOs are predominantly clustered in the blue, while those in Perseus and Auriga are mainly located in the red. Furthermore, FUV colors for Taurus YSOs show a strong correlation with near-infrared (NIR) colors, whereas Perseus and Auriga YSOs follow a different relation. Additionally, we detected a trend where FUV colors become bluer as FUV magnitudes increase across all three clouds. These findings suggest that Taurus YSOs possess fewer dust grains and accrete more efficiently than their counterparts in Perseus and Auriga. We also identified a trend where FUV luminosity increases with mass for all YSOs, though the relationship varies between clouds. Finally, GX-UVW1 - GX-UVW2 colors for Taurus YSOs correlate with FUV luminosity, a relation that is weaker in Perseus and Auriga. These results indicate that Taurus YSOs are less dusty and have more direct lines of sight to the FUV-emitting regions. Overall, the data support the conclusion that Taurus YSOs are less dusty than those in the other clouds, a conclusion consistent with previous studies. Ultimately, GX-UVW1 - GX-UVW2 color is proposed as a useful indicator for characterizing the interstellar medium (ISM) in the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga clouds. Modern document retrieval and information retrieval systems are increasingly leveraging deep neural networks, including graph neural networks. This paper explores using such systems to retrieve tables within scientific documents, which are typically not natively suited for graph representations. We propose an effective representation scheme for documents that includes table pages, enabling the application of graph neural networks to retrieval tasks. Scientific articles often contain multiple tables that serve as crucial links between related documents within a field; consequently, we have developed and evaluated the use of graph neural networks for retrieving table pages.

First, we introduce a graph model for document and information retrieval where nodes represent documents and tables, while edges represent relationships between them. We demonstrate that this model significantly outperforms a baseline using link analysis algorithms like HITS and SVD, even when utilizing publicly available training data.

Second, we show that deep neural networks excel at approximating kernel functions for information retrieval, a capability that allows for generalized representation encoding. We extend this approach to representation encoding within graph neural networks, successfully applying it to retrieve table pages in PDF documents.

Our results indicate that combining a well-designed representation model for documents and tables with graph neural networks creates a highly effective system for table retrieval. This approach surpasses document representation models and remains robust against changes in the training dataset. Furthermore, graph neural networks facilitate the integration of textual content from surrounding paragraphs, enhancing retrieval performance by leveraging both the table and its context.

Finally, we conclude that deep neural networks offer promising avenues for developing novel document retrieval and information retrieval retrieval models, including the potential application to table retrieval using text surrounding the tables.

The authors are currently developing a public dataset for training and evaluating document-based table retrieval models, which will be released to support further research and enable fair comparisons of retrieval performance.

Current research into games of incomplete knowledge centers primarily on signaling strategies, largely because existing tools for analyzing these games are insufficient. This short paper advocates for a new approach that expands the analysis of multi-phase incomplete knowledge games to include non-signaling strategies. Our proposed methodology offers methodology for evaluating the value of communication, generating equilibrium payoffs, and investigating the role of cognitive structures. Through two communicationless games that highlight the significance of non-signaling strategies, we demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed framework. These findings suggest the necessity for further research to develop more sophisticated cognitive structures. To facilitate such advancements, we release Com2Phase, a JavaScript library designed to handle games of incomplete knowledge with both cognitive and non-cognitive structures. Com2Phase employs the extensive normal form representation introduced in [1] and includes algorithms for signaling and non-signaling strategies. The library is comprehensive enough to serve as a foundational tool for research in games of incomplete knowledge. Available at https://github.com/brandonr8/com2phase, Com2Phase can be utilized to develop increasingly complex cognitive structures, thereby significantly enhancing communication structures within these games.

Population and health surveys serve as vital instruments for health and development planning. This study evaluates the sustainability of a survey designed to assess health service utilization, reproductive health, and HIV/STI prevalence among women of reproductive age in Maputo City, Mozambique. The research analyzes stakeholder engagement, sampling design, data collection, data analysis, and reporting from the perspectives of local partners, government officials, and the international funding organization. It further examines the trade-offs inherent in balancing sustainability against sample representativeness and dataset depth. By addressing these compromises, the paper offers valuable insights and recommendations for enhancing the sustainability of future population and health surveys. A central recommendation involves adopting a collaborative funding model where resources are shared between government partners and external funding bodies. Such a partnership would foster capacity building, strengthen government systems, and ensure adherence to international standards. Additionally, the study underscores the significance of involving government counterparts from the earliest planning stages through to final data dissemination. To improve sample representativity, adopting a multi-stage sampling design could help overcome limitations in sample size and coverage. Finally, to prevent sample clustering, the use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for field agent navigation is proposed. Finally, to maximize utility for stakeholders, findings indicate a need for expanded analytical coverage and broader data collection to better address local health and development needs. Implementing these recommendations has the potential to significantly increase the value and impact of such surveys. A case study involving the 2019 Integrated Household Survey (IHS) in Maputo City serves to illustrate how these suggestions can be applied. This case study demonstrates the practical challenges faced during planning, data collection, analysis, and reporting, while outlining specific steps taken to address them. The IHS findings reveal a strong commitment to achieving a sustainable population and health survey program in Mozambique. This paper was prepared as an output of the IHS project. Data organization and retrieval are fundamental components of many computer systems. This study addresses efficient exact multi-collection membership inquiry, a task involving multiple collections where users check if specific items belong to any of them. We introduce a novel system that represents each collection using an approximate membership structure featuring no false negatives, thereby ensuring that membership in that collection can be definitively confirmed. Our system utilizes a new data structure called the negative trie, which models the union of several item sets. The trie is constructed by merging the negations of the sets' contents, which are defined as tries representing the items themselves. This design allows for rapid determination of if an item belongs to a collection and the calculation of how many members remain. Experimental results on a 100-node CPU demonstrate that our system outperforms the baseline approach, which treats each collection as a separate set. Specifically, our method reduces both the time required for membership checks and the memory consumption per collection. Furthermore, we extend the system to support parallel membership inquiries. The proposed structure is well-suited for resource-efficient data storage and retrieval applications, such as information security and search engines. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/taiki-y/negative-trie. The paper can also be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01202v2. We investigate spinor particle-molecule transformation via laser-induced three-body recombination in ultracold spin-1 bosonic atoms. The process comprises two sequential steps: first, three spin-1 atoms ($1^1$S) form a molecule in the excited state ($2^1$) via three-body recombination; second, this excited-state molecule transitions into an identical molecule in the ground state through laser-induced radiationless decay. Each spin-1 atomic system is modeled using $(N-2)$-body effective Hamiltonians. To address the particle-to-molecule transformation problem for a system with odd $N$, we employ the $(N-3)$-body and even-$N$ scattering frameworks to construct the three-body and particle-to-molecule transition amplitudes, respectively. The calculated particle-molecule transition probabilities show significant dependence on the initial spin state of the spin-1 atomic system. Notably, a symmetry-based argument indicates that this dependence is particularly pronounced when transitioning from the excited to the ground molecular state. These findings offer a fresh perspective on spinor particle-molecule problems and may facilitate the direct detection of parity-violating effects in three-body systems. Additionally, the proposed formalism could be valuable for studying three-body recombination in ultracold spinor systems. Finally, we outline potential applications of this proposed process in the context of parity violation. **Keywords:** Three-body recombination; Three-body problem; Particle-to-molecule transformation; Spinor systems. This study introduces a framework for the smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method grounded in the ideal multi-scale (IMS) approach, originally developed for continuum mechanics. By utilizing a kernel-based constitutive relation, the model ensures fully explicit numerical stability. The multi-phase fluid-solid interaction (MPFPI) method is derived from this framework and evaluated against existing SPH-based techniques. Through comparisons with multi-block lattice-Boltzmann method results and experimental data, the research demonstrates the versatility and precision of the proposed MPFPI approach, while also addressing key challenges in calculating fluid-structure interactions. Ultimately, the study confirms that SPH serves as a robust tool for simulating complex fluid-structure interactions across both liquid and elastic solid phases. Machine learning serves as the backbone for data analysis, pattern recognition, and optimization. Although quantum-enhanced machine learning is a rapidly expanding field, its practical realization remains hindered by challenges in quantum data encoding and the noise inherent in current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This study presents the first comprehensive experimental evaluation of quantum enhanced learning, specifically unmonitored and monitored classification, across the full stack of quantum algorithms using state-of-the-art superconducting processors. The investigations span the largest scale yet achieved for these experiments, involving up to 61 qubits and 1 million data points on real hardware. The monitorless framework examines angle-based encoding, Pauli fanout state preparation, and mid-circuit measurement, while the monitoring framework adds a layer of quantum error correction via syndrome decoding. Our results indicate a quantum advantage for both approaches, with monitored learning outperforming the best classical baseline by 3.66%. Furthermore, the failure of monitorless methods under significant noise is effectively mitigated by monitoring, demonstrating that mid-circuit errors can be corrected using quantum computers smaller than those required for the algorithms. These findings provide the first empirical evidence for a quantum enhanced learning stack under noise levels relevant to near-term hardware and establish a pathway for future large-scale machine learning applications. We introduce a method for enhancing the pitch manageability of the popular pitch-conditioned text-to-speech system, FastPitch, utilizing a form of timbre-preserving pitch augmentation (TPA). This augmentation generates an auxiliary mel-spectrogram that retains the original speaker's identity and adjusts pitch by shifting all F0 values to a specified target pitch. By training the speaker encoder on both the original and auxiliary mel-spectrograms, we demonstrate that TPA-enhanced FastPitch significantly improves pitch manageability without compromising the TTS system's core capabilities or overall performance. Quantitative evaluations confirm that the timbre-preserving nature of TPA effectively prevents speaker drift. Furthermore, we show that the model can seamlessly utilize the original mel-spectrograms during inference while being trained on these augmented datasets. Although various pitch augmentation techniques exist, this paper demonstrates that a relatively simple yet effective TPA-based approach can substantially boost pitch manageability. Additionally, we observe that a smaller encoder capacity is sufficient for the TPA-enhanced model, resulting in reduced computational costs for both training and inference. These findings indicate that the TPA method is versatile and can be applied across a wide range of speaker encoders. Finally, we make our implementation and experimental code publicly available to foster future research and development in improved pitch manageability. This study introduces Hopper, an efficient Multi-hop Transformer designed for Spatiotemporal Inference that displays superior performance. Hopper executes both Graph Inference and Transformer Attention in an interleaved manner, completing each time step in linear time relative to the number of time steps. The precise measurement of the $W$ boson mass is essential for Standard Model (SM) research and serves as a critical gauge for new physics. This study details the first results from the CMS experiment at the LHC regarding the precise determination of the $W$ boson mass, utilizing $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.8 fb$^{-1}$. The $W$ mass is extracted by fitting the data to simulated events produced in association with bottom quarks ($W\to\ell\ell + b\bar{b}$). The final result, incorporating all systematic uncertainties, is $m_W = 80.25 \pm 0.08$ GeV. This finding aligns with other recent direct measurements of the $W$ mass but deviates from the SM prediction derived from indirect measurements at the precision level of this analysis. The discrepancy suggests a potential new physics contribution that could be interpreted as a charged Higgs boson with a mass of approximately 300 GeV or as the charged component of a two-Higgs doublet model (2HDM) with $\tan\beta \sim 20$. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that the $W\to\ell\ell + b\bar{b}$ channel offers competitive precision for determining the $W$ boson mass. Enhancing the data sample size through the inclusion of additional integrated luminosity from Run 2 and Run 3 of the LHC could lead to even more precise determinations. Consequently, this method represents a promising avenue for future $W$ mass measurements at the LHC. This analysis was conducted by the CMS collaboration. Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as effective solutions for remote coverage across various settings, such as homes, warehouses, and offices. Despite advancements in TPR capabilities and vision systems, significant challenges remain regarding video quality when utilizing lower-resolution cameras. This study presents findings from a subjective user experience study involving 20 participants testing two distinct TPR camera models. The research examined how rendering methods and tracking algorithms influence participants' perceptions. Key findings indicate that larger field-of-view (FoV) adjustments are perceived as less smooth, and that both camera and scene motion negatively impact subjective quality. This work is the first of its kind to assess TPRs through the lens of subjective quality, a critical factor for both end-users and potential adopters. Ultimately, understanding the drivers of perceived quality is essential for developing TPRs that deliver a more satisfying user experience. The experiment's results support several key hypotheses, demonstrating that scene motion has a more pronounced effect on perceived quality than camera motion, and that TPR users are highly sensitive to FoV rendering methods and model tracking. These insights aim to guide future TPR design improvements and help existing users make informed decisions. The study's findings are supported by statistical analysis, including ANOVA and Spearman correlation tests, which confirm the significance of the observed effects. The paper concludes by outlining potential implications for TPR design and suggesting directions for future research. Additionally, the study provides a link to the interactive TPR testing tool used in this research, along with a data repository for the study's results and analysis code. This accessibility aims to facilitate further research into TPR quality of experience. Mafia, or Werewolf, is a widely enjoyed social game of deduction. In the first scenario, citizens and witches oppose a band of murderous Mafia; in the second, players act as wolves hunting villagers, with one of the wolves being a cunning cunning wolf who eliminates other wolves without fear of retribution. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective algorithm to simulate these games. We outline the algorithm and its variations, analyze its behavior, and present simulation results for specific configurations. Our findings indicate that the algorithm accurately mirrors key characteristics of the actual games. Furthermore, we suggest potential avenues for future research, including the statistical properties of the algorithm, the impact of varied player strategies, and the development of optimal strategies for the distinct roles. This could be achieved through computer simulations, statistical modeling, or, in the case of computer-based computer simulations, by applying multi-agent reinforcement learning techniques. This approach has previously been utilized in simulated board games, successfully producing near-optimal strategies for various roles in the game Mafia. Additionally, our previous study demonstrated that the cunning wolf significantly increases the wolves' victory rate, which further supports this claim. The mass distribution of the solar system's giant planets may reflect the physical conditions of the protoplanetary disk during their formation. This study investigates the impact of simultaneous gas accretion by multiple giant planets on their final masses and on the configuration of the disk, specifically focusing on pressure bumps generated at the edges of accretion gaps. We modeled concurrent accretion onto Jupiter and Saturn, assuming their final separation was established during this phase. Our results indicate that concurrent accretion allows the combined mass of Jupiter and Saturn to be lower than a scenario where they formed sequentially. Specifically, if the disks' response to gap formation is included, the mass of the Jupiter-Saturn pair can be reduced by up to 50% compared to a single accretor scenario, while achieving the same growth of the leading planet. Conversely, if the disk's response to gap formation is neglected, the total mass of the two planets increases by approximately 10% in the concurrent accretion scenario relative to the single accretion scenario. These findings highlight the critical role of the pressure bump mechanism in regulating accretion and in shaping the final mass hierarchy of giant planets. Consequently, this process must be accounted for when using these planets as probes to understand the formation and evolution of the solar system. We also outline potential applications of our findings for interpreting the masses of exoplanets in multi-planet systems. Finally, we present the initial outcomes of a similar study concerning the accumulation of Jupiter, Neptune, and Uranus. This work serves as a foundation for future research into the multi-body formation and evolution of giant planets. A paper detailing the evolution of the Uranus-Jupiter-Nepptune system will be published alongside this study. Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are renowned for their exceptional electrical conductivity in the single-nanotube regime, a trait attributed to the high carrier mobility that facilitates efficient sensing. However, the contact resistance inherent to metal-CNT junctions and the scarcity of reliable sources for high-quality CNTs have historically hindered the scalable production of high-performance devices. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have turned to CNT films, which enable conduction through multiple parallel channels. While these films offer lower resistance, they suffer from two significant drawbacks: a substantial proportion of non-conductive or poorly conducting nanotubes, and imperfect network topology due to imperfect contacts. This study presents a design utilizing a specific armchair CNT network, optimized to function primarily through phonon-supported electron-phonon coupling. Our findings indicate that phonon-supported electronic conduction is the dominant mechanism, allowing for the observation of room-temperature electron interference patterns. This evidence stems from measuring phase-dependent coherent transport signatures, such as a splitting conductance peak, in both single and multiple CNT networks. We propose that phonon-supported conduction is viable because CNT networks possess a higher density of states, allowing for stronger coupling with phonons. Consequently, this research opens a pathway to developing high-performance CNT-based sensors and switches by leveraging phonon-supported electronic conduction. This demonstrates that phonon effects are critical in nanotube transport and suggests that phonon engineering could significantly enhance the performance of nanotube-based electronic devices. Ultimately, this work advances the goal of creating highly efficient, low-cost CNT networks capable of detecting minute physical stimuli. Additionally, it offers a new perspective on nanotube conductivity, potentially enabling the engineering of electronic devices with tunable conductivity. By controlling the phonon environment, one can modulate conductivity, thereby constructing analog electronic devices alongside traditional digital ones. This capability to switch between phonon-mediated and electron-mediated conduction marks a significant step toward designing hybrid digital and analog electronic devices. Finally, this work may inspire the design of carbon materials that utilize phonon-supported electronic conduction to achieve tunable conductivity. Such materials could include carbon nanotube fabrics, carbon nanotube aerogels, and other carbon nanostructures. By controlling the phonon environment, the electronic properties of these materials could be precisely tuned. This represents a paradigm shift from the conventional focus on electron mobility to one centered on electron-phonon coupling. This study introduces a novel fuzzy clustering technique designed for high-dimensional data with variable features. In this model, the cluster similarity measure incorporates two dimensions: an object fuzzy partition matrix and a data feature weight matrix. The objective function minimizes the total distance, calculated as the sum of data-cluster distances and the penalized deviation of feature weights from their mean values. To address the issue of uncertain cluster counts in high-dimensional data, we apply the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) to automatically determine the optimal number of clusters. Experimental results from the UCI machine learning repository demonstrate that this model effectively handles high-dimensional data and surpasses the standard FKM algorithm. The proposed model is iterative, with each step updating the data partition matrix and feature weight matrix based on the previous iteration's values until convergence. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits numerical stability in its update steps. Future research will explore extensions to other clustering methods, such as spectral clustering and DBSCAN. Quantum gravity frameworks, such as string theory, predict a black-pivot worldwide symmetry that breaks Lorentz invariance in the UV regime while preserving Poincaré symmetry. Although this pivot can be absorbed into a field redefinition of the field strength as an additional U(1) gauge transformation, its disruption signifies a non-abelian nature of the ultraviolet gauge symmetry. We establish a new constraint on the black-pivot disruption in ultraviolet quantum gravity theories, derived from observational data regarding cosmic birefringence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the disruption mechanism inherent to the black-pivot worldsymmetry stands as the sole method capable of generating birefringence while maintaining Poincaré symmetry. Finally, we establish a numerical limit on the disruption parameter that any specific quantum gravity theory must satisfy. These findings are particularly pertinent to string theory and other low-energy effective models, where the black-pivot symmetry is anticipated. These results underscore the significance of worldwide symmetry disruption as a viable phenomenon for ultraviolet quantum gravity theories, the detection of which would offer valuable insights into their structure. Additionally, we introduce the concept of world-triplet, which transforms under duality transformations of the field strength as multiplications by U(1) transformations for each polarization. This concept is broadly applicable in low-energy effective theories and is expected to be realized in quantum gravity theories beyond those utilizing the black-pivot symmetry. We propose that world-triplet symmetry should be regarded as a necessary symmetry in quantum gravity. Finally, we explore the connection between worldwide symmetries and the oblique parameters of electroweak physics. These symmetries can contribute to the $b$ and $W$ oblique parameters, offering a novel mechanism for violating electroweak precision constraints. This possibility may be investigated by analyzing the disruption of worldwide symmetries through world-birefringence observations. This approach offers a distinct advantage over conventional methods relying on world-birefringence, as it allows for the exploration of purely imaginary pivot parameters, which are otherwise inaccessible. Furthermore, it enables the study of theories with very high pivot scales, as determined by the magnitude of the pole in the field strength's propagation. These findings are especially relevant to string theory and other low-energy effective models, where the black-pivot symmetry is expected. We demonstrate that the disruption of worldwide symmetry can be verified through the violation of the null test of polarization evolution in the CMB.
