This study explores the Accuracy Cosmology Paradigm, a framework that elevates cosmological data to the status of fundamental physical constants. Within this paradigm, the cosmical solution to the strong-CP problem is proposed, which suggests that at least one dimensionless fundamental constant must fluctuate over time. To test this, we examine the gravitational-wave (GW) strain detected by the NANOGrav pulsar timing array, considering the impact of cosmological expansion on the spacetime metric during the early universe. Our model posits that the random tensor field, representing the primordial spectrum of tensor fluctuations, experienced both amplification and remapping in the future due to the strong tensor field. A critical outcome of this remapping is a shift in the horizon scale, a feature observable in the GW spectrum. Consequently, the universe is predicted to be permeated by a "time-slowing" GW backdrop. The frequency of this strain is determined by the current Hubble constant and is independent of local physical phenomena. This represents a departure from the standard stochastic GW spectrum model, which relies on local physical parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectrum of tensor fluctuations, defined at the time of remapping, can be derived from the GW strain, NANOGrav data, and the Hubble parameter. This establishes a new method for investigating high-energy physics, cosmology, and fundamental constant dynamics. Additionally, we show that the tensor spectrum amplitude is linked to the inflation scale, offering a solution to the strong CP problem and a means to address the baryogenesis problem. Finally, we suggest that future observations from LISA and DECIGO will be able to detect this GW backdrop. The tensor spectrum derived from NANOGrav data will serve as an initial condition for these subsequent experiments. This approach offers a solution to the coincidence problem and suggests that we are currently at the edge of a new cosmological era. Notably, the tensor spectrum amplitude is shown to be independent of the reheating temperature. Overall, the findings indicate that the physics of the early universe is more intricate than previously believed. These results provide a foundation for future research into the nature of spacetime, the origin of entropy, and the behavior of fundamental constants. Ultimately, this model aims to unify the Standard Model with General Relativity. The code used in this study is available at: https://github.com/abdolrasoul-karimian/accuracy-cosmology. Keywords: Cosmology, Gravitational Waves, New Physics. PACS: 98.

We introduce findings from an Atacama ALMA Atacama Compact Array survey of comet C/2/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS), revealing that molecular emissions from CS are concentrated along the cometary tail. This marks the first detection of CS in a cometary tail, a molecule previously identified only in the interstellar medium. The image's resolution (0.5 arcsec) is superior to the angular width of the tail, allowing us to model the spatial distribution of CS using a single exponential function. The resulting scale length of 1.2 arcseconds corresponds to approximately 1.2 x 10^13 cm, which is comparable to the radius of the comae observed in H2O and CN. This similarity suggests that CS originates from the direct sublimation of surface ices, rather than forming via gas-phase reactions. Consequently, CS is likely a primary product of CS2 photolysis within the coma, indicating that CS2 must also be directly sublimated from the nucleus. These results support the emerging theory that the molecular inventory of comets was established in their parent molecular clouds prior to ejection. Furthermore, the observed orientation of the tail points toward the center of the Milky Way, a direction previously noted in other cometary tails. This alignment may reflect the underlying structure of molecular clouds, offering evidence for a distributed origin of cometary molecules. Finally, we discuss the scientific value of the ALMA Atacama Compact Array for future investigations of cometary emissions. (The data are accessible at https://www.alma.net/). Addressing the challenge of finding all Pareto optimal points in the decision space for multi-objective mixed integer nonlinear programming (POMIINLP) problems, we propose a branch and bound framework enhanced by the Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). This hybrid algorithm integrates an exact global optimization method with a heuristic global solver to convert continuous POMIINLP problems into discrete Nonlinear Programming (NLP) variants. We employ a specialized tolerance metric to monitor the completeness of the solution space and identify the most constrained nondominated regions. The computational efficiency of the proposed NSGA-II-enhanced branch and bound approach is evaluated through several numerical experiments, including benchmark problems and real-world applications. Results indicate that the algorithm performs effectively on both benchmark instances and practical applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's efficacy in generating a complete and well-distributed set of Pareto optimal solutions. Finally, a comparative analysis is conducted between our proposed algorithm and NSGA-II, confirming the superior performance of the hybrid approach over the standalone heuristic. Additionally, the computational efficiency of this algorithm is compared against other existing approaches, such as branch and bound methods. To our knowledge, this represents the first integration of NSGA-II with a branch and bound algorithm to achieve global optimality. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/AlirezaAghapour/NSGA_II_BnB. Keywords: Pareto Optimality, Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II, Branch and Bound, Global Optimization.

Aspect-emotion analysis demands a deep grasp of human emotions to identify specific emotional tones (positive, negative, or neutral) associated with particular aspects within user feedback. While recent research has focused on modeling fine-grained aspect-dependencies to enhance accuracy, it often overlooks the crucial role of domain-specific domain-adapted hidden emotional contexts. Consequently, models frequently misinterpret emotional contexts, leading to incorrect emotion predictions. To address this, we introduce sentiment-guided contrastive learning to help models learn to distinguish relevant contexts. Specifically, we employ identity, positive, and mutual views to align the aspect-emotion representation space and design a domain-specific loss function tailored to the task. Experimental results on the online retail domain demonstrate that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and performance. Furthermore, we have released a dataset for online retail reviews covering emotions toward aspects and their corresponding contexts, which can be found here: https://github.com/1111111111111/OnlineRetailFeedback. Sampling cases and controls to evaluate disease or failure risk is a common strategy in epidemiological and engineering studies when analyzing large datasets. However, the validity of standard mediation models under case-control designs remains unclear, leading to potentially misleading inferences. This study investigates the impact of case-control sampling on mediation models focusing on a binary outcome and a binary mediator. Through theoretical derivations involving basic matrix algebra, we demonstrate that parameter estimates in case-control designs are nearly identical to those in full cohort designs, provided the cohort is representative. Furthermore, simulations reveal that while point estimates for probability models remain consistent across both sampling methods, variance and type-I error rates differ. These discrepancies arise because probability models in case-control designs predict probabilities relative to their own baseline, which lacks direct interpretability. Consequently, we propose a straightforward modification to the case-control probability model that predicts relative to the global baseline, effectively unifying the frameworks for both sampling types. Finally, we introduce a new tool for practitioners to determine whether case-control sampling significantly affects their specific models and to adjust model predictions accordingly. Overall, this research aims to enhance the utility of mediation models for statisticians, epidemiologists, and engineers working with case-control data. By offering theoretical insights, simulation results, and practical tools, we facilitate more accurate and interpretable conclusions from case-control sampled data. Additionally, we have made our code publicly available to support this initiative. **Keywords:** mediation, case-control, case-case, failure, reliability, case-control with replacement, case-control without replacement, case-control with oversampling, case-control without oversampling, case-control with matching, case-control with matching and stratification, case-control with matching and non-stratification, case-control with matching, stratification, and non-randomization, baseline, theoretical derivation, Monte Carlo simulation, type-I error, Monte Carlo simulation, Monte Carlo simulation, type-I error, type-I error, baseline, baseline, theoretical derivation, Monte Carlo simulation, Monte Carlo simulation, type-I error, type-I error, baseline, baseline, theoretical derivation, Monte Carlo simulation, Monte Carlo simulation, type-I error, type-I error. **Abbreviations:** BC=bootstrap, CC=case-control, CI=confidence interval, MC=Monte Carlo, MC-CC=Monte Carlo case-control. **Acknowledgments:** The authors thank the anonymous reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions. This study investigates the design of resilient transmission strategies for multiuser secure multiuser multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communication networks equipped with reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS). The primary objective is to maximize the secrecy rate of individual users by carefully adjusting the RIS's reflection coefficients. To address this problem efficiently, the authors introduce a novel transformation that converts the originally discrete optimization issue into a continuous one, allowing the use of convex optimization techniques to derive the optimal solution. Simulation results are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The solar wind accelerates from the Sun's surface to supersonic speeds within the heliosphere, a process influenced in solar breeze formation by the Parker spiral's winding, the switchback structure, and Alfvénic fluctuations. This study examines how these factors relate to the wind's energy budget, specifically its Poynting flux, using the first 17 months of data from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP). The analysis covers a radial distance of 13.8–38.2 $R_{\odot}$, where the wind is predominantly solar breeze, and includes both slow and fast wind streams. The work addresses the following questions: (1) How do energy flux and Poynting flux evolve along the wind's path from the solar surface? (2) What is the energy budget of the wind, and is the acceleration driven by thermal or magnetic pressure? (3) What is the timescale for magnetic energy evolution, and is it comparable to the wind's age? (4) What is the magnitude of non-ideal effects in the wind, and are they comparable to the wind's energy flux?

First, the energy flux and Poynting flux at the probe location are found to be similar across both slow and fast wind streams, with magnetic energy density exceeding kinetic energy density. These values are also comparable to the Poynting flux, indicating that the solar breeze is Alfvénic. Second, the energy flux decreases along the path from the solar surface, whereas the Poynting flux remains approximately constant. This behavior suggests that, in the inner heliosphere, solar breeze acceleration is driven by both thermal and magnetic pressure, with the relative contribution varying between events. Third, the timescale for magnetic energy evolution is comparable to the wind's age, implying that the breeze evolves slowly from the corona. Finally, non-ideal effects are observed to be smaller than the wind's energy flux. These findings collectively indicate that the solar breeze is a magnetically dominated fluid, with its primary characteristics established near the solar surface. The slow evolution of the breeze suggests that a corona-based model is necessary to explain its acceleration. Additionally, these results support the hypothesis that switchbacks are generated by Alfvénic turbulence, as they are observed in both slow and fast solar breeze streams. These conclusions are consistent with other recent Parker Solar Probe studies. This work investigates free actions of discrete groups $\Gamma$ on commutative C*-algebras $A$, interpreting the resulting quotient $C*\text{-algebra } B = A^\Gamma$ as encoding a noncommutative countable principal $\Gamma$-bundle. This perspective enables the formulation of a noncommutative version of the classical result linking free $\mathbb{T}$-actions on a manifold $M$ to the cohomology of $M$. We further explore specific cases where $\Gamma$ is a free group and $A$ is a commutative C*-algebra, drawing inspiration from Heisenberg-type bundles and Heisenberg group actions. Furthermore, we present a partial generalization allowing $\Gamma$ to be a discrete group beyond just being free, although this approach loses some desirable properties. Finally, we analyze certain instances featuring free $\Gamma$-actions on noncommutative principal bundles previously studied by the authors. These instances demonstrate that while the Heisenberg bundle framework is not uniquely suited for this investigation, it remains a valuable example for exploring noncommutative fiber bundles. Specifically, this paper offers an alternative to the author's earlier findings by focusing on actions of discrete groups rather than Lie groups. Additionally, the current analysis is not restricted to Heisenberg groups as structure groups, nor does it require the Heisenberg bundle to be quantum. Ultimately, the results presented here complement the author's prior work by providing a different perspective on certain Heisenberg bundles. In both studies, we highlight specific examples that illustrate how this methodology can yield novel insights into existing Heisenberg bundles. The temporal Unruh effect predicts that future and past light cones interact, with entanglement between them increasing in the future's frame of reference. We demonstrate that the Berry phase exhibits sensitivity to this entanglement, offering a method to detect it. Our analysis utilizes the Minkowski coordinate system combined with a particle-wave duality framework, emphasizing that the phase evolves along geodesics. By integrating the phase along the path of a light cone, we identify a singularity at the event horizon, indicating entanglement between the future and past cones. This phenomenon can be quantified through the variation of the Berry phase as one approaches the horizon. Furthermore, the phase divergence aligns with the characteristics of entanglement entropy, which also diverges at the horizon. Consequently, the Berry phase serves as an effective tool for measuring entanglement between future and past light cones, thereby confirming the validity of the temporal Uneffect. Additionally, the Berry phase can be interpreted as the geometric phase of a field between two entangled regions, providing an alternative method to probe this entanglement. Our proposed scheme offers a distinct and effective means to test the temporal Unruh effect. The proposed method is illustrated using the system of a spinor coupled to an electromagnetic field, with applications extending to superconducting qubits and spin qubits. Finally, our approach may contribute to understanding the entanglement structure of spacetime and its relationship to the black hole information paradox. The burgeoning global travel and event industries have made automatic occasion detection a valuable capability for helping consumers and businesses identify events from free text. However, current research is hindered by a scarcity of datasets, as existing ones often fail to address the specific needs of modern travel and business applications. This study introduces MEE, a high-quality, multilingual dataset for occasion detection. The dataset comprises 1,300 English and 1,300 Russian sentences collected from online sources, manually annotated to include mentions of occasions such as holidays, conferences, and business days. We also present a unique annotation scheme that accommodates various occasion types and enables event disambiguation within sentences. The dataset was manually verified by a second annotator, achieving a high inter-annotator agreement. To validate MEE's utility, we developed a state-of-the-art occasion detection model that relies on fine-tuned BERT representations. Our method attained an F1 score of 0.9109 on English data and 0.8383 on Russian data, representing the first BERT-based approach for this domain. The hard spectral states of black hole X-ray binaries (XRBs) are characterized by a dominant hard X-ray component from a corona, supplemented by a lower-luminosity soft component originating from the accretion disc. In this study, we analyzed the long-term X-ray light curve and spectral data from Cyg X-1 during its hard state in the 2011-2012 outburst. Our results indicate that soft X-ray fluctuations at low frequencies are driven by variations in the stellar breeze, whereas hard X-rays remain unaffected. Furthermore, we observed an anti-correlation between the corona normalization parameter in the hard state and the fraction of emission from the disc. These findings suggest that soft X-ray fluctuations in hard-state Cyg X-1 arise from the modulated stellar wind from the companion star, while the nature of the anti-correlation between coronal strength and disc emission remains unclear. Additionally, we propose that the soft X-ray region is more susceptible to the breeze's impact than the hard region. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates that the stellar breeze influences the soft X-ray region of hard-state Cyg X-1. Future research should explore the relationship between the corona and the disc-wind to determine if their interaction drives the observed spectral-timing characteristics of the hard state. This paper introduces the Collaborative Universal Syntactic and Semantic Analysis (CUSSEA) Framework, which employs a common, language-independent formalism to describe syntax and relations between words and constituents. Relations are denoted using two-dimensional tables that align with natural language structures, where rows represent constituents and columns represent words. The Collaborative Universal Semantic Analysis (CUSAA) framework, a component of the CUSSEA framework, extends this formalism to represent word-argument relations and semantic roles. Through detailed comparisons with existing syntactic and formal approaches, we demonstrate that the CUSSEA Framework offers unification across three dimensions: linguistic data, linguistic theory, and computational applications. Finally, we illustrate how the CUSSEA Framework serves as a bridge between traditional syntactic analysis and state-of-the-art neural models. In light of the rapid advancements in neural networks, such a bridge facilitates a deeper comprehension of neural models and enhances their effectiveness. We provide empirical evidence supporting the CUSSEA Framework's ability to boost Neural Network Performance (NNP). Specifically, we present experimental results from two tasks: (1) the Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) task within the Common Semantic Evaluation, and (2) the Question Answering (QA) task on the Commonsenseqa dataset. The Collaborative Semantic Role Labeling (CSRL) task, which integrates both syntactic and semantic analysis, further demonstrates the benefits of the CUSSEA Framework over neural networks relying solely on word embeddings. These findings highlight the value of the CUSSEA Framework in enhancing Neural Network Performance. The accompanying Code Repository (CR) provides open-source implementations of the CUSSEA Framework, including support for Parsing, Common Semantic Evaluation, and CommonSenseQA. The CR also offers detailed code comments and tutorials to facilitate the understanding and adoption of the CUSSEA Framework. We aim for this framework to serve as a unified foundation for syntactic and semantic analysis, thereby improving Neural Network Performance. Magnetized accretion disks surrounding the remnants of core-collapse supernovae and binary mergers can evolve into rapidly rotating black holes, potentially launching powerful jets. The critical factor determining whether these jets successfully clear the accretion disk is the mass of the remnant black hole. In this study, we investigate the final fate of postmerger neutrino-cooled accretion disks by employing a unified framework that integrates the most recent equations of state for hot, dense matter, utilizing the open-source \texttt{Einstein Toolkit} numerical relativity code. Our analysis focuses on a set of 12 representative simulations, varying binary mass ratios from 0.7 to 1.5, to examine how disk evolution and jet launching are influenced by the gravitational mass of the remnant black hole, $M_{BH}$. Our findings indicate that jets are launched when $M_{BH}$ exceeds approximately $2.5M_{\odot}$, a threshold that remains consistent regardless of the initial disk mass. Furthermore, we observe that higher binary mass ratios result in more massive disks and the development of a more collimated jet. Additionally, we detect a significant amount of ejecta with a mass of roughly $10^{-3}M_{\odot}$, which is primarily helium and oxygen, along with a small fraction of heavier elements. The mass of this ejecta shows a strong dependence on $M_{BH}$, decreasing as the black hole mass increases. Our results suggest that the disks may persist for approximately 1 second, with a potential peak in electromagnetic emission occurring around 1 second post-merger. This suggests that future electromagnetic follow-up observations should be conducted within the first second after the merger. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for constraining the equation of state. By analyzing the light curves from these persistent accretion disks, we can place constraints on the mass-radius relationship of supramassive neutron stars. This method offers a new avenue for exploring compact objects, complementing existing techniques such as gravitational wave observations and the study of millisecond pulsars. This work serves as a proof of concept, and future research will aim to investigate these disks in greater detail. The code and public data used in this study are available at \url{https://github.com/WeiZhang1992/Gravitational-Wave-Signatures-of-Compact-Object-Mergers}. The simulations were performed using the \texttt{Einstein Toolkit} on the National Supercomputer

We investigate the tidal properties and merger rates of massive, early-type galaxies by utilizing the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program's (HSC-SSP) deep imaging survey. Tidal features are quantified through the flux component of tidal ellipticity ($\eta_f$), which is derived from the deVaucouleurs flux profile. By comparing galaxies identified as merging within a radius of $R \leq 100$ kpc based on morphological analysis with those that are not, we examine their $\eta_f$ distributions. Furthermore, by analyzing the $\eta_f$ distributions across different redshift bins, we infer merger rates for early-type galaxies. Our findings indicate that merging early-type galaxies possess significantly higher mean $\eta_f$ values than non-merging ones, with this distinction becoming more pronounced at higher redshifts. Additionally, the difference in mean $\eta_f$ values diminishes as galaxy mass increases. We estimate that approximately 10% of early-type galaxies with stellar masses $\log(M_\odot) \leq 11$ undergo mergers within a radius of 100 kpc during the redshift interval $0 \leq z \leq 1$. These results suggest that tidal ellipticity serves as a valuable proxy for identifying merging galaxies and that the flux component of this metric is highly sensitive to tidal characteristics. Consequently, $\eta_f$ offers a robust method for assessing the merger history of early-type galaxies. This approach is particularly advantageous for large-scale imaging surveys, such as the HSC-SSP, which will eventually cover over 10,000 square degrees. We have made our $\eta_f$ catalog available to the public. (abridged)

This study presents a new theory of gravity, termed the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), which serves as a complement to Relativistic Gravitational Theory (RGT). ASTG is specifically designed to describe the dynamics of Bipel/Bipolar systems. Within this framework, the force vector acting on a particle in motion is directed toward the opposite side of the system's center, perpendicular to the center-line of the bipole. This force is characterized as a \emph{repellent} gravitational effect. The repulsive nature of this force is essential for describing the dynamics of bipolar ejections, a phenomenon that the relativistic theory fails to account for. The paper also addresses the origin of the repellent force, the structure of Bipolar/Emanator systems, and the mechanism behind bipolar ejections. Furthermore, the dynamics of Bipolar systems are demonstrated within the context of ASTG. The findings indicate that ASTG is necessary to provide a comprehensive theoretical model for Bipolar/Emanator systems. The formalism of ASTG shares several similarities with the established RGT. Additionally, the ASTG model for ejection mechanisms aligns with the Emulator model of the Solar System. The Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory paper series is designated as (I) and (II). This work constitutes the sequel, (II). Keywords: Theory of Gravitation, Relativistic Theory of Gravitation, Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation, Bipolar/Emanator systems, Solar System. The origin of fast radio bursts (FRBs) remains unresolved, with faint optical flashes detected from some events offering potential clues. Since even faint flashes are challenging to detect, the optical signatures associated with FRBs may be obscured by the Faint Noises Floor (FNF). This paper examines the detectability of optical emission by simulating FRB-associated light curves under various assumptions and comparing the results against current survey capabilities. Specifically, we analyze optical signals from both concurrent and postponed (delayed) sources. Concurrent emission is modeled as a faint curve superposed on the FNF. For postponed emission from compact sources, we consider scenarios involving a single flash, a flash followed by an exponential decay, and a flash followed by a power-law decay. Additionally, we investigate the feasibility of observing optical emission from FRB sources that have evolved into neutron stars with strong magnetic fields after their burst episodes. Finally, we outline future prospects for detecting faint optical emission from these events. Our findings indicate that the FNF significantly limits the ability to identify concurrent optical emission from "well-defined" FRBs—those exhibiting minimal temporal fluctuations. However, postponed optical emission is generally detectable, with the minimum flash magnitude becoming fainter as the delay time increases. Furthermore, well-defined FRB sources may host neutron stars with strong magnetic fields, which can be observed with magnitudes reaching $m \sim -4$. These results are consistent with recent observations of well-defined FRBs. Consequently, future optical searches should prioritize the observation of well-defined FRBs, as well as a re-analysis of historical data to search for postponed optical emission. This approach may help elucidate the relationship between FRBs and neutron stars. The code used for the simulations is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaoxiaohao1998/FRB_faint_curve. The code will also be utilized to simulate optical curves for other compact objects. This review examines the design principles, optimization strategies, and manufacturing techniques for high-power lasers, utilizing representative examples to illustrate these concepts. We begin with solid-state lasers, transitioning to gas lasers, then returning to solid-state types before addressing photonics-based lasers and light sources. The final section provides a brief overview of free-electron lasers. We aim to offer readers current insights into the design and fabrication of high-power laser systems. Consequently, we stress the need for interdisciplinary research to advance the fabrication processes and technologies required for the high-power laser systems of tomorrow. Although recent language generation models have been trained to incorporate visual inputs to prioritize image content over textual prompts, they frequently neglect this content, produce incoherent output, and fail to render punctuation. By examining how neural models ignore visual controls like punctuation marks and images, we demonstrate that low-level sequence models can effectively integrate visual cues to high-level models that respect image content. This approach yields a new class of models that are more cost-efficient, generate more image-relevant text, produce fewer safety violations, and produce more grammatically correct and punctuated sentences. Furthermore, we show that low-level models can be enhanced with a small, expert-annotated dataset that generalizes well to unseen domains, thereby reducing the data requirements for broader contexts. Finally, we present evidence that low-level models can be trained to explicitly identify "what" and "how much" information is present in images, which facilitates more accurate textual descriptions of images. By enabling models to focus on compositional details, quantity estimation, and low-level features, we aim to promote more accurate and grounded textual descriptions of images. This research represents a step toward models that are more efficient, cost-effective, and relevant to real-world applications. Our code is available at: https://github.com/visogpt/visogpt. This represents a crucial step toward creating models that are more efficient, cost-effective, and applicable to real-world scenarios. Our code is available at: https://github.com/visogpt/visogpt.

This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a ring currency protocol incorporating zero-knowledge proofs, designed to accelerate transaction processing on distributed ledgers like Bitcoin. Specifically, our conditional transaction format reduces processing time by 64%, while our implicit payment method further decreases it additionaly. This performance gain stems from eliminating digital signature verifications during processing. This apparatus modifies the electron bundle's transverse energy distribution during the probe process. The recovered phase space portrait serves to infer the bunch's overall characteristics, such as total charge and RMS beam size, as well as internal inhomogeneities, including non-uniform charge distributions. Furthermore, the paper utilizes these phase space portraits to reconstruct the charge density distribution of bunches that propagated through an air gap, offering a novel method for this analysis that complements existing approaches relying on radiofrequency (RF) deflection, micro-structures, or other diagnostics. This technique demonstrates robust performance across diverse bunch types, including air-gap bundles, with errors under 10% for all analyzed metrics. Additionally, the study examines the method's limitations regarding highly turbulent bunches. Ultimately, this analysis points toward future applications, such as reconstructing charge density for laser-plasma accelerators. The entire study was conducted using Python. Data-informed modeling (DIM) represents a new method for integrating data and models that leverages the unique strengths of both approaches. Its primary objective is to overcome the inherent limitations of relying solely on data analysis or theoretical modeling. This review outlines the fundamental principles of DIM, examines various execution types including theoretical motivations, current status, specific examples, and open challenges, with a focus on particle physics. Additionally, it highlights the necessity of collaborative execution as a solution to resource constraints, thereby facilitating the method's full potential. The article concludes by detailing two prominent collaborative DIM initiatives: AutoEncoder4Higgs and PRL21050089. Given the future emergence of exascale computing, particle physics and the broader scientific community must proactively prepare by fostering interdisciplinary talent, promoting cross-field collaborations, and developing appropriate frameworks. Finally, the review explores how exascale environments can enhance DIM methods, specifically through the utilization of advanced machine learning algorithms like graph neural networks. Ultimately, exascale computing is poised to serve as a catalyst for the future of data-informed modeling. We introduce AskewSGD, an algorithm designed to adapt neural network architectures and weights for high-accuracy inference under tight resource constraints, specifically targeting the skew matrix within convolutional layers. Unlike prior approaches that merely approximate the annealed training process and discard historical information, AskewSGD is derived analytically to precisely optimize the quantized parameter at each training step. Furthermore, we developed architecture and quantization algorithms that utilize the established SGDS parameter to refine the quantized, range-constrained parameter. AskewSGD surpasses the baseline method by achieving an accuracy improvement of 1.6% (equivalent to 20% of the available training budget). Additionally, the resulting Askew architectures and weights demonstrate weights that are 2.5 times sparser and 1.5 times wider, thereby enhancing the model's expressiveness. AskewSGD achieves this without increasing the number of trainable parameters and incurs no additional training time compared to the baseline. Finally, the Askew architecture and the corresponding weights, activations, and gradient maps exhibit rich and diverse patterns that the baseline fails to capture. The Askew architecture and weights are readily available for training on any specific dataset. Additionally, we provide insights into the performance of various quantization schemes and their impact on AskewSGD. Our code will be made public upon request. Dataset: N/A. Code N/A. Soft robotics has gained significant traction due to the unique capabilities offered by these machines. A primary advantage of soft robots is their capacity to generate substantial deformations under external loads, enabling interaction with delicate environments and the manipulation of objects through distributed compliance. Additionally, utilizing pneumatic actuators allows for distributed force generation with these systems. Despite the distinct physical properties of soft robots, there is a lack of comprehensive control strategies that address the full range of soft robot types and materials. This survey examines model-driven control, detailing the various control architectures, materials, and actuation methods prevalent in the field. We provide an in-depth analysis of the current state of practice, highlighting gaps and open challenges. Finally, we argue that future research should concentrate on developing generalizable modeling and control architectures that can accommodate diverse systems. We outline key areas that require further investigation to advance model-driven control toward this goal. By addressing these open challenges, the field can better enable the deployment of soft robots in real-world applications. This work serves as a resource for researchers and practitioners to identify gaps in their knowledge regarding model-driven control and to guide the formulation of new challenges for advancing the field. Table-oriented fact verification demands table dissection, a method that isolates a fact's subcomponents from a table to form verification questions. These questions, paired with specific cell locations within the table, guide further verification. To investigate whether decomposing facts into smaller units early in the pipeline could enhance performance, we examine table disintegration, which involves extracting sub-components from both queries and user-provided facts. Our findings reveal that while discourse information is crucial, it is not entirely necessary for table dissection. We show that leveraging linguistic indicators, such as prepositions, can significantly boost performance. Furthermore, we explore if combining dissection with table semantic enhancement improves outcomes, a hypothesis confirmed by experimental results. We also demonstrate the applicability of our approach to agnostic table dissection by integrating it with TABFact, resulting in performance gains. The code is accessible at https://github.com/roberta-tavakoli/table_dissection. The associated paper can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7271000. The experiment code is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7271001. Finally, we outline our conclusions and suggest several directions for future research. Confrontational Networks (CN) are a type of adversarial network designed to map noisy inputs deterministically to a manifold of realistic data points. While prior research has focused on conditioning these networks using raw attributes like class labels, weather conditions, or image rotation angles, this approach often fails when attributes are abstract, such as the average brightness of textual regions in face images. This paper introduces a novel hidden-space attribute conditioning method that is more robust to such abstract attributes and demonstrates superior generative quality across various datasets. Our findings suggest that directly embedding attributes into latent vectors is less effective than projecting them into a higher-dimensional space and subsequently embedding them from there. Additionally, we present an experimental comparison of this work against other recently proposed attribute conditioning techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexgarcia22/face-conditioning. The authors can be contacted at {alex.garcia22, joel.kirkham} at uoregon.edu. Phase samplers enable hierarchical sampling of periodic signals, enabling the study of quantum devices exhibiting quantum noise and coherence characteristics contingent on measurement timing. In this work, we present a modeling approach for various experimental configurations involving multiple interleaved sampling frequencies, demonstrating that accurate representation of the sampler phases is essential for interpreting data. We discuss measurement scenarios where the sampling phases function as random variables, inducing time-dependent random modulation of the signal. Furthermore, we evaluate the parameters of diverse modeling approaches for such setups, comparing their accuracy and computational complexity. We provide a method for determining the effective sampler phases from known hardware parameters and propose a generic fitting procedure to infer effective sampler phases when direct parameter determination is unfeasible. We illustrate that neglecting the time-dependence of sampler phases can result in the incorrect assignment of modulation frequency to the signal device. Additionally, we show that ignoring the stochastic nature of the sampling phases leads to incorrect estimation of the device's coherence time. We conclude that the proposed modeling framework is applicable to a broad spectrum of experimental setups, such as sideband modulation and microwave modulation, which can be sampled using phase samplers. This framework can also be adapted to pulse modulation scenarios, provided pulse timing is sufficiently precise to be treated as a deterministic variable. We anticipate that this research will assist experimentalists in designing more sophisticated modulation experiments and in publishing more accurate quantitative data. We provide open-source Python code to facilitate the application of this research to new experimental scenarios. We hope our findings will encourage a more precise characterization of phase samplers and a deeper understanding of modulation experiments involving multiple interleaved modulation frequencies. We believe this will enhance the accuracy of quantum device characterization and foster a more nuanced understanding of the devices under study. All findings in this work are based on simulated data, and we anticipate that similar issues may arise in real-world experiments. We aim that this research will facilitate more careful consideration of the experimental design and modulation scheme in new setups. We hope this will contribute to a more precise and nuanced understanding of the devices being developed. Finally, we emphasize that the proposed modeling framework is applicable to a wide range of modulation experiment types. We believe this research will facilitate more careful consideration of the experimental design and modulation scheme in new setups. We anticipate that this will contribute to a more precise and nuanced understanding of the devices being developed. Lastly, we stress that the findings in this work are based on simulated data, and we expect that similar issues may arise in real-world experiments. We believe that this research will encourage more careful consideration of the experimental design and modulation scheme in new setups.

We present a method to assign distance labels $L(v)$ to the vertices $v$ of a weighted graph $G$, ensuring that $L(v)$ approximates the shortest path distance $D(v, s)$ from every vertex $v$ to all source vertices $s$ within a $(1, c)$-additive range. This process is termed "distance tagging." Our primary finding is that for any planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, an embedding $E$ into the grid $\mathbb{Z}^2$ can be computed in $O(n \log n)$ time such that the label $E(v)$ for every vertex $v$ $(1, 2)$-approximates all shortest path distances from $v$ to source vertices in a subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ of size $O(\sqrt{n})$. Crucially, our algorithm functions correctly even if up to $f$ vertices fail, provided that $f$ is known in advance; in this resilient scenario, the approximation factor becomes $(1, (2+4f/n)c)$. Furthermore, we establish that for any constant $c < 2$, there exists a family of outerplanar graphs where no embedding exists in the grid $\mathbb{Z}^2$ that $(1, c)$-approximates all shortest path distances from a set of $k=\sqrt{n}$ sources. Additionally, we demonstrate that distance labeling schemes, which require $D(u, v)$ to be recoverable from labels alone rather than relying on sources, cannot achieve an error bound of $o(n)$ even for outerplanar graphs. Finally, we propose an alternative embedding algorithm for planar graphs into the grid $\mathbb{Z}^2$ that $(1, 3)$-approximates all shortest path distances from $k=\sqrt{n}$ sources within $O(n \log n)$ time; this approach remains resilient to $f$ vertex failures with an error bound of $(1, (3 + 16f/n)k)$. To our knowledge, this represents the first embedding algorithm capable of $(1, c)$-approximating all shortest path distances from $\sqrt{n}$ sources while remaining resilient to a constant fraction of vertex failures. Our findings are supported by a C++ implementation available at https://github.com/ehrmann/planar-embedding. This study investigates two-entity correlations within a lossy Bose-Hubbard framework subject to a pumping force. The analysis utilizes both moment and spectrum domain techniques to examine on- and off-site two-body correlations. Employing a controlled approximation, the correlations are decomposed into a dominant correlated component and a sub-dominant term representing the decay of the correlation function. The results indicate that site-specific, frequency-dependent, spin-exchange-enhanced, and bi-entity bosonic distributions are generated in the pumping-depleted dephased system. Conversely, in the absence of such exchange coupling, only frequency-dependent correlations are observed. These findings suggest that the model is effective for generating the specified two-entity bosonic distributions in both two- and three-mode configurations. The outcomes also demonstrate the viability of the methods for investigating multi-entity correlations in the system. Furthermore, these techniques are applicable for studying two- and three-body correlations in other lossy Bose-Einstein condensate models. Finally, a classical-conditional interpretation is provided for the correlation functions derived via the spectrum domain method. This work examines the existence and regularity of weak solutions to divergence-form elliptic equations where the coefficients possess a bounded current in $W^{-1,\infty}$. The primary innovation lies in establishing the existence of continuous weak solutions through a truncation argument applied to the adjoint operator. This methodology facilitates various applications, including handling rough coefficients within small perturbation principles, analyzing $p$-harmonic equations with small data, and addressing small perturbations involving bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms. Notably, these findings represent the first of their kind applicable to a broad spectrum of operators. Furthermore, employing a convex integration strategy, we derive $L^q$ regularity for the coefficients under the condition that their determinant has an absolute value less than 1. These results are among the most general achieved to date in the context of small perturbations of elliptic equations with rough coefficients. Additionally, the paper explores specific problems within geometric measure theory. Specifically, we investigate the existence and regularity of minimal currents and their boundaries within a divergence structure, as well as establish novel variational dimension reduction theorems. Finally, we present a resolution to a significant problem posed by De Giorgi in his 1965 treatise on the regularity of surfaces. This solution relies on a convex integration method inspired by recent breakthroughs in the study of area minimizers in higher dimensions. The resolution successfully addresses several questions raised by De Giorgi, which remain largely unresolved by traditional techniques. Beyond these results, the paper includes numerous applications to variational problems, many of which appear to be unprecedented. These derive from the observation that the techniques developed herein extend beyond the scope of classical methods. The extension is achieved by utilizing the full structure of the divergence equation rather than merely its weak formulation. This necessitates working with currents instead of distributions and developing a corresponding theory of distributions with vector values. This approach enables the derivation of strong convergence properties for the curl of vector fields and the boundedness of the operator mapping vector fields to their curl. The paper begins with an extensive introduction to the subject and its connections to other fields. It subsequently outlines the equation and coefficient classes considered, followed by an exposition of the main results. A significant portion of the work details the analytical tools required for the proofs, followed by their application to specific problems. Throughout, we have strived to maintain the equations' geometric interpretation. Anomaly detection is extensively researched and utilized across various disciplines, including signal processing, image analysis, and neurobiology. This study introduces a unified framework that integrates existing methods within the context of Gaussian processes and their extensions. We demonstrate the flexibility of this approach by unifying prior art and highlighting potential future directions. Our evaluation assesses several models on 27 datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository to benchmark performance. Furthermore, we examine applications in signal processing within non-stationary environments and neural activity in primary visual cortex. Finally, we advocate for the adoption of Gaussian process-based anomaly detection in neuroscience. This paper serves as a comprehensive guide for researchers in machine learning, signal processing, and neuroscience seeking to leverage out-of-sample anomaly detection capabilities of Gaussian processes. By providing a framework to compare existing methods and suggest new ones, we aim to facilitate the broader adoption of these techniques in the scientific community. Access to our code is available at https://github.com/fernandocosta99/dgp-ad. Access to our data can be found at https://github.com/fernandocosta99/neurodata. Keywords: Anomaly Detection, Distributional Gaussian Processes, Out-of-Sample Prediction.

Periodic driving of a quantum system typically induces rapid heating, a phenomenon known as Floquet heating. However, in open systems open to an environment, periodic driving can simultaneously facilitate energy exchange with the environment, potentially preventing such heating. We investigate this within the context of an optical-lattice Bose gas interacting with a reservoir. We demonstrate that Floquet heating can trigger three-body losses from the gas, a process that can be halted by populating a specific state at $k_\pi=\pi$ (a Mott-insulator state). This selection of a $k_\pi$-like state arises from the existence of a "time crystal" like eigenstate within the open system, a concept we term a "quasi-time crystal." This quasi-time crystal supports a "quasi-time crystalline" scar-like state of the open system. This scar-like state is scarred from the Floquet-heating-driven destruction of the Mott-insulator state, which would otherwise occur. Consequently, Bose aggregation is generated through the destruction of this Mott-insulator state. Our findings provide a pathway to controlling, preventing, and engineering quantum degradation in open systems. Furthermore, our study offers a novel approach to understanding open quantum systems by elucidating the relationship between the quasi-time crystal and the scar-like state. These insights may offer new perspectives on interpreting and designing quantum systems that exhibit time-crystalline behavior. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 030401, 2021) [Phys. Rev. Non-repetitive optical clocks represent the next generation of optical time-frequency standards, expected to achieve superior short-term stability compared to current non-repetitive microwave clocks. This study presents the first statistical time-domain analysis of a non-repetitive optical clock, based on 20 hours of data from a prototype device. The proposed statistical model characterizes the data using two key parameters: an all-optical free-running noise floor of approximately 1.2×10⁻¹⁸ at 1 second, and a relative drift rate (RDR) of 1.5×10⁻¹⁶/s. The paper also discusses RDR compensation techniques and their impact on these metrics. Furthermore, it demonstrates that applying an Allan variance filter to the data reveals the fundamental measurement noise inherent to the clock. Finally, the research confirms that non-repetitive optical clocks can be modeled as the sum of Gaussian white phase noise, linear phase noise, and a mixture of Gaussian white frequency noise with modified loop detuning, as well as with loop feedback. Finally, the paper compares these fundamental characteristics against those of current non-repetitive microwave clocks. The results indicate that once technical limitations are resolved, the performance of non-repetitive optical clocks will significantly surpass that of non-repetitive microwave clocks. The research code is accessible at https://github.com/JulienBertin2000/AllanVariance. Additionally, the findings were partially presented at the OFS Conference 2021 in Madrid, Spain, in a poster session. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that the development of non-repetitive optical clocks is on a sound trajectory. Future endeavors should prioritize addressing technical constraints to fully realize the potential of this technology. This paper introduces an energy-aware framework designed to reconstruct Software-Defined Networking (SDN) services and adapt resource allocation within the Internet of Things (IoT) by integrating Fog Computing and SDN principles. This approach aims to enhance Quality of Service (QoS) in resource-constrained environments while ensuring energy efficiency. To achieve this, we propose a failure recovery mechanism for network services and applications, mitigating the collaboration challenges between Fogs and Intermediate Network devices. The study addresses real-time Service Chain (SFC) provisioning and Failure Recovery Mechanisms (FRM) in resource-limited settings, focusing on the dynamic recovery of service chains and the efficient redistribution of resources. The proposed framework utilizes a heuristic algorithm for rapid service recovery, alongside an asset management tool for cost-effective deployment. We employ the Network Calculus (NC) model to define service chains and their Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees, alongside an optimization problem to mitigate failures. Furthermore, we suggest an energy-aware resource allocation algorithm for SFC provisioning in both Fogs and Intermediate Network devices. Finally, we evaluate the proposed solutions through detailed analysis regarding resource consumption, energy usage, and computational complexity. Results indicate that the NC model effectively defines QoS for services and applications, while the Asset Management Tool facilitates energy-aware, cost-effective SFC deployment. Additionally, the Fog-assisted FRM ensures efficient and rapid service recovery, and the resource allocation algorithm demonstrates effective SFC provisioning. The use of NC model-based service chains and an NC-aware FRM has significantly reduced recovery times. Additionally, the asset management tool enables SFC deployment in cost-effective and energy-aware manners. The combined energy-aware resource allocation algorithm and energy-aware asset management tool have substantially lowered overall energy consumption. Consequently, this approach offers an effective solution for real-time SCB provisioning and FRM, facilitating efficient and cost-effective SFC deployment. Ultimately, the proposed energy-aware framework provides an effective solution for SFC provisioning, recovery, and mitigation in the future of energy-aware IoT. This IoT framework is expected to support various real-time applications, including traffic management, smart healthcare, and smart city initiatives. The ultimate goal is to achieve energy-aware, cost-effective, and real-time SFC provisioning for the emerging IoT ecosystem. This solution is particularly relevant for next-generation applications such as 5G and the Internet of Vehicle (IoV). Achieving this requires an energy-aware framework that provisions, manages, and mitigates failures in real-time SFC resources and services. Although hyperparameter optimization is frequently credited as the primary cause of over-fitting gradient manipulation, research indicates that the selection of loss functions plays an equally critical role. This study employs a deep neural network with a fixed architecture, trained using different loss functions on the same dataset to classify eight German wine varieties. By applying identical hyperparameters and conducting thorough grid searches across various gradient manipulation techniques, we evaluated how each loss function performed under uniform conditions. Our findings demonstrate that the type of loss function significantly influences the outcomes of hyperparameter optimization and subsequent gradient manipulation strategies. Furthermore, our analysis of statistical outputs reveals that certain loss functions offer superior interpretability, enabling researchers to gain deeper insights into the data. Finally, we examined how different loss functions affect both the training and testing processes. To support reproducibility, we provide Python code for our experiments in a public repository. This work serves as a foundational reference for the selection of loss functions within the context of hyperparameter optimization and neural network gradient manipulation. The holographic error correction condition (HECC) is a specific class of error correction codes that maintain a duality between the bulk and boundary, a requirement essential for black hole physics. It has been demonstrated that certain families of holographic codes satisfy this condition; however, no example of a simple holographic code with power-law correlations has been identified that meets the HECC. In this study, we introduce a new family of codes known as Hyper-INVERTIBLE MERA (Hyper-INVERT). This code is a simple, bulk-centric approximate holographic error correction code derived by stacking layers of invertible quantum channels that possess a known inverse. Notably, this code does not fulfill the HECC but exhibits boundary correlation decay rates ($\alpha$) that approach power-law behavior as $\alpha \sim 1/(4\beta)$ when $\beta \to \infty$. Furthermore, we establish that any class of codes formed by stacking unital, invertible quantum operations fails to meet the HECC. Consequently, constructing simple codes that satisfy the HECC with power-law associations remains a difficult challenge that likely necessitates more complex architectures. Additionally, we prove that any code generated by sequentially applying unital quantum operations cannot correct dephasing noise. Finally, we illustrate that the Hyper-INVERT code fails the bulk-decodability test for most codes, despite being bulk-decodable for a specific subset of error operators. This finding contradicts the common simplification that any code capable of error correction is also bulk-decodable. We anticipate that these negative results will be valuable in clarifying the necessary conditions for black hole physics. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the structure of holographic error correction and address several open questions in the field. Future research should aim to develop simple codes that satisfy the HECC with power-law associations to better understand the link between holography and quantum information. Furthermore, it is crucial to determine whether the concept of bulk-decodability is necessary for black hole physics or if alternative conditions can be utilized. Finally, further investigation is needed to understand the relationship between holographic duals and quantum error correction to gain deeper insights into black hole physics. This paper serves as a foundational step toward achieving these goals. Additionally, we demonstrate that any class of codes formed by sequentially applying unital quantum operations cannot correct dephasing noise. This finding highlights various challenges in quantum error correction, such as the non-unitality of error correction and the non-convexity of the quantum error correction condition. The Galactic core is a highly complex environment, necessitating the use of complex dynamical models to characterize its population. Previous research has employed various techniques, including orbit integration, to define a "simple" core using these models. This study presents an alternative approach to generating synthetic fibers by sampling the action space. Unlike methods that rely on arbitrary dynamical model parameters, our method targets a specific physical quantity to ensure the resulting fiber sample meets the desired target. Specifically, we examine the action-space distribution of the maximum distance between two fibers, which serves as a proxy for the maximum 3D separation between stars. By analyzing this distribution, we can determine a target distance to sample from, thereby generating a fiber population with the specified target property. Furthermore, we can infer physical properties of the Galactic core by sampling this target space. Using action-distributions from statistical samples of Galactic core fibers, we observe that the distribution of the maximum star separation between two random fibers is not Gaussian. Instead, it is characterized by a power-law tail with an index of approximately $-2.5$. The scale of the distribution is approximately $100\,\mathrm{pc}$. We also discuss how to construct a dynamical model based on these results. Our approach is general and can be applied to other components of the Milky Way by simply selecting a different target quantity. This research was conducted as part of the CRESST project, and we provide open-source code for our synthetic fiber generator. Additionally, we have made the resulting population of Galactic core fibers publicly available. Our findings suggest that the Galactic core is likely dominated by pairs of stars. While this conclusion is based on statistical characteristics, we also explore how it might be reflected in the physical distribution of the core. We conclude that Galactic core dynamics are likely dominated by close encounters. However, we also note that action-based models, which are based on integrable systems, may not be the most suitable framework for investigating the core's dynamical behavior. Consequently, we outline potential future research directions. This paper is the second in a series; the first will be published separately. The distribution of action-space variables for Galactic core fibers is also examined. In the first paper, we will analyze the distribution of maximum line-of-sight velocity dispersion. This study introduces and evaluates an ideal Distributed Conservation Voltage Reduction (DCVR) program tailored for primary-secondary network configurations where distribution transformers are grouped by zone. Within each zone, secondary network losses and energy usage are minimized by adjusting sub-transmission voltage levels at every sub-station. Crucially, these operational decisions are guided by voltage constraints in the primary network and power flow limits at the sub-station substations. To address this, we formulate and solve discrete DCVR instances using a zonal aggregation model combined with a two-stage stochastic programming approach that accounts for uncertain power flows and voltages. Furthermore, a decomposition algorithm is developed to enhance computational efficiency. Finally, numerical results demonstrate the proposed method's performance, highlighting its ability to reduce distributed losses by up to 1.5% while maintaining primary power flow limits and transformer voltages within acceptable ranges. This study advances the non-stationary multi-armed bandit framework by introducing arm-dependent lags within a specialized bandit model. In this setting, each arm features a non-stationary parameter that evolves over time, yet the information available to the learner at any given moment reflects the arm's parameter from a previous, randomly determined turn. We examine a specialized variant of this problem where arms possess distinct and variable lag durations. Under a specific regret formulation, we derive an upper-bound expression for this regret. This finding is significant because it demonstrates, for the initial time, that specialist bandits can achieve upper bounds comparable to those of stationary problems, provided the number of arms is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we propose a novel algorithm, the Sequential Shifted Thompson Sampling (SST) family, which adapts standard Thompson Sampling to handle delayed observations. Additionally, we introduce a modified Thompson Sampling algorithm, RST, designed for scenarios involving uniform but unknown lags. The theoretical findings for both models yield corresponding lower bounds for their respective regret formulations, establishing a tight bound analysis for this problem. Notably, these tight bounds indicate that the presence of specialist arms does not elevate the lower bound above that of a problem with non-specialist arms and zero lags. This contrasts sharply with existing bandit models that incorporate arm-dependent lags and demonstrate how our tight bound result surpasses similar analyses in current literature. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through numerical simulations. This paper serves as the companion to \cite{Borovikov2022}, which presents a matching lower bound for the same problem. Together, they offer the first tight bound analysis for this class of bandit problems. Our approach is applicable to various decision-making contexts, including online advertising, where ad impressions vary in duration, and e-commerce, where product reviews are subject to random delays. In these scenarios, relying solely on the most recent observation can be suboptimal, as it may not accurately represent the current state of an arm, particularly when some arms exhibit shorter lags than others. Consequently, the specialist bandit model is the appropriate framework for addressing such challenges. Similar issues also arise in clinical trials, where treatments may have delayed effects. In these cases, using only the latest data can be misleading, as it might fail to capture the true efficacy of arms with shorter lags. Therefore, the specialist bandit model provides the necessary foundation for addressing these complexities. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first research to integrate specialist bandits with arm-dependent lags

Creating a text-generation model that produces outputs as close to human-like as possible is a highly promising avenue for future dialogue research. However, this challenge remains difficult because simply collecting large datasets of human conversations is insufficient on its own. To address this, we introduce a new framework called LEATHER (Learning Structure to Enhance Authenticity in Human-TYPE responses). Our method involves training a neural structure over a large dataset of human conversations and evaluating various neural structure loss functions to identify the one that most effectively learns to mimic human dialogue responses. We demonstrate that the unitary LEATHER structure surpasses other models, including GPT-2, in producing human-like dialogue text. Furthermore, in comparative studies with real human participants, subjects rated the text generated by our model as more human-like than that of GPT-2. Additionally, subjects reported perceiving more empathy, helpfulness, and friendliness in the LEATHER-generated responses compared to GPT-2. Finally, our ablation studies indicate that the size of the human conversation training dataset is a critical factor for the success of this approach. The code and data required to replicate our experiments are available at our project's GitHub repository: https://github.com/Prashant-1998/LEATHER. **Background:** Accurately predicting structural loads on offshore wind turbines is vital for lowering development expenses. While physical-based load models offer high fidelity, their complexity hinders the creation of spatial load maps. Conversely, statistical proxy models are simple and enable rapid spatial mapping, yet they lack physical interpretability. This study investigates the use of Gaussian process (GP) regression as a proxy model for offshore wind-turbine loads. **Methods:** GP regression was applied as a proxy model for turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) using time series data collected from a wind turbine. GP regression and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks were compared based on prediction accuracy, uncertainty quantification, and computational demands. The GP model's ability to generate a spatial map of TKE was also assessed. **Results:** The GP proxy model outperformed the LSTM network in both prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification. Additionally, GP regression produced a TKE spatial map that aligns with physical expectations. **Conclusions:** GP regression emerges as a robust proxy model for offshore wind-turbine loads. Its capacity to quantify uncertainty is particularly valuable for future applications, such as reliability assessments. Furthermore, GP is a computationally efficient and rapidly converging method. **Statement of Novelty:** GP regression is a robust and rapidly converging proxy model for offshore wind-turbine loads. The model's ability to quantify uncertainty is particularly valuable for future applications, such as reliability assessments. Furthermore, GP is a computationally efficient method that outperforms LSTM networks in both prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification. Gaussian process regression serves as a robust and rapidly converging proxy model for offshore wind-turbine loads. The model's ability to quantify uncertainty is especially valuable for future applications, such as reliability assessments.

Social media platforms have evolved into essential tools for information dissemination, a capability demonstrated by the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Turkey. This study examines Twitter data from October 10, 2020, to analyze user behavior regarding both natural disasters and general topics. We present the findings of our investigation into Izmir social media responses to the October 2020 earthquake, specifically focusing on information sharing patterns and the most influential accounts. The event generated approximately 100,000 tweets, driven by a mix of influential news organizations and the public. Our results indicate that news organizations predominantly promoted official updates, whereas public tweets often contained irrelevant content. Furthermore, we identified that public interest in the earthquake peaked at 18:00, approximately one hour after the initial occurrence. This study offers valuable insights for future researchers and emergency response teams, enhancing their ability to disseminate and monitor news during crises. The complete dataset from this research is accessible at: https://aops20.tau.ac.il/our_works/EarthQuake2020.zip. This work was partially funded by the Advanced Research Center at Tel-Aviv University.

Keywords: Social Media, Twitter, EarthQuake, Influential Users, Information Sharing.

This study examines the infinite genus $R_\infty$ characteristic for specific nilpotent quotients of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups, derived from orientable $[n, 2]$-dimensional manifolds containing $[n, 2]$-dimensional handles. Extending the scope of our prior work, which focused solely on nilpotent quotients of $R_\infty$-space groups featuring cyclic handles, this report addresses the case where handles consist of finite nilpotent groups $N$. We determine the $R_\infty$ characteristic across all possible $R_\infty$-type pairings applicable to these quotients. Furthermore, we present several examples involving quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups and conclude with an open problem. Finally, additional examples are appended that extend our analysis to $R_\infty$ characteristics in the context of $[n, k]$-dimensional manifolds.

Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for probing the dynamics of chemical and physical systems, yet extracting system information from the inverse problem typically demands multiple simulations. This paper introduces a forward-optimization method grounded in forward dynamics to resolve the inverse problem in time-resolved spectroscopy. This approach enables the simultaneous inversion of time-resolved data for both linear and nonlinear vibrational spectroscopy, including techniques like pump-probe spectroscopy, IR 2D spectroscopy, and Raman spectroscopy. The study presents the application of this newly developed forward-optimization method to two experimental cases: time-resolved Raman spectra of iodomethane and Raman 2D spectra of liquid water. The results demonstrate that the forward-optimization method successfully yields information regarding both the initial conditions and potential energy surfaces. Consequently, this technique is anticipated to be a highly valuable tool for characterizing the dynamics of chemical and physical systems. The open-source software implementing this methodology is publicly accessible at https://github.com/taekyungkim/PySOL. PySOL supports a diverse range of time-resolved spectroscopy methods, encompassing both electronic and vibrational spectroscopy. Electronic time-resolved methods include transient absorption spectroscopy, time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, and photoemission 2D spectroscopy. Time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy offers a distinct advantage over other electronic methods by providing momentum-resolved information. Time-resolved photoemission 2D spectroscopy offers the benefit of delivering both momentum and energy-resolved information. VR2D supports a variety of time-resolved vibrational spectroscopy methods, such as IR pump-probe spectroscopy, IR 2D spectroscopy, Raman pump-probe spectroscopy, and Raman 2D spectroscopy. The VR2D implementation provides significant advantages over other vibrational 2D spectroscopy methods by offering both frequency and time domain information. This allows for the calculation of both linear and nonlinear responses for any vibrational spectroscopy method that can be derived from the one-body density matrix. The PySOL implementation is available on various platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. PySOL is distributed as an open-source, free software package that offers both vibrational and electronic 2D spectroscopy capabilities. Context-based naturalistic driving data is essential for comprehending driver behavior within the actual road environments where it occurs. However, existing public datasets often omit critical environmental contextual information needed to explain driver decisions and behaviors. To address this gap, this paper introduces SceNDD (Scenario-understanding Naturalistic Driving Dataset), a large-scale, multi-modal dataset comprising over 100,000 trips from 10,000 drivers in Seoul, South Korea. Collected via advanced in-vehicle sensors, the data includes rich contextual details such as road type, surrounding land use, and points of interest. The dataset encompasses diverse scenarios, including various road types, land use contexts, points of interest, and inclement weather. Accompanying the data is a suite of tools for analyzing temporal dynamics and spatial contexts, as well as exploring driver behavior. These tools facilitate the examination of driver incursions and conflicts across different contextual backgrounds and support the creation of trip-level feature sets for machine learning applications. The release of SceNDD will enable researchers to investigate how behavioral features vary across contexts and how behaviors emerge from contextual factors. Additionally, the provided analysis tools offer a foundation for developing trip-level features to assist in understanding and predicting driver behavior and incursions in context-based settings. We intend to host the data and tools on an open portal to support future applications. The full details of SceNDD are available at https://scend.net. Boundary entropy represents an additional component of entropy that emerges when a bulk conformal field theory (CFT) interacts with a boundary. This boundary entropy arises from the intrinsic renormalization group (RG) flow between boundary fixed points and serves as the sole indicator of this process. Beyond its standard role, boundary entropy can be extended to scenarios involving interfaces within 2d CFTs. In these scenarios, boundary entropy acts as the exclusive signal of RG flow occurring between interface fixed points. Furthermore, boundary entropy provides a quantitative assessment of the information disruption caused by boundary insertion. This reflected entropy exhibits significant applications in black hole physics, offering a framework to explore the relationship between boundary entropy and boundary entanglement. Consequently, this work aims to compute the boundary entropy associated with a reflected entropy term in a 1d interface CFT model. The resulting boundary entropy successfully identifies the RG flow from one interface fixed point to another. Additionally, we examine the influence of the operator product expansion (OPE) coefficient on boundary entropy and determine the scaling dimension of the scalar operator from the calculated value. These findings offer new insights into the characteristics of boundary entropy. Ultimately, our results contribute to the broader understanding of boundary entropy within 2d CFTs. We present findings from our empirical study on channel estimation within OFDM systems supporting Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS), focusing on scenarios with a flawed hardware receiver and a truncated cyclic prefix (CP). Flawed hardware, characterized by non-linearities, can degrade performance in both standard and RIS-aided OFDM. This study evaluates the performance of standard and RIS-aided OFDM channel estimation techniques under conditions of flawed hardware, truncated CP, and model order selection challenges. To address these issues, we propose a novel channel estimation framework for RIS-aided OFDM that utilizes a reduced number of RIS reflection measurements. This approach combines Extended Learning Machine Bayesian (ELM-Bay) channel estimation with a new unbiased minimum variance estimator. Simulation results confirm the efficacy of this proposed method. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of truncated CP on OFDM channel estimation, observing that while short CPs can yield performance gains in standard OFDM, they may degrade performance in RIS-aided OFDM when using Elman networks. Consequently, we develop channel estimation algorithms for RIS-aided OFDM that operate with truncated CPs requiring only a fraction of the reflection measurements typically needed. Additionally, we investigate the effects of flawed hardware on standard and RIS-aided OFDM channel estimation, demonstrating that ELM-Bay algorithms can surpass conventional methods in terms of performance. Finally, we detail the impact of model order selection on RIS-aided OFDM channel estimation, noting that improper model orders can lead to significant performance degradation. We conclude by offering recommendations for selecting an appropriate model order to mitigate these adverse consequences. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive examination of channel estimation challenges in OFDM systems with flawed hardware and truncated CPs specifically regarding their application to RIS-aided communication. Our work offers a robust solution to enhance RIS-aided channel estimation performance, effectively addressing the challenges posed by flawed hardware and truncated CPs. Our research significantly advances the field of RIS-aided channel estimation, paving the way for more reliable and efficient wireless communication systems. Our work is original and has not been published elsewhere. We invite readers to explore the associated code and data for reproducibility.
