The Individual energy assessment (I-A) Integral Fluctuation Theorem (IFT) establishes a universal relationship among the mean, variance, and higher-order cumulants of stochastically defined random variables. This framework is significant for analyzing and quantifying fluctuations in diverse nonequilibrium processes. The I-A IFT can be derived from the time-reversal symmetry of the path probability weight (PPW) within a probabilistic framework. In this approach, the PPW remains generic and is not constrained by the boundary conditions of the system's evolution. Consequently, the I-A IFT holds universally and can be applied to systems ranging from stochastic thermodynamics to quantum nonequilibrium. This paper outlines the derivation of the I-A IFT using a generalized probabilistic framework. It demonstrates that while the I-A IFT can be proven via a niche argument relying on the detailed balance of transition probabilities, this derivation lacks the depth of the path-based probabilistic framework. Furthermore, the study establishes the equivalence between an earlier formulation of the I-A IFT and the more general probabilistic framework. Finally, it introduces a novel method for experimentally determining the second-order cumulant of a stochastically defined random variable without perturbing the system's dynamics. This non-invasive technique utilizes two-time correlation functions and offers a fresh perspective on fluctuation analysis. The proposed methodology is validated through a concrete example. These findings offer a new perspective on fluctuation theory and tools for fluctuation analysis that differ from conventional techniques. They may prove beneficial for both experimentalists and theorists engaged in fluctuation analysis. Additionally, these results hold value for fluctuation theory itself. The proposed results contribute to fluctuation theory.

Keywords: Stochastic Thermodynamics, Quantum Nonequilibrium, Quantum Thermodynamics, Quantum Fluctuation Theorem, Quantum Jarzynski Equality.

We examine the stability of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds by performing deformations along the NUT direction. First, we conduct explicit computations for specific manifolds, identifying cases where no nontrivial instantons exist on the corresponding noncompact symmetric spaces. We demonstrate that the space of deformations for these nontrivial $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons is isomorphic to the space of harmonic 3-forms. Furthermore, we establish that the space of deformations for these instantons does not vanish for certain quotient manifolds derived from them. Finally, our findings indicate that numerous well-known instantons defined on six-dimensional Euclidean space fail to extend to the associated manifolds. Through our analysis of geometry and curvature, we prove that these extensions are obstructed. Additionally, we explore methods for constructing nontrivial deformations of instantons. As an application, we verify the existence of a 1-parameter family of instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds that are locally homogeneous and possess nontrivial holonomy. This result supports our conclusion that the obstruction to extending $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons is integral and arises from the curvature term. Our work offers a novel perspective on $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons by revealing a link between their obstructions and curvature. Specifically, we show that curvature prevents certain $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds from existing, a phenomenon that contrasts with the case of Yang-Mills connections. This finding underscores the distinction between $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons and standard Yang-Mills connections. Our results suggest that the curvature term is essential for a comprehensive understanding of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons. Furthermore, the nontrivial extensions of instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds may facilitate the study of gauge theories on manifolds with nontrivial holonomy groups. Our work represents the first step toward a deeper exploration of gauge theories in higher dimensions. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the existence of nontrivial deformations and the vanishing of the space of harmonic 3-forms. Our findings suggest that studying deformations of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds can yield insights into the topology of these manifolds. Mobile applications utilizing cellular tower triangulation have emerged as a strategy to curb the spread of infectious diseases, including COVID-19, by establishing and maintaining social distancing. This study evaluates the privacy of Coronav\u{i}rus-SUS, a Brazilian contact tracing application. We conducted an analysis of the application's source code, which revealed insufficient encryption on the communication channel between the application server and mobile clients. Furthermore, the server's log data contained unencrypted personal information, such as phone numbers and user IDs. Our experimental results demonstrated that the server could potentially identify individual users by correlating tower tower-IDs with location data. Consequently, we contend that the privacy of Coronav\u{i}rus-SUS is compromised, a conclusion supported by both our code review and location analysis. We offer several recommendations to enhance the application's confidentiality. These findings may serve as a strategy for the software engineering community to develop more effective and secure contact tracing applications in the future. To the best of our knowledge, this research represents the first of its kind. We believe that the methodologies developed in this study can be applied to other contact tracing applications. The code and documentation are accessible at: \url{https://github.com/fernandocosta99/Coronavirius-SUS-Case-Study}. The paper was submitted to TIIS. This study introduces a quantum-enhanced neural network designed to accelerate data processing and inference. The research addresses two primary challenges: encoding quantum data into equatorial states on the Bloch sphere and developing neural networks that utilize this encoding. Equatorial encoding is identified as an optimal strategy for quantum data processing, particularly for applications involving image data. The study develops two distinct quantum neural network architectures, one utilizing a single hidden layer and the other employing multiple signal and noise propagation paths. Quantum neural networks are constructed by replacing classical neurons with spheres and classical connections with spherical caps. In the single-layer model, the output is determined by a weighted combination of data points from this layer. For the multi-path model, spherical layers are represented by multi-member teams, where the path between data points involves interactions between respective members. These team outputs are aggregated using spherical arithmetic (mean and product). The multi-path structure is specifically designed to handle scenarios where input data points are uncertain regarding their correct classification. In these cases, noise is represented by data points reflected across the equatorial plane relative to their corresponding team members. The proposed quantum neural networks are evaluated using the CIFAR-10 dataset, which consists of 60,000 RGB images of size 32x32 across 10 classes (animals, vehicles, and objects), with 5,000 samples per class. The input vector $x$ is defined as $x = (r_1, g_1, b_1, r_2, g_2, b_2, \ldots, r_{16}, g_{16}, b_{16})$. Results indicate that the single-layer network achieves accuracy comparable to the classical version, while the multi-layer model yields an accuracy improvement of approximately 10%. Additionally, the classical single-layer network demonstrates uncertainty in classifying certain inputs. The network outputs are described using probability distributions, and uncertainty is quantified via standard deviation. Calculations for both classical and quantum networks were performed using the Qiskit framework. The classical single-layer network exhibits uncertainty for some inputs, whereas the quantum version successfully classifies all of them. Furthermore, the quantum multi-path structure maintains high accuracy despite uncertainties in the input data. Leveraging this embedding, the code creator produces a Coq proof script that verifies the correctness of the generated C code within Coq. An extensive experiment conducted on the MISATUN framework demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach. The results indicate that the superficial embedding successfully automates a significant portion of the proof generation process. The authors demonstrate that combining Ramanujan's findings on zeta values at negative even integers with Hurwitz's evaluation of Bernoulli polynomials yields new formulas for H-Zeta values at negative odd integers. Furthermore, they show that Rogers' derivation of the reflection formula for the Hurwitz Zeta function, which relies on the alternating harmonic series, combined with Ramanujan's expressions for the gamma function, his identity concerning the digamma function, and his 1914 paper on the evaluation of $\zeta (2k+1)$, produces formulas for the H-Zeta function. Through this approach, the digamma function, rational numbers, $\pi$, $\log 2$, and H-Zeisel function values can determine the values of the Hurwitz Zeta function. Consequently, the digamma function's series representation and a variant of Ramanujan's formula for computing $\pi$ are utilized. These outcomes provide computational tools to validate Ramanujan's 1914 conjecture regarding the non-rationality of odd zeta values and to investigate the structure of their $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra. Ultimately, these results offer additional support for T. M. Apostol's efforts in exploring the connection between the odd zeta function and the polygamma function. Finally, an identity linking odd zeta values to their polygamma components is established. All findings are supported by examples and tables. Keywords: Zeta function, Hurwitz Zeta function, generalized harmonic series, Ramanujan's identity for the digamma function, Ramanujan's formula for $\pi$, A. T. M. Hossain's identity for $\pi$.

We provide an explicit, heavily computational determination of the $V$-structure within complex circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology for a complex projective space $CP(V)$, where $V$ is a complex representation of a finite cyclic group $G$. This formulation explicitly details the cohomology classes governing the $G$-equivariant theory. Our results are derived through the application of a recently formulated trace formula. Although highly explicit, the formula remains conceptual, avoiding dependence on specific choices of bases. While our focus is on finite cyclic groups, the formula extends to any finite group $G$ with a fixed $G$-representation $V$, though such cases would demand greater computational explicitness. Additionally, we establish a formula for the case where $G$ acts trivially on $V$, which is also valid in the context of topological T-duality. For the space of based maps $\mathcal{Map}_*(V, S^2)$, where $V$ is a representation of a finite group $G$ and $G$ acts trivially on $S^2$, we identify a subring of complex circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology that corresponds to a specific subring of nonequivariant elliptic cohomology. This identification is achieved via a natural map that is shown to be surjective. This finding aligns with the expectation that map spaces are highly connected. However, the map space cohomology is not entirely captured by our formula; the discrepancy between the two methods grows with the number of generators of $G$. We illustrate this difference using finite abelian groups as a case study. Furthermore, we present a formula for a related theory involving an $SU(2)$-representation, which is also relevant to the study of ALE spaces. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our explicit formula and a recent result by Adams and Jarvis concerning equivariant K-theory. Additionally, we address the question of whether there exists a universal formula applicable to all complex circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology theories possessing a $H$-representation $V$ of a finite group $H$. We demonstrate that no such universal formula can exist. To address this limitation, we propose a modification to the definition of complex circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology. Under this revised definition, we establish that a universal formula does exist and is universal. We indicate that the proof utilizes ideas from representation stability. To facilitate key exchange between two participants, Signal employs a multi-layer key agreement approach that mandates the sharing of specific secrets alongside the session key. Specifically, the platform requires a globally shared global code, a user-specific identity key, a safety number, a safe code, and a three-digit PIN code. This study examines the usability of these secrets from the perspective of enthusiastic Signal users, a group presumed to possess strong platform knowledge. Our research involves a grounded theory study where we analyze user interactions with Signal's security features, focusing on their perceptions, understandings, and experiences with the app's multi-layer key agreement secrets. The findings reveal that, contrary to expectations, these users hold significant gaps in knowledge regarding Signal's security architecture, which they have not previously encountered. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that Signal's security mechanisms are not considered usable by these users, as they tend to prioritize usability over security. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that Signal's multi-layer key agreement secrets are not usable even among enthusiastic users, suggesting that similar challenges may affect the broader user base. This has profound implications for the platform's ability to foster a security-aware user base. To address this, we propose several avenues for future research, including exploring the impact of a security-focused design mindset on users' knowledge and perceptions, as well as investigating the relationship between user design attitudes and their knowledge of Signal's security architecture. Additionally, we aim to examine the effects of our proposed Security Awareness Design (SAD) on users' knowledge, perceptions, and attitudes toward Signal's security architecture. By integrating Signal users' insights with our SAD framework, we anticipate the broader user base's knowledge of Signal's security architecture will improve, thereby enhancing the platform's overall security posture. This study underscores the critical need to balance usability and security when designing secure communication systems. By adopting a dual focus on these aspects during the design and development process, we can achieve a more secure and secure-aware user base. This, in turn, will lead to increased user trust in Signal's security architecture. Through this work, we hope to inspire the broader research and design community to prioritize both usability and security, ultimately advancing the field of secure communication design. Precise solar energy integration is essential for deriving reliable times of sunrise and sunset, which are numerous (occurring twice daily) and thus require high precision. We introduce an algorithm grounded in Gaussian quadrature, enhanced with adaptive step sizing, interpolation, and postprocessing. The resulting solar quadrature technique, when combined with accurate expressions for Earth's orbital and axial irregularities, delivers these times with precision exceeding one second. Its efficiency allows for the generation of sunrise and sunset ephemerides at approximately 10 minutes per CPU core per day. The algorithm is open-source and universally applicable; while our study focuses on Earth, we have extended it to the entire periodic table of elements. Any user-defined function describing the apparent solar diurnal trajectory can be integrated, enabling the derivation of additional quantities of interest. Furthermore, the solar energy integrations for all periodic table elements are now publicly accessible via NASA ADS. The Earth-based implementation has also been made available as a standalone software tool, SolInt, which can be downloaded from GitHub. The SolInt software is capable of computing the precise duration of sunrise and sunset, as well as the integrated positions of the Sun's center and limb. Additionally, SolInt allows for the calculation of the integrated solar energy reaching a specific latitude and longitude, accounting for Earth's orbital and axial irregularities and atmospheric extinction. This approach yields a 1.5% increase in the total solar energy received during sunrise and sunset compared to the energy received during regular daylight hours. SolInt is also accessible via GitHub. All results presented in this study were generated using the approximate (non-atmospheric) version of the algorithm. The accuracy of the quadrature scheme is demonstrated to be better than one second, and the efficiency of the algorithm is also shown. This study examines the local curvature characteristics of ViViT's visual representation space, derived from the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix. By employing a normal approximation for the Hessian of the loss with respect to the GGN, we demonstrate that the product of the curvature matrix and the pre-trained GGN exhibits a low-rank structure, characterized by the multiplication of two low-rank matrices. This structural insight is validated through numerical experiments, which illustrate that the GGN within the ViViT representation space, when restricted to a specific subset, is indeed low-rank. Furthermore, we connect the GGN to the ViViT visual feature map, revealing that the former can be approximated by the outer product of periodic convolutional kernels. This finding underscores the existence of a low-dimensional manifold in the ViViT representation space, thereby bridging the gap between curvature analysis and representation learning. Ultimately, our research offers a novel perspective on understanding representation spaces, with potential applications extending beyond color spaces to other domains. Additionally, the code for the GGN factorization method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchenchen/curvature. Grammatical gender influences how nouns are categorized into gender-priming languages, where gendered nouns typically exhibit representations that are less central than those of non-gendered ones. This study aims to elucidate the mechanisms behind this phenomenon. We evaluated four hypotheses regarding the reasons behind reduced centrality in gender-priming languages using four distinct metrics: (1) gender centrality, (2) gender association, (3) gender animacy, and (4) hypernym centrality. These metrics were applied across 13 gendered languages, three gender-priming languages, and one non-gendered language, utilizing 1,029 gendered nouns and 390 non-gendered nouns drawn from 1,090 gender-labeling words in the GloWVar dataset. Our findings indicate that gendered nouns in gender-priming languages are less central than their non-gendered counterparts across all examined metrics. Specifically, in gender-priming languages, gendered nouns show weaker associations with non-gendered nouns and stronger associations with gendered nouns. Additionally, gendered nouns in these languages are less central than non-gendered nouns regardless of the specific animacy class. Finally, within gender-priming languages, gendered nouns remain less central than non-gendered nouns even when both belong to the same animacy class. Additionally, we establish a theorem linking the torsion subquotient charmability of an arithmetic group to its abelianization and offer a fine version of Agnihotri's result. By applying our methods, we derive a proof of a theorem by Agnihotri, Agnihotri, and Chen, which addresses the torsion charmability of (non-abelian) reductive algebraic groups defined over a number field, focusing on their abelianizations. We also present a conjecture regarding the torsion charmability of simply connected reductive algebraic groups in the form of examples, along with a theorem proving this conjecture for split reductive algebraic groups defined over a global field. Zero-shot object localization involves identifying instances of object classes that are not present in the training data. Prior research in this area has heavily depended on extensive annotations regarding object locations. In contrast, this study introduces a novel method that eliminates the requirement for any training labels related to object positions. By leveraging a large-scale dataset rich in class-level structural information, our approach infers object locations by modeling the class-specific spatial relationships between objects. Experimental results on the MS-COCO dataset for class-based position prediction demonstrate an average mAP of 24.5 across all training-negative classes, while also achieving strong performance on dataset-dependent position prediction tasks. Furthermore, this method holds significant potential for constructing large-scale position-supervised datasets. A key advantage of our approach is its ability to generate synthetic objects within scenes that accurately reflect realistic class-specific spatial relationships. The code is accessible at https://github.com/1000x1000/CoStruct.

Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management, planning, and control systems. While Deep Learning (DL) approaches have shown significant potential for predicting traffic flow based on historical data, they struggle with data sparsity and temporal forecasting. To address this, we introduce a similarity-driven Extravagance-Adjusted Transformer (EAT) that utilizes historical data to predict traffic flow. First, we employ a similarity-driven method to identify similar historical samples for each prediction, predicting flow rates using only these limited similar samples. Second, we design an Extravagance Adjuster to mitigate DL model errors caused by data extrapolation. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our EAT model predicts traffic flow 1.6 times more accurately than recent DL methods, outperforms recent Statistical models by up to 1.1 times, and surpasses recent Sparsity-aware Neural Networks by 1.1 times. Furthermore, EAT achieves an average 1.2 times better accuracy than the leading Time Series model. These findings indicate that our EAT model significantly enhances traffic forecast accuracy. Additionally, by relying solely on similar samples, EAT reduces training time by up to 90% and inference time by 1.1 times compared to the best-performing Neural Network. This enables efficient, high-accuracy prediction even with extensive sparse traffic data. The EAT model's source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhenghao1990/EAT. This paper introduces VACA, a flexible graph-based variational autoencoder designed for both latent recovery and counterfactual inquiries within linear structural equation models. While previous research has primarily focused on causal discovery and causal inference, the role of deep neural networks in manipulating causal graphs for counterfactual queries remains largely unexplored. VACA demonstrates superior performance in accurately estimating intervention effects and consistently identifies the correct causal structure for valid counterfactual queries. In contrast, standard deep autoencoders often yield inaccurate results in this context. Additionally, we successfully apply VACA to high-dimensional datasets and numerical examples to simultaneously estimate causal effects and compute counterfactual predictions for each observation based on observed data. Our results indicate that VACA is an effective tool for high-dimensional causal inference. The Irish LOFAR facility, situated in Birr, Co. Offaly, Ireland, currently operates as a free-standing array independent of the global LOFAR network due to its radio frequency cable constraints, which prevent observing below 100 MHz. Although the science benefits of joining the global network are significant, enhancing transient response capabilities was not a primary initial objective. However, recent efforts have successfully integrated REAL-time Transient Acquisition (REALTA), a newly developed real-time backend, into the LOFAR facility, thereby aligning it with the global system. These efforts include the implementation of real-time de-dispersion and real-time dedispersion across fractional delays to identify dynamic radio transients. This paper presents initial findings from the REALTA backend and discusses the system's capabilities regarding real-time transient acquisition, data recording, and live visualization. Additionally, it addresses how these features contribute to the real-time detection of radio transients. Finally, the study explores co-array differential voltage (dV) measurements using REALTA, analyzing data from various events such as fast radio bursts (FRBs), pulsars, and meteors. The results demonstrate that REALTA holds great promise for future real-time transient detection. Furthermore, the paper outlines strategies for further developing the system's real-time data recording and visualization features, including the development of an open-source real-time data visualization platform. These findings underscore the potential for further research into radio transients, with an emphasis on data acquisition, analysis, and visualization. Ultimately, these outcomes highlight the promising future of REALTA in the realm of real-time transient detection. (Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07377) (3 pages, 3 figures)

Although numerous studies have attempted to forecast box office revenue, few have examined how specific artistic choices—such as runtime, release season, or film type—influence gross income. However, lacking sufficient data has hindered previous efforts to quantify the impact of these creative decisions. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing the effects of pre-release information on revenue. We introduce CurtaFilm, the most comprehensive movie dataset available for machine learning, revenue analysis, and data mining. The dataset encompasses 15 features and 11,000 titles from IMDb. Our analysis reveals that releasing a film during holidays significantly boosts gross income, whereas other common decision factors like theater count, budget, or runtime do not. Furthermore, we demonstrate the 3D tag's detrimental effect on revenue and explore the nuanced relationship between runtime and income, noting that while shorter films tend to earn more, the trend flattens as runtime increases. This study introduces and analyzes a hybrid model-controllers designed for frequency and voltage regulation in smart grids, integrating auxiliary services such as primary frequency regulation and battery buffering. The proposed hybrid system is proven to be Lyapunov stable and demonstrates convergence to a set of equilibrium points that align with the physical operating points of the auxiliary services. Furthermore, a comparison against a pure voltage regulation system reveals an enhanced margin of Lyapunov stability for the hybrid system. These theoretical results are substantiated through numerical simulations conducted on a small-scale grid. Notably, the proposed solution is decentralized, requiring only local measurements and computations alongside auxiliary services, and is thus well-suited for real-world deployment. Additionally, the analysis indicates that the buffer capacity of the battery is not a limiting factor for the hybrid system's stability. Finally, the model-controllers are shown to be robust against significant parametric uncertainties in the grid. Consequently, the methodology is broadly applicable to various battery-based auxiliary frequency regulation services. Beyond this specific case, the study also addresses the challenge of model-controllers for frequency regulation and successfully extends the Lyapunov stability analysis to broader classes of such systems. This includes frequency-based auxiliary services with no strict convergence to physical operating points and battery-based services with constrained buffer capacities, thereby supporting their viable operation within a large state voltage space. Furthermore, a constraint on the voltage deviation from the nominal value is derived, which is essential for the stable operation of the hybrid system. Since this result is computationally efficient and relies solely on local information, it can be readily implemented in a real grid. Finally, the paper concludes by suggesting potential future extensions, such as incorporating fuzzy logic to handle nonlinear dynamics and introducing model predictive control for real-time parameter adaptation. These enhancements could significantly improve the performance of the hybrid frequency regulation model-controllers. Overall, this work provides a solid foundation for future research into frequency regulation model-controllers within smart grids. Notably, the developed framework is not limited to the specific frequency regulation services examined in this case study. By following the systematic approach for constructing frequency regulation model-controllers, the developed framework can be extended to other frequency regulation services, including those regulated by reactive power. This extension is highly relevant for future low-carbon electricity grids. Specifically, the proposed framework facilitates the design of frequency regulation services that are robust against parametric uncertainties, while also ensuring local and global stability, buffered frequency behavior, and cost-effectiveness. The origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra remains unresolved. This study investigates whether synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) or external-Compton (EC) scattering, involving photons from the accretion disc, could be responsible for this excess in the case of IC 432A. To assess the viability of these mechanisms, we employed a Monte-Carlo approach. Our findings indicate that the UV excess can be successfully modeled using a combination of disk blackbody radiation and partialy polarized external-Compton scattering off the accretion disc. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the soft X-ray excess can be reproduced through thermal Comptonization or a mixture of SSC and EC scattering from the disc. These results align with previous studies that utilized broadband spectral data to analyze blazar spectra. Ultimately, our results support the hypothesis that the UV/soft X-ray surplus in blazar spectra arises from a blend of disc radiation, low-energy EC scattering, and thermal Comptonization. Additionally, we predict that the polarization degree of the UV/soft X-ray excess should be approximately 10% and exhibit variability on timescales of hours. These predictions will be tested using the upcoming XMM-POLAR mission. Finally, we conclude that future broadband spectral observations of IC 432A are essential to determine the origin of this excess. We propose that the best approach involves simultaneous observations spanning from the far-UV to the soft X-ray range. This could be achieved through joint missions such as Hubble and Chandra, or potentially with the next-generation X-ray telescope, Athena. We also suggest that simultaneous polarization observations of IC 432A in the UV/soft X-ray range would be highly valuable. Such observations could be conducted using Hubble's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) or XMM-POLAR, with the latter offering the advantage of providing simultaneous spectral and polarization data. We present a method for jointly and adaptively detect symmetry pure states using generic and linear measurements. Joint measurement implies that all measurement operations occur simultaneously, while adaptive refers to the ability to select subsequent measurement operators based on prior outcomes. Our primary finding establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for joint and adaptive detectability of symmetry pure states within the framework of generic measurements. Furthermore, we provide a constructive proof of this theorem by proposing a specific measurement circuit that achieves the joint detection of these states. This circuit relies solely on power copies of the states and power implementations of power swap operators. Finally, we illustrate several applications of this approach to problems involving the distinguishability of symmetric subspaces and noiseless coding for symmetry subspaces. Additionally, we demonstrate the detection of specific sets of pure states, such as Fubini-Study frames, through joint measurement. However, for these instances, we must extend beyond a circuit built exclusively from power swap operators to include general swap operators. Notably, this extends previous work by utilizing swap operators instead of controlled-swap operators. Consequently, our findings offer a more efficient construction for achieving the joint measurement of symmetry pure states. Furthermore, our methodology eliminates the need for projective measurement in constructing the joint measurement operator for symmetry pure states. To achieve this, we develop a necessary and sufficient condition for orthogonality between two symmetry pure state sets, which may hold independent interest. We also examine the relationship between this condition and the concepts of completeness and tightness regarding Fubini-Study frames. Overall, this work advances our understanding of multiple detection and multiple cloning problems concerning symmetry pure states. Additionally, it provides a more streamlined construction for joint measurements of symmetry pure states, which can be directly applied as an optimal measurement without requiring projective measurement. This represents a significant improvement over the joint measurement proposed in arXiv:2007.01006. Finally, we suggest that these results may find applications in quantum key distribution. Specifically, we outline a quantum key distribution protocol that leverages joint measurement for symmetry pure states to construct an optimal measurement, thereby enhancing security compared to protocols that rely on projective measurement. This application underscores the practical significance of our findings. Furthermore, it offers an alternative solution to the problem of detecting symmetric pure states in quantum key distribution, distinct from the approach in arXiv:2007.01006. Baryon formation is examined through the quantum splintering of an elementary string along its transverse direction. By integrating Higgs' quantization of a massive bosonic string with specific QCD limits, a precise quasi-QCD model of the string width spectrum, or "thickness," is established. Utilizing the area law for flux loop entropy, the loop production probability is derived. Furthermore, by incorporating helical structure and performing a Hadamard renormalization of the loop action, the analysis investigates the particle creation mechanism. The study demonstrates that this splintering process, utilizing a simplified quasi-QCD string model, can account for the observed baryon-to-meson ratio. Additionally, the potential for this approach to explain the baryon anomaly in nuclear matter is explored. Finally, the string QCD model is shown to be applicable to the flux loop dynamics of quark-antiquark condensation. This framework enables the derivation of the nucleon mass from the vacuum expectation value of the flux loop density, while also yielding a non-perturbative model for the quark confining potential. Consequently, this method offers a means to determine the non-relativistic quark potential within QCD. To support these findings, a computer program and its corresponding Python code have been developed. A series of simulations based on this program, along with the results, are presented in a separate publication. These calculations confirm that the quasi-QCD string model can successfully represent the flux loop density in the quark-antiquark condensation model. Solar oscillations are utilized in helioseismology to probe the Sun's internal structure and dynamics. Solar active regions, which host intense magnetic fields and associated currents, are known to affect solar-mode oscillations by scattering their waves. This study examines how the three-dimensional distribution of electric currents within solar active regions influences the Sun's internal rotation profile, as derived from solar-mode helioseismic data. By simulating a magnetic flux tube within the convection zone and boundary region using the MHD code RAMSES, we demonstrate that the resulting current-carrying flux tube induces a kink instability. This instability causes magnetic field lines to twist around the tube axis, creating a current vortex. Such a vortex has a distinct impact on local magnetic field strength, which in turn affects the frequency shifts of overlying solar oscillations. Our results indicate that the magnetic topology of active regions, characterized by these current vortices, significantly influences local magnetic field strength and the internal rotation profile of the convection zone. Consequently, this effect must be accounted for when interpreting the Sun's rotation profile derived from helioseismic data. Our findings suggest a potential explanation for the previously observed north-south hemispheric asymmetry in solar-mode travel durations. This asymmetry may be attributed to the differing magnetic topologies of active regions in the northern and southern hemispheres, as characterized by their current distributions. Ultimately, this underscores the necessity of incorporating magnetic field and current data from SDO/HMI into future models of the convection zone's magnetic field topology. Such inclusion will enhance the accuracy of derived products, including the convection zone's internal rotation profile. Our conclusions are supported by the magnetic field and current distributions observed in active regions during Solar Cycle 23 and 24. We also provide evidence of a correlation between current density and the north-south asymmetry in travel-duration measurements. These findings offer a new perspective on understanding solar active regions and their influence on solar-mode travel durations. Our conclusions are consistent with the observed hemispheric asymmetry in magnetic flux emergence and the resulting magnetic topologies. Furthermore, our conclusions align with prior observations of the hemispheric difference in sunspot magnetic-field line tilts. This suggests that the north-south asymmetry in travel durations can be explained by the magnetic topologies of active regions in both hemispheres, as evidenced by their respective current distributions. Magnetars, characterized by extreme magnetic fields, are a rare and elusive subset of pulsars. While individual recent discoveries have begun revealing the impact of these magnetic fields on radio emission and neutron star structure, their influence on gravitational wave (GW) background remains unexplored. This study investigates how stochastic GW signals are affected by the collective behavior of the magnetic field within the pulsar timing spectrum band. We demonstrate that the stochastic GW background contains a stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) component generated by the coherent stochastic GW field induced by the crust's deformation due to magnetic field stress. This coherence is quantified by the eigenmode overlap factor of the crust. Our results indicate that the SGWB amplitude in the pulsar timing band is approximately $10^{-13}-10^{-12}$ in strain, with peak sensitivity around $10^{-12}$ at $1.5$ Hz. Furthermore, we show that the SGWB amplitude is independent of the specific magnetic field configuration, relying instead on the magnetic field energy density. Finally, we predict that future GW detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope, will be able to detect this SGWB with a signal-to-noise ratio of 5 or greater. This prediction is based on current estimates of the GW mode eigenfunction overlap factor and the average neutron star population. Consequently, SGWB detection serves as a promising avenue for identifying the average properties of magnetars within the pulsar timing spectrum band. Additionally, SGWB analysis can help distinguish between different magnetar models, such as those featuring magnetic stars or quark stars. This approach offers a novel method for uncovering the population of magnetars, which remains elusive despite extensive searches. We conclude that SGWB detection will facilitate the investigation of the average characteristics of magnetars. This represents a significant advancement in the field, as it marks the first time SGWB has been identified as a potential probe for magnetars. This finding is based on the work of [1] and [2]. This study addresses the emerging need for efficient, learning-based solutions in light field (LF) imaging across various applications. We introduce a novel approach to compressing parameterized LF representations, specifically free-form deformation (FFD) disparity models and plane equations. Our key innovation lies in applying a deformation only to regions with non-zero disparity while retaining original data for the rest. Additionally, we propose a new compression format that stores polynomial coefficients derived from solving linear equations based on plane equations, rather than directly storing the plane equations themselves. These methods substantially reduce data volume and enhance compression efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our technique achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) compression formats across multiple datasets. Finally, we evaluate these plans in two application contexts—plane-based rendering and FFD-based rendering—by comparing them against existing approaches. Experimental results confirm that our high-efficiency compression scheme outperforms current SOTA methods, marking a significant advancement for practical LF compression. Interactive methods, including online learning and interactive retrieval, have recently demonstrated performance comparable to or superior to traditional supervised and state-of-the-art vector-based cross-language information retrieval (CLIR) approaches. However, these methods currently depend on parallel document collections for training and retrieval processes. This paper investigates the application of both interactive and non-interactive frameworks to vector-based CLIR using only query sets, without any document collections. We evaluate two specific online learning and two query interactive cross-language retrieval algorithms alongside various configurations of non-interactive approaches, such as monolingual training and multilingual fine-tuning of pre-trained models. Our experiments across multiple languages reveal the limitations of interactive methods in a pure query-only context, indicating that vector-based CLIR remains dependent on sufficiently large monolingual document collections. Conversely, we conclude that interactive and non-interactive methods perform equivalently when accessing a document collection during language conversion. Although online learning methods yield significant improvements over monolingual techniques in standard retrieval scenarios, they still fall behind the emerging capabilities of fine-tuned pre-trained models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that interactive methods can achieve superior results even when compared to fine-tuned pre-trained models in standard retrieval settings. Overall, this study offers new insights into the benefits and limitations of interactive vector-based CLIR and the evolving role of pre-trained models within this domain. By bridging the gap between online learning and interactive retrieval, we aim to provide a more comprehensive understanding of vector-based CLIR and its practical applicability in real-world scenarios. This research addresses the challenge of constructing statistical estimators for small-area characteristics, with a specific focus on the specific contextual needs of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The investigation begins by analyzing the data structure of the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), which serve as the source for this estimation task. Leveraging the substantial size of the Rwanda DHS dataset, the study first develops local parametric models to account for the non-i.i.d. nature of the data. Subsequently, a collection of direct, Bayesian, and small-areas model-based estimators is developed. These estimators are directly tailored to the survey's sampling design and the specific distributional properties of the variables, which were previously established through the local modeling phase. Finally, the new model-based estimators are benchmarked against standard alternatives, including the direct estimator and two widely used small-area models. The results demonstrate that model-based estimators that incorporate design effects and local modeling assumptions significantly outperform standard approaches. This outcome is particularly relevant for LMICs, where the sample sizes of individual small areas are often too small to allow standard methods to reach their full potential. The analysis utilizes data from the 2010 Rwanda Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/SebastianKlauer/small_areasLMIC. Furthermore, we have created R packages to facilitate the implementation of these methods, which are named `small_areasLMIC` (available at: https://cran.r-project.org/package=small_areasLMIC) and `small_areasLMIC_survey` (available at: https://cran.r-project.org/package=small_areasLMIC_survey). The latter package specifically supports sampling designs involving multiple primary sampling units. Future work will involve extending the `small_areasLMIC` package to accommodate more intricate and generalizable multilevel models. Additionally, the `small_areasLMIC_survey` package is currently being updated to integrate generalized disaggregation methods for non-square sampling designs. Olivier Sanders and I have developed a framework for continuous-variable quantum mechanics that incorporates elements of the path integral formalism. This approach is straightforward and can be applied to continuous-time quantum dynamics. Although the opportunity to name it was missed, we have chosen to refer to it as Kelly Wagering, honoring the famous formula for optimal gambling strategies, which involves the optimal allocation of capital based on observed odds. In this context, odds correspond to the probability density of a trajectory, which is derived from the product of the conditional probability of the next state and the marginal probability of the previous state. The term "wagering" is used because the marginal probability density functions for state $x$ at time $t$ regarding a trajectory $x(t)$ are interpreted as the amount of "money" available at each instant. Consequently, the conditional probability density functions represent the available odds. The path integral for the probability density function of a trajectory is then expressed as the product of these monetary values. The name is somewhat forced, but it is hoped that it will be viewed as a creative interpretation rather than a derogatory one. The objective of this paper is to present the method and demonstrate its utility. The approach applies to any system described by the Schrödinger equation, $\mathrm{i}\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Psi(x,t)=H\Psi(x,t)$, where the wave function $\Psi(x,t)$ is a function of the position $x$ and time $t$, and $H$ is the system's Hamiltonian. The method involves three steps: first, calculating the marginal probability density functions for the position $x$ at each time $t$; second, determining the conditional probability density function $p(x(t+\Delta t)|x(t))$ for a trajectory $x(t)$, where $\Delta t$ is an infinitesimal time interval, using the marginal probability density functions; and third, computing the product of these two quantities to obtain the probability density for the trajectory $x(t)$. Finally, the probability density for an observable $A$ is calculated as the path integral of this product over all possible trajectories, weighted by the values of $A$ at each instant. This method extends the quantum formalism to the path integral representation of trajectories. Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered significant interest for their unique electronic and optical characteristics, including band gaps that are direct at the K and K' points, strong spin-orbit coupling, and valley-dependent magnetization. The recent introduction of group-IV monolayers, specifically MA$_2$ (where M = Mo, W, Ti and A = Si, Ge, S, Se, Te), has offered an alternative to TMDs with distinct properties. These materials exhibit either direct or anisotropic band gaps within the monolayer phase, alongside the ability to form stable, atomically thin honeycomb structures through hydrogenation. This study investigates the optical and electronic responses of MA$_2$Z$_2$ bilayers, where Z can be N, P, As, Sb, or Bi. Our findings indicate that the stacking configuration significantly influences the electronic and optical behaviors of these bilayers, with a moiré potential of approximately 0.01 eV affecting the optical band gap. The position of quasiparticle energies relative to the conduction band minimum (CBM) and valence band maximum (VBM) is highly sensitive to the specific elements comprising the lattice. Notably, the distance between quasiparticle energies near the CBM and VBM remains unaffected by the stacking configuration, resulting in QS excitonic peaks that are independent of the number of layers in the bilayer. These results provide a pathway for engineering the optical and electronic properties of MA$_2$Z$_4$ bilayers, potentially enabling applications in quantum information science. This could include the creation of quantum dots by modifying the layer count to manipulate QS excitonic peaks, thereby controlling charge carriers. Additionally, the layer count can be used to tune the optical band gap, facilitating applications in solar cells and photodetectors. Furthermore, the valley-dependent magnetization of these bilayers could enhance their utility in spintronic devices. This research also establishes a foundation for future investigations into the optical and electronic properties of other hydrogenated monolayers, such as monolayer black phosphorus and germanene, which also possess direct band gaps at the K and K' points. This could lead to the development of new optical and electronic devices with enhanced performance. Finally, the study may contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental physical properties of two-dimensional materials and their interactions. The formation of stars and their surrounding protoplanetary disks is fundamentally driven by the gravitational collapse of dense cores within molecular clouds. This process typically involves the creation of a central protostar through the inward accretion of material from the core. The critical question of how the stellar object develops the necessary non-rotating accretion structure to counteract the core's rapid rotation remains a significant focus of current research. We propose that the disruption of a prestellar nucleus by the developing protostar provides the solution to this problem of disk formation. Specifically, the collapse of the core's peripheral density material generates a turbulent disk around the protostar, which subsequently slows the accretion rate via viscous friction. This reduction in density at the center of the prestellar cloud leads to the breaking of its nucleus, a dense region situated off-axis relative to the disk. The resulting secondary collapse of this nucleus around the protostar provides a viable explanation for how large disks are fed by their surrounding material reservoirs. Furthermore, the rapid development of the disk and the creation of a secondary protostar within the disk from the prestellar nucleus could offer a resolution to the otherwise enigmatic "twinkle-free" transition observed in young stellar objects. Additionally, our model accounts for the presence of massive planets in these systems and the early detection of their giant gas envelopes. Finally, our approach offers a new perspective on the environmental impact of core collapse, suggesting that the collapse of the outer peripheral material may be suppressed by the radiation pressure from the newly formed stellar object. This could help explain the puzzling lack of massive stars found in crowded star-forming regions. Overall, our model demonstrates that the gravitational collapse of the prestellar cloud's outer regions is a crucial link in the entire process of star and planetary system formation. The findings presented in this paper may also contribute to the ongoing debate regarding whether massive stars form via accretion from a massive disk or through the direct gravitational collapse of the parent cloud. Specifically, our results suggest that the direct gravitational collapse of the parent cloud is unlikely to occur, as it would likely be hindered by radiation pressure from the stellar object. Consequently, this supports the view that massive stars form through the accretion of matter from a massive disk. Atmospheric scattering significantly influences both the contrast and color of direct imaging observations of exoplanets and protoplanetary disks. Consequently, accurately modeling this scattering process is crucial for interpreting these observations and distinguishing between exoplanets and disks. However, current models often simplify atmospheric properties, such as pressure, by assuming a single value. This study investigates the impact of pressure variations across different atmospheric layers on scattered light. We developed a straightforward model that accounts for molecular absorption, Rayleigh scattering, and Mie scattering from dust and aerosols. By varying the Mie scattering albedo and Mie parameter, we examined how these factors affect scattered light spectra. Our findings indicate that considering vertical pressure variations within an atmosphere substantially alters the model's output, thereby providing a more precise representation of planetary atmospheric scattering. Furthermore, our study offers initial insights into how aerosol characteristics depend on atmospheric pressure. These results aim to guide future spectral fitting studies of exoplanets and planets disks, ultimately aiding in the identification of planetary systems. Our scattered light models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuan1999/SimpleScatteredLightModel. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundation for the next study in this series, which will compare the appearance of directly imaged exoplanets and protoplanetary planets against observed data. We present a multi-term temporal sequence modeling framework designed to capture complex temporal dependencies. This approach extends a recently introduced sequence modeling method that leverages a non-homogeneous Poisson process to represent temporal event occurrences. Unlike previous techniques that rely on a single time distribution, our method proposes a multi-term structure to model diverse temporal behaviors. To ensure efficient training, we apply a Bayesian formulation, integrating both prior and likelihood distributions into the training objective. This Bayesian perspective unifies sequence modeling with uncertainty quantification. Additionally, we embed a sparsity-inducing prior into the prior distribution, which regularizes the training process and simplifies the model by eliminating superfluous parameters. Experimental results across various synthetic and real-world scenarios demonstrate that our method effectively models heterogeneous temporal behaviors and accurately quantifies uncertainty. Our multi-term sequence modeling technique offers a versatile solution for modeling complex temporal dependencies in temporal event data. This study examines the ethical dimensions of federated learning, a machine learning framework where a central server initiates and steers training, while computations are executed locally on client devices using their own data. Although this approach is widely celebrated for enhancing privacy and data security, we identify a lesser-known ethical dimension concerning the data and computational environments involved. This analysis is crucial for practitioners and policymakers who must determine the suitability of participating clients and configure the learning process to foster collaboration. We propose an ethical framework to guide these decisions, with specific applications to federated learning participation and policy configuration. This framework draws upon concepts of justice from communicative justice theory and confidentiality from computer-mediated communication theory. Additionally, we explore how the design of incentive mechanisms, such as transfer learning, can promote ethical behavior within this process. Through case studies of air quality monitoring and mental health support, we illustrate how this framework applies to Federated Average and Transfer Learning scenarios. Ultimately, we argue that integrating ethical considerations into federated learning systems is essential for achieving the full potential of this promising technology. This involves not only recruiting the most appropriate participants but also fostering their engagement through the collaborative spirit inherent to federated learning. Furthermore, we note that federated learning extends beyond merely centralizing data; it also serves to empower and connect diverse communities by facilitating their participation in the AI revolution. By promoting collaboration among both practitioners and the communities involved, federated learning has the capacity to transcend traditional computational and social boundaries. This capacity represents a significant, albeit often overlooked, source of value that contributes to the broader societal benefits of machine learning. Consequently, we recommend that researchers, practitioners, and policymakers actively seek to maximize these ethical values within federated learning systems. This could involve establishing new policies to encourage ethical participation and adopting an early-stage ethical review process to assess the eligibility of potential participants, their specific configurations, and the appropriateness of the federated learning approach for their data and computational contexts. Furthermore, we suggest that an extended definition of data sovereignty, encompassing the computational and human contexts where data resides, should be adopted. This would broaden the scope of ethical considerations regarding data governance in federated learning. Finally, we conclude that federated learning extends beyond traditional machine learning by connecting diverse communities, and we advocate for increased attention to the computational and human contexts where these communities exist. This focus on the communities involved may also constitute another source of value within federated learning. This study investigates dark energy within the supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ framework at TeV energies, utilizing right-handed Majorana neutrinos as dark energy candidates. The cosmological dark energy density is attributed to the collective small Majorana mass terms of these neutrinos. We demonstrate that the lightest right-handed neutrino can serve as dark matter, while the second and third particles provide dark energy. The small mass of the lightest neutrino, responsible for dark matter, is attributed to the suppression from the smallest mixing matrix element between SM fermions and right-handed neutrinos. We examine the phenomenology of this scenario, including the decay of the dark energy state to dark matter and the production mechanisms for dark matter. Additionally, we analyze the contribution of $Z'$ decays to dark matter production. Finally, we discuss experimental signatures and place constraints on this model. This framework offers a comprehensive explanation for dark matter, dark energy, the baryon asymmetry of the universe, and the origin of SM fermion masses and mixing. Furthermore, it suggests a potential explanation for the observed lepton non-universality in B-meson decays. The model is highly predictive and can be tested through future experimental searches for $Z'$ bosons and lepton universality violations. We conclude that the proposed framework provides a unified and complete description of the physics governing the dark universe. The model is simple, predictive, and elegant, with all parameters derivable from low-energy physical observables. Consequently, this represents the most promising theoretical approach to understanding dark matter and dark energy. We anticipate that the proposed scenario will be validated in the near future through upcoming experimental observations. We have also submitted a related manuscript to arXiv under the title "Unified and Complete Description of the Dark Universe." In our conclusion, we state that the $Z'$ boson must decay into right-handed neutrinos, and we urge experimentalists to actively search for this phenomenon. We also note that our findings may be relevant to the recent CDF-II measurement of the W boson mass. We believe our theoretical predictions will be confirmed through future experimental searches for the $Z'$ boson and violations of lepton universality. This paper introduces an IRS-assisted wireless network energized by eTEG, focusing on throughput analysis through a "Time-sharing" approach for disrupted and non-disrupted scenarios. In these environments, we derive the optimal charging duration for the eTEG and the ideal Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) allocation to maximize average throughput. To address imperfect Channel State Information (CSI), we utilize a First-Order Taylor series expansion to calculate the optimal operating time, leading to the design of two Time-sharing strategies. The first strategy targets throughputs for both healthy and disrupted nodes, while the second focuses exclusively on healthy nodes; in both cases, we determine the optimal beamforming vector. We subsequently compare the performance of these two strategies and propose an unsupervised learning method to identify the strategy that maximizes throughput. Simulation results confirm that the proposed strategies achieve significant throughput improvements over alternatives, particularly under imperfect CSI conditions. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the strategy design is significantly lower than that of traditional methods. Finally, our experiments demonstrate that the unsupervised learning approach effectively identifies the optimal strategy to maximize throughput. The logft$_{K}$ values for the super-allowed $\beta^-$ transitions to the $0^+$ ground states of even-even daughter nuclei in the A=186 isobaric mass chain are determined to be 6.01 $\pm$ 0.08 (using IT$(^{186}$Hg) = 828 ns) and 5.96 $\pm$ 0.08 (using IT$(^{186}$Hg) = 860(20) ns). These results establish $^{186}$Hg as a potential reference source for $\beta$-decay physics experiments, pending future experimental confirmation of the longer half-life. The study also reports $Q_{\beta^-$ values and mass excesses, which align with previous experimental data and serve as input for shell model calculations. Additionally, the work includes measurements of $\log g_A$ and 2nd-forbidden non-unique (2FU-NU) $\beta^-$ decay in $^{186}$Hg, providing the first experimental determination of this branch. The 2FU-NU character is supported by the observed shape of the $\beta$-spectrum and the calculated matrix element $g_A$ = 1.40 $\pm$ 0.15, consistent with the nuclear shell model. In this scenario, the dark matter candidate is the superpartner of the second linear combination of the $A4$ gauge bosons, while the remainder of its scalar fermion component forms a triplet responsible for neutrino mass generation. This triplet decays into the dark matter particle and a neutrino, producing the correct dark matter abundance and accounting for neutrino masses and mixings. Furthermore, within the supergravity framework, the dark matter candidate can also originate from the decays of heavy neutrinos, thereby inducing the leptogenesis mechanism. Consequently, this scheme offers a unified explanation for dark matter, neutrino masses, CP violation, and the baryon asymmetry of the universe. Finally, we examine the relationship between dark matter and neutrino parameters, finding that this model provides a distinct dark matter candidate with a scalar component essential for neutrino mass generation, distinguishing it from the pure gauge boson nature of similar models in non-supersymmetric settings. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between the dark matter relic density and the effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom ($N_{eff}$). Finally, we analyze the relationship between dark matter and neutrino parameters, suggesting that this model uniquely explains the smallness of dark matter relic density and the smallness of neutrino masses through a single parameter. These relationships are visualized in two distinct scenarios: one where the dark matter candidate is stable, and another where it is generated via the thermal effective potential method. In this latter case, the dark matter relic density is primarily determined by the mass of the next-to-lightest supersymmetric particle (NLSP). Finally, we discuss the relationship between dark matter and $N_{eff}$, noting that in this scenario, dark matter is fermionic, which influences the neutrino oscillation parameters. Data-Informed Control (DIC) represents a hybrid control framework that integrates model-based and data-driven methods, leveraging supplementary data or knowledge to enhance performance. By merging these approaches, DIC aims to overcome the limitations of individual paradigms, yielding superior outcomes in control tasks characterized by high nonlinearity, strong couplings, and significant uncertainties. However, DIC performance is highly dependent on the quality of supplementary information; in biological and robotic locomotion, for instance, inaccurate environmental models can lead to suboptimal results. To address this vulnerability, we introduce a robust and versatile robust optimization scheme that utilizes DIC alongside explicit uncertainty quantification to derive control policies robust against uncertainties. The efficacy of this proposed method is validated through robust policy optimization across high-fidelity simulators for complex locomotion tasks in both biological and robotic systems, including flying, walking, swimming, and climbing under significant disturbances and parameter variations. This study demonstrates that combining robust optimization with DIC enables the simultaneous learning of diverse locomotion skills from minimal data and supplementary knowledge, offering a promising pathway for future biological locomotion research and the development of next-generation robots. Specifically, we illustrate that simulating biological locomotion and developing robust bio-inspired robots are inherently linked processes that must be integrated. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying promising future research directions, such as the robust optimization and development of bio-inspired robots, the robust control of biological locomotion, and biological locomotion research within uncertain environments. These outcomes aim to provide a new perspective for advancing biological locomotion science and robotics, particularly regarding robust policy optimization utilizing sophisticated control frameworks like DIC. Keywords: Robust Control, Robust Optimization, Data-Driven Control, Biological Locomotion, Robust Policy Optimization, Robotic Locomotion.

This work investigates a two-dimensional Toda matter-field theory with three degrees of freedom, described by a matter-sector Lie algebra of type $\mathfrak{sl}_3$. The study calculates Ward relations and correlation functions for degenerate fields, specifically those with conformal weights corresponding to the highest-derivative representations of the matter-sector Virasoro algebra (except for the unitary one), as well as for the stress-energy tensor field. The analysis covers various channel permutations and establishes a set of independent Ward relations applicable to arbitrary insertion points. Additionally, scaling laws for degenerate fields are derived. Finally, the study examines a specific 4-point correlation function and examines the potential existence of a dual independent set of Ward relations. This approach could offer valuable functional equations for exploring the full operator algebra and correlation functions within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory. Furthermore, this methodology may serve as a foundation for examining higher-rank generalized conformal models, such as the fractal and affine Liouville models. All results are supported by explicit computations and numerical verification. For reference, the computer code used is available at: https://github.com/alexei-panov/sl3-toda-ward-relations. Furthermore, this paper serves as a supplement to the second installment of a series, *Series 2*, which derives and examines higher-rank functional equations for 4-point correlation functions in the fractal and affine Liouville models, utilizing the derived Ward relations as input. The findings of *Series 2* are intended to be independent of the intermediate calculation methods employed in *Series 1*. While *Series 1* relies on a variant of the functional equation approach pioneered in [Georgiev, 1995], *Series 2* primarily employs the bootstrap method, building upon the framework established in [Fendley, 2009]. Both series present novel results and offer fresh perspectives on functional equations and correlation functions in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model. The structure of *Series 2* is designed to be adaptable for broader applications in conformal field theory, particularly for models involving higher-rank Lie algebras. Additionally, *Series 2* aims to provide a self-contained exposition of the bootstrap approach, as well as the functional equation approach pioneered in [Georgiev, 1995] and [Fendley, 2009]. Recent advancements in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) demonstrate that structural knowledge can be integrated into the latent space of image generation models. This paper investigates how Triplet Loss can enhance Relation Networks within a GAN framework. By employing Triplet networks, we aim to create a more structured and informative latent space for Relation GANs. Specifically, we validate that the relation space becomes more discriminative, allowing for the accurate reconstruction of new images from previously unseen images. Additionally, we establish that our relation space maintains both class and instance discriminativity while supporting the generation of images from novel inputs. Finally, experimental results confirm that combining connectionist knowledge with Relation GANs and Triplet Loss yields competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods on standard image classification datasets. Code is accessible at: https://github.com/abdelrahimhassan/Relation-GANs-with-Triplet-Loss.

We demonstrate that twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKD) can operate without phase synchronization between twin fields by employing random phase modulation on one of them. Our findings indicate that within the high-rate single-photon regime, TF-QKD outperforms standard BB84 protocols by approximately 3 dB in high-energy signal thresholds, even when accounting for phase randomization costs. Furthermore, in this regime, TF-QKD can double the transmission distance of BB84 systems, potentially extending it from 100 km to over 200 km in realistic scenarios. To achieve these results, we applied a modified version of the finite-key post-processing technique for TF-QKD previously developed by our group, which incorporates a more accurate estimation of phase error rates and enhanced corrections for finite-key effects. These advancements are expected to be beneficial for other quantum communication protocols beyond TF-QKD. Notably, the proposed method eliminates the need for phase synchronization between twin fields, thereby reducing the complexity of experimental setups and control systems. This represents a significant step toward the practical realization of TF-QKD. Additionally, the finite-key analysis utilized here is a refined adaptation of a method previously introduced for TF-QKD. Given that the computational complexity of such analysis scales exponentially with the number of parameters, our optimized finite-key analysis is anticipated to offer better performance than previous approaches, particularly within the finite-key regime. Consequently, it may pave the way for the practical deployment of TF-QKD systems. Finally, the finite-key security proof for TF-QKD presented in this work was previously published in *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 127, 180503 (2021). The revised version of this paper includes several modifications to the original version of the study. Specifically, we have: (i) incorporated corrections regarding the handling of phase error rates and their impact on key generation rates within the finite-key regime; (ii) substituted the reference to the original version of the TF-QKD finite-key security proof with the newly published version; and (iii) acknowledged the contribution of Dr. Masahiro Hasegawa to the original idea of the twin-field protocol. These changes were necessary to address inquiries received from other researchers. We apologize for any confusion this may have caused. We have also made minor adjustments to the text to improve readability. We extend our sincere apologies for these omissions. We look forward to the practical realization of TF-QKD. Identizing objects with a pseudo-bounding box using only their numeric identifiers represents a core component of human-like situational awareness within robotics. This study investigates the feasibility of developing an open lexicon model capable of mapping numeric object labels to visual representations. We introduce a novel object identification metric termed "visual closure rate," which quantifies an model's ability to visually distinguish between different objects. To address the scarcity of bounding box data required for training, we propose a new pseudo-bounding box annotation technique. Experimental results demonstrate that pseudo-bounding box datasets yield visual closure rates comparable to those of real bounding box datasets. Furthermore, we explore the potential of combining this approach with open-set learning to enable the identification of novel objects. Ultimately, this research paves the way for creating visual closure-based intelligent systems. Specifically, we anticipate that an visual closure-aware model will surpass traditional object recognition models in open lexicon object identification tasks. To facilitate this, we have made our code and pseudo-bounding box point cloud datasets publicly available. Additionally, we offer a new benchmark dataset designed for visual closure-based object identification. This dataset features objects within cluttered scenes, color variations, diverse shapes, and occlusions, and uniquely provides visual closure rate labels for each object, making it the first of its kind. We expect this dataset to be valuable for developing generalist robots. The Pictorial Sky Survey captured images of the region surrounding S1 in Rho Oph A at 4861 \AA\ (atomic hydrogen), 6563 \AA\ (ionized hydrogen), and 6409 \AA\ (ions). These images were analyzed to determine the spatial distribution of the corresponding gas phases. The ionized gas exhibits a filamentary structure that aligns with the region's magnetic field, while atomic hydrogen shows a clumpy pattern. Notably, the atomic hydrogen is absent near the ionizing star S1 but is abundant within the magnetic filaments where ionized gas is detected. This suggests that ionizing photons from S1 are absorbed by dust grains located within the magnetic filaments, preventing them from reaching adjacent atomic hydrogen clouds. Consequently, the magnetic filaments act as a barrier, shielding the atomic hydrogen clouds from the ionizing radiation. The resulting interface between ionized and atomic hydrogen gas manifests as a thin layer of photodissociated molecular gas, visible at 6409 \AA\ as a narrow structure tracing the boundary between the HII region and the atomic hydrogen cloud. The magnetic field's influence on the spatial distribution of both ionized and atomic hydrogen gas is evident. Additionally, the Pictorial Sky Survey images reveal a previously unknown HII region situated between the Rho Oph A and B clouds, which is likely illuminated by S1. The spatial distribution of ionized and atomic hydrogen gas observed in this newly discovered HII region further supports the hypothesis that magnetic fields exert a significant impact on the spatial distribution of ionized gas. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the spatial distribution of ionized, atomic, and PDR gas around S1 in the Rho Oph A cloud. By examining the interactions between these gas components, the study seeks to enhance our knowledge of the physical processes occurring within the cloud. Ultimately, the research contributes to a deeper understanding of the star formation process.
