Though the transformer architecture has proven highly effective for general Natural Language Processing, its application within Vision remains limited. This paper seeks to adapt transformers for vision tasks and assess their efficacy. To achieve this, we examine the primary challenges faced by conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in vision, subsequently outline key innovations that integrate transformers into sight. Finally, we offer a comprehensive review of KITSA-Transformers, a burgeoning subfield, by detailing fundamental concepts through a series of seminal studies, with all resources available at https://github.com/ashrafulhassan/KitSA-Transformers. KitSA-Transformers encompasses Pre-Trained Transformers (KITSA-PTr), Transferable Transformers (KITSA-Tr), and Transferable Subfield Adaptive Transformers (KITSA-TSAT). KITSA-PTr highlights models where pre-trained language transformers are fine-tuned for vision, while KITSA-Tr illustrates approaches that fine-tune image-based models pre-trained on large-scale visual datasets like ImageNet. KITSA-TSAT demonstrates the versatility of transformers across nearly all vision tasks, including super-resolution, object detection, image classification, dense prediction, denoising, deblurring, deforming, segmentation, clustering, regression, and classification. The study concludes by identifying current limitations and proposing promising future research directions. Given its thorough examination of KITSA-Transformers, this work serves as a valuable reference for researchers and students in the domain. Furthermore, it offers an exhaustive analysis of the field's strengths and weaknesses, effectively addressing the gap for an introductory resource on KITS-AI and Machine Learning Subdomains. The authors hope this paper will inspire future research and contribute to the continued advancement of transformers in subfields of vision, computer vision, and image processing. The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare. Keywords: Transformers in Sight, KITSA-Transformers, Deep Learning, Computer Vision, Image Processing, Review. This study evaluates candidate factor models for mortality prediction using data from English, American, and Russian life tables. We demonstrate that a Cointegration Factor Model (CFM), which assumes time-constant factor loadings, performs comparably to a Factor Model with Time-varying Covariates Model (CFM-TVCM), which allows loadings to change, in terms of predictive accuracy. However, the CFM is significantly simpler, making it the more attractive option. Additionally, we introduce a new approach for estimating a discrete-time CFM. This involves constructing a cointegration matrix by ranking the Granger causality between factors and levels, followed by the development of a non-parametric estimator based on local linear regression. The advantages of this new estimator are illustrated through simulations and an analysis of English life table data. A primary obstacle in Neural Architecture Exploration (NAS) is the inherent disruption of the sequential learning process caused by extensive co-learning sessions required to train and evaluate architectures. This work investigates the origin of this disruption and proposes a method to mitigate it by training and evaluating multiple architectures simultaneously in a non-sequential manner. Our approach involves learning a shared feature extractor on several architectures at once, while independently training their specific task-dependent final layers. We demonstrate that this technique effectively reduces co-learning time by up to 90% without compromising the quality of the resulting architectures. The method is demonstrated to be effective across two fields: automatic speech recognition and classification tasks within the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. Furthermore, we show that the learned shared features are transferable between architectures belonging to functionally distinct classes, highlighting the method's ability to balance the exploration of both high-performance and high-generalization architectures. Additionally, we explore the connection between shared features learned by this approach and those found in Neural Process ensembles, offering insights into the method's efficacy. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/NAS-SharedFeatures. Given that the method operates without any form of regularization, we anticipate its applicability to a wide range of additional architectures. The method's ability to learn shared features also offers valuable insights into the internal representations of neural networks. Finally, we demonstrate that the approach can be utilized to regularize the sequence of architecture training, thereby improving the quality of the explored set. Our findings suggest that the shared learning method serves as a versatile tool for addressing challenges in large-scale NAS. The training code for experiments described in this work can be found at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/NAS-SharedFeatures. The methodologies presented here also offer a pathway for learning task-agnostic representations in other domains. The method's versatility as a tool for large-scale NAS is also worth noting. Attribute-Based Time Series (ABTS) extend traditional time series by incorporating extra dimensions, such as geographical locations or individual characteristics. The ability to analyze and visualize these datasets is essential for uncovering hidden patterns, whether for statistical or machine learning applications. However, R currently lacks native ABTS functionality, necessitating the use of various libraries and ad-hoc code, which often results in inconsistent and non-intuitive outcomes. To address this, the `thief` package offers an ABTS solution. This paper reviews `thief` by demonstrating how it facilitates data manipulation, aggregation, grouping, visualization, and examination within R. Through a series of examples, we illustrate these capabilities using both synthetic and real-world data. Ultimately, `thief` provides users with an efficient, intuitive, and consistent approach for working with attribute-based time series in R. Finally, through examples, we demonstrate that $D$ does not satisfy either geodesic $k$-cat$(0)$ or $k$-cat$(0)C$. Within an Agile framework, translators in a localization environment are assessed daily on their output quality to facilitate their inclusion in a quality guarantee process. This evaluation aims to determine their daily dependability, guiding quality managers in assigning future tasks. We introduce a Bayesian approach to assess translator quality in data-driven ways. By modeling human data generation through a generalized beta distribution, we enable the computation of a translator's probability of correctness. This metric serves as a reliable quality indicator in scenarios where direct assessment of output is infeasible, such as when functional testing is unavailable in the target context. Consequently, managers can make data-driven decisions regarding the allocation of future tasks. We validate this methodology using performance data from an industrial case study. The experimental results demonstrate that the Bayesian approach outperforms the traditional method, which relies on a binomial distribution, in terms of accuracy and stability. Specifically, our approach yields higher accuracy in predicting a translator's quality and exhibits superior stability in predicting their probability of correctness. Ultimately, we show that integrating data and methods from diverse domains can significantly enhance the management processes in localization projects. This paper serves as a proof of concept for our proposed methodology. Future research will explore its application in collaborative translation scenarios to improve the efficiency of professional crowd-sourcing initiatives. Finally, we aim to expand this concept to evaluate the quality of machine translation post-editing. The source code for the methodology is available at: https://github.com/fernandagarcia22/bayesian-translator-quality-evaluation. The project was developed in collaboration with industry partners. In an open quantum or classical system subjected to a time-dependent driving field, energy absorption occurs when the system is excited from its ground state. This study examines the linear response of a half-open system to a scalar or vector potential that vanishes at large distances. We present sum-rule analyses of the total energy absorption characteristic, a property independent of the system's initial state. This analysis is based on a complete set of "energy absorption eigenchannels," whose construction relies on solutions to a Schrödinger-like equation. While closely related to "Floquet eigenchannels" derived from the stationary scattering matrix (the large-time limit of the time-dependent S-matrix), the two differ in that the construction of energy absorption eigenchannels does not require explicit knowledge of the time-independent Floquet scattering matrix. We demonstrate this approach through a detailed analysis of energy absorption in hydrogen within a linearly polarized, arbitrarily time-dependent electric field. This methodology is potentially applicable to various quantum systems, serving as a valuable tool for investigating quantum dissipation. Additionally, we demonstrate that our previously established sum-rule analysis of stationary scattering frameworks remains consistent with the standard analysis of bound systems, where scattering states are unphysical. In this context, all energy absorption eigenchannel energies correspond to bound-state energies, and the sum-rule analysis relies on the Coulomb bound-state spectrum. This analysis is uniquely consistent with the standard analysis of bound systems, which is not based on energy absorption eigenchannels. Finally, we discuss the implications of this study for the broader field of nonequilibrium quantum physics. Specifically, we illustrate that the sum-rule analysis of energy absorption, when applied to both bound and scattering systems, serves as a valuable consistency check for the corresponding sum-rule analysis of energy dissipation. While the latter analysis is currently applicable to both quantum and classical systems, it lacks the rigorous derivation found in the energy absorption analysis. Consequently, the sum-rule analysis of energy absorption provides a critical consistency check for the recently developed sum-rule analysis of energy dissipation in both quantum and classical systems. This ensures that the latter analysis remains consistent with the standard sum-rule analysis of bound systems, thereby supporting the broader goals of nonequilibrium quantum physics. Ultimately, this work aims to advance the understanding of fundamental nonequilibrium phenomena, such as energy dissipation, in both quantum and classical systems. These findings contribute to the broader objective of developing a more comprehensive and consistent theoretical framework for analyzing energy dissipation in both quantum and classical systems. Fully connected neural networks, including convolutional architectures, contain numerous redundant parameters that can be eliminated without compromising performance. Although pruning techniques have been applied to various network types, no study to date has attempted to prune a fully connected convolutional network down to the extent of a standard convolutional network. By applying aggressive pruning to such a fully connected structure, we can determine whether a conventional convolutional network represents the "Winning Lottery Ticket" within a fully connected framework. This research investigates three primary hypotheses: first, whether parameters in a fully connected network are as highly redundant as those in a convolutional one; second, whether the sparsity of the winning lottery ticket in a fully connected setting is comparable to that in a convolutional one, specifically regarding convolutional weights; and third, whether the sparsity of the winning lottery ticket in a fully connected network is comparable to that of a mixture of expert (MiE) models, which combine multiple convolutional networks. Our findings indicate that the answers to these hypotheses are largely affirmative. Furthermore, the winning lottery ticket in a fully connected network appears to resemble a mixture of expert (MiE) models, where the set of winning parameters corresponds to those of one or more experts within the MiE structure. This suggests that the winning lottery ticket in a fully connected network may represent the union of experts from an MiE model, where each expert functions as a convolutional network. Consequently, the winning lottery ticket in a fully connected network exhibits characteristics similar to those found in convolutional networks, mixture-of-experts models, and other sparsely activated networks. This implies that if a winning lottery ticket in a fully connected network exists, it likely shares similar attributes with networks containing sparsity. We present a new approach to purchasing lottery tickets by maximizing their anticipated value, which hinges on predicting future winning numbers. While existing solutions, such as past performance analysis or naive forecasts like uniform distributions, fail to adequately solve this problem, we introduce two key innovations. First, we establish the first end-to-end trainable framework for maximizing lottery ticket utility. Second, we propose a transformer-based sequence-to-sequence deep learning model, Transformer-Lottery, which utilizes historical draw data as input to forecast subsequent winning sequences. This model is optimized end-to-end through a custom differentiable non-linear function, which is derived after reformulating the expected value calculation for the super-prize to be differentiable. By training this model on past draw data, we generate probabilistic forecasts of future winning numbers, which are then incorporated into the optimization process. This results in optimized strategies that significantly outperform all baselines, achieving approximately a 10% increase in value. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model can be easily adapted for integration with blockchain technology, enabling decentralized trust and transparency. Finally, we release an open-source implementation of our solution for real-world deployment. Based on our findings, we recommend deploying open-source strategies for new lottery games that have a track record of at least 10 years of past draws. Additionally, we highlight that the value of a lottery ticket is highly time-dependent, suggesting that existing strategies should be deployed immediately to capitalize on current ticket values. To facilitate deployment, we have also released a high-level abstraction of our solution. This allows developers to focus on specific features of their chosen lottery game, such as the number of options, the size of the option pool, and the cost per option, without needing to understand the underlying value maximization logic. In summary, the core contributions of this work are: (1) a new framework for maximizing lottery ticket value by end-to-end optimizing value maximization strategies; (2) a transformer-based deep learning model, Transformer-Lottery, designed to maximize ticket value; (3) a blockchain-integrated implementation for decentralized trust and transparency; (4) a high-level abstraction enabling the deployment of optimized strategies; and (empirical results) demonstrating that Transformer-Lottery significantly enhances ticket value. Additionally, we provide practical guidance for developers and analysts on implementing optimized strategies, including recommendations on when to adopt them. Finally, we offer actionable advice for policymakers and decision-makers, such as setting a minimum threshold of 10 years of past draw results before deploying new strategies.

Valley engineering has become essential for two-dimensional materials due to their essential electronic valley characteristics. This study investigates the impact of various electron-phonon interaction mechanisms on valley dynamics, specifically focusing on time-resolved valley Hall conductivity and optically pumped spin-relaxation time. We systematically analyzed phonon dispersion variations across different two-dimensional substances to identify novel phenomena. Furthermore, we developed a rigorous theoretical framework for electron-phonon interactions that goes beyond the conventional deformation potential model. Our results indicate that modifying the valley response to time-resolved electromagnetic pulses is straightforward by selecting an appropriate pulse frequency. Additionally, we demonstrated that altering the spin-phonon coupling mechanism can significantly influence valley dynamics. These findings offer a comprehensive approach for effectively controlling valley properties and provide a robust theoretical basis to advance the field of valley electronics. The numerical code used in this study will be made available for public use. Additionally, our work identifies several materials with unique electron-phonon interaction features that hold significant promise for future applications. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) and its derivative, t-SNE, are prominent techniques for non-linear dimensionality reduction and data visualization. Designed for Euclidean data, they fail within the non-isometric framework of spherical geometry. This paper introduces VMF-SNE, a method specifically designed for representation and visualization on spherical manifolds. By utilizing the von Mises-Fisher distribution and geodesic distance, VMF-SNE maintains the informational integrity of spherical datasets. Performance assessments demonstrate its distinct advantages over current state-of-the-art geodesic methods. Additionally, the application of VMF-SNE to spherical geometric data yields promising and insightful visualizations. Geometric data utilized includes sample surfaces from diverse Spherical Sine Cardiac Models and molecular structures. Furthermore, the approach offers a new perspective on spherical classification tasks, generating discriminative visual representations of spherical data classes. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan/VMF-SNE. The implementation is written in Python and is available for download. This version supports spherical samples up to 1,000 data points and 100 classes. Future updates will accommodate larger datasets and an increased number of classes. The current release corresponds to VMF-SNE v1.0.0. Future versions are expected to enhance visualization features and expand support for larger datasets. Updates to VMF-SNE v2.0.0 are currently being prepared. To achieve this, the existing Python implementation will be converted into C++ using the C++ spherical machine learning library SML, which is part of the C++ statistical computing environment SHARK. This transition will improve scalability, enabling the processing of larger datasets and more classes. Furthermore, VMF-SNE v2.0.0 will integrate clustering techniques for spherical data, such as spherical k-means and spherical FCM, alongside spherical classification methods like spherical SVM. The enhanced VMF-SNE application will be published under the name Spherical Data Explorer (SDE). This initiative aims to provide users with user-friendly visualization tools for spherical data and accelerate research into new analytical methods for this geometric domain. The C++ implementation of VMF-SNE is scheduled for release as SDE v1.0.0. Future applications will be developed based on the feedback and suggestions provided by the scientific community. All future versions of SDE will be released under the name Spherical Data Explorer (SDE). Through diagrammatic Monte Carlo simulations, we examine the 2D Fermi polaron, consisting of an impurity coupled to a sea of fermions under both continuous and lattice regulations, by analyzing several low-order diagrams. We present findings for both continuous and box ultraviolet (UV) cutoffs, systematically listing the diagrams for the many-body process where a polaron is perturbed once, twice, and finally annihilates. We begin by validating our results against existing literature and then explore multiple combinations of UV cutoff schemes. By comparing many-body diagrams, we observe that a box UV cutoff yields superior performance. Based on comparisons involving diagrams for a single perturbation, we discuss potential divergences in diagrammatic Monte Carlo simulations for the 2D Fermi polaron under a box UV cutoff. Finally, we report a systematic shift in polaron energy for both box and continuous UV cutoffs as the coupling constant increases. This divergence in diagrammatic Monte Carlo for the 2D Fermi polaron, despite being a well-established and extensively studied model, contrasts sharply with results in other field theories. We also address a previously published diagrammatic Monte Carlo study on the 2D Fermi polaron [J. Phys. Conf. Ser. 1181 (2018) 012007] and the implications of its conclusions. We demonstrate that this work relied on UV cutoff-independent diagrams, which are absent in any valid perturbative expansion of the polaron energy. Consequently, we show that the polaron energy derived in that study diverges with an increasing number of perturbations. This raises the question of whether diagrammatic Monte Carlo techniques are viable for the 2D Fermi polaron. We conclude that further investigation is necessary to address this issue. In the appendix, we provide additional diagrams and diagrammatic Monte Carlo results for the 2D Fermi polaron. Additionally, we explore whether diagrammatic Monte Carlo can be applied to the 2D polaron problem by considering a finite number of diagrams and performing numerical integration. We find that a 2D polaron energy based on a finite set of diagrams, combined with UV regularization, exhibits better convergence properties than a finite set of diagrams without UV regularization. However, this UV regularization is artificial and lacks a clear physical interpretation. In the second appendix, we explore whether a 2D polaron energy is independent of UV regularization by comparing a finite set of diagrams with a finite set of loops. This method leverages the natural evolution of a fermionic quantum gas under a Fermi-Hubbard interaction Hamiltonian, which is perturbed by a small superexchange interaction Hamiltonian. This perturbation loads complementary quantum gates into the quantum circuit that simulates the target system. Our hardware-efficient quantum algorithm executes the quantum emulation of the fermionic system using a quantum circuit with a minimal gate count, making it suitable for current noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. We present the results of quantum simulations on this hardware-efficient quantum algorithm for fermionic systems in two and three dimensions. This note explicitly calculates Hitchin systems relative to an arc $\gamma$ with fixed endpoints, which varies within a moduli space of stable marked surfaces of type $(g,n)$. We demonstrate that for a fixed arc, these systems are gauge equivalent to the Hitchin systems associated with the fundamental group of the complement of that arc. Furthermore, we show that the algebra of sections for a reductive structure group (both cases and positive genus) is a gauge equivalence class of subalgebras, which corresponds to the center of a specific subset of induced representations. As an application, we express the multiplicity of a specific irreducible representation of the fundamental group of a stable marked surface as a sum of multiplicities related to a specific representation of the braid group of a marked sphere. Additionally, we derive multiplicities as sums of eigenvalues of the permutation representation of the fundamental group of the marked sphere. Finally, we outline how to recover the original Hitchin system from the one associated with the stable marked surface. These findings are instrumental in establishing the conjecture that the Hitchin system is independent of the chosen stable marked surface. The rise of remote work in software engineering has driven significant interest in examining its effects on project outcomes. While prior research has primarily relied on descriptive statistics to establish basic correlations between remote collaboration and performance, these methods often overlook confounding variables, limiting their ability to uncover complex interactions. Consequently, there is a pressing need for more rigorous analytical approaches to deepen our understanding of remote working in software projects. This study investigates how fully remote setups impact the performance of Agile software projects utilizing Scrum. Through a retrospective analysis of fully remote teams, the study examines the relationship between remote configurations and project success. Data was gathered via online surveys administered to individuals across various roles within agile software development environments. The collected dataset comprised 101 projects distributed across 27 companies. To ensure robust analysis, the study employed multiple methodologies, including chi-square testing, correlation analysis, and logistic regression. Findings indicate a negative association between fully remote work and project success, though this effect is not statistically significant. However, when controlling for company size and whether the company is listed, this relationship becomes statistically significant. These results suggest that the decline in performance is likely driven by the characteristics of organizations adopting remote work rather than by remote methods themselves. Ultimately, this research helps clarify the mechanisms influencing project success in remote settings and offers valuable insights for organizations planning to transition to remote operations. By revealing the specific factors that make remote work beneficial, companies can make more informed decisions about adopting fully remote models. Furthermore, this enhances our overall comprehension of remote working in software engineering, a domain that has received limited attention compared to broader discussions on distributed Agile development. The latter often conflates remote work with distributed methods, which allow teams to operate remotely but do not necessarily mandate it. Ultimately, these insights can guide organizations in making better-informed decisions regarding their remote working strategies. Future research should focus on distinguishing the specific impacts of fully remote models versus remote distributed models to provide a more nuanced understanding of remote working in software engineering. This distinction is crucial for developing effective remote practices and improving organizational decision-making. Additionally, the study's sample includes projects utilizing various remote tools, highlighting the need for further research into the influence of specific tools on project success in remote environments. Such investigation would aid organizations in selecting appropriate tools for remote setups. Overall, this research advances our understanding of remote work in software engineering by providing empirical evidence and statistical analysis, a domain that has previously been overshadowed by broader discussions on distributed Agile methods. This paper presents a generalized formula for the Gau-Wu value of symmetric arrowhead matrices. Using this formula, we detail the computation of the Gau-Wu value for $4\times 4$ symmetric matrices. Since the Gau-Wu function serves as the signature polynomial for real symmetric matrices, calculating the signature of a real symmetric matrix can be derived from its Gau-Wu value; therefore, this work also enables the calculation of the signature for $4\times 4$ symmetric matrices. Additionally, we provide a generalized formula for the Choose Arrowhead Matrix (CAM) associated with a real symmetric matrix, which is derived through elementary row and column operations, and apply this to identify the signature matrix for $4\times 4$ matrices. Finally, we illustrate the methodology with several examples, including various $4\times 4$ block diagonal matrices. The examples cover diverse scenarios, such as matrices with zero diagonal entries, differing signs within diagonal blocks, and differing signs of diagonal elements in diagonal blocks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the signature of a real symmetric matrix does not necessarily follow the pattern suggested by the CAM illustration. The paper concludes with exercises designed to help readers master the techniques presented. The authors hope that the examples and exercises will be beneficial to readers. The concepts and results herein can be viewed as an extension of the diagonalization method for block diagonal matrices found in Linear Algebra textbooks. This study investigates the elliptic motion of beauty quarks within the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) by analyzing the elliptic flow ($v_2$) of B-hadrons, B-mesons, and semileptonic decay electrons originating from beauty-hadron decays. Data were collected by the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider during Pb-Pb collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV, covering event multiplicities ranging from 100 to 5000. Using elliptical coordinates derived from the CMS event plane, the transverse momentum distributions and elliptic flow coefficients for B-mesons and decay electrons were extracted. These findings were compared against results from pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV. The analysis employed two distinct models: elliptical motion, which posits that beauty quarks move along elliptical paths while maintaining constant speed and orientation relative to the shortest axis of the QGP; and the Landau model, which describes motion toward the center of an expanding, elliptically shaped QGP. Both approaches successfully account for the observed elliptic motion of beauty-hadron transformation products, with the Landau model offering a slightly superior fit. Furthermore, the elliptic motion of charm quarks, as previously reported, is compared with that of beauty quarks. The results indicate that, consistent with expectations, beauty quarks exhibit greater sensitivity to the geometry of the QGP than charm quarks. Finally, the thermalization of beauty quarks is confirmed by the momentum-independent $v_2$ observed for B-mesons and electrons in the low transverse momentum region. These outcomes suggest that, similar to light and charm quarks, beauty quarks hadronize predominantly via the coalescence mechanism. Additionally, the findings support the hypothesis that beauty quarks traverse a strongly-coupled QGP with a low viscosity, comparable to that of charm and light quarks. These conclusions are consistent with recent ALICE measurements regarding the nuclear modification factor and average ellipticity of electrons. We present an efficient and precise computational methodology for determining specific topological characteristics of colorful alpha complexes, defined by the intersection of Voronoi regions, along with their complementary spaces, known as color diagrams. These features, which encompass Betti numbers, Euler characteristic, and various persistence diagrams, facilitate a thorough investigation of the topology and homotopy type of the complex. Applications of this approach include analyzing the topological evolution through filtration or deformation, studying point cloud topology via the nearest neighbor ratio, interpreting fiber bundle data, and developing brain network models. Furthermore, an extensive suite of examples, ranging from regular geometric configurations to point cloud approximations of higher-dimensional manifolds, illustrates the results of our method. All computations were performed using the Python package CHAIR. By investigating the topology of colorful alpha complexes, we aim to enhance our comprehension of phenomena influenced by spatial heterogeneity, anisotropy, and non-uniformity. Ultimately, this represents a significant advancement over methods applied to classical geometric reconstruction methods like standard Cech or Delauney complexes. Specifically, we establish an upper bound on the GDoF gain of optimal regulation relative to binary control across all multilevel $K$ user interference networks featuring arbitrary interference channels. This bound demonstrates that the GDoF gain scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ with $K$. Notably, our findings are applicable to scenarios involving cochannel interference, adjacent channel interference, and a combination of both, provided the total number of cochannel and adjacent-channel users sums to $K$. Furthermore, we identify the specific channel configurations that characterize this upper bound. In contrast to prior research, which concentrated on networks with mutual information-based channel constraints, our analysis addresses multilevel $K$ user interference networks defined by finite alphabet power constraints. Additionally, we present an upper bound on the GDoF gain of optimal regulation over multilevel interference avoidance, which remains independent of $K$. Finally, the methodology employed in this work is adaptable to multilevel interference networks with continuous-valued channel coefficients. The emerging algorithm for parametric reconstruction of one-dimensional datasets, recently developed by the authors, is a modification of the classical Peierls-Broyles methodology. This approach utilizes the cumulative distribution function of measurement errors, which are assumed to follow a Gaussian distribution, alongside the average error deviation calculated via the least-squares method. The resulting reconstruction is represented as a piecewise linear function. A critical advantage of this technique is its exceptional stability. This paper investigates the application of this algorithm to both independent and correlated measurement errors using data with an a priori known parametric form. Additionally, the algorithm's utility in reconstructing one-dimensional data sets without a known parametric form is examined. The study also explores methods for error estimation and the assessment of result accuracy. Finally, the algorithm's performance is tested on experimentally obtained data from the LHCb L0 L0MU trigger system. To enhance the accuracy of reconstructed data sets, a specific transformation is applied to the initial data before fitting. This transformation, termed "stitching," relies on the average error deviation and the most probable (Gaussian) error value. Furthermore, the conditions required to ensure the positivity of both cumulative and probability distribution functions are analyzed. Correlation coefficients between errors in this transformed data sets are investigated, demonstrating the improved accuracy of the reconstructed data sets. However, it is noted that error positivity cannot be guaranteed in the original measurement data sets. Additionally, the conditions required to maintain the positivity of error variances are analyzed. The original algorithm is also evaluated for its ability to reconstruct data sets with unknown parametric forms. To achieve this, the average error deviation and the density function of the most probable errors are treated as functional parameters. The cost function is formulated as the sum of the average error deviation and the integral of the density function over the entire parameter space. The minimum of this cost function is determined using the variational method. Achieving multitasking control remains a significant challenge in control theory. This study extends the classical shared computation mechanism to handle multiple tasks simultaneously. The first task is a dynamic system, such as a linear or nonlinear dynamical system, while the second is a static system involving the optimal calculation of the minimum $H_\infty$ norm for a specific interval of linear time-varying systems. An online sampling mechanism is employed to manage task switching. Through the analysis of swap transients, we demonstrate that the optimal shared computation management problem can be transformed into a single-machine scheduling problem from another field. By evaluating three switching policies, we illustrate that a new priority-based policy outperforms the two most common alternatives: pre-emptive lowest-remaining-time and lowest-first-time. Finally, to validate the efficacy of the proposed policy, we present two applications: a nonlinear model predictive control scenario and a biological neuron. Biological neurons are renowned for their multitasking capabilities, a feature that has inspired numerous engineering designs. This paper seeks to contribute to this domain by offering an engineering application that validates the practicality of the proposed switching policy. Specifically, we investigate a biological question: how do biological neurons regulate multiple tasks? Our results indicate that a shared computational unit, governed by a priority-based switching policy, provides a viable explanation for multitasking control in biological neurons. Notably, the optimal switching instants in this priority-based policy can be approximated by comparing the times at which each task was initiated. This finding provides a new perspective on multitasking management in biological neurons. Additionally, our swift convergence to optimality suggests that an approximate switching policy, derived from optimal results, could be implemented on biological neurons. This supports the hypothesis that multitasking in biological neurons is not an inherent property of neurons themselves but rather emerges from their connectivity. Consequently, our findings support the hypothesis that a central computational unit is unnecessary for multitasking control in biological neurons. Furthermore, our results suggest that multitasking in biological neurons is not an intrinsic characteristic of individual neurons. This paper presents the first empirical assessment of a dependent OTA upgrade utilizing simultaneous updates across numerous devices. Our findings indicate that uplink interference is the primary obstacle in OTAs, a problem that intensifies as the network size grows and device density within the access point's coverage increases. To address this, we evaluated multiple existing and new interference mitigation strategies through real-world experiments involving 64 wireless IoT nodes. These methods included distributing devices evenly or unevenly, applying dependent or independent updates, and implementing various dependent update schemes such as package division, sequential installation, and incremental installation. Consequently, we offer specific guidance for designing large-scale mesh networks to ensure the dependable delivery of OTA updates. We evaluated these methods using two distinct updates: the default Luucos-IPCC IoT operating system and the recently released Luucos-RRTC routing extension. The experimental results confirm that all tested interference mitigation techniques are effective for dependent OTA upgrades. Notably, even with multiple simultaneous updates, a dependent OTA deployment can achieve an average installation success rate of 96.9% and an average interference duration of merely 10.5 seconds per device. Interactive exploration is particularly effective for real-time applications involving multiple targets, as it facilitates the rapid acquisition of information regarding their states. This paper addresses the challenge of exploring $N$ targets using a mobile sensor with a cost-limited budget. The targets' locations are unknown but confined within a specific region, and the cost incurred by the sensor depends on its trajectory. We examine the scenario where the cost function results in a NP-hard problem and propose a series of algorithms capable of producing $\alpha$-approximate solutions in polynomial time, where $\alpha$ represents a constant. Theoretically, we demonstrate that these algorithms yield the optimal solution when $N$ equals 2. Furthermore, experimental results indicate that our proposed algorithms deliver satisfactory performance across various practical scenarios. Finally, to illustrate the utility of this algorithm in practical applications, we present a scenario related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Specifically, mapping the spread of the virus to target points and treating surveillance routes as the mobile sensor's path allows for the efficient exploration of numerous targets using a route that minimizes the total infected population. Additionally, the framework for applying these algorithms to a cost function with polynomial complexity is provided. This approach offers a viable solution for practical path planning in scenarios involving a large number of targets. Finally, our work introduces a novel application of cost-limited interactive exploration to the field of public health. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of such an application. To our knowledge, no prior research exists in this area. Our findings regarding the computational complexity of this problem are detailed in a companion paper [1].

By employing the SwiftZVM emulator, we demonstrate that genuine quantum classifiers can be constructed using off-the-shelf components, achieving substantial speedups over both classical alternatives and quantum circuits with higher qubit counts. These practical classifiers remain sufficiently classical-like to permit the creation of adversarial examples. The resulting adversarial robustness of quantum classifiers provides a vital benchmark for assessing and advancing the field's progress. This approach relies on the universal properties of probability amplitudes and adversarial perturbations, ensuring broad applicability. Additionally, we highlight that SWAP test robustness is contingent upon the specific classifier implementation rather than the swap test itself. Finally, we establish a relationship between adversarial instances for quantum classifiers and those of their classical counterparts, offering valuable insights for future research. The widespread adoption of 5G technology has led to increased deployment of base stations across various regions, resulting in significant radio interference between adjacent cells. This interaction necessitates effective modeling and simulation to facilitate resource allocation in 5G networks. Traditional cellular systems typically rely on two primary models for radio interference: the Stochastic Geometry Model and the Multi-Cell Network Model. However, recent advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, have introduced new opportunities for interference resolution. While deep learning approaches have been increasingly applied to cellular interference management in recent years, the geometric characteristics of interference patterns have received limited attention. This study models radio transmission using deep convolutional neural networks, treating output power as a two-dimensional image. By representing geometric information within the power distribution, this approach offers novel insights into leveraging deep learning for cellular interference mitigation, with a specific emphasis on beamforming design. The proposed method employs two distinct deep convolutional neural architectures to demonstrate the effectiveness of geometric information within the transmission space for developing novel deep learning-based beamforming techniques. Experimental results indicate that the proposed deep learning-based beamforming strategy outperforms existing deep learning-based approaches and established techniques such as Zero-Forcing (ZF) and Maximum Ratio Transmission (MRT). Furthermore, an ablation study confirms that the network's ability to capture geometric information within the transmission space is crucial for achieving high beamforming performance. We introduce a new validation command for temporal planning that rigorously confirms the correctness of temporal plan graphs and identifies errors when plans cannot be derived. This command guarantees that any declared plan is indeed a valid plan and that any identified invalid plan truly fails. We provide a rigorous proof of the command's correctness and implement it using the superposition calculus within E-prover, demonstrating that valid plans can be validated efficiently. We integrate the commander into the International Timetable Competition and showcase several examples of what the commander can achieve. These findings support our conclusion that a verified validity check for temporal plans is feasible and can produce useful outcomes. Furthermore, we explore how this capability could inform research into automated planning, such as guiding repair procedures, defining admissible heuristic functions, or assisting in the design of new temporal planning algorithms. Finally, we examine potential challenges and limitations when applying the commander in various research contexts. This work extends the findings presented in [1].

This study examines the rheo-acoustic interaction between a colloidal gel subjected to ultrasonic standing waves and a ultrasonic transducer under shear deformation. The gel, formed by slowly drying a suspension of 1.5 wt% silica spheres in isopropanol, displays distinct responses to these combined oscillations depending on whether shear is applied before or after the ultrasonic field. Pre-applying the ultrasonic field results in a gel with a low storage modulus, whereas shearing it first creates a gel with a high storage modulus; in both scenarios, colloidal gels are acoustically unstable. The findings are illustrated using silica gels, but the underlying mechanisms are expected to apply broadly to other colloidal gels. Classifying documents from STEM fields is essential for building large-scale knowledge bases and enhancing the web's semantic interoperability. However, manually labeling vast collections of files is prohibitively expensive, making supervised learning an attractive alternative. Yet, such learning depends on human-provided samples, and humans are scarce in the field of science. Consequently, there is a pressing need to train models using vast amounts of unannotated data. This study investigates whether the capability to identify the domain of a document can be leveraged through semi-supervised learning, yielding three key findings: first, models trained solely on non-mathematical documents fail to categorize mathematical files; second, cross-domain samples—such as those blending math and physics documents—significantly hinder accurate categorization; and third, using the model's uncertainty as a metric to filter out mathematical files allows for their manual annotation, thereby improving classification accuracy. Furthermore, the paper explores a multi-class neural network architecture incorporating mathematical entity connection to better grasp the content of these documents. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The research paper and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/SeungjaeLee88/STEM-Doc-Categorization. Our code is also available on GitHub. Additionally, the paper includes a tutorial on semi-supervised learning practices. Finally, the authors offer insights into their experiences conducting interdisciplinary research. Keywords: STEM document categorization, semi-supervised learning, mathematical entity connection, STEM knowledge base.

Matching markets serve as the foundation for numerous critical real-world systems, such as college admissions, organ transplantation, and job recruitment. These markets facilitate interactions between buyers and sellers by pairing them based on their respective preferences. However, researchers have long observed that agents within these markets often achieve suboptimal outcomes because they prioritize short-term profits over long-term welfare. This paper tackles the challenge of identifying high-quality matches by proposing a group of reliable matching mechanisms designed to assist agents in securing long-term beneficial relationships. We rigorously analyze the properties of these mechanisms and empirically demonstrate their efficacy through extensive simulations. Our results indicate that compared to existing mechanisms, our proposed methods achieve near Pareto-optimal matchings in realistic scenarios and remain robust even when agents' preferences are uncertain. Furthermore, we show that a significant majority of real-world datasets are compatible with our mechanisms, whereas they are rarely suitable for strict optimal mechanisms like Stable Roommates. Ultimately, we view our methods as a promising alternative to strict optimality, offering a reliable solution for high-quality matching even when not all agent preferences are known. The code required to replicate our experiments is accessible at: https://github.com/ChengyuanLi2000/reliable_matching. Recent evaluations of automatic summarization metrics, such as Abstracting over F-Measure (Abstrct), have demonstrated that performance on existing test collections correlates poorly with human judgment. This paper presents a novel scoring mechanism, SummScore, which assesses summary quality using the cross-encoder model. To ensure efficiency while preserving scoring accuracy, SummScore employs early exit computation and dynamically adjusts the number of generated summaries for evaluation. Empirical results confirm that SummScore achieves strong efficiency and delivers accurate assessments, demonstrating human-level scoring correlations and outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, using SummScore as a learning signal yields significant score improvements for both neural and template-based generative models. Ultimately, SummScore serves as an efficient score predictor and an effective learning objective, offering a promising path to enhance summary quality and accelerate progress in automatic summarization. This work introduces a robust restoration technique capable of recovering unknown real signals from noisy quadratic measurements, specifically including incomplete data and outliers. The process of generating such measurements is termed "quadratic observation." Our recovery approach is grounded in convex optimization, which ensures both the stability and well-posedness of the solution. Relying solely on standard convexity often results in excessive over-smoothed recovery, so we first enhance the fidelity of our recovery function by integrating features like sparsity and edge preservation. Subsequently, we improve the robustness of our recovery by incorporating statistical characteristics, such as heavy tails and sparsity, observed in the measurement error. Theoretically, we demonstrate that our recovery guarantees are tight, meaning no stronger guarantee can be ensured. Furthermore, we prove that our method achieves optimal recovery even when dealing with incomplete observations under entropy constraints. Finally, extensive numerical experiments confirm that this convex recovery method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we illustrate its effectiveness through real-world applications in X-ray computed tomography and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. Our findings indicate that convex recovery from quadratic observations yields significant improvements in image reconstruction, resulting in clearer and more interpretable medical images. In summary, this paper presents a robust algorithm for recovery that offers both theoretical guarantees and substantial practical performance enhancements. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/taehyounkim1222/QO_Restoration. Our implementation is available at: https://github.com/taehyounkim1222/QO_Restoration. The demonstration video can be found at: https://youtu.be/2YQ81111111. These methods are highly promising for future research into recovery based on quadratic observations. Additionally, our approach is well-suited for extension to other inverse problems, such as those involving tensor observations, and for recovering complex signals, for which we have already made preliminary progress. These extensions are expected to yield substantial practical performance improvements. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a unified framework for addressing inverse problems that involve quadratic observations. This will facilitate more accurate recovery, whether the observations are incomplete or the signals are complex. We anticipate that our work will serve as a valuable resource for the community interested in these inverse problems. Our contributions include: (i) a unified approach for recovery from quadratic observations, (ii) tight theoretical analysis, and (iii) a unified framework for future research in this area. Fusing data from cameras and LiDARs is essential for the safe and efficient operation of autonomous vehicles. However, effectively combining these modalities is difficult due to their inherent differences: LiDARs offer precise depth measurements but suffer from noise in point clouds, while cameras capture rich color details despite lacking depth. This paper introduces BEVFusion, a straightforward yet resilient integration approach that combines bird's-eye-view (BEV) features from both sensors without relying on complex calibration or alignment. The method first projects LiDAR point clouds into the BEV plane using ground height, then aligns camera features with the BEV plane via projection. These modality-specific features are integrated using a cross-attention mechanism, which is paired with a simple decoder for object detection and keypoint localization. BEVFusion is easily transferable to most backbones and requires no complex camera-LiDAR calibration or feature alignment, making it suitable for various integration scenarios. Evaluated on the nuScenes dataset, it achieves a 5.1% improvement in 3D detection AP over a baseline using similar BEV fusion, and a 1.2% gain in 2D detection AP. Additionally, it delivers a 3.1% increase in 2D keypoint localization AP. For an ablation study, the entire training process was conducted on the nuScenes dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/CAIR-ETH/BEVFusion. Given its simplicity and effectiveness, BEVFusion is expected to provide a strong baseline for other integration methods. Notably, it has already surpassed previous state-of-the-art results without any modifications to the detector architecture. We anticipate that BEVFusion will serve as a valuable reference for developing future detector architectures and fusion strategies. The experimental code and pre-trained models will be made available to the community. In this study, we demonstrate that dissipative-range turbulence, driven by dissipative heat flux, is a universal characteristic of the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations and similar models, and it influences the statistical behavior of thermal fields during large Reynolds number turbulence. Through statistical analysis, we find that all stochastic thermal fluctuations scale with the Reynolds number $Re$ as $Re^{1/2}$ and match classical hydrodynamic fluctuations in small-scale, high-gradient regions. Consequently, the previously believed universality of intermittency—where all significant statistical properties of the turbulent field, including velocity and temperature intermittency, scale with $Re$—is confirmed. Furthermore, we clarify the physical significance of thermal effects in high-Re turbulence, indicating that they are not merely minor corrections to the inertial range but can fundamentally alter the statistical properties of passive scalar fields. Finally, by linking the turbulent heat transfer coefficient to the turbulent Prandtl number, we provide a physical explanation for its non-unity value and the existence of its empirical analogues. These findings are supported by both analytical and numerical evidence. Specifically, large-eddy simulations of turbulent channel flow at $Re_\tau=18,000$ show that the turbulent Prandtl number $Pr_t$ is approximately 0.8, consistent with experimental data. Additionally, we prove that the asymptotic behavior of $Pr_t$ at very high Reynolds numbers is governed by the asymptotic value of the turbulent Nusselt number, which is typically around 0.8. This confirms the generalization of the Reynolds analogy, which states that turbulent transport of momentum and energy is identical. As a result, the asymptotic behaviors of $Pr_t$ and the Nusselt number at large $Re$ are both asymptotically equal to 1. These conclusions are also validated by direct numerical simulations of the most unstable parallel shear flow. Finally, we propose a universal asymptotic model for $Pr_t$ that is in good agreement with all available experimental and numerical data. This model demonstrates that $Pr_t$ is not a constant but a universal function of $Re$ and the turbulent Peclet number $Pe$, with its minimum value of approximately 0.8 occurring at $Pe=1$. These results are also supported by the recent direct numerical simulation of a turbulent plane jet conducted by the second author. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis of thermal profiles generated within liquids by ultrafast laser pulses of varying durations and energies. The liquid's specific heat capacity is modeled as a function of both energy density and temperature. By incorporating the ultra-short spatial focal spot and the temperature-dependent index of refraction, we simulate complex self-diffraction patterns and subsequently map the resulting heat profiles. This approach demonstrates how the ultra-short focal spot expands during propagation, how the temperature gradient front bends inward due to diffraction, and how the final profile becomes increasingly non-Gaussian as laser pulse duration, energy, and focal spot size increase. These generated profiles are compared against current experimental data. The findings indicate that, given fixed laser pulse duration and focal spot size, the liquid's specific heat response remains relatively consistent across different laser energies. Furthermore, we conclude that for liquid targets, the laser-generated thermal profile is governed by stochastic fluctuations in the liquid's heat response rather than the deterministic non-linear propagation characteristics of light in liquid. This conclusion is supported by the fact that complex self-induced diffraction patterns, while theoretically possible, are rarely observed in experiments. These results are particularly relevant to laser ablation experiments utilizing ultrafast pulses in the picosecond regime. Finally, our findings suggest that the non-linear behavior of liquids, which is well-documented in nanosecond and longer pulse experiments, is significantly suppressed when using laser pulses longer than a few tens of femtoseconds. This suppression is attributed to the liquid's specific heat rising rapidly with temperature, thereby preventing the non-linear expansion of the light beam. Consequently, the liquid's thermal profile is determined by the spatial-temporal evolution of the light profile and the specific heat's dependence on temperature. We demonstrate that the ultra-short focal spot expands during propagation, while heat generated in the shadow region is deflected inward due to diffraction, and the final profile becomes increasingly non-Gaussian as focal spot size decreases. These outcomes are consistent with previously reported ultrafast laser heating profiles in liquids. The paper also examines the influence of ultrafast laser pulses on the temperature distribution of liquid targets, revealing that the temperature distribution is highly non-uniform and spatially localized. This non-uniformity arises from the stochastic nature of the liquid's specific heat response and the non-linear evolution of the light profile. Ultimately, the ultrafast heating profile is characterized by its ultra-short spatial extent, stochastic fluctuations, and non-deterministic spatial-temporal evolution. Designers often rely on digital platforms to develop new products, often embedding conversational context directly into 3D models. This integration enriches designs with conversational semantics, enabling models to be accessed and modified based on natural language instructions. This capability transforms digital models into virtual repositories that can respond dynamically to user queries. This study investigates the conclusion stability of algorithms that locate contexts relevant to design instructions. We focus on the conclusion stability limit, which represents the maximum number of times a function can be restored to a previous state while still responding correctly to a given query. Our findings indicate that a conclusion stability limit of one is nearly inevitable, a result derived from considerations regarding input size and the granularity of context partitioning. Consequently, we argue that achieving dynamic access to digital design resources remains a challenging problem. To address this, we explore algorithmic solutions that partition context into clusters and adjust these groupings in response to design instructions. We further examine the conclusion stability of our proposed algorithms and their ability to balance context partitioning with the precision required to identify the most appropriate design resources. Finally, we validate these findings through practical applications that utilize both synthetic and real-world data. Specifically, we leverage synthetic data generated by a large language model and real data collected from a digital design platform, which records both virtual and physical design artifacts along with their associated conversational context. This data reflects conversations among designers regarding a specific product: a smartphone. Through experiments on this dataset, we provide evidence supporting the conclusion stability limits of our algorithms and their efficacy in dynamically accessing digital design resources. Ultimately, we aim to enhance current solutions for extracting meaning from design conversations, thereby improving how digital design resources are accessed and adjusted to reflect real-world requirements. This work serves as an initial step toward that objective. To achieve this, we have developed an open-source software library that implements algorithms for clustering design contexts and retrieving relevant resources. This library enables researchers and practitioners to evaluate their algorithms, assess their conclusion stability, and easily integrate them into existing solutions for extracting meaning from design conversations. This study introduces new illustrations for the non-resonant singular production of top-bottom associates at the High-Luminosity LHC, utilizing an enhanced version of the Path Ordered Saturated Angular Spectrum (POAS) formalism within Small-x QCD. For the first time, this framework is rigorously applied in the enhanced Small-x POAS scheme to examine the production of colour singlet and octet states in the process $g + q \to Q\bar{Q}b$ at leading order. The investigation centers on the singular kinematical region where the top quark carries the majority of the incoming parton's longitudinal momentum, while the bottom quarks carry negligible fractions. The results reveal that the contributions from the octet configuration are predominantly logarithmically enhanced, rendering them the most significant. Furthermore, the influence of the gluon saturation scale is explored, demonstrating that the POAS formalism operates effectively within the non-linear saturation regime. Additionally, the POAS saturation correction is found to be substantial and positively impacts the cross section. Finally, the POAS saturation effect is evaluated at the parton level, showing that it can reach several tens of percent. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating the non-linear saturation effect into the evolution equations used for precision phenomenology at the HL-LHC. Additionally, predictions regarding the differential cross section for this process are established, which may be valuable for future studies on the production of the $t_b$ system. The necessary code will be made publicly accessible. Finally, the connection between this work and the phenomenology of the $t\bar{t}b$ colour singlet resonance is addressed. The path forward involves investigating the production of colour singlet states within the evolution equations, a task that will be pursued in subsequent publications. This research is motivated by the recent discovery of the $t\bar{t}b$ colour singlet resonance at the parton level. Furthermore, the significance of this study lies in its ability to provide insights into the formation of the $t\bar{t}b$ colour singlet state from the perspective of the POAS formalism. The application of the POAS formalism to the production of colour singlet states is expected to yield significant results, as it is anticipated to generate substantial saturation corrections. Although standard NME approaches treat each operator as a separate feature enhancing the original NMT model, this study proposes a replication mechanism to manage modular knowledge base components within the NME framework. By replicating operators and reusing them across multiple sentences within a context window, the model achieves time efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the replication mechanism boosts both the original and modified systems' accuracy and efficiency, even when the modified system uses more parameters. The approach also increases the proportion of correctly translated subject-predicate-argument triples and overall translation quality. Furthermore, the replication mechanism improves the generalization capability of the modified system, as evidenced by the higher accuracy of the original system on test data and development set data from other languages and domains. Additionally, the study evaluates the sensitivity of the system to context window size and the number of operators included in the replication knowledge base. Finally, the research explores the impact of varying numbers of operators and KBase contents within the replication knowledge base. These findings aim to provide insights for future research on knowledge-enhanced NME systems. Measuring scholarly contributions is essential for advancing science and society. While traditional metrics like impact factors and h-indices rely heavily on journal and author reputations, this study investigates whether a metric derived solely from venue data can accurately reflect research impact. By employing a machine learning approach grounded in decision trees, we demonstrate that venue-specific scores significantly enhance the predictive capability of citations across various disciplines. Our analysis of nearly 1.5 million papers from 2004 to 2018 in computer science, physics, and mathematics confirms that learning from venue alone yields results comparable to those using combined venue and author features. These findings suggest that future impact metrics could be more equitable by depending exclusively on venues rather than being skewed by reputational biases associated with specific fields and authors. Additionally, we examine the temporal evolution of these metrics and their effectiveness in forecasting a paper's "half-life"—the period during which it continues to inspire new research. Furthermore, our venue-based model effectively identifies interdisciplinary papers, a capability that falls outside the scope of current citation-based systems. Finally, we offer recommendations for enhancing the utility of venue scores. Overall, this research lays the groundwork for developing fairer, more interpretable, and transparent metrics to assess research impact. For instance, the venue analysis component contributes to the Open Citation Impact (OCI) metric, which synthesizes open, non-reputational citation data to measure scholarly influence. The code and data required to replicate this study's findings are accessible at https://github.com/venueinsights/replication. Supplementary materials can be found in our previous publication at https://doi.org/10.1145/3447548.3447702. Implementation code is also available at https://github.com/venueinsights/venue_analytics. Our findings indicate that impact factors and similar author-centric metrics suffer from inherent biases, and we explore strategies to mitigate these issues through the development of new metrics. Specifically, our work informs the creation of the Open Citation Impact (OCI) metric, which leverages venue-based reputation and author-independent citation data to offer a fairer and more interpretable assessment of scholarly significance. This study explores neural network validation methods for regulatory applications. Unlike other use cases where predictive accuracy is the primary concern, neural networks in regulation often cannot be validated solely through the comparison of predicted versus actual outcomes. Consequently, we examine supervision techniques such as explainability, semantic alignment, and causal inference to facilitate alternative validation approaches. We introduce a novel semantic alignment method designed to evaluate knowledge validity within neural networks by detecting contradictions against a regulated knowledge graph. Furthermore, we present a new framework for validating causal claims derived from neural networks by leveraging claims extracted from human-generated text. Finally, we outline several lines of supervision that are currently under development. Overall, this work serves as a foundation for future research and development in the supervision of neural network validation. Our proposed methods for causal and semantic validation have been well-received by neurosymbolic researchers, who are increasingly interested in utilizing neural networks to infer knowledge from data and symbolic researchers seeking to train neural networks on knowledge graphs, semantic objectives, or contradiction detection tasks. We aim to facilitate collaboration between these groups to integrate knowledge graphs and common sense reasoning into neural network development and deployment, thereby enhancing transparency and enabling validation via claims from natural language. This synergy is essential for facilitating validation through causal reasoning and for ensuring that causal claims hold up under scrutiny. Additionally, the work supports efforts to enhance model fairness and robustness by utilizing knowledge graphs and causal models. To support these initiatives, we have made our code and data accessible at https://github.com/robertoribeiro/kwNN. We believe these practical developments will advance the fields of neural network-based knowledge inference, symbolically-enhanced neural networks, neural common sense reasoning, code for validating neural networks on knowledge graphs and causal assertions, and the broader application of knowledge graphs and causal models to neural networks. We anticipate that these advancements will improve fairness and robustness within neural network systems. We hope that sharing our code and data will enable other researchers to reproduce and extend these findings. Finally, we look forward to collaborating with regulatory technology companies to implement practical validation methods for neural networks in regulated environments. We believe that fostering collaboration between academic and industrial researchers will significantly accelerate the deployment of neural networks in sensitive contexts. Grouping is a fundamental capability that enables various AI systems, including vision, by condensing vast amounts of data into more manageable representations. While most methods rely on element-to-element similarity, they often struggle with group membership inconsistencies and fail to maintain the structural integrity of the grouping process. To address these challenges, we introduce FunCHOG, a novel approach that leverages overrepresenting element sets and formalizes grouping as a category theory problem. This category-based framework ensures robust grouping and guarantees the preservation of hierarchical structure. FunCHOG demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art models on image datasets, successfully learning groupings from limited examples and retaining them during transfer to unseen datasets. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness on the Viso dataset for visual reasoning tasks and explore its application in robot arm planning. Streaming retrieval within tensor spaces presents significant challenges, particularly when dealing with evolving visual data and under constrained memory conditions. We introduce a novel patch monitoring-based streaming tensor retrieval (STMRT) framework designed for streaming environments with limited memory. This approach utilizes an online tensor ring model as memory, enhanced by patch-based similarity metrics. Specifically, when a new query arrives, its patch similarities to existing queries are monitored and used to expand the set of relevant copies. Subsequently, a tensorization operator maps these selected patches into the tensor representation of the online tensor ring memory. To address memory growth, we implement two strategies: periodic pruning and patch eviction. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that STMRT significantly outperforms various baselines in both accuracy and runtime efficiency. Furthermore, we provide asymptotic complexity analysis and conduct extensive ablation studies to validate our methods. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuan/STMRT. Finally, we release eight new visual streaming datasets to foster research in this domain. We anticipate that our work will establish a robust foundation for STMRT, offering versatile solutions and versatile tools to the research community. Relying on well-established theories and tools, our work demonstrates high reliability and versatility.

This paper investigates Nichols algebras associated with traditional quantum groups. We demonstrate that for extended affine Weyl groups of label type, the dimensions of the first graded component in the Nichols algebra of the tangent space (in the sense of He and Zhang) align with the coefficients of the Weyl-Kac formula for irreducible modules. In contrast, no such correspondence exists for Nichols algebras linked to Kac-Moody quantum groups. Furthermore, we calculate the dimension of the Nichols algebra for Kac-Moody traditional quantum groups and establish an isomorphism between its Nichols class and the weight space of a specific module. Additionally, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the finite-dimensionality of these Nichols algebras and conjecture that their co-Yetter-Drinfeld modules are also finite-dimensional under these conditions. Finally, we construct a family of infinite-dimensional Kac-Moody traditional quantum groups. Finally, this study serves as a supplement to reference [N2].

Three-dimensional isotropic turbulence exhibits a $-5/3$ energy spectrum, a result derived from the Navier-Stokes equations under high Reynolds number conditions and viscous dissipation. Although the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) equation offers a more streamlined framework by omitting viscous dissipation and relying on statistical ensembles, it was uncertain whether it could genuinely represent fully developed chaos or merely model the early nonlinear evolution of waves. Recent studies [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 124301 (2019); Phys. Rev. E 101, 063102 (2020)] established the $-5/3$ spectrum for strongly nonlinear magneto-hydrodynamic Alfv\'en waves. This work extends those findings to establish the same spectral slope for standard three-dimensional isotropic gravitational waves. The analysis encompasses the complete high-energy regime, validating the validity range of the ZK equation, and demonstrates that fully developed inertial wave chaos can be accurately modeled using this simplified equation. Furthermore, the presence of the $-5/3$ spectrum in gravitational wave systems suggests its applicability to a broad spectrum of wave phenomena. This achievement completes the numerical verification of the universal Kolmogorov spectrum for strongly nonlinear waves, thereby confirming the statistical closure of the Zeeman-Kraichnan-Kolmogorov direct-interaction approximation. Additionally, the Kolmogorov cascade's absence of dissipation and the identification of its closure implications may enhance the efficiency of large-scale simulations and deepen the understanding of turbulent dynamics. These universality findings were achieved through the application of a newly developed parallel simulation code. Finally, the study confirms the validity of the ZK model, thereby resolving the longstanding debate regarding the statistical closure of the direct-interaction approximation. This conclusion was reached by demonstrating that the Kolmogorov energy spectrum $E(k) \propto k^{-5/3}$ and the Batchelor spectrum $E(\omega) \propto \omega^{-7/3}$ for isotropic wave turbulence can be derived from the Zakharov-Kolmogorov equation. Furthermore, the derived Kolmogorov-Zakharov equation is shown to be mathematically equivalent to the one previously reported.
