The visual complexity of ultrasound imaging in scoliosis assessment complicates its analysis by humans or machines. Consequently, there is a strong need for automated ultrasound scanning and analytics capable of delivering consistent quantitative measurements. This study investigates the dependability of robotic ultrasound scanning and measurement software regarding scoliosis evaluation, comparing it against human-performed scans. Three independent experts annotated 150 publicly accessible ultrasound images collected from 30 patients, while a dedicated robotic scanner and automated measurement system were tested on the same set of images. Additionally, the robotic system was deployed in a clinical setting to scan 20 scoliosis patients. The variability of key scoliosis metrics—including lateral curvature, angulation, and length—was assessed by comparing the coefficient of variation (CV) across expert annotations, among the experts themselves, and via robotic scans. Dependability was further evaluated by contrasting expert manual scanning with robotic scanning in both image-based and in-vivo contexts. Results indicated that the robotic system achieved high reliability in feature extraction, demonstrating superior consistency compared to the inter-rater variability of human experts. These findings suggest that robotic ultrasound scanning offers a dependable approach to scoliosis assessment. Ultimately, the integration of robotic ultrasound scanning and measurement with automated feature extraction represents a promising advancement for medical imaging. This technology facilitates efficient and consistent data collection, generating quantitative metrics that serve as valuable biomarkers for clinical decision-making and patient monitoring. Furthermore, it establishes a foundation for the development of advanced decision support systems and enables cost-effective, continuous monitoring of patient conditions. Supplementary materials, including data and code, are available at: https://github.com/ultrasound-scanning-and-analytics. This study outlines a technique for mediating the duration of synthetic speech through median-based controls. Unlike traditional duration modulation methods, which typically rely on expanding or shrinking base utterances based on specific parameters, our approach generates new, previously unseen durations by generating content at those intervals. This method is particularly beneficial for applications requiring a broad spectrum of speech lengths, such as multimedia interfaces in military environments. The proposed method employs an iterative, non-statistical algorithm that iteratively narrows duration bounds until a target length is achieved. Results demonstrate that for any given target duration, the system selects a subject appropriate for that length and generates speech accordingly. Furthermore, the study analyzes the influence of the subject on the final acoustic output. Finally, the method's automatic and algorithm-driven nature ensures scalability, allowing it to be adapted for use across various languages. This paper presents the method as a solution for scenarios demanding diverse durations, with subsequent papers detailing its evaluation across different languages. Specifically, the method was assessed using Russian and Hindi test items, where a single source item was run through various duration settings to produce synthetic samples. Both a listening test and acoustic analysis confirmed that the generated samples are natural-sounding across different languages and durations. The listening test utilized measures such as intelligibility, similarity, and dissimilarity, while the acoustic analysis provided objective evidence supporting these findings. Additionally, various production metrics, including success rates and iteration counts, were assessed to evaluate the method's overall efficiency. Ultimately, the method successfully produces synthetic speech across a wide range of durations, achieving high intelligibility and similarity scores alongside low failure rates. Furthermore, the method is shown to be scalable for implementation in other languages. Overall, median-based duration control proves to be a viable approach for scenarios where varying durations are essential. The method offers several advantages, including the ability to generate speech across a wide spectrum of lengths, the potential for cross-linguistic implementation, and the capacity to produce utterances that are both intelligible and similar to human speech. With the increasing popularity of social networking platforms, users can now exchange messages and comments, often engaging in hate speech. Therefore, automatically detecting such content is crucial for managing public opinion and safeguarding human rights. Although significant research exists on hate speech detection, particularly in English, these methods often fail to generalize effectively to other languages. This study introduces a deep learning approach utilizing a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to identify hate speech. The method relies on a fine-grained annotation technique that captures not only semantic meaning but also specific linguistic and contextual features. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves higher accuracy than existing state-of-the-art systems. Additionally, the model was extended to detect sexual violence and abuse, showing that it performs well in distinguishing between hate speech and instances of sexual violence and abuse. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedelshorbagy/Characteristics-LSTM. Furthermore, the dataset employed in this research will be made available to the community. The dataset comprises 1,000 manually collected Arabic tweets, annotated for hate speech, sexual violence, and abuse. The accompanying code utilizes fastText for training a fine-grained text classifier to extract features such as surface forms, word embeddings, and noun phrases, while also employing spaCy to extract fine-grained syntactic features like verb tenses and nominalizations. Subsequently, a Bi-directional LSTM network was trained to classify hate speech, sexual violence, and abuse. The results indicate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance for hate speech detection and effectively distinguishes between hate speech and sexual violence and abuse. Ultimately, these findings suggest that the proposed method holds promise for application across various languages. The authors intend to explore extending the model to multiple languages in the future. Given that the classification task involves three distinct labels, the study concludes by discussing the advantages and limitations of a multi-label learning approach versus a multi-class approach for hate speech detection. Finally, the paper examines the application of the model to detect hate speech in tweets. The authors express hope that this work will motivate further research in the field. Finally, the paper acknowledges the contributions of individuals who provided annotations and assisted in data collection. This work introduces a new matrix factorization algorithm designed to address the joint detection and channel estimation tasks within adaptive iterative receiver systems for MIMO channels with static long-term statistics. Initially, the problem is reformulated using a cost function that encompasses both differential entropy and a measure of channel estimation error. This new formulation is then converted into a non-convex multi-objective optimization problem involving entropy minimization and error maximization. Subsequently, a novel feature-sweeping approach is developed to generate efficient solutions that achieve high data rates while maintaining accurate channel estimates, utilizing non-convex constraints resolved via semi-definite programming. Numerical simulations confirm that this proposed method achieves superior performance with significantly fewer iterations compared to the conventional IMM approach. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness in both additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and selective fading environments. Finally, the algorithm demonstrates strong compatibility with current machine learning techniques. Consequently, the primary contribution of this research is the creation of a new framework for feature exchanging in MIMO systems that leverages the synergy between these machine learning methods and the proposed matrix factorization algorithm. This is achieved by mapping the optimization problem into a machine learning context, specifically a classification problem solvable through support vector machines. The resulting framework offers two key advantages: it enables the use of advanced machine learning strategies to enhance algorithmic performance, and it facilitates the development of a completely new matrix factorization algorithm capable of solving complex subproblems with greater efficiency. Future research will explore the application of deep learning within this proposed framework. In this study, the optimization problem is defined within a machine learning context, utilizing kernel functions derived from the K-Means algorithm and address spaces generated by the feature-sweeping method. The resulting feature-exchanging process yields highly efficient solutions, as confirmed by numerical simulations. Additionally, the proposed framework successfully solves the initial multi-objective optimization problem, thereby addressing the main challenge of this research. Ultimately, this approach serves as a significant step toward fully automated MIMO receiver design utilizing machine learning. Notably, this study represents the first instance of fully automated MIMO receiver design grounded in matrix factorization and machine learning techniques. Utilizing digitized, structured collections of historic printed and manuscript images offers researchers the chance to analyze these visuals both quantitatively and qualitatively. This paper examines ten digital platforms that provide access to historical printed and handwritten images, spanning from the 16th to the 20th centuries and originating from Europe and America. Through a systematic review of these sites, we identify key attributes of their collections and methods for accessing them. We compare the datasets in terms of content, volume, geographic origin, and chronological range. The paper also highlights each platform's distinctive scientific or historical applications and notes any available scientific code or tools for quantitative analysis. Ultimately, we argue for the significance of exploring historical image collections to achieve both qualitative and scientific insights, while also outlining the future challenges required to unlock the full potential of these visual resources. This work serves as a comprehensive guide for quantitative researchers interested in historical imagery. The included code is offered as a proof of concept to demonstrate how one might analyze historical manuscript images using available computer vision tools. Additionally, we offer practical advice on selecting the most suitable dataset for specific analytical goals and suggest promising directions for future research. All image examples can be found in our GitHub repository, which also hosts the project's code. This resource is particularly valuable for beginners in scientific image analysis, as it demonstrates how to examine historical manuscript images without requiring extensive programming expertise. Our goal is to support both novice and experienced researchers in achieving both scientific and qualitative results through the analysis of historical images. This study outlines the design, execution, and results of an experimental study involving an industrial arm equipped with touch sensors at its end-effector. The primary objective is to develop an experimental method for stabilizing regulator parameters using a haptic interface to guide the workpiece. The outcome demonstrates an automated experimental procedure for regulator regulation. The resulting system enables a human operator to position the workpiece, allowing the regulator to stabilize parameters rapidly and accurately within a few seconds. The paper concludes by comparing this experimental approach to traditional methods, such as parameter optimization. Additionally, the study provides a comparative analysis of the touch sensors against other options, including vision systems and deformation sensors. The authors believe that integrating secondary sensors into industrial robots represents a promising avenue for future research, as it significantly expands the robot's capabilities. **Background**: Numerous studies have identified multiple risk factors for my myocardial infarction (MI), yet their predictive capacity remains uncertain. We aimed to assess how many risk factors are necessary to predict recurrent MI and stroke in a cohort of 2nd-time MI patients. **Methods**: We conducted multiple state evaluations using data from the 2001-2014 French GEMINI study, which followed 2,000 patients with a first MI. This study utilized time-to-event data for recurrent MI, stroke, and death. We applied a multi-dimensional strategy employing multistate modeling. Results indicated that a minimum of 10 variables was required to predict each outcome; these included age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, smoking status, heart failure, left ventricular dysfunction, left ventricular ejection fraction, and eGFR. **Results**: The findings demonstrated that these 10 variables could predict each endpoint using at least 90% sensitivity and 80% specificity. Furthermore, we developed a simple risk classification system based on these variables, which successfully stratified the cohort into four groups with significantly distinct risks for each endpoint. **Conclusion**: Our study shows that a small set of variables can effectively predict recurrent MI and stroke in patients with a prior MI. Additionally, we present a straightforward risk classification method that could be applied to various other diseases. **Implications**: This work could facilitate the creation of new decision trees for managing patients following a first MI. Additionally, it may help determine which patients would benefit most from specific preventive measures, such as antiplatelet therapy or statins. **Limitations**: The study's limitations include the fact that it was not designed to identify new risk factors for MI and stroke, and it did not capture patients' physical activity levels. **Funding**: This study was supported by the French Ministry of Higher Education and Research. **Conflicts of Interest**: The authors declare no conflicts of interest. **Availability of data and materials**: Data availability is not applicable. **Ethics approval and consent to participate**: The study protocol was approved by the French National Ethics Committee (Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile-de-Face VI). **Patient and public involvement**: Not applicable. **Registration**: Not applicable. **Competing interests**: The authors have no competing interests. **Authors' contributions**: All authors contributed to the study conception and design. We present a quadrature approach to solve integral equations governing the continuum spectrum of relativistic and non-relativistic electrons interacting with molecules under strong electromagnetic fields. This technique builds upon our previous work (J. Phys. B: At. Mol. Phys. 48 (2015) 105001) that developed multi-dimensional quadrature for molecular targets using complete atomic bases. The development of this quadrature method was driven by the need to achieve the necessary computational accuracy for testing relativistic heavy ion beams as a source of coherent X-ray radiation. By extending the method to multi-center targets, we specifically address the accuracy challenges inherent in multi-electron systems. We apply this quadrature to calculate the photoionization cross section of various molecular targets, including multi-electron systems like H$_2^+$, and compare these results with literature data. Additionally, we demonstrate how to extend the method to compute the continuum spectrum of relative motion in a few-body system. Ultimately, our findings indicate that beam-based x-ray sources could provide unprecedented accuracy for photoionization cross sections and the spectral signatures of molecular targets. This represents a significant advancement in modeling matter interaction with intense electromagnetic fields, a capability that will be essential for interpreting data from upcoming experiments at heavy ion facilities worldwide. These facilities are advancing toward x-ray beams characterized by high brightness, stability, and tunability. These developments hold substantial potential for advancing our understanding of fundamental atomic and molecular processes. Specifically, they offer a unique opportunity to rigorously test and refine our computational and experimental capabilities, thereby driving further innovation and discovery in this field. Finally, we illustrate the specific types of data and insights that can be obtained using our quadrature method. This includes not only traditional observables such as photoionization cross sections and the spectrum of relative motion in a few-body system, but also more complex quantities, such as the response of the target to a two-pulse sequence and the effects of time-varying fields. These capabilities will enable us to probe the electronic structure of the target in unprecedented detail, thereby providing new insights into the underlying physical processes. This level of detail can only be achieved by combining our quadrature method with the full range of capabilities offered by next-generation x-ray beamlines. Such an approach will undoubtedly lead to new and exciting discoveries in the field. To illustrate this, we have included several examples in our paper. This study introduces an algorithm with runtime $2^{kv}n^{1+\omega}$ that resolves the Metric Dimension problem, parameterized by the size of a feedback vertex set $v$. In this context, $\omega$ denotes the matrix multiplication exponent. We leverage this method to develop an algorithm running in $2^{kv}(C\log n)^{v}$ time, which simultaneously determines all possible values of $k$ along with their corresponding frequencies. Here, $C$ represents a universal constant. Additionally, we examine the solve sets for Metric Dimension when parameterized by various structural graph parameters, such as Vertex Cover, Excluded Minor, and Pathwidth. Our findings indicate that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable under Excluded Minor and Pathwidth, utilizing the Courcelle Theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Vertices of Degree at most $d$ and Excluded Minor jointly tight parameterize the problem via a linear function of the parameters, while no other joint fixed-parameter tractability results are established. Finally, we establish that joint fixed-parameter tractability relies heavily on the nature of degrees within graphs. The frequency of the parameter set for Metric Dimension, defined as the minimum required value of $k$ for a graph $G$ with $v$ vertices in a feedback vertex set, is analyzed in detail. This analysis reveals that the problem is frequency-monotone when parameterized by pathwidth. Additionally, it is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized jointly by Excluded Minor and pathwidth, though this does not extend to the scenario where pathwidth is replaced by tree-width. The metric dimension, denoted as $k$, serves as the minimum number of vertices needed to uniquely determine a graph's structure through their distances. Specifically, for a set $S \subseteq V(G)$, every pair of vertices can be distinguished by their distances to at least one vertex in $S$. This study extends the concept of power polynomial sequences to directed areas within the complex plane. Power frameworks for directed areas emerge as a subset of the broader power framework structure defined for directed curves in the complex plane, which was developed in reference [1]. The properties of power frameworks for directed areas are derived from those of their corresponding directed curve counterparts. The framework associated with a directed area $\mathcal{D}$ possesses order $N$ when its $(N+1)$-st moment vanishes while all lower-order moments do not. Given an area parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ defined over a region $\mathcal{U}$ in the $(u,v)$-plane, the choice of origin influences both the order and polynomial order of the resulting power framework. We demonstrate that, for any parametrization of a region, the power framework order for any directed area can be increased to a prescribed integer $K$ by shifting the origin. Furthermore, we prove that for any directed area, there exists a specific parametrization that naturally yields a power framework. We also examine the power polygon derived from such power frameworks. Additionally, we present a direct construction method for power frameworks of directed areas and apply this approach to a subclass of curves known as $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-curves. Finally, we show that for any $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-curve, the power framework order can be elevated to an arbitrary integer $K$. Finally, we establish that for any directed area, there exists an area parametrization that results in a power polygon order of at least $N-1$.

Hothouse Earth scenarios, characterized by elevated CO2 levels, are anticipated to trigger climatic shifts, including the disappearance of ice sheets and percolation of meltwater into the crust. This influx could introduce a novel feedback loop where groundwater discharge into the atmosphere further amplifies CO2 concentrations. To investigate this mechanism, we employed climate models to simulate hothouse conditions and episodic groundwater release. Our findings indicate that, even with moderate groundwater fluxes, air humidity would approach saturation, resulting in a significant rise in the frequency of hothouse-era rainstorms. Consequently, the integration of hothouse groundwater dynamics into climate models could serve as an illustrative method for depicting extreme weather events. The widespread adoption of deep learning (DL) methods has significantly enhanced the accuracy of diagnosing various conditions, including tuberculosis and lung cancer. However, DL models necessitate extensive datasets for training, and human expert labeling is essential, a process that is both costly and time-intensive. Consequently, utilizing a reduced dataset by sampling only a subset of labels is a common strategy to enhance training efficiency. Yet, DL models often struggle to yield satisfactory results when trained on such incomplete data. To address this, we propose a robust label noise reduction mechanism that leverages Bayesian analytics to estimate the probability distribution of class labels for unlabeled images. This approach enables the selection of noisy labels based on an entropy threshold, effectively filtering noise from the mini-batch. Experimental results demonstrate that our mechanism significantly improves the accuracy of DL models across multiple datasets, including chest X-rays, dermoscopic images, and the LUNA16 lung nodule dataset. Timed definitions represent a specialized category of recursive functions governed by colexicographic ordering. This spatial ordering is appropriate for record-like data structures, such as those found in protocol implementations, where every field must be updated before the record becomes valid. We present an alternative formulation of this concept using a monad that encapsulates all possible computation histories for a protocol state, demonstrating that this monad commutes with certain function applications. Leveraging the equations of a monadic transformer, we develop a more flexible solution that extends timed definitions beyond protocols to any function relying on algebraic types. The timeliness of these functions is essential for protocol verification, as protocols must progress through their state histories, rendering backstates inaccessible. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of timed definitions in a protocol authentication proof using the ProVerif verification tool. The approach involves generating a theorem proving the function's co-termination with a provided state, which ProVerif subsequently utilizes during proof construction. Our methodology also addresses theories involving uninterpreted functions that modify algebraic types, effectively mitigating challenges related to uninterpreted function recursion. All proposed solutions have been implemented in the HOL theorem prover. The implementation occurs at the theorem level, meaning the development of co-termination theorems for specific functions is performed manually by the user. Additionally, we demonstrate how to apply timed definitions within the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant using the HOL42K library. Our implementation successfully handles functions defined via coalescing hole filling, a technique employed in both HOL4 and Isabelle2021. However, our solution does not yet support protocols analyzed by the ProVerif tool, as this requires modifications to the ProtVerif specification language. Furthermore, generating the co-termination theorem for a function defined as timed demands significantly more effort compared to standard function definitions. Our work demonstrates that timed definitions constitute a definitional extension rather than an axiomatic one, allowing for straightforward integration into the HOL kernel alongside other definitional extensions like inductive types. This capability offers a distinct advantage over prior research, which often treated timed definitions as axiomatic. This paper introduces an enhanced coherent framework model that incorporates modeling and machine learning techniques to integrate data-driven effects into predictive coherent framework-based models. Specifically, the study investigates how to effectively embed instantaneous, local, and non-local data effects into these models. Specifically, modifications to the transport equations for turbulence kinetic energy and its dissipation rate were achieved by adjusting their production and destruction terms using a weighted ensemble learning method. This approach combines a modeling component with a data-driven component, where their contribution balance is determined by an adaptive weight. Additionally, data effects are introduced to the dissipation rate's budget equation via a memory function. Although local effects are applied to specific turbulence properties, the study demonstrates an effective integration of non-local influences. This is achieved by selecting turbulence quantities at neighboring grid points for the local application, thereby establishing a non-local connection through the discretized grid. The proposed method was validated using the 1/6th scale grid turbulence experiment conducted in the NCAR Large Eddy Simulation Database. Data from the experiment was used to train the methods and verify data compatibility. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm improves the accuracy of data compatibility. Specifically, the predicted time series of turbulence kinetic energy and its dissipation rate show significantly reduced errors compared to the original model. The original coherent framework model, which is a type of Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) model, is widely used in engineering design and numerical simulations. However, the original model's predictions are often inaccurate in regions with strong data effects, such as near boundaries. This discrepancy arises because the destruction terms in the turbulence kinetic energy and dissipation rate equations were derived from linear scaling assumptions, which do not accurately reflect physical phenomena. Consequently, the original model fails to capture instantaneous, local, and non-local data effects. This work aims to resolve this issue by enabling the model to adapt to instantaneous local conditions and non-local data effects through the application of data effects. The proposed method holds significant potential for enhancing the predictive capabilities of various models that rely on the coherent framework. Furthermore, the findings can be extended to other regions exhibiting strong instantaneous data effects, such as wake regions. Future research will explore data effects for other turbulence properties and expand the validation scope to include other regions from numerical simulations. Ultimately, the goal is to facilitate the application of this approach in engineering design and numerical simulations. Extending the polynomial Born-Infeld model established by Manton and Sutcliffe, we introduce the \textit{Born-Infeld/infant Skyrme model}. This hybrid approach integrates two complementary mechanisms for soliton stability: a magnetic field constrained by a small parameter $\epsilon$ akin to $\lambda$ in the nonlinear sigma model, and a potential term that flips sign when $\epsilon$ is treated as negative. Leveraging $O(3)$-symmetry, we employ a shooting method grounded in linear interpolation to identify self-dual static solitons. The resulting family of solutions exhibits a magnetic flux approximately ten times larger than that of the nonlinear sigma model, though their energy remains only marginally lower. Furthermore, their decay rate is significantly slower compared to the standard polynomial model. A comprehensive analysis of both decay rates and magnetic flux demonstrates that the \textit{Born-Infeld/infant Skyrme model} offers a viable framework for studying various physical phenomena. Specifically, we investigate the (anti-)self-dual region to explore potential connections with quantum gravity. We have created and experimentally analyzed hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantennas based on silicon nanospheres integrated with gold nanoparticles to achieve the simultaneous control of particle spacing, size, and shape. These nanoantennas are highly luminous under excitation due to strong photoluminescence from the silicon nanospheres and a high quantum yield of 40% for the embedded gold nanoparticles. The gold nanoparticles also generate localized surface plasmon resonances that can be tuned across the visible spectrum. The presence of these localized plasmons alters the photoluminescence angular distribution by modifying the oscillator strength along different directions. By precisely positioning and arranging gold nanoparticles on the surface of the silicon nanospheres, we successfully designed and fabricated a hybrid nanoantenna with a well-defined, unidirectional photoluminescence pattern. This approach offers a straightforward method for engineering the spatial distribution of energy within the system, thereby enhancing the efficiency of light-matter interactions. This study investigates the electronic structure of silicene supported by h-BN using density functional theory. We examine how Mn adatoms, positioned either above Si or above the boron (B) sites, influence the material's band gap. Results indicate that while Mn adatoms above the Si lattice maintain the Dirac cone characteristic of pristine silicene, they open a tunable band gap when placed above the B sites. The scarcity of training data in multi-category text classification poses a significant challenge, prompting the use of class-level sampling strategies to address class imbalance. This study employs various artificial oversampling techniques to generate synthetic samples for imbalanced classes across English and Turkish news datasets, categorizing the methods into three groups: class-based, related class-based, and target class-based. Following data generation, a classification model is trained and assessed using multi-category metrics. The analysis reveals that class-based and related class-based oversampling consistently yield superior performance compared to other methods. Furthermore, the findings indicate that oversampling enhances the performance of support vector machines and neural networks relative to other classification algorithms. Ultimately, the related class-based oversampling technique delivered the highest performance, achieving micro F1 scores of 0.8441 (English) and 0.8177 (Turkish), with target class-based oversampling following closely behind. This research provides a foundation for developing advanced oversampling methods to minimize the adverse effects of class imbalance in multi-category text classification. Additionally, the study includes Python code for conducting class-level, related class-level, and target class-level oversampling, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ozdemirbasak/Class-Level-Related-Class-Level-and-Target-Class-Level-OverSampling. Related findings are available in Turkish at https://ozdemirbasak.wordpress.com/class-level-oversampling/. Finally, the authors acknowledge that this work represents only a preliminary step toward the most effective oversampling technique; future endeavors will aim to identify the optimal approach by considering factors such as the number of classes, class sizes, and document lengths.

Media coverage of the crisis has been extensive and intense, yet it has sparked intense debate regarding its impact on viewers. While some argue that sensationalist reporting fuels panic, others contend that adequate public information is essential to reduce fear. Despite these conflicting views, there is broad consensus that news media must educate the public and promote health outcomes. Consequently, researchers are increasingly scrutinizing how media reports influence audience perceptions and behaviors. Despite this growing interest, there is a notable lack of empirical evidence linking media coverage to the specific trajectories of COVID-19 cases, fatalities, and audience metrics like page views. Utilizing advanced data analytics, we apply a vector autoregression model to investigate the interconnections among media reports, case counts, mortality rates, and audience size. Our findings indicate that media reports do not exacerbate fear; rather, they correlate with reduced fear and lower case numbers. These results offer valuable insights for policymakers and media professionals, enabling more informed decisions on media content and strategies to mitigate the pandemic's impact. Additionally, we recommend that news organizations prioritize informing vulnerable populations to further limit the virus's spread. This approach would also strengthen the media's role in public education and support the ultimate goal of containing the pandemic. To support these recommendations, we have made the underlying data publicly available to advance research in this domain. By demonstrating the evidence behind informed media consumption, we hope to encourage the public to seek out news reports that provide accurate information, thereby contributing to personal and societal well-being. This study analyzes how polarized electrons and protons interact within the $e\vec{p} \to e\vec{p}$ scattering framework. Utilowing the spin density matrix formalism, we investigate the transfer of polarization from the initial electron to the scattered electron. Our findings indicate that with an incident electron polarization of $P_{in} = 100\%$, the degree of transmitted polarization reaches approximately $P_{out} \approx 90\%$ at momentum transfer values of $Q^2 \approx 10-15\ GeV^2$. The influence of proton spin is explicitly incorporated into our results. We also examine the effects of proton polarization $P_p$ and the impact of proton excitation, which is critical for high-energy elastic scattering. The probability of proton excitation, denoted as $W_{ex}$, is shown to be approximately 10% at $Q^2 = 15\ GeV^2$ when $P_p = 0$. Furthermore, we explore the potential for enhancing transmitted polarization through proton spin-dependent terms, observing that these effects can be amplified by increasing the magnitude of $P_{in}$. The entire analysis was conducted using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. We have provided comprehensive tables, graphs, and plots detailing the outcomes of this work. The presented approach is applicable to other elastic scattering processes, such as $e\vec{p} \to e\pi^+\pi^-$, and the findings are extendable to deep inelastic scattering scenarios. Additionally, we note that the proton's electromagnetic form factors were derived from the JLab database. The accuracy of the transmitted polarization values is supported by the precision of these data. We have also considered the uncertainty associated with the proton's polarization $P_p$. The code employed for numerical calculations is available at \href{https://github.com/abdullahkayaarar/e-p_spin}{https://github.com/abdullahkayaarar/e-p\_spin}. We introduce a method designed to create synthetic training data for specialists by significantly speeding up the training process through the use of optimized subspaces. Unlike previous data-enhanced training approaches, our subspace optimization targets not only the model architecture but also the hyperparameters. Furthermore, we show that combining this data-enhanced training with post-training ensembling enables the creation of reusable, model-based tuning tools. These reusability improvements allow for rapid and reliable deployment of specialists, which is essential for making specialism viable within generalist-specialist systems. Reusable tuning is a critical component of R4D, a framework that replaces the traditional human feedback loop with an automated feedback cycle to continuously improve the performance of multi-specialist systems. This specialisation through division of labour is particularly vital for specialist AI agents operating in distributed environments.

This work forms part of a broader initiative to develop a specialisation framework for autonomous agents. The primary goal is to enhance the overall system performance of autonomous agents by leveraging their ability to adapt and learn from interactions with their environment. By learning from these interactions, specialisation enables agents to develop expertise in specific tasks, thereby increasing the probability of success. This expertise is especially valuable when combined with data-enhanced training and an automised feedback cycle to continuously refine the specialist's training. Additionally, it allows for the learning of tasks that a general AI agent could not have initially learned due to constraints in the state-action space.

Keywords: Specialisation, Autonomous Agents, Robotics, Reinforcement Learning, Hyperparameters.

In this study, we employ a alkaline spin-maser model to illustrate the efficacy of digital simulation methods. We demonstrate the successful adaptation of the spin-maser's dynamics for such a simulation by leveraging the connection between its evolution operator (along the $z$ axis) and the eigenbasis of the two-particle swap operator. Our findings indicate that even a minimal two-spin system can serve as a quantum simulator when digital techniques are applied. Furthermore, we examine the error analysis regarding the approximation of spin-maser evolution, with results showing that two-particle systems can simulate a 200-spin system with an error under 1%. To validate our digital simulation approach, we compare the analytical solution of the spin-maser model against both the digital method and the corresponding quantum circuit. Ultimately, we conclude that digital simulation methods offer a powerful tool for quantum information processing. Specifically, we show that the digital simulation of the spin-maser model can be directly converted into a quantum algorithm for factoring large numbers using Shor's algorithm. Consequently, our work may pave the way for the development of new quantum algorithms and potentially novel quantum information processing tasks. In the broader context of the quantum revolution, our research may contribute to the advancement of emerging quantum technologies. Finally, the successful implementation of these methods may significantly influence the development of emerging quantum technologies. This paper introduces and investigates the Randomized Newton Method (RNM) for N homogeneous agents, each managing a local convex objective, while jointly minimizing their average. We establish convergence rate bounds for both the primal and dual variables under conditions of noise and communication errors. Specifically, we demonstrate that RNM achieves practical linear convergence in both the primal and dual domains, even when noise is present. Furthermore, we apply RNM to a vehicle formation tracking task to validate the theoretical findings. Additionally, we extend the analysis to handle a subset sum constraint, proving linear convergence for the RNM-based solution. Finally, the solution derived from RNM is benchmarked against two state-of-the-art distributed methods to verify the results. Numerical simulations confirm the efficacy of the proposed RNM approach. Additionally, this solution exhibits the fastest convergence speed compared to the other methods. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ashishkumar123456789/NewtonMethod}. This paper details our methodology and findings for the first contest on identifying Hindi and Bengali hate speech. The objective was to classify generated sentences containing hate speech, specifically targeting Dalits, Muslims, and women in Indian contexts. Our team achieved macro F-1 scores of 81.69% and 79.24% for the Hindi and Bengali languages, respectively, securing 1st place within each track. Our baseline approach utilized a BERT-based transformer model with transfer learning, a strategy that proved highly effective across both languages. We also conducted a comparative analysis of various neural networks, including BERT, FastText+Bi-LSTM, RoBERTa, and XLNet, to determine the optimal model through ablation studies. Finally, we discussed the challenges encountered and how they were addressed. This report serves as a comprehensive guide to our approach, offering insights and detailed explanations regarding the applications used. We hope this document assists researchers and students in building similar models. We present a study of such a module utilizing tetraphenyl butane as a polar tracer gas, operated without electric multiplications and equipped with tetrode cathodes for recoil discrimination. Our work provides detailed characterization of the various signals generated by neutron and gamma interactions, aiming to define optimal signal selection criteria to maximize sensitivity in future neutron-based dark matter experiments. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this detector design achieves near 100% detection efficiency for gamma rays up to 1 MeV and identifies approximately 70% of 2 MeV neutrons. Furthermore, our discrimination capabilities yield an equivalent gamma rejection factor of $10^6$ for neutron signals, surpassing the $10^3$ level typically accessible with similar technologies. These results indicate that this class of detectors is exceptionally well-suited for neutron-based experiments, such as the proposed Neutron Decay to Dark Matter searches. Additionally, we discuss how incorporating a tetraphenyl butane target into existing dark matter setups, like the XENON1T experiment, could enable new searches for neutron-based processes in the 1–2 MeV energy range, potentially offering the first constraints on dark matter models predicting keV-scale features. Finally, we outline how this technology can be scaled to achieve the detector sizes necessary for fundamental symmetry searches, including neutrinoless double beta decay. Specifically, we propose a novel large-scale recoil detector using tetraphenyl butane as the polarizer, accessible to fundamental symmetry experiments worldwide. Commercial driving represents a labor sector with some of the lowest wages and the highest instability. The proliferation of commercial vehicles and the rising cost of fuel have driven fuel efficiency into focus, creating an urgent demand for accurate models that can predict fuel consumption. This study addresses the challenge of developing an effective communication strategy to educate commercial drivers about fuel usage. We introduce the Specialist Moderation model, a method for predicting machine learning outputs in high-stakes settings. By applying topological data analysis, we demonstrate that driver expertise is a critical factor influencing how commercial drivers evaluate their own fuel efficiency. Furthermore, we develop a theory of contextual intelligence, a concept for AI designed to be modifiable by contextual experts like commercial drivers. This ensures that commercial driving remains a stable and equitable profession. The code required to run these models is publicly available at https://github.com/robertobertelli/SM. This paper introduces the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge, a competition held concurrently with SemEval-2019 Task 11: Mixed Initiative Discourse Annotation. The challenge aims to advance research on named entity recognition (NER) by testing systems on previously unseen words specifically for pre-defined named entity categories. The dataset comprises 16 major language families, featuring labels for entities such as countries, cities, states, oceans, mountains, rivers, plants, animals, currencies, and languages. The study demonstrates that existing state-of-the-art NER methods perform significantly worse on new words compared to familiar vocabulary, with the performance gap being most pronounced for rare rare words. We invite researchers to participate and help find solutions to this well-established yet deceptively simple NER subtask. Our goal is to foster discourse on the challenges this domain poses for various machine learning techniques and to encourage the creation of new models capable of superior out-of-lexicon (OOl) performance. This paper outlines the dataset, analyzes the challenges faced by current state-of-the-art systems, and introduces the benchmark used to evaluate them. We define two additional evaluation metrics to assess performance relative to the analysis. Finally, we present results from the winner of the competition, which achieved a 20% improvement over the baseline. We demonstrate that the average pathway connecting two points within a Gaussian random field manifold can be characterized by a geodesic in an ambient Riemannian space. By decomposing the metric of this exterior Riemannian structure into a sum of a dominant metric and a perturbation, we establish that the associated geodesic equation simplifies to a straight line under these conditions. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a stochastic field's influence is not uniform; rather, it diminishes rapidly with distance, enabling the approximation of the exterior Riemannian metric as Minkowski when separation exceeds certain thresholds. These outcomes are validated through examples drawn from machine learning, statistical physics, and statistics. Notably, in a multivariate normal distribution, the exterior Riemannian metric depends on the correlation matrix, whereas the geodesic distance between two points is determined by the inverse of this correlation matrix. Additionally, we derive a sufficient condition for a geodesic to approach a straight line and employ this condition to construct applications within stochastic differential geometry. Our work establishes a new framework for analyzing random field manifolds by leveraging exterior Riemannian metrics and their geodesics. Specifically, we demonstrate that the average trajectory of MLEs across diverse Gaussian stochastic field manifolds corresponds to a geodesic within this external Riemannian structure. This insight facilitates a unified methodology for studying random field manifolds using a characteristic metric defined in the exterior space. Furthermore, our analysis of geodesics in these manifolds yields applications in statistical physics, multivariate analysis, and machine learning. For instance, we reveal that within a sphere defined by a correlation matrix, geodesics follow straight lines when the correlation strength is high and curve when it is low. Finally, we model the Bayesian inference process as geodesic motion in this exterior Riemannian structure, where the correlation matrix acts as a Riemannian tensor field. This perspective offers a novel perspective on the behavior of Bayesian inference and the evolution of MLEs in random field manifolds. Our results provide a new analytical tool for understanding the behavior of MLEs by utilizing exterior Riemannian geodesics within a stochastic field manifold framework. Specifically, this approach enables a unified investigation of the convergence properties of MLEs across various statistical models by examining the characteristics of the exterior Riemannian geodesics. The primary finding indicates that for extended film runtimes, word frequency distributions align closely with the overall word rank rank (Slope $S \approx 1$), reflecting a universal feature of large lexical lists. Conversely, shorter films exhibit a "finite-size" effect where high-frequency words dominate the list, resulting in a steeper Slop $S \approx 1.5$ consistent with general finite random texts. Notably, films ranging from 90 to 150 minutes in duration demonstrate a transition from this finite-size regime toward the extended-runtime regime. Furthermore, the standard runtime (approximately 2 hours) appears to optimize the balance between lexical diversity and usability, an effect observed across major Hollywood production companies. Finally, the study confirms that both male and female directors oversee films exhibiting the universal regime, with no significant correlation between director gender and the Slope $S$. The research concludes by proposing a universal model to explain these finite-size characteristics. Let $L(s,\pi)$ represent the $L$-function associated with an irreducible cuspidal automorphic representation $\pi$ of $\mathrm{GL}_n\times \mathrm{GL}_m$. We demonstrate that the Galois conjugates of $L(s,\pi)$ remain bounded whenever $L(1,\pi)$ converges absolutely, provided the dual $L$-functions $L^\vee(s,\pi)$ satisfy a functional equation. This finding offers partial progress toward resolving a conjecture originally proposed by Iwanawa and extended by Deligne. Furthermore, we derive novel boundedness conclusions for special values of $L$-functions linked to automorphic forms on quaternion groups and the automorphic $L$-functions for regular supercuspidal representations of $\mathrm{GL}_2$. Notably, our methodology diverges from the approaches utilized by Deligne and Blasius. Additionally, we establish novel convergence results for special values of $L$-functions for isobaric sums of automorphic $L$-functions. Our proof relies on automorphic methods, whereas an alternative approach combining analytic and representation theory techniques can be derived from the work of Iwanawa and Yoshida. Finally, we examine the applicability of these results to the conjectures of Kohnen and Zagier. Specifically, our methodology yields novel boundedness results for non-holomorphic automorphic forms, including those for $\mathrm{GL}_2\times \mathrm{GL}_1$ and quaternion groups. Our strategy involves utilizing arithmetic data regarding special values of Dedekind zeta functions to link arithmetic data concerning special values of automorphic $L$-functions with regular central critical values. In the case of holomorphic newforms, we employ the Shimura-Taniyama-Weil conjecture and the modularity lift to obtain boundedness results for special values of $L(s,\pi)$ for $\mathrm{GL}_2\times \mathrm{GL}_1$. Furthermore, we utilize the analytic properties of quaternionic Eisenstein series to derive boundedness results for special values of $L(s,\pi)$ for $\mathrm{GL}_2\times \mathrm{GL}_1$. Our work yields the following specific outcomes:

\item[1.] We establish a novel bound for the special values of Dedekind zeta functions.

Using a tight-binding model, this study investigates charge and spin transport in armchair graphene nanostructures by connecting a ferromagnetic source to a non-magnetic drain via leads. The system allows for the independent application of gate voltage and exchange field at the drain. By analyzing the dependence of spin polarization on these parameters, we identify two distinct regimes of spin-sensitive behavior. The first regime exhibits high spin polarization (exceeding 90%) that remains stable across a broad range of dissipation conditions, though it is highly sensitive to variations in gate voltage and exchange field. In contrast, the second regime is characterized by a region of negative differential conductance, where spin polarization approaches unity; however, this behavior is suppressed by dissipation effects, resulting in lower spin polarization. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of these systems in spintronics and quantum information technologies, highlighting the advantages of graphene nanostructures regarding fabrication and defect management. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research in this field. These models and findings are expected to be valuable for advancing spintronics and quantum information science, particularly in developing devices that utilize spin-polarized electrons as qubits for quantum information processing. Specifically, we propose a platform for generating and manipulating spin-polarized electrons using graphene nanostructures, which can serve as spin-polarized qubits in quantum information applications. Additionally, we address the challenges of dissipation in these systems and suggest strategies to mitigate them, which could help overcome current obstacles in graphene-based quantum technologies. The models and results presented here may contribute to new advancements in graphene research, potentially leading to breakthroughs in quantum computing and information processing. Specifically, our work paves the way for the development of graphene-based quantum dots and other devices essential for quantum information processing. We also explore the possibility of using graphene nanostructures to create new types of quantum bits with unique properties, which could expand the capabilities of quantum computing and information processing. The models and findings reported in this work are poised to contribute to new developments in graphene research, opening up exciting new avenues for future progress. In conclusion, our work has the potential to significantly impact the field of graphene research and contribute to new discoveries and innovations in quantum technology. Specifically, the models and results presented here may lead to new breakthroughs in graphene-based quantum dot research and other areas of quantum information processing. By providing a novel approach to generating and manipulating spin-polarized electrons, our findings could unlock new possibilities for graphene research and contribute to new discoveries and advancements in the field. Let $G$ be a simple, connected graph with $p$ vertices. The independence number of $G$, denoted $\alpha(G)$, is the size of its largest induced subgraph that is free of edges. The graph's Hamiltonicity is determined by the minimum degree $\delta(G)$ and the independence number $\alpha(G)$. We introduce the concept of the Hamiltonian independence quantity, defined as $\eta(G) = \delta(G) - \alpha(G)$. This paper demonstrates that if $G$ is a simple, connected graph with $p$ vertices and $\eta(G) > \frac{p}{2}$, then $G$ is pancyclic. Furthermore, we examine how both the Hamiltonian independence quantity and independence number influence the conditions required for $G$ to be pancyclic. We derive sufficient conditions ensuring $G$ is pancyclic and highlight the significance of these findings. Finally, we analyze the relationship between $\eta(G)$ and $\alpha(G)$, proving that for a simple, connected graph $G$ with $p$ vertices, if $\eta(G) \ge \frac{p}{2}$ and $\alpha(G) \le \frac{p}{3}$, then $G$ is pancyclic. The creation of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) during heavy-ion collisions is linked to modifications in particle production mechanisms within the Quark-Gluon Phase (QGP) and the Hadron Resonance Gas (HRG) phase. Inspired by the recently commissioned ISOLDE/ESoMSIS beam at CERN, which enables mixed Au+Au and Cu+Cu interactions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV, we propose measuring thermal radiation from QGP by analyzing the systematic production of charm and strangeness as functions of invariant mass across both system sizes. Furthermore, we suggest investigating the QGP phase by measuring the transverse momentum ($p_T$) spectra of $\Upsilon$ states in both systems, providing the first direct evidence for the suppression of higher excited states. This study also examines the melting of strange quark condensates in the QGP phase through various strangeness observables, such as $K^0_s$-nucleon correlations, which could be conducted using Au+Au and Deuterium+Gold interactions at the same center-of-mass energy. Additionally, we address the enhancement of strange hadron production in Cu+Cu and Deuterium+Au interactions, alongside the potential for observing the strangeness enhancement factor as a function of $p_T$ in both interaction types. Finally, we explore the formation and melting of $K^-$-condensates in the QGP phase by analyzing the momentum spectra of $K^-$ in both system sizes. These analyses are expected to yield new insights into the microscopic mechanisms of thermal hadron production in the QGP phase, thereby clarifying the matter created during heavy-ion collisions. Consequently, these measurements will facilitate a more precise determination of the temperature and chemical potential of the QGP. This can be achieved by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data from both interaction systems, ultimately leading to a more complete understanding of the nuclear equation of state. The proposed measurements will be conducted using the ALICE detector at the LHC. We have also estimated the statistical precision required to observe these phenomena, demonstrating that the required statistics can be attained with $\sim$1 nb$^{-1}$ of data for Cu+Cu and $\sim$10 nb$^{-1}$ for Au+Au at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV. We conclude that these measurements are crucial for understanding the formation and melting mechanisms of hadrons in the QGP phase

This study presents a new approach that merges sparse grid sampling with adaptive spectral Koefman operator estimation to analyze dynamical systems exhibiting diverse behaviors. The method starts by generating a sparse grid based on system observables, which are then sampled according to the system's invariant measure. Subsequently, the linear operator associated with the dynamical system is estimated using adaptive spectral kernel smoothing. This technique isolates dynamic features while filtering out sampling noise, thereby enhancing reconstruction accuracy. The proposed algorithm is highly flexible and broadly applicable, as evidenced by its successful implementation on a chaotic Lorenz-16 oscillator, a quasi-periodic forced harmonic oscillator, and a rigid body performing torque-free motion. These results demonstrate that the algorithm can accurately identify dynamic features across a wide range of scenarios, offering a promising tool for high-dimensional dynamical systems. Additionally, a key advantage of adaptive spectral operator estimation is its independence from sequential time series data, making it particularly suitable for analyzing snapshot ensembles from high-resolution simulations where temporal ordering is unavailable. Finally, the paper discusses the method's potential for advancing data-driven modeling in complex engineering applications within aerospace and other fields. This study introduces the "outside complicated scaling method," a concept distinct from conventional scaling approaches, to enhance the robustness of strong DC field calculations for atoms and molecules within atoms-in-molecules frameworks. The approach's efficacy is confirmed across various systems, including helium, neon, water, and methanol. Its performance is further demonstrated through studies on helium dimers, dimethanol dimers, and the electron detachment region of water, where it significantly outperforms standard scaling methods. The findings indicate that the outer regions of atoms and molecules are essential for achieving accurate ionization rates in these calculations. Additionally, the outer regions of molecules tend to be more critical than those of isolated atoms. The method's effectiveness is further validated by the successful reproduction of experimental photoelectron angular distributions for H2O. Ultimately, this approach substantially improves the reliability of DC scaling calculations for atoms and molecules in strong fields within the outside-in framework. Furthermore, it is observed that outside-in calculations for molecules generally require broader support from outer regions compared to inside-in calculations, which are predominantly influenced by inner regions. This contrasts sharply with the inside-out approach, which focuses exclusively on inner regions and is primarily grounded in the inside-in theory. These insights are expected to be valuable for developing novel and efficient strong-field theories. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a prominent iterative technique for addressing the Schrödinger problem, which seeks an optimal diffusion process connecting two fixed marginal distributions. Typically, this approach yields a solution that minimizes the quadratic path-optimal transport cost. However, solutions may fail to exist when the two marginal distributions are defined on different state spaces. Although prior research has established the Sinkhorn algorithm's convergence in cases where a solution does exist, this study demonstrates that the algorithm still converges to a deterministic constant in "wrong" cases, where no solution is available. This finding confirms the method's robust convergence. Furthermore, these findings are supported by algorithms derived from "augmented" Kullback-Leibler divergence, which offer alternative solutions to the Schrödinger problem. Finally, numerical experiments illustrate the convergence rates of both methods and compare their performance. The code used in this study is accessible at \url{https://github.com/GeoffroyBeyl/robust-schrödinger}. These results present the first convergence guarantees for Sinkhorn iterations in such scenarios and hold significant implications for applications involving matrix scaling and diffusion models with fixed initial and final marginals. Specifically, this paper demonstrates that, contrary to standard practice, the diffusion model can yield a solution even when marginals are defined on different state spaces, provided at least one of them is absolutely continuous with respect to the common ambient measure. Additionally, for a broader class of problems, we prove the existence of solutions and establish convergence rates applicable to both Sinkhorn and augmented Sinkhorn methods. These guarantees not only ensure the convergence of Sinkhorn iterations in "wrong" cases but also enable a unified convergence analysis across both scenarios, supported by a dual analysis. Finally, our work introduces a new class of problems featuring "moving" marginals, for which we propose a novel solution and prove its convergence rates. This effectively extends the primary results of the paper to a wider class of problems. Furthermore, our results provide the first convergence guarantees for the Sinkhorn method in "degenerate" cases, where the Kullback-Leibler divergence acts as a distance metric rather than a divergence. These results underscore the robustness of the Sinkhorn method, particularly given its widespread use in applications ranging from image processing to machine learning. The paper also includes an extensive discussion of these findings. This study measures the cross-sections for the production of pairs of top quarks and antiquarks at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV using proton-proton collisions. The analysis utilizes the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, incorporating an updated Monte Carlo simulation tuned to reflect the higher collision energy. The dataset comprises 329.4 nb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, gathered between the end of Run 2 and the commencement of Run 3, with this work published as a whole for the first time. The integrated cross-section for top quark pair production is determined to be $\sigma_{\mathrm{t\bar{t}}} = 698.7 \pm 1.4 \text{(stat)} \pm 11.1 \text{(syst)}$ pb. This result aligns with Standard Model predictions and with measurements conducted at the lower energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. The top quark mass is found to be $m_{\mathrm{t}} = 172.00 \pm 0.53 \text{(stat)} \pm 0.38 \text{(syst)}$ GeV, consistent with previous ATLAS findings. This paper investigates the localization dynamics within a centrally embedded double Atwood machine (DDA), which consists of three pulleys, each driving two subsystems of two masses connected by different frictionless pulleys. Unlike the widely studied externally driven double Atwood machine, this system offers an analytically distinct model that allows for the examination of both localized and delocalized dynamics. Through an exact analytical approach, we determine the conditions required for dynamics to localize on one of the three DDAs. Furthermore, using an ensemble-averaged model, we demonstrate that the localization transition in the DDA is of the first order. This phenomenon is characterized by hysteresis involving coexisting localized and delocalized states, alongside the emergence of singularities in density and pressure at the critical coupling strength where localization begins. Additionally, our findings indicate that density and pressure within the localized regime are governed by the effective gravitational field of the subsystem. Finally, our results reveal that the delocalized regime is influenced by the initial conditions of the masses. Our analysis of the coexistence region identifies the mechanisms responsible for hysteresis, thereby explaining the system's localization behavior. We conclude that these findings may have potential applications in various technological fields. Additionally, we validate our results through numerical simulations and an experimental realization of the model. Finally, we suggest that these conclusions can be extended to other technically relevant systems, such as nanotubes, by utilizing an external thermal reservoir. To our knowledge, this represents the first study on the localization behavior of a DDA. This research can be easily replicated in undergraduate and high school laboratories. Furthermore, we believe these results will inspire future investigations into mass-pulley systems, including those composed of two, three, or more DDAs. Given the potential technological relevance, we anticipate that this work will inspire researchers to explore the localization properties of the DDA further. Finally, we note that all findings can be easily reproduced in a laboratory setting. Our results may also inspire future research into the localization behavior of the DDA. Let $T_p[q](\beta)$ denote the class of functions $q$ satisfying $T_p[q](\beta) = \{q(z): q \in \mathcal{A}_p(1),\,\,\Re[q(z)] > \beta\}$. Additionally, let $I_{l,m,n}[v](z)$ represent the generalized Bessel function. The primary objective of this paper is to establish sufficient conditions for the subordination $I_{l,m,n}[v](z) \prec q(z)$, where $q$ belongs to the class $T_p[q](\beta)$, and to derive a sufficient condition for the validity of this subordination. Furthermore, we examine specific instances of Bessel functions and their relationship with the function $I_{l,m,n}[v](z)$. Finally, we investigate the univalence properties of the analytic function $f(z) = z + \sum_{j=p+1}^{\infty} a_j z^j$ under the condition that $p(a_j) \prec I_{l,m,n}[v](z)$. Specifically, we demonstrate that $f(z)$ is univalent in the unit disk $|z| < 1$ and determine its region of univalence. Moreover, we establish an inequality for $|f(z)|$ and calculate the coefficient of $a_{p+1}$ when $p=1$. Finally, we present examples to illustrate the applicability of our main theorems.

Urban interaction patterns are often analyzed to forecast viral transmission. However, during the pandemic, people altered their behavior, necessitating comprehensive modifications to both the features and predictive models of these time-series patterns. Data from the Chicago Metropolitan Area, collected via the Chicago Urban Mobility Report, highlights that income-based inequality in cellular phone co-locations was already elevated in 2019. Yet, inequality indices rose sharply in 2020, driven by divergent behavioral responses across income groups. Specifically, while lower-income individuals resumed higher interaction levels, those with higher incomes maintained greater physical distancing. These distinct behaviors resulted in a divergence in the recovery trajectories of interaction patterns for different income classes. Furthermore, the pandemic's impact was not uniform; it affected low-income populations more severely than high-income ones, largely due to the occupational demands of low-income workers to return to physical settings. This divergence in recovery trends poses significant implications for the spatial distribution of viral outbreaks and underscores the need for targeted policy interventions. Additionally, the pandemic's disproportionate effect on low-income groups exacerbates existing socioeconomic disparities, thereby intensifying the challenges these communities face in recovering from the pandemic. Consequently, the models and forecasting techniques developed in this study are essential for evaluating the potential consequences of such inequalities on viral spread and for guiding policy decisions in disaster management and recovery efforts. Finally, our findings contribute to the growing body of research emphasizing the critical role of urban mobility in pandemic recovery, while offering insights for managing social distancing and containment strategies. This research paves the way for future studies on the spatial distribution of viral transmission and its socioeconomic factors. This work is based on the second-place solution from the Chicago Urban Mobility Challenge, a competition organized by Chicago Data Portal. This study introduces various preconditioners designed for multiphase flow equations within heterogeneous porous media, derived using fully implicit black-oil formulations. These equations are discretized via a fully implicit mixed finite-element approach for field variables and integrated Gauss-Seidel algorithms for field separation. The resulting framework enables the application of multiple preconditioners to resolve the complex systems of nonlinear, multiphase flow equations. To evaluate these precursors, four representative test cases were examined: one homogeneous model and three heterogeneous models featuring distinct permeability contrasts in vertical, horizontal, and three-dimensional configurations. Numerical results demonstrate that all preconditioners significantly accelerate the convergence of the fully implicit black-oil equations compared to standard iterative solvers, with several outperforming converged single-phase simulations. Among them, the Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) algorithm paired with a diagonal approximation of the Jacobian matrix yields the most efficient convergence for the separated system. For comparison, the Dual-Grid (DUG) preconditioner was also developed, revealing that while DUG converges rapidly for near-horizontal models, it suffers from slow convergence in highly heterogeneous models with strong gravity effects. Consequently, the DUG algorithm is less suitable for highly heterogeneous multiphase flow modeling in three-dimensional heterogeneous porous media. Finally, a preconditioner based on the Schur complement of the multiphase flow equations was also constructed. Numerical experiments confirm that this Schur-complement-based preconditioner is highly effective for two-phase flow modeling in three-dimensional heterogeneous porous media. In conclusion, a robust preconditioner for two-phase flow in three-dimensional heterogeneous porous media can be built upon the fully implicit black-oil formulation combined with Schur-complement-based matrix inversion techniques. This approach offers a viable alternative to traditional two-phase flow models, such as the relative permeability-based formulation. Future research will explore extending this highly effective and robust preconditioner to fully implicit black-oil models under strong gravity conditions in two- and three-dimensional heterogeneous porous media. Additionally, the method holds promise for nonlinear flow modeling in heterogeneous porous media involving thermal convection, chemical reactions, and other complex processes. We present a theoretical investigation of a bilateral, birefringent optical cavity exhibiting strong unilateral transmission. In this setup, the input line is integrated into one of the cavity's wings, producing a symmetrical configuration. Our analysis reveals that the bilateral chamber maintains all the key properties of its unilateral counterpart, while offering the added benefit of superior noise suppression. Consequently, the bilateral chiral cavity is a viable candidate for implementing nonreciprocal devices within birefringent systems. Specifically, we explore its potential application as an all-silicon photonics component: a nonreciprocal optical buffer. This device would induce a substantial time delay for forward-propagating waves while transmitting backward-propagating waves with 100% efficiency. Such a device would significantly enhance communication network efficiency by enabling the buffering of faulty or re-routable packets without active control. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bilateral chiral cavity can serve as a highly efficient and compact switch for controlling the transmission of optical pulses. In its default state, the device allows full transmission with minimal insertion loss; however, a control beam can completely block the primary signal. The buffer's high reflectivity ensures that the transmitted pulse retains a narrow linewidth, a critical feature for maintaining coherence in quantum systems. We validate these theoretical predictions with single-pulse transmission and reflection data from an experimental silicon photonics chip, confirming the exceptional performance of the bilateral chiral cavity. These findings underscore the potential of chiral cavities to advance various photonic and quantum technologies. Additionally, we highlight promising applications within quantum memory and quantum sensing. Finally, we propose future research directions, including the bilateral chiral cavity's role as a robust, tunable quantum memory. This memory could store photonic qubits with high fidelity and remain accessible only from a single direction, a vital attribute for establishing the fundamental non-commutativity required in quantum information processing. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the bilateral chiral cavity could function as an ultra-sensitive photonic sensor, surpassing the standard quantum limit. We anticipate that these advancements will foster new research avenues in the fields of photonics and quantum physics. To support these conclusions, we provide comprehensive data and detailed demonstrations through numerical simulations, numerical optimization, and experimental measurements. This work demonstrates the high efficiency and robustness of chiral unilateral and bilateral chambers, establishing them as a promising foundation for future technological advancements. Our proposed future research directions are poised to significantly impact the fields of photonics and quantum physics.
