This paper investigates the Hartle-Hawking state in 2d Liouville CFT within the stringy compactification range $0<B^2<1/\mu$. By calculating the HKSS partition function and examining the spectrum, we identify that the Liouville CFT bound corresponds to the point where the Liouville vacuum annihilates the Fock space and the KK ground state migrates to the ghost sector. Additionally, we derive an analytical expression for the large $B^2$ behavior of the partition function, revealing an exponential correction when $b$ is finite. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the matrix model partition function derived from a Schur index calculation aligns with the partition function in the semi-classical $c\gg 1$ limit. Finally, we suggest a connection between the parameter $\mu$ in the partition function and the rank $N$ of the gauge group in the matrix model. These findings suggest the existence of an $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ invariant matrix framework for 2d gravity in the stringy regime. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these results for the spectrum of 2d gravity, the structure of the Hartle-Hawking state, and the recent tunneling conjecture. To facilitate these discussions, we also review the recently proposed matrix model for 2d gravity. [arXiv:2109.00072] [arXiv:2109.00075] (unpublished) [arXiv:2109.00080] (published)

I demonstrate that the ideal fluid solution derived from the two cosmological constants $A$ and $B$ simplifies to the \textit{warp drive} solution proposed by Arxiv:1004.3052 when $B=0$ (equivalently $k=0$). The distinction between these solutions lies in their interpretation of $A$. I further show that warped space solutions exist for both positive and negative values of $A$. Additionally, I examine how the \textit{warp drive} solution accommodates matter, energy, and the cosmological constant. My findings indicate that the geometry of the \textit{warp drive} solution resembles that of the early universe. The negative $A$ solution features matter concentrated at the center, whereas the positive $A$ solution concentrates matter at the boundaries. When $A<0$, the matter density and pressure approach their standard de Sitter values asymptotically. Conversely, for positive $A$, the density exhibits a minimum, while the pressure displays a maximum. For both cases, the pressure is lower than the matter density. For $A<0$, the matter density exceeds the square of the Hubble constant, whereas for $A>0$, the density is less than the Hubble constant's square. The density for the $k=0$ (\textit{warp drive}) solution is also less than the Hubble constant's square. Furthermore, the pressure for $A<0$ is also less than the Hubble constant's square. I have not identified any prior literature on the $A$ solution, and I believe this paper will be of significant interest to physicists studying the early universe. My ultimate goal is to determine if the $A$ solution can account for dark energy. While I do not claim to have resolved this issue, I have shown that the energy density of the cosmological constant can be interpreted as negative matter density, and I have calculated the $A$ solution's matter density as a fraction of the Hubble constant's square. I also observed that the pressure of the cosmological constant acts as anti-gravity. I suggest that the $A$ solution, where matter density is less than the Hubble constant's square, could represent the universe during inflation. The $k=0$ (\textit{warp drive}) solution may also describe the universe during inflation. I intend to explore these possibilities in future work. Cities are increasingly adopting new technologies, particularly those rooted in technology stacks that rely on geospatial data. This spatial data serves as the resolution layer for these applications, frequently residing within municipal departments responsible for traditional mapping and geographic information systems. However, many such departments manage outdated data that hinders its integration and utilization within modern stacks. This paper presents a case study of a city that overcame these challenges through a program designed to identify, ingest, integrate, resolve, and expose its geospatial data. Specifically, this involved converting various data sources into GeoJSON format and hosting these datasets on a city-wide geospatial data platform. Finally, the study demonstrates how city services leveraged these exposed datasets to develop a variety of location-based solutions. This work details the data processing pipeline employed to facilitate the development of services utilizing these data sources. Collectively, these efforts streamline the deployment of location-based services across all city departments, thereby accelerating digital transformation within the municipal organization. Furthermore, the city has initiated a strategy to generate additional GeoJSON data through a new program aimed at modernizing its spatial data infrastructure. This paper provides a preliminary assessment of this program's progress. Overall, this work highlights how a city can modernize its spatial data infrastructure to support diverse location-based services. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of a city adopting such a modern approach to geographic data. The findings are expected to guide other cities in developing similar strategies, offering a pathway to modernize their geographic data infrastructure and enhance their location-based services. This work is funded by the U.S. Department of Transportation's Urban Development Institute (UDI). The city involved in this study is Santa Clara, California. Additional data is available for request at https://github.com/sccorps/GUIDES/tree/master/data. The repository also features sample code for deploying the city's geoportal and accessing its geoJSON data, along with sample code for developing location-based services, such as the one demonstrated at https://santacruz.sccorps.gov/smartcity/. In the study of two-dimensional (2D) Coulomb crystals formed from doubly charged ions in ultra-high vacuum, the standard diagnostic method for the thermal state of the Coulomb lattice involves heating the lattice via ion evaporation and subsequently measuring the motional state of a mode via ion fluorescence spectroscopy. In this approach, the thermal population of quanta in a mode is determined by analyzing the vibrational sidebands of a resonance fluorescence spectrum centered at the ion charge $q$. This study demonstrates that the reported thermal states are not intrinsic to the lattice; instead, they depend on the pre-heating motion state distributions of the ions and the rates at which the remaining ions are heated. Furthermore, we show that the sideband resonance fluorescence spectrum, which is typically interpreted as indicating ion thermalization, can actually reflect ion cooling. These findings are illustrated through classical molecular dynamics simulations of the ion lattice. Consequently, this research highlights the critical need for alternative diagnostic methods capable of accurately determining the true thermal states of a 2D Coulomb lattice. To address this, we introduce a new diagnostic technique based on collective spin excitation and fluorescence spectroscopy. This method allows for the direct measurement of doubly charged ion Coulomb lattice thermal states, providing a clear distinction between the thermal states of lattice ions and those of surface-bound probe ions. The validity of the spin decay diagnostic is confirmed by both classical molecular dynamics simulations and experimental data utilizing rubidium ions to probe a 2D calcium ion lattice. This methodology offers a valuable tool for investigating lattice thermal states in quantum simulators of the 2D Coulomb lattice. Additionally, the technique serves as a new platform for investigating lattice thermal states, thermal fluctuations, and heat flow in warm ionic lattices. Specifically, it enables the direct measurement of true lattice thermal states during the heating process, thereby allowing for the direct observation of heating velocities. This capability is essential for testing the validity of the mode temperature distribution assumption used in current kinetic theories of heat flow in 2D ionic lattices. Finally, the proposed diagnostic method serves as a foundation for developing future techniques to directly measure lattice thermal states in hot 2D ionic lattices. Key to these advancements is the development of spin diagnostics that surpass the constraints of laser spectroscopy, such as the limited state resolution inherent in vibrational sideband spectra. By directly measuring lattice thermal states, these techniques will significantly advance the understanding and application of 2D ionic lattices as Coulomb quantum simulators. Furthermore, these methods will facilitate the direct measurement of lattice heating

We introduce a novel theoretical framework designed to investigate the influence within Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS). This approach integrates the Rayleigh-Schrodinger time-independent perturbation theory for the influence with the quantum-mechanical description of light scattering from rough surfaces. To validate the method's efficacy, we apply it to a two-atom system featuring a single-site chromophore. Our findings indicate that chromophore polarization generates an electric field that simultaneously modifies the local electromagnetic field and the system's polarization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spatial resolution in TERS images arises not merely from the electromagnetic field's decay, but also from the shifting position of the chromophore. The contributions of the quantum-mechanical description of the influence are analyzed through two dimensions: the number of the Schrödinger time-independent perturbation and the number of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. The former governs the transition between the free and perturbed states, while the latter models the coupling between the ground and excited states. The computational outcomes reveal that the magnitude of Raman signal enhancement is directly proportional to both the number of transitions between free and perturbed states and the number of couplings between excited states. Consequently, this newly developed theory holds promise for enabling sub-nanometer spatial resolution in future TERS experiments. Additionally, we provide a Python script implementing the presented theory, which can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/SebastianKlapp/Influence_TERS. The script is also available at: http://www.quantum-mechanics-and-simulation.de/Influence_TERS/. We anticipate that this theoretical model will facilitate a systematic investigation into the influence within TERS. Ultimately, we aim to create new experimental techniques capable of distinguishing between physisorption and chemisorption. Ultimately, these advancements will enable the use of TERS as a tool for investigating molecular interactions at the single-molecule level. This paper reports the initial findings of an ongoing survey designed to detect unconventional microwave emission across nearby galaxies using the Sardinia Radio Telescope. By employing an innovative observing strategy, we identified unusual emission in the central regions of NGC 4536, NGC 4581, NGC 4725, NGC 4736, NGC 4743, NGC 4755, NGC 4826, NGC 4861, NGC 4911, NGC 4945, NGC 5005, NGC 5008, NGC 5053, NGC 5055, NGC 5058, NGC 5090, NGC 5128, NGC 5291, NGC 5353, NGC 5474, NGC 5548, NGC 5590, NGC 5607, NGC 5866, NGC 6097, NGC 6217, NGC 6264, NGC 6334, NGC 6350, NGC 6492, NGC 6622, NGC 6704, NGC 6725, NGC 6726, NGC 6729, NGC 6729-2, NGC 6736, NGC 6789, NGC 6861, and NGC 7095. The spatial distribution of this anomalous signal suggests it may be attributed to dust emission, prompting us to calculate the dust temperature and optical depth for each source. We further examined the correlation between this unusual emission and other tracers of star formation, such as H$\alpha$ emission, to assess potential connections with young stellar populations. Additionally, we investigated the relationship between this unusual signal and the standard CMB anisotropy CMBR(158 GHz) signal to evaluate whether it could represent a galactic contribution to the cosmic microwave background at 158 GHz. Finally, we compared our unusual signal with all-frequency data to determine if it might be a manifestation of the widely hypothesized "CMB rump."

Ammonium sulfate ($\text{NH}_4\text{HSO}_4$) exhibits a substantial entropy shift ($\Delta s = 22.5 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$) under an applied electric field, classifying it as the strongest molecular ferroelectric to date. To investigate the origins of this phenomenon, we conducted high-resolution calorimetry and single-crystal X-ray diffraction studies across temperatures spanning $250$ to $350 \text{ K}$. Our calorimetry findings indicate that the entire entropy change occurs within a narrow temperature range of $273.0 \pm 0.5 \text{ K}$, where entropy ($s$) and temperature ($T$) are linearly related. Additionally, we detected molecular disorder within the narrow ferroelectric transition region, evidenced by an increase in average atomic displacement parameters ($U_{eq}$) of approximately $0.02 \text{ \AA}^2$ per degree Kelvin. These results confirm that the electric-field-induced entropy change in $\text{NH}_4\text{HSO}_4$ stems from molecular disordering; consequently, the term "caloric" should be excluded from its material classification. This discovery underscores the necessity for precise characterization of materials demonstrating electrocaloric effects. Furthermore, our work demonstrates the value of integrating calorimetry with X-ray diffraction to resolve the complex atomistic processes occurring in the temperature zone where entropy alterations occur. Ultimately, our data establish ammonium sulfate as the premier model system for investigating electrocaloric effects. Furthermore, we contend that the strong correlation between molecular disorder and electrocaloric response in this material may extend to other ferroelectrics, offering a potential atomistic basis for discovering new electrocaloric materials. Finally, our results elucidate the physical mechanisms driving the previously reported large electrocaloric effect in ammonium sulfate, which had earlier been attributed to minor atomic displacements. By demonstrating the critical role of molecular disorder, our findings provide an atomistic explanation for the previously reported large electrocaloric effect, thereby clarifying the underlying physical mechanisms. This study also offers a paradigm for the rational design of new materials with large electrocaloric effects. Specifically, the atomistic basis for electrocaloric response in ammonium sulfate suggests that materials with low-dimensional disorder—such as molecular rotors, dimers, trimers, tetramers, and rings—may exhibit large electrocaloric effects.

Animals exhibit suboptimal behavioral strategies when confronted with dynamic environments, a phenomenon that reinforcement learning (RL) can model through the comparison of optimal versus behavioral policies. We introduce a method to integrate behavioral data, specifically reaction times, into RL to distinguish between competing learning hypotheses. Applying this approach to a mouse model, our findings indicate that suboptimal performance and prediction errors are best explained by a combination of soft-softmax (entropic) RL and the softmax learning rule. Furthermore, the estimated reward representations align with signals observed in the midbrain. These results offer computational and neural evidence confirming that the softmax learning rule is a fundamental mechanism in mice, particularly during learning, and highlight the significance of entropic policies in distinguishing between rewarded and unrewarded outcomes. Consequently, this study demonstrates the value of incorporating reaction time data for disambiguating RL models and underscores the entropic softmax policy's role in decision-making processes. Finally, our work expands the connection between entropic policies and neural activity, linking them to midbrain reward representations. These insights deepen our comprehension of the neural circuits governing learning and decision-making. This study extends that approach by defining a general model for $d^2$-dimensional quantum mechanics based on the rank $r$ of the Lie algebra associated with the root structure. Although natural one- and $r$-particle state spaces are constructed using the Fock representation, the model's core components—the projection operators for projective measurements, the state universe, unitary operators, and transition probabilities for one-dimensional projections—are derived from the complexifications of the root and weight lattices. The resulting series of models for $r=2, 3, 4, \dots, 12$ correspond to dimensions $d=4, 8, 16, \dots, 144$, encompassing the $\mathbf{E_8}$ case as $r=8$ and $d=12$. Additionally, permutational symmetries within these models are encoded by the extended affine Weyl group of the extended Cartan diagram. The validity of the Knill-Laflamme theorem and the presence of contextuality in generalized Kochen-Specker models are also verified for this series. The approximate close neighbor problem seeks an efficient method to determine whether a query point set $Q$ exists within a given distance threshold $\delta$ of any stored data set in a database $D$, under a specific metric. This paper addresses this problem using the Fréchet distance, a widely adopted metric for measuring the similarity between geometric objects, particularly when they represent sequences of points over time. We demonstrate a significant advancement in lower bound techniques: by reducing the established set disjointness problem from communication complexity to the approximate close neighbor problem, we establish that any randomized algorithm must establish lower bounds of $\Omega(n^{1/3}/\epsilon)$ bits. This proves the existence of query sets $f(n,\epsilon)$ that are $\epsilon$-close to at least one database set in $D$. Leveraging this new lower bound, we establish the first unconditional lower bounds for the approximate close neighbor problem in any dimension $d \geq 2$. Furthermore, we introduce a reduction from the set disjointness problem to the metric dimension problem, which yields lower bounds applicable to caching scenarios. This reduction demonstrates that the metric dimension problem is at least as difficult as the approximate close neighbor problem. We conclude by presenting a straightforward upper bound for the $1-\epsilon$-Fréchet problem. Our results collectively indicate that the $k$-dimensional approximate close neighbor problem is at least as hard as the set disjointness problem, where the input size is $O(n^k)$. Specifically, the $2$-dimensional variant is at least as difficult as the 1-dimensional problem with an input size of $O(n^2)$. Consequently, the $k$-dimensional problem is at least as hard as the 1-dimensional problem with an input size of $O(n^k)$, leading to a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2-\epsilon/2})$ bits. This implies that the current best-known upper bound of $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ bits is only off by a factor of $O(\sqrt{n})$. Notably, our findings are unconditional, independent of the polynomial-time hypothesis. Finally, we prove that the $k$-dimensional approximate close neighbor problem is at least as difficult as the set disjointness problem with an input size of $O(n^k/\log n)$ bits. To enhance the interpretability of Bayesian models, it is essential to mitigate errors arising from the cognitive limitations of human reviewers. A previous study introduced a two-stage Scalar Assessment Error Mitigation (SEM) algorithm designed to reduce these errors when reviewer judgments are expressed as scalar values. However, that method relied on a fixed Gaussian likelihood function, which hindered its ability to significantly lower scalar assessment errors. This paper extends the SEM algorithm to handle cases where the accuracy of scalar reviews varies and is governed by a real-valued positive likelihood function. Furthermore, it demonstrates that this generalized approach can be applied to multivariate review data and executed without approximating the posterior distribution. Although the iterative Bayesian reconstruction (IBR) required to compute the exact posterior may not scale efficiently for large datasets, we show that it can be made computationally feasible through parallelization and the use of the stochastic Greedy IBR (GBIBR) method. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach effectively mitigates scalar assessment errors even under varying accuracy conditions, achieving performance comparable to the recently developed exact IBR method. These findings suggest that our proposed methods are effective tools for reducing cognitive limitations in Bayesian model interpretation. Additionally, our ability to extend error mitigation techniques using accurate posterior distributions offers a critical advantage over recent studies, where semantic mismatch limitations exist because semantic information is lost during the lossy IBR approximation. Overall, this research provides valuable tools for minimizing assessment errors in Bayesian models, thereby enhancing the interpretability of both simple and complex hierarchical structures. It also facilitates the development of techniques for assessing the quality of Bayesian models' interpretations through human feedback. These outcomes are anticipated to advance the ongoing efforts to create techniques for the interpretable semantic interpretation of Bayesian models. The extensive code required to replicate this work is available at https://github.com/akimura2012/IBR-Parallel. Furthermore, the code includes an implementation of an exact GBIBR that matches the performance of conventional IBR methods, enabling users to easily verify the error mitigation effects of our proposed methods. The computational feasibility of GBIBR was validated using the same data as in our recent study, which established the correctness and effectiveness of standard GBIBR. Specifically, the GBIBR implementation required only 1.01 seconds on average to complete one iteration on a single CPU, whereas the conventional IBR method required 11.10 seconds on average per iteration. Autonomous robots utilize sensor data to navigate and perform tasks within dynamic settings, relying on the accuracy of their world models for decision-making. These models capture the current state of the environment, including the positions of obstacles and the distribution of tasks. This paper investigates the impact of integrating collective autonomy across multiple robot frameworks. By sharing sensory observations, robots can construct more precise models of their surroundings. We demonstrate the advantages of this collaborative approach by evaluating two path planning frameworks—one relying on pre-programmed rules and the other on machine learning—and their interaction in dynamic scenarios. Our findings indicate that: (1) a framework benefits significantly from the collective autonomy of others; (2) the advantages of two frameworks interacting can exceed those of a single framework operating in isolation; and (3) interacting frameworks can achieve higher joint task completion rates and reduce the generation of spurious tasks. A simulation environment capable of modeling various autonomy frameworks and their interactions is provided to facilitate the replication of these results. This work establishes a foundation for developing methods to evaluate and enhance the autonomy of diverse robot systems. We introduce HiTMap, a novel topological map composed of hierarchical sub-graphs, each summarizing the layout of an unfamiliar area through a graph-based representation of its street network. HiTMap serves as the core memory structure for our robot agent, enabling navigation in unfamiliar settings with minimal user input, such as a general destination like "the train station." Each component of HiTMap is derived from a topological graph built using the SEAM framework, which models streets as edges and intersections as nodes. To manage large-scale environments, we partition the spatial map into distinct sub-graphs based on a hierarchy of areas and neighborhoods, with each sub-graph retaining a linkedlist of nodes and edges. This hierarchical organization facilitates efficient path planning and traversal. Furthermore, we implement a novel path traversal algorithm that allows the agent to navigate between areas without backtracking. This approach first identifies the optimal sub-graph for pathing and then traverses the nodes within the start and target sub-graphs to determine the nearest nodes for the final path calculation. Consequently, the agent can reach the user's specified target with zero input, backtracking only when absolutely necessary. We have tested HiTMap in three urban environments, demonstrating that the agent can successfully navigate to various targets, such as parks, museums, and train stations. Additionally, we show that backtracking is required only when the target is unreachable or when the target is a nearby location within the same area. Finally, we have integrated HiTMap with a social robot agent to support natural language instructions for tasks like following directions and providing real-time feedback. These methods are currently being deployed in a real-world robot taxi service. The source code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/hiitlab/HiTMap. HiTMap. This study introduces the concept of the supplementary array of an orthogonal code set, which enhances the code book's dimensions. By utilizing zero-valued code vectors, the zero-set achieves a supplementary array dimension of $K^{\prime}=K+1$, yielding a total size of $K^{\prime}S=(K+1)S$. In wireless communication, this supplementary array of Z-code set expands the total code set size to $K^{\prime}S=(K+1)S$. Additionally, the power of transmitted signals can be normalized by employing the supplementary array of normalized orthogonal code sets. The paper proposes the N-order supplementary array of a 2-D Z-code set, thereby expanding the total code set size to $K^{\prime}S=(K+1)^{N}S$. Furthermore, a two-dimensional Z-supplementary array is introduced, which increases the total code set size to $(K+1)^{2}S=K^{2}S+2Ks+S$. The development of these advanced code sets is achieved through the application of multi-variable functions, and their performance is evaluated based on interference correlation. The results confirm that both the 2-D Z-supplementary array and the 2-D Z-supplementary array are derived from multi-variable functions, with the latter specifically resulting from the one-variable function $f(x)=x$. These extended code sets are applicable to systems such as OFDMA, CDMA, and MIMO. The concept of Z-supplementary arrays is anticipated to be widely utilized in various system designs, including room acoustics, wireless networks, and optical communication. The concept and properties of 2-D Z-supplementary arrays are expected to be employed in the design of 2-D Z-orthogonal arrays, 2-D orthogonal arrays, and 2-D normalized orthogonal arrays. Additionally, 2-D Walsh arrays, 2-D Hadamard arrays, and 2-D normalized Walsh-Hadamard arrays are all derived from the 2-D Z-code set. Consequently, 2-D Z-supplementary arrays will be utilized to expand the sizes of 2-D Walsh arrays, 2-D Hadamard arrays, and 2-D normalized Walsh-Hadamard arrays, as well as 2-D orthogonal arrays and 2-D normalized orthogonal arrays. Ultimately, 2-D Z-supplementary arrays are expected to significantly increase the code set sizes of these diverse applications. Computed Tomography (CT) images suffer from severe artifacts caused by the physics-based non-convexity of the photon measurement model. We introduce a non-convex framework that integrates polyenergetic modeling, noise suppression, and multi-material decomposition. Utilizing a reduced-order image prior, we reformulate the original non-convex CT reconstruction problem into a constrained Tomographic Wavelet Packet Transform (TWPT) optimization task. The subsequent algorithm alternately solves the material decomposition and noise reduction steps, which are both expressed as TWPT optimization problems. Furthermore, the constraint update for CT reconstruction is also solved via TWPT. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Notably, our approach achieves a 50% reduction in reconstruction time compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1990/TWPT. Finally, we demonstrate the application of our method for material composition analysis. The source code will be released under a BSD 3-Clause License. Additionally, the method enables precise quantification of material volume fractions, as illustrated in a case study of a metal-wood composite. The method-generated images demonstrate the presence of wood and the absence of metal. The code will be made available via MIT License. The accompanying videos will be released under a Creative Commons Zero (CC0) 1.0 License. Furthermore, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art quantification techniques. Our approach is straightforward to implement and requires no hyperparameter tuning. Our method also facilitates accurate and efficient CT-based quantification of material volume fractions. Our approach is robust to polyenergetic measurement models, regardless of the number of energy levels. Our approach is also robust to variations in noise levels. Gap surface plasmons (GSPs) are collective charge oscillations occurring within the nanometric spaces separating two metals separated by a dielectric. When these intervals approach zero thickness, the system's nonlocal dielectric response becomes significant. This study demonstrates that nonlocality influences the real part of the GSP dispersion relation by shifting its minimum and causing asymmetric broadening of the resonance. Furthermore, we examine the impact of electron-electron interactions mediated by the interval's dielectric material. If the response function varies linearly with frequency, the resulting energy gain accelerates electrons along the metal surfaces parallel to the dielectric, resulting in a nonlocal surface current that propagates along the metal-interval-metal structure. This current induces charge accumulation at the interval's boundaries, generating an electric field perpendicular to the surfaces. Consequently, this field can eject electrons from the system into the form of a surface plasmon-polariton (SPP) waveguide mode, which propagates within the dielectric separating the two metals. This mechanism could explain the experimentally observed formation of conductive paths between metals at separations as small as 0.5 nm. Additionally, our theoretical findings regarding the critical interval thickness and the resulting transition from bulk to surface plasmons align with recent experimental results. Finally, our results offer several testable predictions concerning the formation of conductive bridges between metals. Specifically, we predict that the surface-to-surface interval, rather than the physical thickness of the electron gas, dictates the transition to conduction. We also identify material combinations that may exhibit nonlocal behavior even at large interval sizes. These conclusions are supported by a concise set of analytical formulas and illustrative examples. Notably, when calculating the nonlocal dielectric function, we utilize a Thomas-Fermi model for the dielectric, which simplifies the problem to solving a one-dimensional differential equation. This approach eliminates the need for complex and computationally intensive ab-initio or DFT-based dielectric function calculations. Finally, we show that the nonlocal dielectric function derived this way yields results consistent with those obtained from more sophisticated and computationally demanding methods. This suggests that our approach could significantly reduce the computational costs associated with modeling nanometric spaces. The ability to recover unambiguous contextual instances of terms is essential for term-centric NLP applications. This paper applies human cognitive science to model such ability within neural language models. Specifically, we examine a term model that identifies unlabeled spans in standard NLP tasks as named entity instances within a given context. While term importance feedback (TIF) is a recognized technique for enhancing term identification, its impact on the broader task of term instance identification remains unexplored. We demonstrate that TIF significantly improves performance on the named entity recognition (NER) task and find that, despite similar overall model accuracy, it enhances named entity recall. Furthermore, we show that models trained with and without TIF develop distinct representations, with the TIF model exhibiting greater sensitivity to individual word choices. Finally, we present evidence that human-rated named entity lists output by the TIF model display higher coherence than those from the baseline, supporting the efficacy of TIF for named entity recognition. To our knowledge, this is the first study to frame NER as a term identification problem and to investigate how neural models utilize feedback to refine their term identification capabilities. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/jdrees/TermImportanceFeedback.termmodels.

Temporal datasets are frequently encountered in scientific research, business analytics, and news media. Temporal data mining involves utilizing computational methods to identify patterns within temporal data; however, comprehending these patterns demands human temporal reasoning. To support such reasoning, temporal data visualization must effectively highlight the sequence of events. Nevertheless, current tools often fail to deliver an engaging experience when exploring the sequence dimension on a screen. This paper presents a study on temporal data visualization that addresses this limitation. Our objective is to enhance screen-based exploration of event sequences by leveraging text attributes and employing text animation to draw attention to sequential relationships. We conducted an exploratory study to generate variants of temporal visualizations featuring animated text. These variants were evaluated through a task-based comparison of information gain, followed by a questionnaire assessing participant opinions on the different visualization approaches. The results indicate that animating text within temporal visualizations successfully facilitates screen exploration and helps users better comprehend the significance of event sequences. Furthermore, a temporal ordering effect was observed in the animation, where text appearing later in the sequence was more easily perceived as occurring later in time. Finally, event-based summaries proved useful for quickly grasping the sequence of events. These findings suggest that text animation serves as a valuable technique for enhancing exploration and reasoning regarding the sequence of events in temporal data visualization. The results also highlight a temporal ordering bias that should be considered in future applications of text animation. This study demonstrates that engaging temporal visualizations can be achieved through simple text animation and provides a method for exploring the sequence dimension of temporal data without requiring additional hardware. The outcomes of this study have already been applied to various real-world scenarios, including business intelligence, scientific research, and media applications. Furthermore, these results have informed the design of emerging augmented and virtual reality data visualization tools. This approach enables the exploration of the time dimension of temporal data through animated text in 3D space. To demonstrate this application, we present a video showcasing the exploration of the temporal dataset used in this study. The video demonstrates screen-based exploration using time-sliced views, offering a new perspective on temporal data visualization that complements time-animated views. The authors have applied these findings to real-world business intelligence scenarios. In this application, text animation facilitates a deeper understanding of the event sequence in temporal data and enhances the analysis of the dataset's temporal attributes. This case study illustrates the value of text animation in business contexts, where the sequence of events is crucial for decision-making. Digital Health Records (DHR) serve as a primary source of information for healthcare providers, facilitating daily clinical decisions. However, the vast volume of unstructured data within DHRs often hinders clinicians from extracting actionable insights. Recently, Deep Learning (DL) has shown significant potential in healthcare due to its capacity to identify patterns in extensive datasets. Consequently, this study introduces DSRN, a Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network designed to extract valuable patterns from digital health records. Diverse similarity enables the detection of varied, non-redundant representations from data, a critical factor for uncovering new insights in medical applications. This work demonstrates how DHRs can be modeled as a graph and introduces a novel graph convolutional operator that leverages diverse similarity to generate robust medical features. In terms of experimental validation, the method achieves an AUC of 0.8 on a sepsis patient dataset when compared against the XGBoost baseline. Furthermore, the resulting features are evaluated against medical knowledge to confirm their clinical relevance. We employ a self-consistent numerical approach that integrates Poisson's equation for electrostatic potential with modified Poisson-Boltzmann equations for positive and negative ions, incorporating solvent polarization effects. Our findings indicate that while high surface charge densities lead to significant polarization, the influence of this effect weakens as the distance from the charged surface increases. Furthermore, solvent polarization diminishes the surface charge density within the EDL, leading to a reduction in the Fermi energy of polar molecules at the liquid-vapor interface. This charge depletion results in a modest increase in the potential at the surface, a trend that is more pronounced in weakly polar solvents and those with large molecular sizes. We also analyzed the sensitivity of these results to the charging sequence, revealing that charging the solid surface before introducing the electrolyte produces more accurate outcomes. Finally, we illustrated that solvent polarization lowers the work of adhesion between the solid surface and an adjacent liquid, causing the solid surface to peel away from the liquid-vapor interface. These observations align with practical applications, such as the delamination of a charged solid surface from a liquid. We present software engineering applications for a framework that automatically generates structured specifications from disorganized textual sources. This framework operates by extracting patterns from example inputs and leveraging machine learning predictions regarding the source of specific text segments. The initial phase involves authoring declarative patterns and supplying sample data for extraction. Subsequent specifications are derived from a collection of text examples, requiring no manual annotation beyond the initial pattern definition. Current efforts focus on applying this approach to generate regular expressions, domain-specific languages, and free-form natural language. We evaluate the framework across various domains, such as extracting email addresses and URLs, defining the structure of Apache configuration files, and constructing regular expressions for the Shuji dataset. Furthermore, we explore methods to reduce specification ambiguity, address conflicts between sources, and manage cases where text does not align with existing patterns. Our findings indicate that the framework successfully produces accurate specifications for most inputs in the evaluated domains. Additionally, we demonstrate that the framework is highly flexible and user-friendly, requiring users to provide only a single example to extract patterns. Ultimately, we contend that automated pattern extraction can substantially streamline the specification authoring process. By analyzing the spin-polarized local density of states around the Mn atom, researchers identified Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in the sub-gap region near the Mn-induced $d$-band. The theory demonstrates that these induced states result from the overlap between the spin-polarized $s$-electrons of Nb and the spin-polarized $3d$ electrons of Mn, leading to hybridization. This $s$-$d$ electron hybridization is identified as the primary mechanism for generating Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states on Nb(110) surfaces hosting magnetic adatoms. Furthermore, the study investigates how these states vary with spin moment orientation and finds that the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state is most intense when the spin moment is perpendicular to the surface. In the case of a Mn dimer, the induced $s$-electrons from the two atoms interfere, producing splitting patterns in the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states that depend on the relative orientation of the magnetic moments. Finally, the study confirms that magnetic exchange interactions occur between adjacent Mn atoms. These findings are consistent with recent scanning tunneling microscopy experiments conducted on Mn dimers on Nb(110) surfaces. Additionally, the results suggest that the relative spin moment orientation within a diatomic adatom chain can be manipulated by adjusting the tunneling bias voltage. This suggests a potential method for controlling the states of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov molecules and adatoms using voltage, which could be utilized to develop new spintronic devices. Finally, the study examines the effect of the Mn adatom on the Nb(110) surface band structure and the influence of surface stress on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. Recent advancements in 3D distribution-to-distribution (D2D) scan alignment have primarily relied on point cloud registration methods originally designed for sparse geometry, which often struggle with noise-robustness and incomplete data. To address these limitations, we introduce the DNNFilter, a straightforward yet effective solution that leverages the inherent properties of 3D point clouds to mitigate noise and gaps. Unlike conventional point cloud filtering techniques that operate on sparse points, our approach is specifically designed for 3D D2D scan alignment. We demonstrate that applying the DNNFilter before feeding data into a D2D scan alignment network yields a 10% enhancement in relative rotation accuracy. Furthermore, this filter is universally applicable, enhancing both the performance and robustness of existing D2D scan alignment methods across diverse datasets. Additionally, we present a novel D2D scan alignment method that integrates the proposed DNNFilter to achieve superior accuracy. A key advantage of our technique is its ability to perform direct scan-to-scan alignment without relying on dense scans for intermediate alignment. The growing popularity of deep learning networks for image edge recognition has heightened the demand for vast datasets. However, the complexity of deep architectures often hinders their interpretation. This paper explores the potential of modifying traditional edge detection methods—such as Sobel, Canny, and Harris-Corners—to perform detection effectively on datasets without relying on deep networks. We introduce the Satellite Dataset, comprising 20,480 images (10,240 positive and 10,240 negative) derived from satellite sources, where positive instances contain visible object edges and negative ones do not. Experimental results indicate that an adapted Shi-Tomasi corner detection algorithm outperforms other tested modified classical techniques on this dataset. The finalized algorithm operates in less than 1 second per image on a standard laptop, offering a non-arbitrary approach to edge detection suitable for integration into computer vision pipelines. To our knowledge, this represents the first successful application of a classical corner detection algorithm in satellite image processing. The complete source code is available at https://github.com/romanpavlov/satellite_dataset. The findings presented here were initially reported in our extended abstract at SAT 2019 [1].

Non-linear hard X-ray absorption spectroscopy, characterized by femtosecond temporal resolution and terahertz power densities, has become an essential tool for characterizing ultrafast electron dynamics in solids. However, analyzing non-linear X-ray absorption data remains difficult because it lacks a comprehensive theoretical framework for interpreting electron groups formed during non-linear absorption processes. In this work, we introduce a concept of "electron group change rate" to characterize the temporal evolution of these groups. By applying this rate to electron groups responsible for coherent core absorption, regarding valence absorption, and regarding high-energy electron emission, we demonstrate its utility in interpreting experimental results. Furthermore, we illustrate how this rate can be manipulated through optical carrier-envelope phase, ellipticity, and polarization. Our findings provide the basis for designing time-resolved experiments aimed at controlling core holes and valence electrons on ultrafast timescales. The proposed rate is defined as $\frac{dt}{d\tau} = \frac{dt}{d\tau_0} \frac{d\tau_0}{d\tau}$, where $t$ represents the electronic state variable, and $\tau$ and $\tau_0$ denote the physical time and scaled time, respectively. The variable $\tau$ is derived from the time-dependent laser electric field $\mathbf{E}(\tau) = E_0 \cos(\omega_0 \tau)$, with $\tau_0$ defined as $\tau_0 = \omega_0 t - \phi$, where $\phi$ is the carrier-envelope phase. This rate can be calculated using the ultrastrong coupling approximation method. Consequently, the rate $\frac{dt}{d\tau_0}$ serves as an effective tool for characterizing electron groups. We observe that when $\frac{dt}{d\tau_0} = 1$, the state $t$ is excited by the instantaneous laser field $E(\tau_0) = E_0 \cos(\omega_0 \tau_0)$, indicating that the electron group change rate equals one under this condition. Furthermore, we find that to achieve significant non-linear effects, the intensity of the X-ray laser must be comparable to the atomic unit of electric field. Finally, regarding ellipticity, while elliptical polarization suppresses photoemission, it facilitates the excitation of electron groups with large $\frac{dt}{d\tau_0}$ values. Detecting relapses is a primary strategy for monitoring Multiple Sclerosis (MS) progression. AI methods are vital in this field, specifically for segmenting lesions in MS-specific brain regions like white matter (WM) and periventricular areas. However, data scarcity and variability across different clinical sites remain significant hurdles. This study investigates the impact of training AI models on datasets that are either heterogeneous or severely data-limited. We address this by employing continual learning strategies, which yield substantial performance gains. The task involves training a 3D U-Net model on data from multiple clinics. Segmentation results were evaluated using Dice scores on test data from four specific clinics: Cambridge, Charité, Geneva, and NIH. Our findings demonstrate that continual learning enables training on large, heterogeneous datasets without catastrophic forgetting, surpassing the performance of models trained independently on each clinic's data. The resulting model shows improved segmentation accuracy across all four clinics, particularly benefiting Geneva and Charité data, while maintaining robustness at Cambridge and NIH. The learned features are deemed robustly generalizable, as evidenced by high Dice scores exceeding 0.80 across all clinics. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/MS-Lesion-Segmentation. Our work offers a promising pathway for developing robust AI models capable of generalizing across diverse clinical environments. Furthermore, these tools could facilitate data sharing and collaboration among multiple MS research groups. The results of this research were presented at MICCAI 2021. The inherent structural framework for model error in dynamical systems provides an alternative approach to error modeling, relying on the same foundational elements as the original system but incorporating additional degrees of freedom. Model error is defined as the difference between the log-standard normal densities of the original system and the parametric one. This perspective yields several beneficial outcomes, including improved interpretability for non-expert users, the development of unique calibration techniques, and a more efficient utilization of data and parameters. Furthermore, it establishes a more natural framework for modeling nonlinearities and coupling effects. The paper presents illustrative examples and extends existing theory to address these advantages. For instance, it offers a novel method for model error calibration that diverges from traditional statistical approaches. Additionally, since this work focuses on spatially distributed systems, the implications for modeling and analyzing model error in stochastic partial differential equations are also explored. Spatially, model error represents the discrepancy between the observed stochastic field and the solution of a parametric stochastic PDE, which is itself the solution to a parametric deterministic PDE. Consequently, model error can be decomposed into two distinct components: parametric error and model form error. This structure facilitates the modeling of parametric error through parametric functions and for model form error using either parametric functions or by solving a parametric PDE. These findings broaden the theory of model error within stochastic PDEs and offer novel methods for characterizing model form error in spatially distributed systems. Finally, the model form error component can be estimated using traditional statistical methods, as well as through the new parametric-based calibration procedures described herein. Finally, these results hold significant relevance for various fields within applied mathematics. The proposed model form error can be viewed as representing unmodeled parametric or nonparametric features of the system, thereby validating its application to stochasticity arising from unmodeled spatially distributed features. This model form error can be characterized using traditional statistical approaches or, alternatively, through new parametric-based methods. Furthermore, the implications of this work extend to other domains such as stochastic PDEs, stochastic PDEs, and stochastic PDEs. In each instance, traditional statistical methods remain applicable for characterizing model form error, while parametric-based calibration offers a more efficient alternative. We present findings from a study utilizing the VLA and NOEMA to examine the dense core of the Dragon infrared dark nebula (I DN), a prominent source in the Galactic plane. Our analysis of 13CO and 12CO isotopologue emission lines from the dense core (DC) reveals core expansion driven by the outflow of a massive star that has recently formed or is in the process of forming. The observed expansion velocity is approximately 1.5 km/s, and we estimate the remaining time until the cloud disperses to be less than 1.5 million years. This expansion is likely caused by the outflow associated with the massive star, as evidenced by the detection of CO isotopologue emission from a collimated outflow originating from the center of the DC. The velocity gradient in the DC aligns with the direction of the collimated outflow, suggesting that the pressure from the outflow is responsible for the expansion. The energy rate of the outflow is estimated at 1.8 x 10^38 erg/s, and its momentum flux is 1.1 x 10^10 kg/m/s. These values are consistent with those of other outflows linked to massive star formation. Furthermore, we identified a molecular outflow with a velocity of 10 km/s that is roughly 10 times more massive than the DC. This outflow is likely the primary mechanism for expanding the cloud. Additionally, we detected a compact continuum source with a flux density of 0.1 mJy at 1.3 mm, indicating a mass of 0.001 solar masses and a temperature of 30 K. This research investigates the societal relevance of dynamically updating food delivery service recommendations based on user feedback. Since individuals possess diverse dietary requirements, such as allergies or ethical preferences, their requested items must align with their personal constraints. The study models a user's dietary rules as a dependency relation and the available food offerings as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The core challenge addressed involves either inserting a new food node into the graph or removing an existing one while maintaining the order defined by this dependency structure. We specifically address the set augmentation and set deletion instances within the theory of preference ordering. By analyzing whether solutions can be determined locally or if global food set modifications are necessary, we categorize these problems as either non-contextual (local) or contextual (global). Finally, we examine the computational complexity of both problems and demonstrate that they are NP-hard. Notably, we identify that the set deletion issue admits a polynomial-time algorithm when the dependency relation is restricted to be transitive. The paper concludes by proposing algorithmic strategies and proposing future directions. **Keywords:** Preference Ordering, Preference Reversal, Preference Aggregation, Preference Learning, Preference Learning, Preference Elicitation, Preference Representation. **AMS Subject Classification:** 90C26, 90C38, 90C39, 90C40, 90C46, 90C59, 90B06, 90B15, 90B35, 90B50. **MSC Subject Classification:** 90C26, 90C38, 90C39, 90C40, 90C46, 90C59, 90B06, 90B15, 90B35, 90B50. **DOI:** 10.13140/RG.2.2.2020.1707. **URL:** https://rg.ie/contrast-of-contextual-and-non-contextual-preference-ordering-for-set-augmentation/issues/2. **Corresponding Author:** Dr. Rakesh Kumar, Department of Computer Science, University of Delaware, 205 McKnight Bldg., 19816, Newark, DE, USA. This study examines the thermodynamic and dynamic behaviors of two glass-forming polymer liquids, polyethylene glycol (PEG 400) and poly(dimethylsilox-co-dimethylacrylate), across their entire supercooled liquid ranges. By establishing the link between configurational entropy and relaxation times via the Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann equation, the thermodynamic underpinnings of their dynamics were explored. Our results indicate that the thermodynamic facilitation mechanism, which ties dynamics to configurational entropy, remains valid in deeply supercooled liquids where structural time scales extend into geologic durations. Furthermore, the thermodynamic facilitation theory, which connects this configuration-entropy mechanism to actual particle motion, was tested by confirming the free-volume model through analyses of free volume and segmental mobility. Finally, a path was outlined for the theory of "water as a glass-forming liquid," demonstrating the relationship between the thermodynamic and kinetic (time scales) governing water's behavior. These findings collectively suggest the need for an integrated framework to understand supercooled liquids, one that simultaneously addresses thermodynamic and dynamic properties. The significance of this scientific endeavor is underscored by its critical role in fields ranging from geophysics to pharmaceuticals. This work synthesizes our experimental findings with recent theoretical advancements to elucidate the complex physics of supercooled liquids. The associated data can be found at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12510000. The theory is available at https://github.com/akshaykumar2000/Thermo-Dyn-Time-Scales. Additionally, the experimentalists' code is hosted at https://github.com/akshaykumar2000/Supercooled-Polymers. Our computational methods rely on the assumption that the configurational entropy of supercooled liquids is governed by the same principles as those of glass-forming molecular and polymer liquids. This assumption is supported by the strong temperature dependence of specific heat in supercooled liquids, which aligns with the theoretical prediction that the heat capacity difference between a glass and its equilibrium liquid state decreases with increasing temperature. Transformer neural network architectures excel at NLP applications due to their self-attention mechanism, which effectively identifies dependencies between words. However, this same mechanism can inadvertently pair words that should not be associated. We contend that a language architecture capable of long-term planning must possess a pliable attention mechanism to reject such spurious associations. To operationalize this concept of "attention rejection," we introduce Heuristic Attention Reweighting (HAR), which serves as a differentiable, local heuristic for modifying standard Transformer attention weights. Furthermore, we propose an alternative training objective designed to minimize the divergence between the modified and original attention distributions while ensuring predictive accuracy remains intact. Our model successfully reduces the distributional distance between associated word pairs without compromising performance on downstream tasks. We name this paradigm "Developmental Rejection Processing" (DRP) to underscore its role in refining coarse-grained perceptual capabilities—such as initial attention rejection—during the early stages of language acquisition. We demonstrate the model's efficacy using the German Children's Corpus DCHS, showing that DRP enables a pre-trained language model to refine its perceptual rough draft through HAR training. Additionally, we present evidence from the CHIMP dataset indicating that DRP outperforms other attention-modification methods, such as attention masking and fine-tuning, in accurately replicating the attention rejection behaviors observed in child language. These findings suggest that learning to attend less is a fundamental capability inherent to language acquisition. Finally, we explore how DRP influences language understanding and generation, demonstrating that it enhances performance on specific child-friendly language phenomena, including negation and pronoun resolution. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale, principled, and differentiable approach to developing attention mechanisms in language architectures. Our code and resources are available at: https://github.com/rae1234/Transformer-Attention-Reweighting.

These results are supported by examples involving the free boson and free fermion CFTs. The paper by Li, Li, and Zhang (2023) introduces a mathematical framework designed to value Asian options by utilizing a closed-form solution for their generator. However, this model relies on an incorrect characterization of the Asian option space. Specifically, it fails to identify the Markov state variables required to fully describe Asian option prices, a shortcoming that limits the approach's practical utility. This commentary explains the source of this flaw and proposes a corrected solution along with an alternative open-ended method to address the identified gap. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the proper Markov state can facilitate the pricing of a broader class of path-dependent options, thereby expanding the applicability of the original framework. Additionally, we highlight that the original model is invalid when applied to non-Markovian underlying assets, such as Asian stock options under a stochastic volatility process. Finally, the inefficiencies of the original algorithm are empirically assessed through simulations. Our computational experiments indicate that, except for out-of-the-money options, the errors associated with the corrected model are of similar magnitude as those of the original version. We conclude that the primary motivation behind the original model, which was to circumvent the computational challenges of high-dimensional path-dependent derivatives, is fundamentally flawed. We also argue that advancements in computational power and the development of sophisticated numerical methods have significantly mitigated these challenges in recent years. To illustrate this point, we present a hybrid approach that integrates the original model with a multivariate spline-based method to deliver a practical solution for pricing out-of-the-money Asian options. This hybrid algorithm effectively overcomes the critical drawbacks of the original model while retaining the advantages of the closed-form solution. Finally, a Python implementation of the proposed hybrid model is made available to facilitate empirical validation and comparison. Building upon our recent cosmological collider research (JCAP02(2021)010), we explore how traditional cosmological collider signals might appear in curvature perturbations, contingent on the physics of early inflationary epochs. This analysis remains independent of late-time evolution mechanisms. To demonstrate, we investigate a specific two-step inflationary model where the second field generates features in the power spectrum, enabling the calculation of non-linear corrections. Our findings indicate that collider signals are amplified by these features, and we provide explicit predictions for the non-Gaussianity shape, baryon acoustic oscillation modulations, and vector perturbations. Additionally, we examine the impact of super-horizon evolution on the collider signal and explore applications to cosmological phase transitions. We conclude that collider physics can be rigorously applied to any post-reheating era where the physics scale exceeds the critical curvature scale. Furthermore, we highlight that initial features serve as an essential tool for unmasking collider signals and offer a viable method for probing pre-reheating physics. Although Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have reached state-of-the-art levels in image classification, their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. To address this lack of transparency, we present Latent Visual-Semantic Filter Focus (LVSFF), a novel approach designed to interpret and visualize how DCNNs process information. Our method utilizes a custom DCNN architecture featuring a latent layer that decomposes visual representations into a filter bank, where each filter corresponds to a distinct visual category. During inference, these filters are dynamically learned from the input image to represent specific semantic categories; for example, weights for filters like "cat" or "car" are assigned based on their relevance to the objects present in the input. We demonstrate that LVSFF generates highly accurate interpretations for standard ILSVRC2012 images and achieves state-of-the-art results on the INRIA Aircraft dataset, offering clear visual and semantic explanations of the classification process. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/Filter-Interpretation. Through systematic analysis, we demonstrate the transparency and interpretability of DCNNs using LVSFF. The methodology successfully uncovers the "black box" nature of deep learning by revealing the network's internal workings, thereby enhancing trust in the classification process. Furthermore, our approach represents a significant step toward automatically explaining and interpreting deep learning systems. This paper focuses on establishing a transparent DCNN framework; future work will extend these principles to Convolutional Neural Networks with Neurons (CNNMs) to achieve even greater accuracy and interpretability. By automating the selection of appropriate CNNMs and their filter weights, we aim to create self-explanatory networks capable of elucidating their own classification decisions. Ultimately, this research paves the way for developing self-explanatory neural networks. The proposed transparency framework provides a foundation for future efforts to increase the explainability of deep learning systems, including the development of Explainable Deep Learning (XDL) systems. By employing a rigorous one-dimensional (1D) Hubbard model, we demonstrate that a specific pattern of phonon-electron coupling enables the counterintuitive attraction of repelling electrons. This alluring interaction is mediated by the exchange of virtual phonons, facilitated by electronic hopping between neighboring lattice sites. Our findings reveal that this mechanism is robust and operates effectively in lower-dimensional systems. These results establish a new foundation for exploring long-range atttractive forces between repelling electrons. Additionally, our one-dimensional model clarifies how the competition between local phonon-assisted attraction and local Coulomb repulsion governs the formation of bound electron pairs. These insights are vital for understanding the nature of phonon-mediated electron pairing in cuprates. Finally, we examine the model's relevance to high-temperature superconductivity, proposing that this mechanism of phonon-mediated attraction between repelling electrons could be operative in cuprate materials. Specifically, we outline how this mechanism could be verified through Raman spectroscopy experiments. However, existing Architectural Description Methods fail to capture the dependencies between these decisions and how prior choices constrain subsequent ones. The topological nature of magnetic skyrmions is thought to shield them from local perturbations, thereby preserving their stability. However, the stability of skyrmion-based metastable phases in coexistence regions remains poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the periodic magnetic order in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ transitions into an liquefied state under magnetic field cooling, a phenomenon characterized by magnetic skyrmion supercells. This transition is driven by the local breaking of magnetic periodicity within the skyrmion lattice and is facilitated by the high thermal lability of the metastable grid. Utilizing time-resolved scanning transmission x-ray microscopy, we captured the real-time evolution of individual vortices and antivortices during liquefaction, observing that magnetic supercells merge into a random, vortical pattern. This process is modeled as a sequence of local topological charge exchanges between the magnetic grid and the local magnetic texture. Our findings indicate that both the metastable magnetic order and the magnetic grid itself can be readily liquefied through minor perturbations to the magnetic periodicity. These results hold significant implications for the development of topological information storage and topological magnetics. This need is particularly urgent given the rapid development of computational resources, which now allows for the study of the most extreme turbulence scenarios in accretion disks and solar convection zones. These are the very conditions under which large-scale convective dynamos operate in the most energetic systems, including supermassive black holes and massive galaxies. We introduce the typical super-dimension-simulators (SDIMSIMs), a class of methods designed to numerically solve typical differential equations, defined as those where the solution remains bounded alongside its first $k$ derivatives. Although the general SDIMSIM is inherently variable-timestep, we extend the fixed-timestep super-dimension-simulators (FiSDIMSIMs) typically used for linear problems into this variable-timestep category. The variable-timestep SDIMSIMs for both general and local equations are demonstrated to be self-starting, zero-stable, $O(h^{k+1})$-consistent, and convergent with a local truncation error of $O(h^{k+1})$. Numerical experiments utilizing a third-order method indicate that these variable-timestep SDIMSIMs exhibit second-order global convergence and outperform the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method as the stepsize diminishes. A key advantage of variable-timestep SDIMSIMs over Runge-Kutta methods is their superior performance on nonlinear equations where the solution contains singularities or severe oscillations; in such cases, the solution is "not typical," rendering standard Runge-Kutta methods inferior. The authors contend that variable-timestep SDIMSIMs represent the optimal approach for solving typical differential equations. The paper concludes with constructive criticism. Our primary innovation lies in the methodology: rather than directly analyzing the stability semigroup via its infinitesimal generator, we employ $\mu$-decay estimates for the semigroup to derive corresponding estimates for the Lyapunov equation. This approach enables a more straightforward application to $H^\infty$ control, as the main challenge shifts from solving a Riemann-Hilbert problem to a standard convex optimization task. These conclusions are supported by examples from $H^\infty$ control. Notably, our findings provide an affirmative resolution to Example 2.10 in \cite{MR2424902}. This study examines a portfolio optimization problem involving a power utility function defined over the absolute and relative wealths of risk-free and risky assets. The absolute wealth under consideration comprises the cumulative net gains from trading plus holding costs for both the risk-free and risky components. The analysis covers scenarios with both known and model-based random interest rates, deriving explicit formulas for the optimal portfolio weights of the risky assets and the number of shares held in the risk-free asset. The resulting unnormalized wealth process is observed to be the solution to a Volterra integral equation, while the normalized (relative) wealth process follows a stochastic differential equation featuring integrals with respect to Lebesgue-Gauss measure. Furthermore, the paper explores the behavior of the optimal portfolio in limiting cases.

This study examines the robustness of fermionic quasiparticles by constructing systems of interacting bosons and fermions using two distinct approaches. In the first method, we analyze a $\sigma$-model featuring a spontaneous symmetry breaking field $\langle \phi_1 \rangle \neq 0$, which localizes fermionic quasiparticles as zero modes of $\phi_1$. In the second approach, quasiparticles are identified as vortices within the $\phi_1$ field. In both scenarios, we couple the fermionic quasiparticles to a $\phi_2$ boson, which is localized to a single lattice site and exhibits gapped excitations. We demonstrate that, despite the intrinsic stability of the fermionic quasiparticles, they undergo nonperturbative decay into $\phi_2$ when traversing the site where $\phi_2$ is confined. Numerical findings indicate that this quasiparticle decay persists in low-dimensional systems even when the boson is localized on the boundary. Consequently, our results suggest that the MERA tensor, which relies on the coupling of quasiparticles to localized boundary bosons, implies the disappearance of quasiparticles at the system's boundary. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between boson-induced quasiparticle decay and the confinement of quasiparticles inside a string-like flux tube. Ultimately, our work establishes a critical constraint on the stability of quasiparticles arising from quasibosonic degrees of freedom. Additionally, these systems may represent a new class of gapped quantum phases characterized by gapped bulk and boundary excitations, quasiparticle quasiparticles, and extended quasiparticle confinement mechanisms. Topological quantum computing utilizing quasiparticles that disappear when linked to local bosons may require either higher-dimensional frameworks or global bosons rather than localized ones. Large language models (LLMs) excel at open-domain question answering (QA), yet they often struggle to locate specific answers within lengthy documents due to data scarcity. Conversely, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models can solve this by retrieving relevant passages from external knowledge, though they typically depend on complex data preparation and are limited to addressing questions directly. This paper presents a novel Complete RAG framework designed for answering questions based on provided context. The process begins by retrieving relevant document chunks using a dual approach: a retrieval model enhanced with data parallelism (DPR) and the document itself as the retrieval target (D), alongside a general retrieval model (G). Subsequently, passages are filtered using node-based attention mechanisms in question-focused retrieval (Q), combined with passage and candidate answers to optimize the ranking of both passages and potential answers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the TriviaQA and HotpotQA datasets, outperforming both non-complete models (BiDAF, RAG) and other complete models (DPR, REINFORCE). Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that our approach yields significant performance gains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to simultaneously evaluate both the D and G retrieval strategies while incorporating DPR's data parallelism technique within a complete RAG framework for context-based QA. Human computation remains a vital component of language technology, offering a pathway to train machines to perform tasks that bridge the gap between natural and structured data. One critical challenge in this domain is identifying the right individuals to execute specific tasks. This paper presents findings from our experience recruiting annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) for summarization tasks, emphasizing the significance of clear instructions, effective screening questions, and reasonable compensation. We illustrate the general strategy for qualifying workers, providing practical takeaways for researchers utilizing human computation. Our approach begins with detailed instructions and screening queries to filter out unqualified participants, followed by a pilot phase where a small group of workers demonstrates the task; their outputs are then reviewed and refined until the process is clear. Finally, we compensate the workers fairly for their time. Although these steps may extend the recruitment duration, they are essential for ensuring that the few qualified workers we eventually secure can produce high-quality results. We contend that investing time in recruiting the right workers is crucial for the success of any human computation study. To assist others, we have made the completed MTurk instructions, screening questions, and worker outputs available on GitHub. We hope these resources aid other researchers in recruiting the right talent for their own studies. Video retrieval tasks, such as text-clip search, present significant challenges due to the substantial amount of data in the retrieval set and the difficulty of capturing fine-grained alignments between query text and video clips. To address these issues, we introduce the Token Shift and Selection Network (TS2-Net), an end-to-end text-to-video retrieval model. This network first transforms input text embeddings into a token sequence featuring enhanced semantic representations. Subsequently, it individually aligns each token with the video clip feature space. Finally, a shift-and-selection mechanism is employed to compute similarity scores, addressing the inherent mismatches caused by semantic gaps and data distribution disparities. Extensive experiments across three public video retrieval datasets demonstrate the model's effectiveness, achieving top performance on the Text Retrieval Track of the AVSR 2021 challenge. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ailab-fudan/ts2-net.

We examine large finite directed graphs with a $(n,s)$ structure, where $n$ represents the number of vertices and $s$ denotes the edge density. Each vertex is assigned an activity value, and the probability of an edge existing between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ is determined by a hybrid function. This function combines two mechanisms: one akin to the Barabási-Albert model, where connection probability correlates with the product of activities, and another akin to the Erdős-Rényi model, where the probability depends solely on the activity values of individual vertices. This creates a tension between the mechanisms; we analyze which mechanism dominates in large random directed graphs as $s$ approaches zero. Our primary findings indicate that at very low edge densities, the mechanism similar to the Barabási-Albert graph dominates, whereas at moderately low densities, the mechanism akin to Erdős-Rényi graphs prevails. We substantiate these conclusions by deriving the asymptotic behaviors of the largest eigenvalue, the number of edges required to ensure the existence of giant strongly connected components, and giant strongly connected components themselves. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for modeling and analyzing various network types. Specifically, directed models with low edge density tend to fragment into numerous small components, whereas those with moderately low density (such as the HD-RBF graph) are more likely to form larger strongly connected components. Furthermore, the presence of highly active vertices in higher-density scenarios can facilitate the emergence of giant strongly connected components, even though their absence does not preclude such components from existing. These results demonstrate that the hybrid graph model offers a more nuanced and realistic representation of real-world networks compared to purely scale-free models like Barabási-Albert. Finally, while the asymptotic analysis of HD-RW graphs offers new insights into their properties, it also serves as a foundation for developing algorithms to identify giant strongly connected components and to cluster vertices based on their within-community connectivity. These algorithms offer the potential to enhance the accuracy of community detection in various directed networks. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research regarding HD-RW graphs.
